nodes.t: Everything the mind knows about valuation.
Everything the mind knows about accounting.
Everything the mind knows about technical analysis.
Everything the mind knows about macro and policy.
Everything the mind knows about rates and credit.
Everything the mind knows about options and derivatives.
Everything the mind knows about commodities.
Everything the mind knows about trading and market structure.
Everything the mind knows about risk and portfolios.
Everything the mind knows about statistics and inference.
Everything the mind knows about behavior and bubbles.
Everything the mind knows about games, poker and decisions.
Everything the mind knows about negotiation and haggling.
Everything the mind knows about private markets.
Everything the mind knows about asset management.
Everything the mind knows about the ai buildout.
Everything the mind knows about crypto.
Everything the mind knows about market history.
Everything the mind knows about machine learning.
Everything the mind knows about models and reality.
Everything the mind knows about information edge.
Reading price and volume for trend, momentum, mean reversion and structure; worth only what its signals earn out of sample on the asset in question.
A Japanese trend system: conversion and base lines and a cloud built from 9, 26 and 52-period midpoints, plotted 26 periods ahead.
A trailing stop set a multiple of ATR from the midpoint; the trend flips when the close crosses it.
Wilder's stop-and-reverse level that accelerates toward price as a trend extends.
A volume-weighted RSI on typical price.
Levels at 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% and 78.6% of the last big move, watched as likely pauses; their power is mostly that many traders watch them.
Minervini's stage-two checklist: price above rising 50, 150 and 200-day averages stacked in order, near the 52-week high and well off the low.
A price divided by a benchmark's, against its own average: is it leading or lagging the market.
nodes.f: RS = (P / B) / SMA252(P / B) - 1

nodes.t: The average return after a signal or event against all days, with errors that respect overlap; how every technical signal here is judged.
Nine pass-fail tests of profitability, leverage, liquidity and efficiency; high scorers among cheap stocks outperformed in Piotroski (2000).
nodes.f: F = sum of 9 binary tests

nodes.t: A weighted sum of balance-sheet and earnings ratios that predicts distress; Z'' is the version for non-manufacturers.
Eight ratios that flag a higher chance of earnings manipulation; above -1.78 is the usual cut-off.
How much of reported profit is cash: cash conversion, accruals, stock pay and capitalized costs.
Revenue growth plus free-cash-flow margin of at least 40% marks a healthy growth company.
nodes.f: growth + FCF margin >= 40%

nodes.t: Return on equity split into margin times asset turnover times leverage, to see which one is doing the work.
nodes.f: ROE = NI/Sales x Sales/Assets x Assets/Equity

nodes.t: Learning a policy that maximizes reward over time from experience; in sizing, the state is what the market looks like and the action is how much to hold.
Offline reinforcement learning: repeatedly fit the value of each state and action to reward plus the discounted best next value on recorded data.
nodes.f: Q(s,a) = E[r + gamma max Q(s', a')]

nodes.t: Reinforcement learning when actions do not change the next state, as when one investor's trades do not move the market.
Stock and Watson's discounted mean-squared-error weights: models that forecast well recently get more weight.
nodes.f: w_k ~ 1 / sum delta^(t-s) e_ks^2

nodes.t: One interface to every data source the engine reads, with priorities, fallbacks, provenance and a connection check.
Owning the path to the customer: when products are easy to copy, the firm that already reaches billions of users or the enterprise seat wins the new feature.
Ben Thompson's argument that internet winners own the user relationship and commoditize suppliers, so demand, not supply, is the moat.
The users, devices, seats or developers a firm already serves; new AI features ship to them on day one.
Sales reach and channels that turn a product into revenue faster than a rival with a better product can.
Share price divided by earnings per share: how many years of today's profit the price pays for.
nodes.f: P/E = Price / EPS

nodes.t: Price over the earnings analysts expect for the next twelve months; flattered when forecasts are too high.
nodes.f: Forward P/E = Price / expected EPS(next 12m)

nodes.t: Price over the ten-year average of inflation-adjusted earnings (Campbell and Shiller); smooths the cycle and predicts ten-year returns far better than one-year returns.
nodes.f: CAPE = real price / mean(real EPS over 10 years)

nodes.t: The CAPE earnings yield (1/CAPE) minus the real ten-year yield: the extra return stocks offer over inflation-protected bonds.
nodes.f: ECY = 1/CAPE - real 10y yield

nodes.t: Earnings per share over price, the inverse of P/E; comparable to a bond yield.
nodes.f: E/P

nodes.t: P/E divided by expected growth in percent; Lynch's rough check that a growth company is not overpriced for its growth.
nodes.f: PEG = (P/E) / growth%

nodes.t: Enterprise value over earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; compares firms with different debt.
nodes.f: EV / EBITDA

nodes.t: Enterprise value over revenue; used when profits are small or distorted.
nodes.f: EV / Revenue

nodes.t: Price over accounting equity per share; the classic value metric, weaker where assets are intangible.
nodes.f: P/B

nodes.t: Annual dividends over price; once a strong predictor of returns, weaker since buybacks replaced dividends.
nodes.f: D/P

nodes.t: Dividends plus net buybacks over market value: total cash returned to owners.
Free cash flow over market value; cash, not accounting profit, that the business could hand back.
nodes.f: FCF / market value

nodes.t: Buffett's measure: net income plus depreciation minus the capex needed just to keep the business where it is.
Value as the sum of future cash flows, each divided by (1 + discount rate) for every year of waiting.
nodes.f: V = sum CF_t / (1+r)^t + TV / (1+r)^T

nodes.t: Solving a DCF backwards: the growth a price already assumes, which can then be checked against how often companies achieve it.
The revenue or earnings growth a price needs to be fair; the engine's main test of irrational pricing.
How often companies of a given size have achieved a given growth rate historically; the outside view on a forecast.
The value of all cash flows after the forecast years; often most of a DCF, which makes long-duration stocks rate sensitive.
nodes.f: TV = CF_(T+1) / (r - g)

nodes.t: The return required to wait for cash; the risk-free rate plus a risk premium.
The blend of the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt, weighted by how the firm is funded.
nodes.f: WACC = E/V re + D/V rd (1 - t)

nodes.t: What shareholders require: the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium in the CAPM.
nodes.f: re = rf + beta ERP

nodes.t: The extra return investors expect from stocks over safe bonds; low when stocks are expensive relative to yields.
Comparing the stock earnings yield with the ten-year Treasury yield; popular but criticized for mixing a real and a nominal yield (Asness 2003).
nodes.f: E/P vs 10y yield

nodes.t: Total stock market value over GDP; Buffett's 2001 rough gauge of how expensive the market is.
nodes.f: market cap / GDP

nodes.t: Market value of firms over the cost of replacing their assets; above one invites building more.
nodes.f: q = market value / replacement cost

nodes.t: How much investors pay for a unit of profit or cash across the market; high levels mean lower long-run returns on average.
The average return a rational investor anticipates; not a forecast of any one year.
What a business is worth to an owner from its future cash, independent of the quote today.
Buying well below estimated value so errors in the estimate do not cost money (Graham).
After-tax operating profit over the capital tied up to earn it; growth creates value only when ROIC exceeds the cost of capital.
nodes.f: ROIC = NOPAT / invested capital

nodes.t: Net income over shareholders' equity; inflated by leverage and buybacks.
nodes.f: ROE = NI / equity

nodes.t: A durable advantage (scale, network effects, switching costs, brand, patents) that keeps returns above the cost of capital.
Returns that come from investors paying more per unit of earnings, not from earnings growth; it reverses.
Changes in analysts' forecasts; rising estimates tend to lead prices for a while.
Consensus forecasts of earnings; historically too optimistic a year out.
Net income divided by shares outstanding; buybacks raise it without raising profit.
The rate profits rise; over long periods it tracks nominal GDP for the market as a whole.
Buying assets for less than they are worth on fundamentals (Graham, Buffett, Klarman).
Paying up for companies whose earnings should compound fast for long; works when growth persists.
How sensitive a stock's value is to the discount rate; far-off cash flows mean long duration, like a long bond.
Valuing each business line separately and adding them, often revealing a conglomerate discount.
Market value of equity plus debt minus cash: the price of the whole business.
nodes.f: EV = equity + debt - cash

nodes.t: The tendency of stretched quantities (valuations, margins, volatility) to drift back toward their long-run average.
Dividends over earnings.
A company repurchasing its own stock; returns cash and raises EPS, and is a steady buyer in the market.
Assets minus liabilities on the balance sheet.
The yield on government bills or bonds, the return for waiting without default risk; the base of every discount rate.
The interest rate a company pays to borrow, after the tax saving on interest.
The cash a business would produce if it stopped growing: revenue less costs and the capex needed only to maintain it.
Mauboussin and Rappaport's method: read the expectations a price implies, then judge whether they are likely to be revised.
The rhythm of expansion and recession; earnings, credit and commodity demand all ride it.
A breakdown in funding and trust that forces selling across markets at once.
The slow move by some reserve managers and trade partners away from the dollar, visible mainly in central bank gold buying.
The US Energy Information Administration's weekly inventory data and monthly Short-Term Energy Outlook.
One series moving before another; useful for forecasting only if it survives out of sample.
The exchange of cash and securities after a trade; US stocks settle the next business day.
What an asset earns if prices do not move: a bond's yield over funding, a currency's rate gap, a commodity's roll; it predicts returns across asset classes (Koijen et al. 2018).
Fitting flexible models to data to predict; in markets the signal is weak, the data short and the world changes, so most of the work is validation.
Judging a model on data held out from fitting, repeatedly; in time series the held-out data must come after, and overlapping labels must be purged.
Refitting on an expanding window and forecasting only the next block, as a trader would have.
Dropping training rows whose label window overlaps the test period, plus an embargo after it, so the model cannot peek (Lopez de Prado 2018).
A gap left after each test block before training resumes, against leakage through serial correlation.
Holding out every combination of k of N time blocks, purged; gives many backtest paths and the probability of backtest overfitting.
Training data that contains information from the test period: overlapping labels, revised data, features computed with future values.
Many decision trees on random subsets of rows and features, averaged; robust, but it cannot extrapolate beyond the data (Breiman 2001).
Trees added one at a time, each fitting the previous ensemble's errors (Friedman 2001); powerful and easy to overfit.
Least squares with a penalty on the size of coefficients, which shrinks noisy estimates toward zero.
Penalizing complexity so a model fits signal rather than noise.
Simple models miss real structure; complex ones chase noise; with low signal to noise the simple side usually wins.
Finding the past months most like today and asking what followed; transparent, and only as good as history's resemblance.
Averaging several models; simple averages of forecasts are hard to beat (Rapach, Strauss and Zhou 2010).
Averaging individual predictor forecasts, which beat each one out of sample for the equity premium.
How much a model's held-out error grows when one feature is shuffled; misleading when features substitute for each other.
Which inputs a model relies on; in-sample importance flatters noise, so the engine measures it out of sample.
When today's inputs come from a different distribution than the training data, so the model is extrapolating.
Measuring how far today sits from its nearest historical neighbours, against how far typical months sit from theirs.
Relationships that change over time; the main reason market models decay.
Mean squared error of probability forecasts; the skill score compares it with always forecasting the base rate.
Whether events forecast at 30% happen about 30% of the time.
The chance a model ranks a random positive case above a random negative one; 0.5 is a coin flip.
Whether one forecast's errors are reliably smaller than another's, with errors robust to overlap.
A second model that decides whether to act on a primary model's signal and how big, rather than its direction (Lopez de Prado).
Labelling a trade by which comes first: a profit target, a stop or a time limit.
Asking large language models to read news and predict returns; promising results are hard to separate from look-ahead in their training data.
How much of a series is predictable; for monthly stock returns it is tiny, which is why flexible models overfit.
Loss from decisions based on wrong or misused models (the Fed's SR 11-7 definition, 2011).
Critical review of a model by people with the skill, independence and authority to change it (SR 11-7).
Stating what a model assumes and testing each assumption on the data before trusting the output.
How wrong an assumption can be before the model's conclusion flips: the cost that erases an edge, the correlation that breaks a hedge.
Choosing the decision that stays acceptable over the widest range of errors in the model, instead of the one that is best if the model is right.
Decisions that hold up across many plausible worlds, not just the most likely one.
Alternative histories resampled from the data, in which a decision is re-run to see how often it still holds.
Anomalies earn less after they are published: about 26% lower out of sample and 58% lower after publication (McLean and Pontiff 2016).
Shrinking a backtest's Sharpe ratio for the number of strategies tried; the haircut is larger for modest Sharpes (Harvey and Liu 2015).
Across 888 Quantopian algorithms, backtest Sharpe ratios explained almost none of live performance (Wiecki et al. 2016).
How fat-tailed a variable is in sample-size terms: 0 for the Gaussian, 1 for the Cauchy; it says how much more data the same confidence needs.
nodes.f: kappa = 2 - (log n - log n0) / log(M(n)/M(n0))

nodes.t: Taleb and Douady's test: if losses accelerate as a shock grows, the position is fragile; if they slow, it is antifragile there.
Avoid ruin first; distrust thin-tailed models; prefer convex payoffs; judge by exposure, not forecasts.
For non-perishable things such as ideas or technologies, longer survival so far implies longer expected survival.
Trusting forecasts and advice more when the source bears the cost of being wrong.
Every valuation is a story and numbers; the story must be possible, plausible and probable, and the numbers must follow from it.
Turning a business story into growth, target margin, reinvestment through sales to capital, a cost of capital, terminal growth at most the risk-free rate, and a chance of failure.
Revenue added per dollar of capital invested; sets how much a company must reinvest to grow.
nodes.f: reinvestment = change in revenue / sales-to-capital

nodes.t: The chance a young or stretched business does not survive, weighed against its value as a going concern.
The return premium that makes the index equal the present value of its expected cash yield, growth and a terminal rate equal to the risk-free rate (Damodaran).
Market-neutral quant funds lost heavily on August 7 to 9, 2007 as crowded positions were unwound (Khandani and Lo).
A deployment error ran old code on one server and lost $460 million in 45 minutes.
Knowing something material before the market prices it, legally: better sources, faster reading, deeper analysis or a different time horizon.
Filings, transcripts, regulators' data and the original papers, read before anyone's summary.
10-Ks, 10-Qs, 8-Ks, proxies and Form 4s on EDGAR; full-text search finds a phrase across every filing.
Form 4 reports of executives' buying and selling; clusters of buying carry more signal than selling.
Data beyond prices and filings: shipping, satellite, card spending, app downloads, job postings, web traffic.
Specialist writers (SemiAnalysis, Stratechery, Doomberg, SixSigma, BowTied Bull) who go deep where sell-side coverage is thin; read for facts and frameworks, check their incentives.
What management says and refuses to say; changes in wording across quarters are a signal.
Treat any tip, thread or newsletter as a lead to check against a primary source, never as the source.
Paid calls with industry practitioners; useful for context, a legal risk near material non-public information.
Sales recognized in the period; the top line every margin is measured against.
The rules for when a sale counts as revenue; aggressive timing pulls future sales forward.
Revenue minus the direct cost of goods, over revenue; pricing power shows up here first.
nodes.f: (Revenue - COGS) / Revenue

nodes.t: Operating income over revenue.
Net income over revenue.
How much profit rises for a rise in sales when costs are fixed; cuts both ways.
Revenue, costs and profit over a period.
What a company owns and owes at a point in time.
Cash from operations, investing and financing; harder to flatter than earnings.
Cash generated by the business in the period, before investment.
Operating cash flow minus capital spending: cash left for owners.
nodes.f: FCF = OCF - capex

nodes.t: Spending on long-lived assets such as data centres, fabs and power plants.
The spending needed just to keep capacity where it is; often approximated by depreciation.
Spreading an asset's cost over its useful life; a short life lowers profits now, a long one flatters them.
The years over which an asset is depreciated; servers set at five to six years when the economic life may be shorter.
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; ignores the cost of the assets that earn it.
EBITDA with management's chosen exclusions; read the adjustments.
Earnings that exclude items management calls unusual, often including stock pay; higher than GAAP by design.
US Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, the audited standard.
Pay in shares; a real cost to owners through dilution even though it uses no cash.
Earnings not yet backed by cash; high accruals predict lower future returns (Sloan 1996).
nodes.f: (NI - OCF) / assets

nodes.t: Operating cash flow over net income; below one means profits are not turning into cash.
nodes.f: OCF / NI

nodes.t: How well reported profit reflects durable cash generation.
Receivables and inventory minus payables; swings in it move cash without moving profit.
Cash collected before the service is delivered; flatters cash flow while it grows.
Goods held for sale; a build-up can signal weak demand or a coming price war.
The premium paid in an acquisition over the fair value of net assets; written down when the deal sours.
A write-down when an asset is worth less than its book value.
Debt minus cash.
Net debt over EBITDA, a lender's first measure of how stretched a borrower is.
nodes.f: net debt / EBITDA

nodes.t: Operating income over interest expense.
nodes.f: EBIT / interest

nodes.t: Long-term rental commitments, now on the balance sheet; data-centre leases are large and long.
Obligations kept outside the reported balance sheet through vehicles or guarantees.
The average of the last n prices, updated each period; smooths noise to show the trend.
An equal-weighted moving average.
A moving average that weights recent prices more, with weight 2/(n+1) on the newest.
nodes.f: EMA_t = a P_t + (1 - a) EMA_(t-1)

nodes.t: The average of the last 200 trading days (about ten months); price above it is the most common definition of an uptrend.
The average of the last 50 trading days; the medium-term trend.
Hold stocks when the monthly price is above its ten-month average, else cash (Faber 2007); the engine tests it on 155 years.
The 50-day average crossing above (golden) or below (death) the 200-day.
Wilder's 0 to 100 gauge of recent gains against losses over 14 periods; above 70 is called overbought, below 30 oversold.
nodes.f: RSI = 100 - 100 / (1 + avg gain / avg loss)

nodes.t: Labels for prices that have risen or fallen fast; on their own they rarely predict reversals in trending markets.
Appel's moving average convergence divergence: the 12-period EMA minus the 26-period EMA, against its own 9-period EMA.
nodes.f: MACD = EMA12 - EMA26; signal = EMA9(MACD)

nodes.t: A 20-period average with bands two standard deviations above and below; band width tracks volatility.
Wilder's measure of daily range including gaps; used to size stops.
Wilder's average directional index: trend strength, not direction.
Where the close sits within the recent high-low range, 0 to 100.
A running total of volume signed by the day's direction.
Volume-weighted average price over a session; an execution benchmark as much as an indicator.
nodes.f: sum(P v) / sum(v)

nodes.t: Shares or contracts traded; conviction behind a move.
Price levels where buying or selling has gathered before; self-fulfilling when many watch them.
A move through support or resistance or to a new high.
The year's extreme prices; stocks near highs tend to keep doing better (George and Hwang 2004).
Buying what has risen and selling what has fallen over months, across many markets; paid in crises (Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen 2017).
The tendency of recent winners to keep winning for months (Jegadeesh and Titman 1993).
nodes.f: 12-1 month return

nodes.t: An asset's own past year return predicting its next month (Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen 2012).
Trend followers' habit of making money in long sell-offs.
Price making a new high while an oscillator does not; a warning, not a signal.
How many stocks share in a move; narrow rallies led by a few giants are fragile.
Running total of advancing minus declining stocks.
A breadth gauge of the trend under the index surface.
Put volume over call volume; extremes read as fear or greed.
Levels at 38.2, 50 and 61.8 percent of a move; widely used, without reliable evidence.
The fall from the previous peak; the loss that tests whether an investor can stay invested.
nodes.f: P_t / max(P) - 1

nodes.t: Finding a rule that worked by trying many; its backtest overstates its future (Sullivan, Timmermann and White 1999).
The rise in the general price level; erodes cash and bonds and decides what the Fed does.
The BLS index of consumer prices; the headline inflation measure.
Inflation without food and energy; the Fed's guide to the trend.
The personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge.
The overnight rate the central bank sets (the fed funds rate in the US).
A guide that sets the policy rate from inflation's gap to target and output's gap to potential.
nodes.f: i = r* + pi + 0.5 (pi - pi*) + 0.5 gap

nodes.t: How far the economy runs above or below its potential.
Central bank bond buying to push down long rates and add reserves.
Letting the central bank's bonds roll off; drains reserves.
The ease of funding and trading; ample liquidity props up risk assets, scarce liquidity breaks them.
Banks' deposits at the Fed; the system's cash.
Where money funds park cash at the Fed; once it is empty, drains come out of reserves.
An index of how easy credit, equity and dollar conditions are (Chicago Fed NFCI).
The value of everything an economy produces; nominal GDP growth bounds long-run profit growth.
A broad, lasting fall in activity; earnings fall, defaults rise, and stocks typically drop a third.
Inflation falling without a recession.
High inflation with weak growth; the worst regime for a stock and bond portfolio.
The share of the labour force without work.
A recession signal when the three-month average unemployment rate rises half a point above its prior-year low.
Monthly US job gains; the market's most-watched data release.
Government spending above revenue; financed by issuing bonds.
The stock of bonds a government owes; its interest cost rises with rates.
The amount of new duration the market must absorb, from Treasuries and corporate issuers.
The world's reserve and funding currency; a strong dollar tightens global conditions and weighs on commodities and gold.
Taxes on imports; raise prices and can lower growth.
Output per hour; the only lasting source of higher real wages and margins.
The rise in pay; feeds services inflation.
Cash and deposits in the economy.
A sudden jump in oil prices from lost supply; raises inflation and lowers growth.
Currencies' prices against each other; set by rate gaps, growth, flows and risk appetite.
Borrowing in a low-rate currency to hold a high-rate one; earns slowly and loses fast in crises.
The benchmark long-term rate; it sets mortgage rates and the discount rate on long-duration stocks.
Yields on bills and two-year notes; follow expected policy rates.
Yields by maturity; its slope reflects expected policy and the term premium.
Short rates above long rates; historically preceded most US recessions with a long, variable lag.
Trades on the curve's slope widening or narrowing.
The extra yield for locking money up long instead of rolling short bills; rises with supply and inflation uncertainty.
The yield after inflation, observed on TIPS; the true cost of money.
Nominal yield minus the TIPS yield: the inflation the bond market prices.
Treasury bonds whose principal rises with CPI.
The percentage change in a bond's price for a one-point change in yield; long bonds have high duration.
nodes.f: dP/P = -D dy

nodes.t: How duration itself changes with yield; long bonds gain more when yields fall than they lose when they rise.
nodes.f: dP/P = -D dy + 0.5 C dy^2

nodes.t: Moves opposite the yield.
An ETF of 20+ year Treasuries; the book's classic hedge, which fails when stocks and bonds fall together.
What a bond earns if yields do not move: its coupon over funding plus the price gain as it rolls down the curve.
The extra yield on corporate debt over Treasuries; widens before and during stress.
Bonds rated below investment grade; behave half like stocks.
The weakest rated borrowers; cracks show here first.
Bonds rated BBB- or better.
Failure to pay; default rates rise in recessions and when rates stay high for borrowers who refinance.
What creditors get back after a default.
Insurance against a borrower's default, quoted as an annual spread.
Investors who sell government bonds to punish fiscal excess, pushing yields up.
Implied volatility of Treasury options; the VIX of bonds.
The gap between swap rates and Treasury yields; negative when dealers' balance sheets are full.
How new debt is sold; weak demand (tails, low bid-to-cover) moves yields.
The right, not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) at a set price before a date.
The right to buy at the strike; pays when the price rises above it.
The right to sell at the strike; insurance against a fall.
Buying one put and selling a lower one: cheaper insurance that stops paying below the lower strike.
Buying a put and selling a call: free or cheap protection that gives up gains above the call.
Selling calls against stock held: income that caps upside.
Buying (or selling) both a call and a put: a bet on (or against) a big move.
The 1973 formula that prices a European option from spot, strike, time, rates and volatility.
nodes.f: C = S N(d1) - K e^(-rT) N(d2)

nodes.t: The volatility that makes the option price fit Black-Scholes; the market's priced uncertainty.
The volatility prices actually showed; usually below implied, which pays option sellers on average.
Implied minus realized variance; the insurance premium option sellers collect, and lose in crashes.
Downside puts priced at higher implied volatility than calls: crash insurance demand.
Cboe's 30-day implied volatility of the S&P 500; the fear gauge.
Option sensitivities: delta (to price), gamma (delta's change), vega (to volatility), theta (to time), rho (to rates).
How much dealers must buy or sell as prices move to stay hedged; negative gamma amplifies moves.
Options expiring the same day; now a large share of S&P 500 option volume.
Call minus put equals spot minus the discounted strike; arbitrage keeps them aligned.
nodes.f: C - P = S - K e^(-rT)

nodes.t: Exchange-traded contracts to buy or sell later at a price agreed now, marked to market daily.
A private agreement to trade later at a set price.
Spot minus futures; converges to zero at expiry.
Collateral posted against a leveraged position; margin calls force selling in falls.
A position that gains when the main bet loses; it costs something on average.
Cheap, far out-of-the-money protection that pays only in crashes (Spitznagel, Taleb).
Raw materials traded in bulk: energy, metals, grains, softs and livestock.
How most investors hold commodities; returns come from spot, roll and collateral (Gorton and Rouwenhorst 2006).
Futures above spot, usually when inventories are ample; rolling long positions loses money.
Futures below spot, usually when supply is tight; long positions earn as they roll.
The gain or loss from replacing an expiring future with the next; positive in backwardation.
The benefit of holding the physical commodity when supply is short (Kaldor, Working).
Futures equal spot plus financing and storage minus convenience yield; low inventories mean backwardation.
nodes.f: F = S e^((r + u - y)T)

nodes.t: Financing plus storage costs of holding a commodity until a future date.
Keynes's idea that hedgers pay speculators a premium, so futures sit below the expected spot price.
Stocks of oil, gas, metals or grain; the buffer that sets the curve's shape.
The producers' group that sets output quotas; its spare capacity caps price spikes.
Production that can be added quickly; low spare capacity makes prices jumpy.
The US government's emergency oil stock.
The North Sea benchmark for most of the world's oil.
The US benchmark, delivered at Cushing, Oklahoma.
The gap between the two benchmarks; cointegrated, with deviations that close over weeks.
The refining margin: product prices minus crude.
nodes.f: 3:2:1 crack

nodes.t: Soybean meal and oil value minus soybean cost: the crusher's margin.
Power price minus the gas cost to make it: the gas plant's margin.
Henry Hub in the US, TTF in Europe, LNG in Asia; strongly seasonal and storage driven.
Gas cooled to liquid and shipped; links regional gas markets, a fifth of it through Hormuz.
A store of value with no yield; driven by real yields, the dollar, fear and central bank buying.
Reserve managers buying gold to diversify away from dollars; a steady bid since 2022.
Half precious metal, half industrial input.
The industrial metal of wiring and grids; Dr. Copper for its read on growth, and a data-centre input.
Currencies of exporters (AUD, CAD, NOK, BRL, ZAR) that move with their commodities.
Steel's raw material; China's construction cycle sets its price.
China consumes about half the world's metals; its credit cycle drives the metals cycle.
Wheat, corn, soybeans and their oils; weather and stocks-to-use drive prices.
The USDA's monthly world supply and demand estimates for crops.
Coffee, cocoa, sugar, cotton: tropical crops prone to weather shocks.
The CFTC's weekly breakdown of futures positions by trader type; extremes in speculators' positions mark crowded trades.
The old saying that stocks do better from November to April than from May to October; the engine tests it since 1871 and since 1950.
Regular calendar patterns: gas peaks in winter, grains around harvest; in stocks, mostly folklore.
A decade-long price boom from a demand surge meeting slow supply.
The shift to electricity and renewables; raises demand for copper, power and gas backup.
The chokepoint for about a fifth of world oil and LNG; its closure in 2026 is the book's live oil shock.
The gap between the best buy and sell quotes; the toll for immediacy.
How much can trade without moving the price; vanishes when needed most.
Resting limit orders at each price.
An order to trade only at a set price or better; may not fill.
An order to trade now at the best available price; certain fill, uncertain price.
An order that becomes a market order when a price is hit; can fill far away in a gap.
The difference between the expected and actual fill price.
How much a trade moves the price against itself; grows with the square root of size (the square-root law).
nodes.f: impact ~ sigma sqrt(Q / V)

nodes.t: Impact scales with the square root of the order's share of daily volume, across markets.
Trading a large order fast (more impact) or slow (more price risk) optimally (2000).
Turning a decision into fills at low cost: slicing, timing, venue choice.
Time-weighted average price: an even pace of trading.
The cost from decision price to final fill, including what never filled.
How far price moves per unit of order flow when informed traders hide among noise traders (Kyle 1985).
Trading against someone who knows more; the reason spreads exist (Glosten and Milgrom 1985).
A dealer who quotes both sides and earns the spread while managing inventory and adverse selection.
A dealer's exposure to positions accumulated while making markets.
Automated trading at microsecond speed, mostly market making and arbitrage.
Delay between a signal and an order reaching the market.
Wholesalers paying brokers for retail orders, which they fill inside the spread.
Venues without public quotes; a large share of US volume trades off exchange.
A large trade negotiated privately and printed at once, often at a discount.
Borrowing shares to sell, hoping to buy back cheaper; losses are unbounded.
Shorts forced to buy as prices rise, driving prices higher.
The fee to borrow shares to short.
A demand for more collateral; forced selling begets more selling.
Borrowing to hold more than one's capital; magnifies gains, losses and the risk of being forced out.
Cutting positions to reduce leverage, often all at once.
Exchange-wide trading halts after large falls.
US stocks settle one business day after trade since 2024.
Authorized participants swap baskets for ETF shares, keeping prices near NAV.
Forced buying and selling when index weights change.
Individual investors' share of trading; surges in manias.
Profiting from a price gap between equivalent assets; limited by capital and risk (Shleifer and Vishny 1997).
Commissions, spreads, impact and taxes; they turn many backtested edges negative.
How much of a portfolio trades each year.
The standard deviation of returns; the most common, and incomplete, measure of risk.
How much an asset moves with the market; the CAPM's measure of risk that cannot be diversified away.
Return beyond what the asset's risk exposures explain; mostly luck after costs (Fama and French 2010).
Sharpe's 1964 model: expected return rises only with beta.
nodes.f: E[r] = rf + beta (E[rm] - rf)

nodes.t: How two returns move together, from -1 to 1; it rises in crises, when diversification is needed most.
Positive when inflation drives both; then bonds stop hedging stocks.
How often assets crash together; correlation understates it.
Holding assets that do not move together to lower risk without lowering expected return.
Too much in one name, sector or factor; the AI book's defining risk.
Excess return over volatility; the standard risk-adjusted score.
nodes.f: SR = (r - rf) / sigma

nodes.t: Like Sharpe but counts only downside volatility.
The worst peak-to-trough loss; the number that ends careers and funds.
The loss not exceeded with a given confidence over a horizon; silent about the tail beyond it.
The average loss beyond the VaR; describes the tail.
Extreme moves far more often than a bell curve allows; kurtosis above 3.
A rare, extreme, unforeseen event that is explained only afterwards (Taleb).
The bet size that maximizes long-run growth: edge over odds; full Kelly is wild, half Kelly is common.
The chance of losing the whole bankroll; falls exponentially with bankroll over variance.
nodes.f: ~ exp(-2 mu B / sigma^2)

nodes.t: How much to put in each bet; more important than which bets.
A rule to exit after a set loss; limits damage, adds whipsaw.
Returning weights to target; sells winners and buys losers.
Weighting assets so each adds equal risk, usually with leverage on bonds (Bridgewater's All Weather).
60% stocks and 40% bonds; it suffered its worst year in 2022 as both fell.
How much hedge per unit of exposure; the minimum-variance ratio is the regression slope.
nodes.f: h* = cov / var

nodes.t: Tilting toward characteristics with long-run premia: value, momentum, quality, size, low volatility, carry.
Cheap stocks beating expensive ones over long periods; it suffered a lost decade to 2020.
Profitable, stable, low-debt companies earning more than their risk suggests.
Low-risk stocks earning as much as high-risk ones.
The book's loss in a chosen bad scenario.
Weighing a few coherent futures instead of one forecast.
Many funds in the same trade; exits become stampedes.
A period with its own rules (low inflation, high inflation, crisis); links and hedges change between them.
Active return over tracking error.
Fitting a line (or plane) through data to measure how one variable moves with others.
The regression that minimizes squared errors.
The share of variation a model explains in-sample; flattering.
How much better a model forecasts than the historical mean on data it never saw (Campbell and Thompson 2008).
nodes.f: 1 - SSE_model / SSE_mean

nodes.t: The chance of a result at least this extreme if nothing were going on; not the chance the idea is wrong.
An estimate over its standard error; above 3 is the modern bar for a new factor (Harvey, Liu and Zhu 2016).
How much an estimate would vary across samples.
Standard errors that allow for autocorrelation and changing volatility (1987).
Resampling the data to see how much an estimate could vary (Efron 1979).
Resampling blocks of random length to keep time dependence (Politis and Romano 1994).
Running many tests guarantees some false positives; Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg corrections adjust for it.
A step-down correction that controls the chance of any false positive.
The expected share of false findings among those declared (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995).
A model that fits noise; great in-sample, poor after.
How often the in-sample winner falls to the bottom half out of sample (Bailey et al. 2017).
A Sharpe ratio adjusted for how many strategies were tried and for fat tails (Bailey and Lopez de Prado 2014).
Judging a model only on data it was not built on.
Using information in a backtest that was not available at the time.
Studying only what survived (funds, stocks) and so overstating returns.
Monthly averages of prices create spurious autocorrelation of about 0.25 (Working 1960), flattering trend rules on averaged data.
A series whose statistical behaviour does not drift; prices are not, returns roughly are.

nodes.n: Unit root and the ADF test
nodes.t: Testing whether a series wanders like a random walk (Dickey and Fuller 1979).
Two wandering series tied by a long-run relationship; their spread mean-reverts (Engle and Granger 1987).
Betting on the spread of two related assets returning to normal.
Whether one series' past improves forecasts of another; prediction, not proof of cause.
Telling cause from correlation: experiments, natural experiments, or structural assumptions stated out loud.
A hidden common cause that makes two things move together; the robustness value says how strong it would have to be.
The share of variance an unseen confounder must explain to erase an estimate (Cinelli and Hazlett 2020).
Learning causal direction from non-Gaussian data: the cause is the variable whose residuals look independent of it (Shimizu et al. 2006).
What would have happened had one cause been different, holding the rest.
Each series regressed on the past of all; impulse responses trace a shock through time.
The path of every series after a one-time shock to one.
The share of forecast-error variance coming from other variables' shocks (Diebold and Yilmaz 2012).
Shocks spreading across markets beyond what fundamentals justify.
Estimating which variables are linked once all others are held fixed, with most links set to zero.
Correlation after removing what other variables explain.
Keeping only what survives refits on many half-samples, with a bound on false findings.
Tracking a hidden quantity that drifts, updating with each observation.
A model in which the data switch between hidden regimes with fixed probabilities (Hamilton 1989).
Volatility that clusters: today's variance depends on yesterday's shock and variance (Bollerslev 1986).
Answering by simulating many random worlds.
Revising a belief in proportion to how much more likely the evidence is under it than under the alternative.
nodes.f: posterior odds = prior odds x likelihood ratio

nodes.t: The belief before the evidence.
How probable the evidence is under a hypothesis.
Error bars calibrated on past errors rather than an assumed distribution; the adaptive version keeps coverage when the world shifts.
Combining rival models with the weights that forecast best out of sample.
Whether multi-period variance grows faster (momentum) or slower (mean reversion) than a random walk (Lo and MacKinlay 1988).
How heavy the tails are; 3 for a bell curve.
Asymmetry of returns; stocks crash down more than they jump up.
The power-law exponent of the tail; below 3 means variance is barely defined for practical purposes.
Ignoring how common something is in general when judging a specific case.
Losses hurt about twice as much as equal gains please (Kahneman and Tversky 1979).
People judge outcomes as gains and losses from a reference point, overweight small probabilities and feel losses more.
Estimates pulled toward an arbitrary starting number (Tversky and Kahneman 1974).
Believing one knows more than one does; makes people trade too much (Barber and Odean 2000).
Following the crowd because others are; feeds bubbles and crashes.
Buying because prices are rising and others are getting rich.
Overweighting what happened lately.
Assuming recent trends continue; buys high and sells low.
Seeking evidence that agrees with what one already believes.
Selling winners too soon and holding losers too long.
Treating money differently by its label or source.
Believing after the fact that one saw it coming.
Fitting a tidy story to random events.
Believing a run must reverse.
Staying in because of what has already been spent.
Choices changing with how the same facts are presented.
Investors trading on non-information; their sentiment can move prices further than arbitrage can correct (De Long et al. 1990).
Mispricing that persists because correcting it is risky and capital is limited (Shleifer and Vishny 1997).
Soros's loop: prices change fundamentals, which change prices (rising stocks fund more AI capex).
Prices far above any reasonable value, sustained by expectations of further rises; ends in a crash.
A broad speculative frenzy (Kindleberger's Manias, Panics, and Crashes).
When stability has bred enough leverage that a small shock forces a collapse.
Graham's moody business partner who offers prices daily; to be used, not obeyed.
The market's mood; extremes are contrarian signals over months, not days.
Buffett's advice to be fearful when others are greedy and the reverse.
Shares bid up by online retail crowds and short squeezes (2021).
Cheap, volatile shares overpriced for their small chance of a huge gain.
Believing skill governs what chance governs.
Imagining a decision has failed and asking why, before making it (Klein).
Evidence written down in advance that would reverse a decision.
Judging a case by the base rate of similar cases before its details.
The group of similar past cases used for a base rate.
The probability-weighted average outcome; the right target for repeated bets, the wrong one for ruinous ones.
nodes.f: EV = sum p_i x_i

nodes.t: How widely results scatter around expected value; short runs are dominated by it.
The price of a call against the pot; call when equity exceeds call / (pot + call).
nodes.f: call / (pot + call)

nodes.t: Pot odds including what can be won on later streets if the draw hits.
A hand's share of the pot on average against the opponents' range; the engine simulates it.
All the hands an opponent could have given their actions; think in ranges, not single hands.
The value of a bet from the chance opponents fold.
Betting a weak hand so a stronger one folds; in equilibrium, bluffs keep bets credible.
Acting last, with more information; worth money in poker and in markets.
Unintended signals of strength or weakness.
Emotional decision-making after losses; the trader's version is revenge trading.
Keeping each bet small relative to capital so variance cannot end the game.
An unexploitable strategy, a Nash equilibrium; limit hold'em heads-up was solved in 2015 (Bowling et al.).
Deviating from equilibrium to profit from an opponent's mistakes, at the risk of being exploited back.
A set of strategies where no player gains by changing alone.
Randomizing between actions so an opponent cannot predict and exploit.
Each does better defecting whatever the other does, yet both do worse than if they cooperated; the AI capex race.
Hyperscalers each spending more because the others do, even if all would earn more spending less.
Coordination under noisy private information: when a crowded trade runs (Morris and Shin).
Depositors withdrawing because they fear others will; gates in private credit are a run's brakes.
One side knowing more; prices, spreads and contracts adjust for it.
Costly actions that reveal private information (dividends, buybacks, insider buying).
Winning an auction often means having overestimated the value.
A price set by competing bids: English, Dutch, sealed-bid; Treasuries and IPOs are auctioned.
Laying out choices, chance events and payoffs to compute the best path.
How much a piece of information would raise the expected value of a decision before it is known.
Judging decisions by their process and odds, not by how one outcome turned out (Duke).
Judging a decision by its outcome alone.
Whether the average over many people equals one person's average over time; leverage breaks it.
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement (Fisher and Ury 1981): what you do if this deal fails; it sets your walk-away.
The worst price at which one would still deal.
Zone of possible agreement: the gap between the buyer's and seller's reservation prices.
The first number anchors the deal; bold first offers win more on average (Galinsky and Mussweiler 2001).
An extreme anchor drags the counterpart's estimate toward it, unless they counter with their own.
Shrinking concessions signal approaching a limit.
Alternating offers over a shrinking pie: the more patient side gets more (Rubinstein 1982).
nodes.f: first mover share = (1 - d2) / (1 - d1 d2)

nodes.t: Splitting the surplus over each side's outside option in proportion to bargaining power (Nash 1950).
What tilts the split: patience, outside options, deadlines and information.
Willingness to wait; in Rubinstein's model, the source of bargaining power.
Most concessions happen near deadlines; the side without one gains.
One proposes a split, the other accepts or both get nothing; people reject offers they find unfair.
People pay to punish unfair offers, so the selfish optimum often fails.
Trading concessions on issues each side values differently to create value.
Bargaining over price with uncertain walk-away points; the best opening offer balances a better price against the chance of no deal.
nodes.f: p* = (hi + cost) / 2 for a uniform buyer value

nodes.t: Blocks, OTC bonds and private stakes trade by negotiation, not on a screen; information and urgency set the discount.
Funds that buy companies, usually with debt, improve them and sell within about five years.
Buying a company mostly with borrowed money secured on it.
Minority stakes in fast-growing, already profitable companies.
Funds backing young companies for a share of the few that win big.
A handful of investments return the whole fund.
A private company valued above $1 billion.
Raising money at a lower valuation than before.
A venture round of $100 million or more; AI labs now raise in the billions.
Capital flowing to AI companies, now the majority of venture dollars.
Committed capital not yet invested.
Capital raised by new funds; falls when distributions dry up.
A fund drawing committed money from its investors.
Cash returned to fund investors from exits.
Sales of portfolio companies by IPO, to a company, or to another fund.
A company's first sale of shares to the public.
The fund's reported value of what it holds; marks lag public markets.
Managers' estimates of private holdings; smoothed, which understates volatility and correlation.
Private assets look calm because they are rarely priced (Asness calls it volatility laundering).
The discount rate at which a fund's cash flows net to zero; flattered by early distributions and subscription lines.
nodes.f: sum CF_t / (1 + IRR)^t = 0

nodes.t: Total value (distributions plus NAV) over paid-in capital.
nodes.f: (D + NAV) / paid in

nodes.t: Distributions over paid-in capital: the cash actually returned.
nodes.f: D / paid in

nodes.t: Remaining value (NAV) over paid-in capital.
nodes.f: NAV / paid in

nodes.t: Multiple on invested capital for a deal.
Private fund cash flows judged against investing the same cash in a public index (Kaplan and Schoar 2005).
A fund's cumulative cash flow dips in early years (fees and calls) before rising.
Yale's 2002 model of a fund's calls, growth and distributions, used to plan commitments.
The year a fund starts investing; returns cluster by vintage.
The manager's share of profits, typically 20% above a hurdle.
An annual fee on committed or invested capital, typically 1.5 to 2%.
The return investors get before the manager earns carry, often 8%.
General partners run funds; limited partners (pensions, endowments) provide the money.
Buying existing fund stakes or assets from investors who want out, usually at a discount to NAV.
A new fund a GP creates to keep holding an asset its old fund must sell.
Borrowing against a fund's portfolio, sometimes to pay distributions.
A fund borrowing against investors' commitments to delay calls; raises IRR without raising profit.
Loans made by funds rather than banks, mostly to mid-sized private companies at floating rates.
A fund lending straight to a company.
A listed or non-traded fund that lends to private firms; its discount to NAV is a stress gauge.
Interest paid by adding to the loan instead of cash; rising PIK is a warning.
Limits on withdrawals from semi-liquid funds when requests exceed the cap.
A listed shell that raises money to buy a private company; boomed and busted in 2021.
Money a firm manages; fees scale with it.
Picking securities to beat a benchmark; on average it cannot, before costs (Sharpe 1991).
Holding the index at low cost; now about half of US fund assets.
A fund that holds a market index (Bogle's 1976 first).
An exchange-traded fund; trades all day, usually tracks an index.
A pooled fund priced once a day.
A lightly regulated pool using leverage, shorts and derivatives, paid a fee plus a share of gains.
Hedge funds running many small teams under tight risk limits; correlated de-grossing is their tail risk.
The classic 2% fee plus 20% of profits.
What managers charge; the one certain drag on returns, falling for decades.
A fund's annual cost as a share of assets.
Falling fees as money moves to passive funds.
Money moving into or out of funds; persistent outflows from active equity, inflows to ETFs and money funds.
Funds holding bills and repo; a record pile of cash on the sidelines.
How investors are already placed; crowded positions limit who is left to buy.
BofA's monthly poll of global managers' cash, allocations and the most crowded trade.
Quarterly US filings of large managers' holdings, 45 days late.
Few active managers beat the market by more than chance would produce (Fama and French 2010).
Volatility of a fund's return relative to its benchmark.
Charging active fees while hugging the index.
Promising quick withdrawals on assets that are slow to sell.
Asset managers merging for scale as fees fall.
Owning the index's stocks directly to harvest tax losses.
Funds that shift from stocks to bonds as retirement nears; steady automatic buyers.
Yale's heavy use of private assets (Swensen); its illiquidity bit in 2008 and after 2022.
Hyperscalers' spending on data centres, chips and power; four hyperscalers guided about $725 billion for 2026 (April).
Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle: the cloud giants funding the build.
Renting computing over the internet; where AI is sold.
Chips that train and run AI models; Nvidia dominates, custom chips are rising.
Chips designed by the hyperscalers themselves, with Broadcom and others.
Stacked memory that feeds AI chips; sold out and pricey in 2026.
Buildings of servers, power and cooling; the physical AI buildout.
Electricity needed by data centres; grids and gas plants are the binding constraint.
Running trained models to answer queries; the demand that has to pay for the build.
Building a model from data with huge compute.
The units AI models read and write; usage measured in tokens.
Money customers pay for AI services; still small against capex.
Whether AI revenue will earn more than the cost of the capital spent on it.
Suppliers investing in customers who then buy their chips; inflates demand signals.
Sellers lending buyers the money to buy their products; a 1999 telecom echo.
Specialist GPU clouds such as CoreWeave, financed with debt secured on chips.
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and others building frontier models; huge private funding rounds.
Whether AI raises output per worker enough to justify the spend.
Governments funding national AI computing.
Chips boom and bust with inventories and capex; memory most of all.
A fixed-supply digital asset; to some digital gold, to others speculation.
The case that bitcoin is a scarce store of value like gold.
Bitcoin's four-yearly cut in new supply.
Spot bitcoin and ether ETFs approved in 2024; flows now move prices.
Tokens pegged to the dollar and backed by bills; large buyers of Treasuries.
A programmable blockchain and its token, ether.
Lending and trading on blockchains without intermediaries.
Recording real assets such as funds and bonds on blockchains.
The crash that began the Great Depression; stocks fell 89% by 1932.
A sudden, deep fall; correlations jump and liquidity disappears.
OPEC's embargo quadrupled oil prices; stagflation and a 48% stock fall followed.
A 20% one-day fall, amplified by portfolio insurance.
A surprise Fed tightening that crushed bonds.
A leveraged hedge fund whose convergence trades blew up; a Fed-brokered rescue followed.
The 2000 tech bubble; the Nasdaq fell 78% and took 15 years to recover; the AI buildout's most cited parallel.
A housing and credit bust that froze funding; stocks fell 57%.
A minutes-long collapse and rebound in US stocks.
Yields jumped on hints of slower QE.
Short-volatility products collapsed in a day.
A 34% fall in five weeks, then a policy-fuelled recovery.
GameStop squeezes, SPACs and crypto peaks.
Stocks and bonds fell together as the Fed hiked fastest in 40 years.
Silicon Valley Bank failed on duration losses and a digital bank run.
A sudden yen rally forced carry trades shut and spiked the VIX.
Sweeping US tariffs in April 2025 drove a sharp, brief sell-off.
The Strait of Hormuz disruption that lifted Brent above $120; the Fed hiked 25bp on September 16.
The annual interest a bond pays as a percentage of its par value, fixed at issue for a fixed-rate bond. It sets the cash flows but not the yield, which depends on the price paid.
nodes.f: annual coupon payment / par value

nodes.t: The principal amount a bond promises to repay at maturity and the base on which coupons are calculated. Bond prices are usually quoted as a percentage of par.
A bond's quoted price excluding accrued interest. Markets quote clean prices so the price does not jump on coupon dates; the buyer actually pays the dirty price.
nodes.f: clean price = dirty price - accrued interest

nodes.t: The full price a buyer pays for a bond: the clean price plus interest accrued since the last coupon date. It equals the present value of all remaining cash flows.
nodes.f: dirty price = clean price + accrued interest

nodes.t: The portion of the next coupon earned by the seller since the last coupon date, paid by the buyer at settlement. Its size depends on the day count convention.
nodes.f: accrued = coupon x (days since last coupon / days in coupon period)

nodes.t: The rule for counting days when computing accrued interest and discount factors, such as actual/actual for Treasuries, 30/360 for corporates and munis, and actual/360 for money markets.

The single discount rate that equates a bond's price to the present value of its promised cash flows if held to maturity. It is an internal rate of return that assumes coupons are reinvested at the same yield.
nodes.f: price = sum of CF_t / (1 + y/k)^(k t)

nodes.t: The yield computed assuming the issuer redeems a callable bond at the first (or a specified) call date and call price rather than holding it to maturity.
The lowest yield among yield to maturity and the yields to every possible call or put date, giving the most conservative yield a holder of a bond with embedded options can expect absent default.
nodes.f: ytw = min(ytm, ytc over all call dates)

nodes.t: Annual coupon income divided by the bond's current price. It ignores pull to par, so it overstates return on premium bonds and understates it on discount bonds.
nodes.f: current yield = annual coupon / clean price

nodes.t: A yield annualized by doubling the semiannual rate, the convention for US Treasury notes and bonds. It lets bills and other instruments be compared with coupon Treasuries on a common basis.
nodes.f: bey = 2 x semiannual yield

nodes.t: The quoting convention for Treasury bills: the discount from face value as a fraction of face, annualized on a 360-day year. It understates the true return because it uses face value and a 360-day year.
nodes.f: discount yield = (face - price)/face x 360/days

nodes.t: The yield on a zero-coupon bond for a given maturity, the correct rate for discounting a single cash flow at that date. The set of spot rates forms the zero curve.

The interest rate for a future period implied today by the spot curve, such that investing to the far date equals investing to the near date and rolling at the forward. It embeds expectations plus term premium.
The curve of coupon rates at which bonds of each maturity would price exactly at par. It is the curve most often shown for Treasuries and swaps, and is derived from or used to build the spot curve.
A bond that pays no coupons and is bought at a discount, returning par at maturity. Its Macaulay duration equals its maturity, making it the purest exposure to a single point on the curve.
nodes.f: price = par / (1+y)^T

nodes.t: Building a zero-coupon curve sequentially from coupon bond or swap prices: solve the shortest maturity first, then use those spot rates to strip each longer instrument's final cash flow.
The risk that coupons and principal must be reinvested at lower rates than the original yield. It works against price risk: falling rates raise bond prices but reduce reinvestment income.
The risk that a bond's market value falls when yields rise. It grows with maturity and falls with coupon, and is measured by duration and convexity.

Bond prices move inversely to yields along a convex curve: a given yield drop raises price more than the same yield rise lowers it for an option-free bond. Longer, lower-coupon bonds are more sensitive.
nodes.f: dP/P = -D_mod x dy + 0.5 x C x dy^2

nodes.t: A bond priced above par because its coupon exceeds the prevailing yield for its maturity and risk. Its price drifts down toward par as it approaches maturity.
A bond priced below par because its coupon is below the prevailing yield. Part of its return comes from accretion toward par, which can be taxed differently from coupon income.
The convergence of a non-defaulting bond's price toward par value as maturity approaches, regardless of where it was bought. It makes realized return at maturity predictable when held.
A bond the issuer may redeem early at set prices, usually after a protection period. The holder is short a call option, so the bond has negative convexity and caps price gains when yields fall.
nodes.f: callable bond = straight bond - call option

nodes.t: A bond the holder may sell back to the issuer at par on set dates. The embedded put limits price declines when yields or spreads rise, so it yields less than a comparable straight bond.
nodes.f: putable bond = straight bond + put option

nodes.t: An indenture provision requiring the issuer to retire part of a bond issue on a schedule before maturity, by open-market purchase or calls at par. It reduces credit risk but shortens average life.

A bond whose coupon resets periodically to a reference rate plus a fixed spread. Because the coupon tracks market rates, its rate duration is close to the time to the next reset, while spread duration remains.
nodes.f: coupon = reference rate + quoted margin

nodes.t: A bond with no maturity that pays coupons indefinitely, typically callable by the issuer. Its value is coupon divided by yield, so duration is long and roughly equal to (1+y)/y.
nodes.f: price = coupon / yield

nodes.t: A bond the holder can exchange for a fixed number of issuer shares. It combines a straight bond floor with an equity call option, so it behaves like debt when the stock is low and like equity when high.
nodes.f: conversion value = conversion ratio x share price

nodes.t: Buying convertible bonds and shorting the issuer's stock in a delta-hedged ratio to capture cheap embedded volatility, carry and credit mispricing. It suffers when credit spreads widen or short borrow becomes scarce.
A bond that repays principal gradually with each payment rather than in a lump sum at maturity, like a mortgage. Its weighted average life is shorter than its final maturity.
A bond that repays all principal at a single maturity date with no call, put or sinking fund. Most Treasuries and many corporate bonds are bullets.
The legal contract between an issuer and bondholders, administered by a trustee, setting out payment terms, covenants, call provisions, events of default and remedies.
Promises in a debt contract that restrict the borrower, such as limits on additional debt, liens, asset sales or payouts. Affirmative covenants require actions; negative covenants forbid them.
The ranking of claims in a capital structure that determines payment order in bankruptcy: secured debt first against its collateral, then senior unsecured, subordinated, and finally equity.
Debt backed by a lien on specific collateral, giving the lender first claim on that asset's value in default. It typically carries lower yields and higher recoveries than unsecured debt.
Debt that ranks behind senior debt in liquidation and is repaid only after senior claims are satisfied. It pays a higher yield to compensate for lower expected recovery.
Subordinated financing that sits between senior debt and equity, often with PIK interest or warrants. It earns high returns for low recovery and is common in buyouts.

The full return on a bond over a horizon: coupon income, reinvestment income and the price change from rates, spreads and roll-down. Starting yield is its best single predictor over a duration-length horizon.
nodes.f: total return = coupon + reinvestment + price change

nodes.t: Projecting a bond's total return over a chosen holding period under assumed yield curve and spread scenarios, decomposing it into carry, roll-down and price effects.
The present-value-weighted average time to receive a bond's cash flows, in years. A zero-coupon bond's Macaulay duration equals its maturity; coupons pull it shorter.
nodes.f: D_mac = sum(t x PV(CF_t)) / price

nodes.t: The approximate percentage price change for a 1 percentage point change in yield, assuming cash flows do not change. It is Macaulay duration divided by one plus the periodic yield.
nodes.f: D_mod = D_mac / (1 + y/k); dP/P = -D_mod x dy

nodes.t: Duration computed by repricing a bond for small up and down shifts in the benchmark curve, letting cash flows change. It is the correct measure for callable bonds, MBS and other instruments with embedded options.
nodes.f: D_eff = (P_down - P_up) / (2 x P_0 x dy)

nodes.t: The dollar change in a position's value for a one basis point change in yield. It lets positions of different size and maturity be compared and hedged in dollar terms.
a: dollar value of a basis point
nodes.f: DV01 = modified duration x price x 0.0001

nodes.t: Modified duration multiplied by market value, the dollar sensitivity to yield changes. The dollar price change for a 100 basis point move is about one hundredth of that figure. Portfolio dollar duration is the sum of position dollar durations.
nodes.f: dollar duration = D_mod x market value; dollar change for 100bp approx D_mod x market value x 0.01

nodes.t: The sensitivity of a bond or portfolio to a shift in one maturity point of the curve, holding others fixed. A set of key rate durations sums to effective duration and reveals exposure to curve shape changes.

The percentage price change of a credit or spread product for a 100 basis point change in its spread, holding the benchmark curve fixed. For fixed-rate bonds it is close to modified duration; for floaters it can be much larger than rate duration.
A credit risk measure equal to spread duration multiplied by spread, reflecting that spreads move proportionally to their level. Bonds with equal DTS have similar expected excess return volatility.
nodes.f: DTS = spread duration x OAS

nodes.t: Convexity computed by repricing for up and down curve shifts with cash flows allowed to change. It is negative for callable bonds and most MBS over common rate ranges.
nodes.f: C_eff = (P_down + P_up - 2P_0) / (P_0 x dy^2)

nodes.t: A price-yield profile where duration shortens as yields fall and lengthens as they rise, so gains are capped and losses grow. It arises from embedded short call options in callable bonds and mortgage-backed securities.

The correction between futures-implied and forward rates (or between other payoff structures) caused by daily margining or nonlinear payoffs. Futures rates exceed forwards by an amount rising with volatility and maturity squared.
nodes.f: approx 0.5 x sigma^2 x t1 x t2

nodes.t: Interest rate sensitivity estimated by regressing a security's returns on Treasury yield changes. It can differ sharply from model duration for high yield bonds and equities, where spreads often fall when yields rise.
The mismatch between the duration of a firm's assets and liabilities, scaled by leverage. A positive gap means equity value falls when rates rise, the core risk in bank and insurer balance sheets.
nodes.f: gap = D_A - (L/A) x D_L

nodes.t: Managing a balance sheet so asset cash flows and rate sensitivities fund liabilities under changing rates, central to banks, insurers and pensions. Key tools are duration matching, gap analysis and hedging.

Structuring a bond portfolio so its value at a horizon is protected from small parallel rate shifts by matching duration to the horizon and keeping portfolio PV at least equal to the liability, with convexity at least as large.
Building a bond portfolio whose coupons and maturities exactly fund a schedule of liabilities, removing reinvestment and rate risk at the cost of flexibility and usually expense.

Running pension or insurance assets to hedge the rate and inflation sensitivity of liabilities, often with long bonds and swaps plus a separate return-seeking portfolio. Leveraged versions need collateral when yields jump.
A portfolio of bonds with evenly staggered maturities, reinvesting each maturing rung at the long end. It spreads reinvestment risk across time and provides predictable liquidity.

A bond portfolio concentrated in short and long maturities with little in the middle. Compared with a bullet of equal duration it has more convexity, gaining in large parallel moves and in flattenings.
Concentrating bond holdings around a single maturity, often to match a liability date. It carries less convexity than a barbell of the same duration but usually more yield when the curve is concave.

A common error: treating a bond's quoted yield as its expected return. Realized return differs because of defaults, calls, reinvestment rates, spread and rate changes before maturity, and the yield quoted may be gross of expected losses.
Taking more credit, duration, illiquidity or leverage to restore income when safe yields are low. It compresses risk premia and leaves portfolios exposed when the cycle turns.

The simplification behind single-number duration that all yields move by the same amount. Real curves twist and bend, so portfolios with equal duration can perform very differently; key rate durations correct for this.

The empirical regularity that a high-quality bond portfolio's starting yield closely forecasts its annualized return over a horizon near twice its duration, because price changes and reinvestment offset over that span.
An upward-sloping curve where longer maturities yield more than shorter ones, the typical shape when investors demand term premium and policy is not unusually tight.
A curve where short and long yields are similar, often seen late in tightening cycles as short rates rise toward long rates. It offers little reward for extending maturity.
A curve where intermediate yields exceed both short and long yields, often when markets expect policy tightening followed by easing. The hump is a curvature factor in curve models.
A curve move in which long yields rise more than short yields. It often reflects rising term premium, inflation worries or heavy supply rather than expected policy hikes.
A curve move in which short yields fall more than long yields, typically when markets price imminent policy easing, as often happens entering a recession.
A curve move in which short yields rise more than long yields, the usual signature of a central bank hiking cycle with credible long-run inflation expectations.
A curve move in which long yields fall more than short yields, often from falling inflation expectations, flight to quality, duration demand or long-end central bank purchases.
The 10-year Treasury yield minus the 2-year yield, the most watched gauge of curve slope. Inversion has preceded US recessions with variable and long lags, along with some false signals.
The 10-year Treasury yield minus the 3-month bill yield, used in the New York Fed's recession probability model. It captures the gap between current policy and long rates.
The 30-year yield minus the 5-year yield, a gauge of the long end's slope. It responds strongly to term premium, pension demand and long-end supply.

A three-leg curve trade going long or short a middle maturity against the opposite position in wings on both sides, weighted to be duration neutral. It bets on curvature and is sensitive to convexity differences.
nodes.f: fly = 2 x y_belly - y_short - y_long

nodes.t: Sizing the legs of a curve or spread trade so their DV01s offset, making the position insensitive to small parallel moves and isolating slope, curvature or relative value.
nodes.f: notional_2 = notional_1 x DV01_1 / DV01_2

nodes.t: Principal component analysis of yield changes finds three factors explaining nearly all variation: level (parallel shifts), slope (steepening and flattening) and curvature (belly versus wings), a result associated with Litterman and Scheinkman (1991).

The theory that long yields equal the average of expected future short rates, so forwards are unbiased forecasts. Empirically it fails: forwards overpredict future rates on average, implying a positive term premium.
nodes.f: y_n = average of E[short rates over n periods]

nodes.t: The theory that investors require extra yield to hold longer bonds because they carry more price risk, so the curve slopes upward even with flat rate expectations. It is an early statement of term premium.

The theory that each maturity segment is priced by its own supply and demand because investors such as banks, pensions and insurers stick to preferred maturities. Preferred habitat is a softer version allowing switching for enough yield.

The view that investors favor particular maturities but will move for sufficient yield, so local supply and demand shocks, such as QE purchases or pension demand, move term premia in specific curve segments.

A parametric yield curve model from Nelson and Siegel (1987) using level, slope and curvature terms with an exponential decay parameter. It fits smooth curves with few parameters and is widely used by central banks.
Comparing each bond's yield with a fitted curve to find securities trading rich (yield below fit) or cheap (above fit), the basis of Treasury relative value trading.
nodes.f: residual = market yield - fitted yield

nodes.t: Taking offsetting positions in closely related instruments, such as two Treasuries, bonds versus futures or swaps versus bonds, to capture small mispricings, usually with high leverage and repo financing.

The most recently auctioned Treasury of each tenor is on-the-run and trades with the best liquidity and repo specialness, so it usually yields slightly less than older off-the-run issues of similar maturity.
A term structure model that specifies a stochastic process for the instantaneous short rate and derives bond and option prices from it. Examples include Vasicek, Cox-Ingersoll-Ross and Hull-White.
nodes.f: dr = a(b - r)dt + sigma dW (Vasicek form)

nodes.t: A one-factor short-rate model from Vasicek (1977) with mean reversion and constant volatility, giving closed-form bond prices. Its Gaussian rates can go negative.
nodes.f: dr = k(theta - r)dt + sigma dW

nodes.t: A one-factor short-rate model from Cox, Ingersoll and Ross (1985) where volatility scales with the square root of the rate, keeping rates non-negative under a parameter condition.
nodes.f: dr = k(theta - r)dt + sigma sqrt(r) dW

nodes.t: A no-arbitrage extension of Vasicek with a time-varying drift calibrated to fit today's yield curve exactly, widely used to price callable bonds, swaptions and MBS.
nodes.f: dr = (theta(t) - a r)dt + sigma dW

nodes.t: A general framework from Heath, Jarrow and Morton (1992) that models the evolution of the entire forward curve, with no-arbitrage drift fully determined by forward rate volatilities.
A model where yields are linear in a few latent or macro factors, giving tractable bond prices. Fitted versions decompose long yields into expected short rates and term premium.
nodes.f: y_n = a_n + b_n x X_t

nodes.t: A widely cited estimate of the Treasury term premium from Adrian, Crump and Moench's affine model, published by the New York Fed. Estimates are model dependent and can differ from other models.
The constant spread that, added to every point on the benchmark zero curve, discounts a bond's cash flows to its market price. It reflects credit and liquidity risk plus any option value.
nodes.f: price = sum CF_t / (1 + z_t + Z)^t

nodes.t: A bond's yield minus the interpolated government bond yield of the same maturity. It is simple and widely quoted but ignores curve shape.
nodes.f: g-spread = bond yield - interpolated treasury yield

nodes.t: A bond's yield minus the interpolated swap rate of the same maturity, common in European credit and for comparing bonds with swap-funded investors' hurdle.
nodes.f: i-spread = bond yield - interpolated swap rate

nodes.t: The spread over the floating rate an investor receives after buying a fixed-rate bond and swapping its coupons to floating. It is a common measure of credit spread for banks and is compared against CDS.
The spread over the benchmark curve after removing the value of embedded options, computed by averaging over simulated rate paths. It is the standard comparison spread for callables and MBS.
nodes.f: OAS = Z-spread - option cost

nodes.t: A US government discount security maturing in one year or less, sold at weekly auctions and quoted on a bank discount basis. Bills are the core collateral and cash-equivalent asset of money markets.
A US government coupon security with an original maturity of 2 to 10 years paying semiannual fixed coupons. The 10-year note is the global benchmark for long-term rates.
A US government coupon security with an original maturity above 10 years, currently 20 and 30 years. Long bonds carry the highest duration and convexity in the Treasury market.

The market for US government debt, the largest and most liquid bond market and the benchmark for global risk-free rates and collateral. Trading runs through primary dealers, principal trading firms and interdealer platforms.
A 2-year US Treasury whose coupon resets weekly to the latest 13-week bill auction rate plus a fixed spread set at issue. It carries almost no rate duration.
Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal of Securities: Treasury coupons and principal traded as individual zero-coupon bonds. They give pure zero-coupon exposure and long duration.

Non-marketable US savings bonds whose rate combines a fixed real rate set at purchase with a semiannually reset inflation component tied to CPI-U, with annual purchase limits and early redemption penalties.
nodes.f: composite rate = fixed + 2 x semiannual inflation + fixed x semiannual inflation

nodes.t: Banks and broker-dealers designated by the New York Fed as trading counterparties for open market operations, obliged to bid in every Treasury auction. Their balance sheet capacity shapes Treasury liquidity.
Forward trading in a Treasury security between announcement and issue date, settling on issue. The when-issued yield just before the auction deadline is the benchmark for measuring an auction's tail.
Total bids received in a Treasury auction divided by the amount sold. A higher ratio signals stronger demand, though tail size and bidder mix are usually more informative.
nodes.f: bid-to-cover = bids tendered / amount accepted

nodes.t: The amount by which a Treasury auction's high yield exceeds the when-issued yield at the bidding deadline. A tail signals weak demand; a stop-through, where the auction clears below the when-issued yield, signals strength.
nodes.f: tail = high yield - wi yield at 1pm
