nodes.t: Treasury auction bidders who submit through primary dealers or the New York Fed, a category that includes foreign central banks and many investment managers. Their share is read as a proxy for end demand.
Non-dealer bidders who submit Treasury auction bids for their own account directly to the Treasury, such as domestic funds, banks and pensions. Dealers absorb what directs and indirects do not take.
The US Treasury's quarterly announcement of coupon auction sizes and borrowing plans, informed by the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee. Changes in coupon sizes or guidance can move term premium.

The proportion of marketable Treasury debt in bills. Raising it shortens debt maturity and reduces duration supply, easing long yields at the cost of more rollover and rate exposure for the government.
The average time to maturity of a government's outstanding marketable debt. A shorter maturity makes interest costs respond faster to policy rates and increases refinancing exposure.

The Treasury repurchasing outstanding off-the-run securities before maturity, funded by new issuance, to support market liquidity and smooth cash balances. Buybacks restarted as a regular program in 2024.

The ease of trading Treasuries without moving prices, measured by bid-ask spreads, market depth and price impact. It has deteriorated in stress episodes as debt outstanding grew faster than dealer balance sheets.
An SEC rule requiring many cash Treasury and repo trades to clear through a central counterparty such as FICC, aimed at reducing counterparty risk and settlement failures and enabling netting.

A clearinghouse that becomes buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer, netting exposures and collecting margin. It cuts bilateral counterparty risk but concentrates it in one systemically important entity.
Trades that do not settle on time because a seller cannot deliver the security. Fails rise when a bond is scarce and repo rates go near zero; the Treasury fails charge penalizes them.

Exchange-traded futures on baskets of deliverable Treasuries across several tenors, settled by physical delivery of the bond chosen by the short. They are the main tool for hedging and expressing duration views.

The deliverable bond in a futures basket that maximizes the short's profit at delivery, determined by price relative to conversion factor. The futures price tracks the CTD, and switches in CTD alter futures duration.
nodes.f: CTD minimizes price - futures price x conversion factor

nodes.t: The price per unit of par at which a deliverable bond would yield 6 percent, used to adjust the invoice price for different bonds in a Treasury futures basket.
nodes.f: invoice price = futures price x CF + accrued

nodes.t: The financing return earned by buying a deliverable bond, selling the future and delivering. The bond with the highest implied repo is usually the cheapest to deliver; comparing it with actual repo shows basis richness.
nodes.f: irr = (invoice price + coupons - cash price)/cash price x 360/days

nodes.t: The set of choices held by the short in a bond future: which bond to deliver, and when in the delivery month. Its value makes the futures price lower than a simple forward on the CTD.

Buying cash Treasuries financed in repo and shorting the corresponding futures, earning the gap between implied and actual repo. Highly levered, it can force rapid unwinds when repo margins or futures margins rise.
The reference CPI on a given date divided by the reference CPI at issue, used to scale a TIPS bond's principal and coupons for inflation. Reference CPI uses non-seasonally adjusted CPI-U with a lag.
nodes.f: adjusted principal = par x index ratio

nodes.t: The guarantee that a TIPS bond repays at least its original par at maturity even after cumulative deflation. The floor is worth more on newly issued bonds with little accrued inflation.
Government or corporate bonds whose principal or coupons are indexed to a price index, delivering a real yield. Examples include US TIPS, UK index-linked gilts and euro area linkers tied to HICP.

A derivative exchanging a fixed rate for realized inflation over the term, usually zero coupon. Its fixed rate is the market breakeven used to read inflation expectations without TIPS liquidity distortions.
nodes.f: pay (1+fixed)^T - 1 vs receive CPI_T/CPI_0 - 1

nodes.t: The implied average inflation rate for the five years starting five years from now, from breakevens or inflation swaps. Central banks watch it as a gauge of long-run inflation expectation anchoring, though it includes risk premia.
Extra yield nominal bond holders demand for bearing uncertainty about future inflation. It makes breakeven inflation differ from expected inflation, alongside TIPS liquidity premia.
nodes.f: breakeven = expected inflation + inflation risk premium - liquidity premium

nodes.t: Debt issued by US states, cities and other public entities, usually with interest exempt from federal income tax and sometimes state tax. The market is large, fragmented and dominated by retail and fund buyers.
A municipal bond backed by the issuer's full faith, credit and taxing power rather than a specific revenue source. Its credit depends on tax base, debt burden, pensions and governance.
A municipal bond repaid from a specific project or enterprise's revenues, such as water, airport, toll road or hospital fees. Credit rests on the project's coverage ratios rather than taxing power.
The taxable yield needed to match a tax-exempt municipal yield after taxes, used to compare munis with taxable bonds. Higher-bracket investors gain most from the exemption.
nodes.f: TEY = muni yield / (1 - marginal tax rate)

nodes.t: A high-grade municipal yield divided by the Treasury yield of the same maturity, the main relative value gauge for munis. Low ratios mean munis are rich unless tax rates justify them.
nodes.f: ratio = AAA muni yield / treasury yield

nodes.t: A US tax rule under which bonds bought at a discount larger than 0.25 points per year to maturity have the accretion taxed as ordinary income instead of capital gain, which can cause muni prices to fall sharply below that threshold.
nodes.f: threshold = par - 0.25 x years to maturity

nodes.t: A municipal bond whose repayment is secured by an escrow of Treasuries funded by a new issue, so it carries essentially government credit until its call or maturity date.
Issuing new bonds more than 90 days before an old issue's call date and escrowing proceeds to retire it, locking in lower rates. Tax-exempt advance refundings were eliminated by the 2017 US tax law.

A tax-exempt municipal bond whose proceeds benefit private entities, such as airports or housing. Interest may be subject to the alternative minimum tax, so it yields more than comparable non-AMT bonds.
A long-maturity municipal floater whose rate resets daily or weekly and which holders can put back at par, backed by a bank liquidity facility. VRDNs are core holdings of tax-exempt money funds.

The recurring supply and demand pattern in munis driven by heavy coupon and principal reinvestment around summer and winter months and by fund flows around tax season, which tends to make munis richer when net supply is negative.

The US bankruptcy chapter for municipalities, available only if state law authorizes it. Unlike corporate cases, creditors cannot force liquidation and courts cannot order tax increases, making recoveries uncertain.

A financial guaranty in which an insurer promises timely payment of principal and interest if the issuer defaults, wrapping the bond with the insurer's rating. Its value collapsed for many wraps when insurers were downgraded in 2008.

A privately owned, federally chartered financial company created to support credit in sectors such as housing and agriculture, including Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and the Federal Home Loan Banks. Their debt trades near Treasuries on an implied guarantee.
The Federal National Mortgage Association, a GSE that buys conforming mortgages and guarantees MBS backed by them. It has been in federal conservatorship since 2008.

The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, a GSE that buys conforming mortgages and guarantees MBS. Its securities are fungible with Fannie Mae's in the UMBS TBA market; it is also in conservatorship since 2008.
The Government National Mortgage Association, a US government agency that guarantees MBS backed by FHA, VA and USDA loans. Its guarantee carries the full faith and credit of the United States.

A system of regional GSEs that lend secured advances to member banks and insurers, funded by consolidated debt. They act as a lender of next-to-last resort in banking stress, before the discount window.
Unsecured bonds and discount notes issued by GSEs and federal agencies. They yield slightly more than Treasuries for weaker liquidity and an implied, not explicit, guarantee, and are often callable.
A mortgage meeting Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac size and underwriting limits, so it can be sold into agency MBS. Larger loans are jumbos and must be held or securitized privately.

Pooling loans or receivables in a bankruptcy-remote vehicle that issues securities paid from the pool's cash flows, often in tranches of differing seniority. It transfers credit and funding to capital markets.
Pass-through securities backed by pools of residential mortgages and guaranteed by Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac or Ginnie Mae, so holders bear prepayment and rate risk but essentially no credit risk.
A security that passes the pool's scheduled principal, interest and prepayments, minus servicing and guarantee fees, directly to holders pro rata each month.

The forward market for agency MBS in which buyers and sellers agree on issuer, coupon, maturity, price and settlement date, but specific pools are announced just before settlement. Its liquidity underpins US mortgage rates.
Selling a TBA for one month and buying it back for a later month, effectively lending MBS and borrowing cash. When the price drop is large, the roll is special and implied financing is cheap.
MBS pools traded by their specific characteristics, such as low loan balance or high loan-to-value, that predict slower prepayment, commanding a payup over TBA.
The risk that borrowers repay mortgages early, mostly by refinancing when rates fall, returning principal when reinvestment yields are low. It is the source of MBS negative convexity.
The risk that falling rates accelerate prepayments, shortening an MBS's average life and capping price gains just as reinvestment yields drop.
The risk that rising rates slow prepayments, lengthening an MBS's average life and duration when prices are falling, compounding losses.
The annualized percentage of a mortgage pool's outstanding balance expected or observed to prepay, derived from the monthly single mortality rate (SMM). It is the standard prepayment speed measure.
The gap between a borrower's mortgage rate and current mortgage rates, the main driver of prepayments. Pools with rates well above market are in the money and prepay fast.
nodes.f: incentive = note rate - current mortgage rate

nodes.t: Homeowners with mortgages far below current rates staying put to keep cheap financing, depressing home sales, housing supply and MBS prepayment speeds.
The gap between rates offered to borrowers and current-coupon MBS yields, reflecting originator capacity, guarantee fees and servicing values. It widens when lenders are capacity constrained.
The spread of the par-priced current coupon MBS yield over Treasuries or swaps, the standard gauge of mortgage valuation. It widens with rate volatility and when the Fed or banks stop buying.
Dynamic duration hedging by mortgage holders and servicers who sell Treasuries or pay swaps as rates rise and duration extends, and buy as rates fall. The flows can amplify rate moves.
The average time until each dollar of principal is repaid, weighted by principal amount, used for amortizing and prepayable securities in place of maturity.
nodes.f: WAL = sum(t x principal_t) / total principal

nodes.t: A structure that redirects mortgage pool cash flows into tranches with different prepayment and maturity profiles, such as sequential, PAC, support, IO and PO classes.
A CMO tranche with a fixed principal schedule that holds within a band of prepayment speeds, protected by support tranches that absorb excess or shortfall prepayments.

MBS split into an IO receiving only interest and a PO receiving only principal. IOs gain when prepayments slow and rates rise; POs gain when prepayments speed up, making them powerful prepayment hedges.
The right to collect mortgage payments for a fee, an asset that behaves like an IO strip: it gains value when rates rise and prepayments slow and loses when refinancing surges.

Residential mortgage securities without a GSE or government guarantee, backed by jumbo, non-QM or other loans, where investors bear credit risk through subordination. The subprime segment was central to the 2008 crisis.

Securities backed by pools of commercial real estate loans, typically with prepayment lockouts or yield maintenance. Credit risk depends on property cash flows, refinancing conditions and loan concentration.
Securities backed by pools of consumer or commercial receivables such as auto loans, credit cards, student loans and equipment leases, usually short and tranched with credit enhancement.

An actively managed securitization of broadly syndicated leveraged loans, funded by floating rate tranches from AAA to equity. Coverage tests divert cash from junior tranches when collateral deteriorates.
A securitization of bonds, loans or other structured products into tranches. CDOs of mortgage securities concentrated correlated housing risk and suffered large losses in 2008.
A slice of a securitization or structured deal with its own priority, size and risk. Losses hit junior tranches first; senior tranches are protected by the subordination beneath them.
The contractual order in which a structured deal's collections pay fees, interest and principal to tranches, including triggers that redirect cash to senior classes when tests fail.
Features that protect senior investors in a structured deal from losses, including subordination, overcollateralization, excess spread, reserve accounts and third-party guarantees.
Collateral par exceeding the notes issued, a cushion that absorbs losses before rated tranches. In CLOs, OC tests compare collateral par with tranche balances and divert cash if breached.
nodes.f: OC ratio = collateral par / tranche par and above

nodes.t: The portfolio loss levels at which a tranche starts and stops absorbing losses. A 3 to 7 percent tranche loses nothing until pool losses exceed 3 percent and is wiped out at 7 percent.
Bank bonds backed by a ring-fenced pool of mortgages or public loans that stays on the bank's balance sheet, giving investors dual recourse to the issuer and the cover pool. They are large in Europe.

A contract exchanging fixed-rate payments for floating-rate payments on a notional amount. Paying fixed shorts duration; receiving fixed adds duration. Swaps are the main tool for hedging and expressing rate views.
nodes.f: swap value = PV(fixed leg) - PV(floating leg)

nodes.t: The term structure of fixed swap rates across maturities against a floating index such as SOFR, used as the discount and pricing benchmark for derivatives and much corporate credit.
A swap exchanging a fixed rate for the compounded overnight rate, such as SOFR, fed funds or ESTR, over the term. OIS rates read off the market's expected policy path with little credit risk.
Discounting collateralized derivative cash flows at overnight rates because posted collateral earns roughly the overnight rate. It became market standard after 2008 replaced single-curve discounting.
The ISDA document governing collateral for OTC derivatives: eligible collateral, thresholds, margin frequency and interest on posted cash. Its terms change a derivative's value and funding cost.
An option to enter an interest rate swap at a set fixed rate on a future date. Payer swaptions profit when rates rise, receivers when they fall; swaption vol is a core rates volatility market.
A cap is a series of call options on a floating rate (caplets) paying when the rate exceeds a strike; a floor pays when it falls below. Floating rate borrowers buy caps to limit funding costs.
nodes.f: caplet payoff = notional x accrual x max(L - K, 0)

nodes.t: An OTC contract fixing an interest rate for a future period on a notional, settled in cash against the realized reference rate. It is the single-period building block of swaps.

Exchange-traded futures settling on average or compounded SOFR over a reference period, quoted as 100 minus the rate. They replaced eurodollar futures as the main instrument for trading the policy path.
nodes.f: price = 100 - rate

nodes.t: CME futures on 3-month USD LIBOR, for decades the most liquid short-rate contract and the basis of the strip used to read policy expectations. They were converted to SOFR futures in 2023.
nodes.f: price = 100 - LIBOR

nodes.t: Futures settling on the average effective federal funds rate in a calendar month, quoted as 100 minus the rate. They are the standard source for market-implied FOMC meeting probabilities.
nodes.f: implied rate = 100 - price

nodes.t: A swap exchanging two floating rates, such as two tenors of one index or two different indices. Its spread prices funding, credit or liquidity differences between the rates.
The spread between the swap rate matched to a Treasury future's CTD and the futures-implied yield, used to trade swap spreads with futures and to hedge corporate issuance.

Rate volatility quoted in basis points per year rather than percent of the rate level, the market convention for swaptions and the measure behind the MOVE index. It suits low or negative rate regimes.

An option pricing model from Bachelier (1900) assuming the underlying follows arithmetic Brownian motion, allowing negative values. It is the standard quoting model for rate options under normal volatility.
nodes.f: call = (F-K)N(d) + sigma sqrt(T) n(d), d = (F-K)/(sigma sqrt(T))

nodes.t: Black's (1976) adaptation of Black-Scholes to options on forwards and futures, assuming the forward is lognormal. It is the classic model for caps, floors, swaptions and commodity options.
nodes.f: call = DF x [F N(d1) - K N(d2)]

nodes.t: A stochastic volatility model from Hagan and coauthors (2002) used to interpolate and extrapolate rate option volatility smiles through four parameters: alpha, beta, rho and nu.

Debt issued by a company, paying a spread over government yields for credit, liquidity and optionality risk. Most trade over the counter, in dealer and electronic markets, with far less liquidity than Treasuries.

A rating agency's ordinal opinion of an issuer's or security's relative default risk, on scales such as AAA to D. Ratings drive regulatory capital, index eligibility and mandates, so changes can force selling.

Firms such as S&P Global, Moody's and Fitch that publish credit ratings, mostly paid by issuers. The issuer-pays model and their role in rating mortgage CDOs before 2008 drew criticism over conflicts.
The letter grade ladder with plus and minus (or 1, 2, 3) modifiers, where each step is a notch. BBB- or Baa3 is the lowest investment grade rating; BB+ or Ba1 is the top of high yield.
An agency's signal of likely rating direction: an outlook (positive, negative, stable) over roughly one to two years, and a watch or review for a nearer-term decision after a specific event.
Movement of issuers between rating categories over time, summarized in transition matrices. Downgrades cluster in recessions and are more common than upgrades for lower-rated credits.
A bond downgraded from investment grade to high yield. Forced selling by IG-only holders often pushes prices below fair value around the downgrade, a pattern fallen angel strategies try to exploit.
A bond upgraded from high yield to investment grade, opening it to a larger investor base and usually tightening spreads.
Bonds rated near the investment grade boundary, roughly BBB- to BB+, where index and mandate rules make spreads jump around rating changes.
The concern that a large share of investment grade debt rated BBB could be downgraded in a recession, overwhelming high yield buyers and widening spreads.
Sales driven by rules, margin calls, redemptions or rating limits rather than views on value. It creates temporary price dislocations that patient capital can buy.

The likelihood a borrower defaults over a horizon, estimated from ratings history, structural models or market spreads. Risk-neutral PDs from spreads exceed real-world PDs because spreads contain risk premia.
The fraction of exposure lost when a borrower defaults, equal to one minus the recovery rate. It depends on seniority, collateral and the default cycle.
nodes.f: LGD = 1 - recovery rate

nodes.t: The average credit loss anticipated on an exposure, used in pricing, provisioning and capital. Spreads must cover expected loss plus a risk premium for unexpected loss.
nodes.f: EL = PD x LGD x EAD

nodes.t: The approximation linking a credit spread to default intensity and loss: spread roughly equals hazard rate times loss given default. It converts CDS spreads into implied default probabilities.
nodes.f: spread = hazard rate x (1 - recovery)

nodes.t: The instantaneous conditional default intensity: the probability of default in the next instant given survival so far. Reduced-form credit models use it to price CDS and risky bonds.
nodes.f: survival(t) = exp(-integral of lambda)

nodes.t: A structural credit model from Merton (1974) treating equity as a call option on firm assets with strike equal to debt. Default occurs when asset value falls below debt at maturity, linking spreads to leverage and asset volatility.
nodes.f: equity = call(assets, debt face, T)

nodes.t: The number of standard deviations firm asset value sits above the default point, from a Merton-style model. Moody's KMV mapped it to empirical expected default frequencies.
nodes.f: DD = (ln(V/D) + (mu - 0.5 sigma^2)T) / (sigma sqrt(T))

nodes.t: A credit model that treats default as a random jump arriving with a hazard rate, calibrated to market spreads rather than to firm balance sheets. Jarrow and Turnbull, and Duffie and Singleton, are standard references.
The finding that investment grade spreads are far larger than historical default losses and structural models imply, attributed to risk premia for default timing in bad states, liquidity and taxes.

The portion of a credit spread above expected default loss, compensating investors for bearing default risk that tends to hit in bad times and for illiquidity. It is the source of long-run credit excess returns.
nodes.f: premium = spread - PD x LGD

nodes.t: The return on a credit bond or index above duration-matched Treasuries or swaps, isolating the reward for credit risk from the reward for rate risk.
nodes.f: excess return = total return - duration-matched treasury return

nodes.t: The sensitivity of a bond's spread changes to the market spread, typically higher for longer, lower-rated and wider bonds. DTS captures much of it.

The recurring expansion and contraction of credit availability: loose lending and tight spreads late in expansions, then rising defaults, wider spreads and tighter standards in downturns. It often leads the business cycle.
The share of issuers or debt by value that defaults over a period, usually trailing twelve months. High yield default rates rise sharply in recessions and drive spread levels.
nodes.f: default rate = defaulted issuers / issuers at start

nodes.t: The share of high yield bonds trading with spreads above 1000 basis points over Treasuries. It tends to lead the default rate by several months.
The tendency of borrowers to default together because of shared exposure to the economy or a sector. It barely affects expected portfolio loss but drives tail losses and senior tranche risk.
A model linking individual default times through a normal dependence structure, popularized for CDO pricing by Li (2000). It understated joint tail defaults and became a symbol of model risk in 2008.
The yield gap between lower- and higher-rated bonds, such as BBB minus AAA or Baa minus Aaa. A long-running series of it is a common gauge of credit stress and recession risk.
The component of corporate spreads not explained by expected default risk, from Gilchrist and Zakrajsek (2012). It measures credit market risk appetite and predicts economic activity.
The spread of a bond's yield to worst over the government yield of matching maturity, the standard spread quote for high yield bonds with call schedules.

The period after issue when a bond cannot be called, or can be called only at a premium, protecting investors from early refinancing. High yield bonds commonly have non-call periods followed by stepped call prices.

A call provision letting the issuer redeem early at the present value of remaining cash flows discounted at Treasury plus a small spread, so investors are largely compensated. Common in investment grade bonds.
nodes.f: price = max(par, PV at treasury + make-whole spread)

nodes.t: A covenant letting bondholders sell bonds back, typically at 101, if the issuer is acquired or control changes, protecting against leveraging buyouts.
The extra spread a new bond offers over the issuer's existing bonds' fair value to attract buyers. It widens in volatile markets and when supply is heavy.
nodes.f: nic = new issue spread - fair secondary spread

nodes.t: The volume of new corporate debt sold in primary markets. Heavy supply can pressure spreads, while issuance windows close in stress, making refinancing harder for weak borrowers.
A concentration of corporate or real estate debt maturing in a short window, which raises default risk if refinancing must happen at much higher rates or in a closed market.

The cost and ease of trading corporate bonds, which are fragmented into many issues and trade infrequently. Liquidity premia widen in stress, and TRACE data plus electronic and portfolio trading have improved transparency.
FINRA's Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine, which publishes US corporate and agency bond trade prices and sizes, bringing post-trade transparency to OTC bond markets.
Trading a basket of many bonds as a single package at one price, often against ETF creation or index rebalancing. It has grown with bond ETFs and lowers execution costs for large lists.

Senior secured floating rate loans to below investment grade companies, often to fund buyouts, syndicated to institutional investors and largely held by CLOs. They have higher recoveries than bonds but weaker covenants than in the past.
An institutional tranche of a leveraged loan with minimal amortization and a bullet at maturity, sold to CLOs and loan funds, distinct from amortizing bank-held term loan A.
A committed bank line a company can draw, repay and redraw up to a limit, paying a commitment fee on undrawn amounts. Revolver draws often spike in stress as firms hoard cash.
Loans without maintenance financial covenants, relying only on incurrence tests. They delay defaults and give borrowers room, but can lower eventual recoveries as value erodes before lenders can act.
A covenant requiring the borrower to meet financial tests, such as maximum leverage or minimum coverage, every quarter. Breaches give lenders an early seat at the table.
A covenant tested only when the borrower takes a specific action, such as issuing debt, paying dividends or selling assets. It is the standard type in high yield bonds.

A distressed borrower's use of loose documents to restructure debt outside court, such as uptiering some lenders or moving assets beyond creditors' reach. It can transfer value between creditor groups.
An offer to swap existing debt for new debt, cash or equity worth less than the original promise, to avoid bankruptcy. Rating agencies usually treat it as a default.
Bonds and loans of companies in or near default, trading far below par. Investors buy them for recovery value, often targeting the fulcrum security to gain control in restructuring.
The most senior class of claims that will not be paid in full in a restructuring, which therefore receives most of the reorganized equity. Identifying it is central to distressed investing.
US reorganization bankruptcy in which the debtor keeps operating under court protection while negotiating a plan to restructure claims. An automatic stay halts creditor collection.
The bankruptcy principle that senior creditors must be paid in full before junior classes or equity receive anything. In practice deviations occur through negotiated settlements.
New lending to a company in Chapter 11, granted super-priority status by the court to fund operations during the case. Lenders often use it to steer the restructuring.
The risk of a sudden loss when an issuer defaults, beyond what gradual spread moves would suggest. Hedging spread duration alone does not remove it.
nodes.f: JTD = exposure x (price - recovery)

nodes.t: The risk that the other party to a trade defaults before settling its obligations. It is mitigated by collateral, netting and central clearing, and priced as CVA.
The reduction in a derivative's value for the expected loss from counterparty default, the market price of counterparty risk. DVA, FVA and other XVAs are related adjustments.
nodes.f: CVA = LGD x sum(EE_t x PD_t x DF_t)

nodes.t: When exposure to a counterparty rises just as its credit quality falls, such as buying CDS protection on a bank from a correlated bank. It makes counterparty losses larger than independent models suggest.

Additional Tier 1 capital: perpetual, deeply subordinated bank securities that convert to equity or are written down when capital falls below a trigger or regulators intervene, with cancellable coupons.
Resolution authorities imposing losses on a failing bank's creditors by writing down or converting debt to equity, instead of using taxpayer money. Bail-in-eligible debt counts toward TLAC and MREL.
Measures of a bank's loss-absorbing equity relative to risk-weighted assets or total exposure, such as CET1 and the leverage ratio, set under Basel rules to keep banks solvent through losses.
nodes.f: CET1 ratio = common equity tier 1 / risk-weighted assets

nodes.t: Standardized tradable baskets of single-name CDS, such as CDX investment grade and high yield in North America and iTraxx Europe and Crossover. They roll to new series every six months and are the most liquid credit hedges.
A tranche of losses on a CDS index between attachment and detachment points. Tranche prices imply a correlation between defaults and once formed a liquid correlation trading market.
A defined occurrence that triggers payment on a CDS, such as bankruptcy, failure to pay or, for some contracts, restructuring. The ISDA Determinations Committee decides whether one has occurred.
A committee of dealer and buy-side members that rules on whether a CDS credit event or succession event has occurred and sets the terms for the settlement auction.
The auction held after a credit event to set a single final price for the reference obligations, so all CDS settle in cash at par minus that recovery price.
nodes.f: payout = notional x (100 - auction price)/100

nodes.t: Standard CDS pay a fixed running coupon, such as 100 or 500 basis points, with an upfront payment exchanged to make up the difference between that coupon and the market spread.
nodes.f: upfront approx (spread - coupon) x risky duration

nodes.t: The CDS spread minus the bond's spread over the risk-free curve (often asset swap or Z-spread). A negative basis lets investors buy the bond and protection for a near-riskless spread, subject to funding risk.
nodes.f: basis = CDS spread - bond spread

nodes.t: Credit default swaps referencing a government's debt, used to hedge or express country risk. Contracts on major advanced economies are often quoted in a different currency from the debt to capture redenomination risk.

A swap in which one party pays the total return of a reference asset (income plus price change) and receives a floating rate plus spread. It gives synthetic, leveraged exposure without owning the asset.

Short-term unsecured promissory notes, usually up to 270 days, issued by companies and banks to fund working capital, mostly bought by money market funds. The market can freeze in stress, as in 2008 and 2020.

An exchange-traded fund holding a portfolio of bonds that trades intraday on an exchange. It often trades more easily than its underlying bonds and becomes a price discovery venue when bond markets are stressed.
The gap between a bond ETF's market price and its NAV. NAVs use stale or modeled bond prices, so large discounts in sell-offs usually mean the ETF is showing the true clearing price first.
nodes.f: premium = (price - NAV)/NAV

nodes.t: Most bond funds keep a roughly constant duration by selling aging bonds and buying new ones, so they never mature and do not pull to par. Recovery after rate losses comes from higher reinvestment yields over about a duration's span.
A bond ETF holding bonds that all mature in one year and liquidating then, so it behaves like an individual bond with diversification and pull to par.
A standardized 30-day yield for US bond funds based on the portfolio's yields net of expenses, giving a closer estimate of forward income than the trailing distribution yield.
The benchmark index of US investment grade taxable bonds, combining Treasuries, agencies, agency MBS and corporates weighted by market value. It is tracked by the largest bond funds and ETFs.
The predictable lengthening of bond index duration at month end when new longer bonds enter and shorter ones drop out, prompting index-tracking investors to buy duration.

ETFs tracking investment grade or high yield corporate bond indexes. They are used for tactical exposure and hedging, and can be shorted or optioned, though their prices embed both rate and spread moves.

A rush into safe, liquid assets such as Treasuries, bunds, the dollar and the yen during stress, lowering safe yields and widening spreads. It underpins the negative stock-bond correlation in growth shocks.

The extra value investors place on Treasuries for their safety, liquidity and use as collateral, which lowers their yields below otherwise equivalent safe assets. Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen documented it.

A debt claim expected to hold value in nearly all states, such as top-rated government bonds, used as collateral, a store of value and a pricing benchmark. Global demand for them exceeds supply in stress.
Assets pledged to secure a loan or derivative exposure that the lender can seize on default. Haircuts, eligibility and reuse rules shape funding markets and transmit stress.
The US central bank, made up of the Board of Governors, twelve regional Reserve Banks and the FOMC. It sets monetary policy, supervises banks, runs payment systems and acts as lender of last resort.

The Federal Open Market Committee: seven Fed governors plus the New York Fed president and four rotating Reserve Bank presidents. It meets eight times a year to set the fed funds target range and balance sheet policy.
The policy statement released after each FOMC meeting, and minutes released three weeks later describing the debate. Markets parse small wording changes for signals about the policy path.

A chart in the Fed's quarterly Summary of Economic Projections showing each FOMC participant's view of the appropriate year-end fed funds rate for coming years and the longer run. Dots are projections, not commitments.
Quarterly FOMC participant projections for GDP growth, unemployment, PCE and core PCE inflation, and the policy rate, released with the March, June, September and December statements.

Speeches, testimony, press conferences and interviews by Fed officials used to shape expectations. Markets weigh the chair, governors and New York Fed president most; a blackout period silences officials before meetings.
A Fed report published eight times a year summarizing anecdotal conditions from contacts in each of the twelve districts, giving qualitative color on activity, labor markets and prices.
The Federal Reserve's statutory goals of maximum employment and stable prices, plus moderate long-term interest rates. The Fed defines price stability as 2 percent PCE inflation over the longer run.

A monetary framework in which the central bank publicly commits to a numerical inflation goal and sets policy to hit it over the medium term. Pioneered by New Zealand around 1990 and now standard among major central banks.

The framework the Fed adopted in 2020, aiming for inflation that averages 2 percent over time and tolerating moderate overshoots after undershoots. The Fed revised its framework in 2025 and dropped the makeup element.
A framework targeting a path for the price level rather than the inflation rate, so past misses must be made up. It can strengthen stimulus at the lower bound but is harder to communicate.
A proposed framework in which the central bank targets the level or growth of nominal GDP, letting inflation absorb supply shocks while stabilizing total spending.
Insulation of monetary policy decisions from short-term political control, linked empirically to lower and more stable inflation. Threats to it raise inflation expectations and term premium.
The rate at which depository institutions and GSEs lend reserve balances overnight, unsecured. The FOMC sets a target range for it as its main policy rate.
The volume-weighted median rate on overnight fed funds trades, published daily by the New York Fed. It normally sits inside the target range just below interest on reserves.
The rate the Fed pays banks on reserves held at the Fed, its main tool for setting the floor of overnight rates under an ample reserves regime. Banks rarely lend below it.

The Fed's floor system in which reserves are abundant enough that small changes do not move short rates, which are set by administered rates (IORB and the ON RRP rate) rather than by daily reserve adjustments.

A policy framework in which a central bank keeps reserves scarce and steers the overnight rate within a band set by a lending rate above and a deposit rate below, using frequent open market operations.
The reserve quantity below which banks start bidding up money market rates because they want to hold more. Its uncertain location determines how far QT can go before repo stress appears.
Central bank purchases or sales of securities, outright or through repo, to add or drain reserves and steer short rates. Conducted for the Fed by the New York Fed trading desk.
The Fed's portfolio of Treasuries, agency MBS and other assets acquired through open market operations, managed by the New York Fed. QE grows it; QT shrinks it through runoff.

The Fed's assets (mostly Treasuries and MBS, plus loans) and liabilities (currency, bank reserves, the Treasury General Account and reverse repos). Changes in its composition drive reserve supply and liquidity.
nodes.f: assets = currency + reserves + TGA + ON RRP + other

nodes.t: Monthly limits on how much maturing Treasury and MBS principal the Fed lets roll off without reinvesting during QT. Amounts above the caps are reinvested, smoothing the drain on reserves.

A market heuristic equal to the Fed's total assets minus the Treasury General Account and ON RRP balances, proxying reserves available to the financial system. Its correlation with asset prices is unstable.
nodes.f: net liquidity = fed assets - TGA - ON RRP

nodes.t: The US Treasury's operating cash account at the Fed. When it rises from tax receipts or debt issuance, reserves fall one for one, all else equal; when the Treasury spends it down, reserves rise.
A statutory cap on total US federal debt. When binding, the Treasury uses extraordinary measures and draws down its cash; resolutions bring a surge of bill issuance that drains reserves.

The estimated date when the Treasury would exhaust cash and extraordinary measures under a binding debt ceiling and could no longer pay all obligations. Bills maturing near it trade at elevated yields.
Central bank communication about the likely future path of policy, either open-ended, date-based or tied to economic thresholds. It moves longer rates by shaping expected short rates.

The sequence of future policy rates priced into fed funds futures, SOFR futures and OIS, often expressed as basis points of cuts or hikes by a meeting date. It contains term premia, so it is not a pure forecast.

The real short-term rate consistent with full employment and stable inflation, neither stimulating nor restraining the economy. It is unobservable and estimated with wide uncertainty, for example by the Laubach-Williams model.
nodes.f: nominal neutral = r* + inflation target

nodes.t: A policy setting with the real policy rate above the neutral rate, intended to slow demand and inflation. How restrictive policy is depends on the uncertain neutral rate and on financial conditions.
The nominal policy rate minus expected or recent inflation, the measure of how tight monetary policy really is. A falling inflation rate with a fixed nominal rate passively tightens policy.
nodes.f: real policy rate = policy rate - expected inflation

nodes.t: Milton Friedman's observation that monetary policy affects the economy with delays that are long and uncertain, often a year or more for activity and longer for inflation, making policy prone to overshooting.
The channels through which policy changes reach spending and inflation: interest rates, credit supply, asset prices and wealth, the exchange rate and expectations.

The constraint that nominal policy rates cannot fall much below zero because people can hold cash instead. It pushes central banks toward QE, forward guidance and negative rates when more stimulus is needed.

A situation, described by Keynes, in which rates are so low that further money creation fails to stimulate spending because people hoard money. It is associated with the zero lower bound and deflation risk.
Setting policy rates below zero, as the ECB, BOJ, SNB and others did in the 2010s, charging banks on excess reserves. It eased conditions but squeezed bank margins and had limits from cash hoarding.
An estimated policy rate that can go below zero to summarize the stance of unconventional policy at the lower bound, as in the Wu-Xia shadow rate.
A central bank commitment to cap or target a specific bond yield by buying whatever quantity is needed, as the Bank of Japan did with 10-year JGBs from 2016 and the Fed did in the 1940s.
A Fed program, first in 1961 and again in 2011 and 2012, selling short-term Treasuries and buying long-term ones to lower long yields without expanding the balance sheet.
The mechanism by which central bank bond purchases lower yields: removing duration from private hands reduces term premium and pushes investors into riskier assets.
A central bank's role in lending to solvent but illiquid institutions in a panic to prevent fire sales and bank runs from spreading.
Walter Bagehot's (1873) rule for crises: lend freely, to solvent firms, against good collateral, at a penalty rate. It remains the reference model for central bank crisis lending.

The Fed's standing facility lending to banks against collateral, with primary credit priced at the top of the fed funds target range. Stigma has historically kept banks from using it until stress is severe.
Banks' reluctance to borrow from the discount window for fear it signals weakness to markets or supervisors, which limits the facility's ability to calm funding stress.
The Fed's permanent facility offering overnight repo loans against Treasuries and agency securities to primary dealers and eligible banks at a set rate, acting as a ceiling on repo rates.
A Fed facility letting foreign central banks borrow dollars against their Treasury holdings, so they need not sell Treasuries into a stressed market for dollars.
a: foreign and international monetary authorities repo

nodes.t: Arrangements in which the Fed lends dollars to foreign central banks against their currency, which they then lend to local banks. They cap offshore dollar funding stress, as in 2008 and 2020.

Fed programs under Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act lending broadly to nonbanks or markets in unusual and exigent circumstances, with Treasury approval, such as commercial paper and corporate credit facilities.
An emergency Fed facility, used in 2008 and 2020, that bought commercial paper directly from issuers through a special purpose vehicle to keep short-term funding markets open.

A 2023 Fed facility created after Silicon Valley Bank failed that lent to banks for up to a year against Treasuries and agency debt valued at par rather than market value, easing run pressure from unrealized losses.

The market for repurchase agreements: selling securities with an agreement to buy them back, which is economically a collateralized loan. It finances dealer and hedge fund positions and is central to money market plumbing.
nodes.f: repo interest = cash x repo rate x days/360

nodes.t: Repo in which any of a broad class of securities, such as Treasuries, is acceptable collateral. The GC rate is the base funding rate; individual bonds in demand trade special below it.

When a specific bond is in high demand to borrow, its repo rate falls below general collateral, letting holders borrow cash cheaply. Specialness adds value to owning that bond, typically on-the-run issues.
nodes.f: specialness = GC rate - specific repo rate

nodes.t: Repo in which a clearing bank handles collateral selection, valuation and settlement between cash lenders, such as money funds, and borrowers, such as dealers. Bank of New York Mellon is the main US tri-party agent.

Repo negotiated directly between two counterparties, cleared or uncleared, where collateral is delivered to the lender. Hedge funds finance much of their Treasury positions this way, sometimes at zero haircut.
The difference between collateral market value and cash lent, protecting the lender against collateral price falls. Haircuts set leverage and rise in stress, forcing deleveraging.
nodes.f: max leverage approx 1 / haircut

nodes.t: A dealer's reuse of collateral posted by clients to secure its own borrowing. It increases collateral velocity and market liquidity but can trap client assets when the dealer fails.

The Secured Overnight Financing Rate, a broad measure of overnight Treasury repo costs published by the New York Fed. It replaced USD LIBOR as the main dollar reference rate for loans and derivatives.

The London Interbank Offered Rate, a survey of unsecured bank borrowing costs at several tenors. It was the main floating rate benchmark for decades until manipulation scandals and thin underlying trading led to its retirement.
The global move from LIBOR to near risk-free overnight rates such as SOFR, SONIA and ESTR, completed for most USD tenors in mid 2023, requiring contracts to add credit spread adjustments.
The gap between term LIBOR and the OIS rate of matching tenor, a gauge of bank credit and funding stress. It spiked during the 2008 crisis.
nodes.f: spread = 3m LIBOR - 3m OIS

nodes.t: Limits on bank-affiliated dealers' capacity to warehouse bonds and intermediate repo, from leverage ratios, capital rules and internal limits. They cause dysfunction and wider spreads when selling surges.

A US capital requirement on large banks equal to Tier 1 capital divided by total leverage exposure, including Treasuries and reserves, regardless of risk. It can make safe, low-margin intermediation costly.
nodes.f: SLR = tier 1 capital / total leverage exposure

nodes.t: The post-2008 international bank regulation framework raising capital quality and quantity and adding leverage, liquidity coverage and net stable funding requirements.
A Basel III rule requiring banks to hold high-quality liquid assets at least equal to projected net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period. It shapes bank demand for reserves and Treasuries.
nodes.f: LCR = HQLA / 30-day net outflows >= 100%

nodes.t: Assets counted toward the liquidity coverage ratio, led by reserves and Treasuries at full value, with agency MBS and other assets subject to haircuts and caps.
Spikes in repo and FX swap costs around quarter and year ends when banks shrink balance sheets for regulatory snapshots, such as G-SIB surcharge calculations, reducing intermediation.
Rules requiring banks to hold a minimum share of deposits as reserves. The Fed cut them to zero in March 2020; in an ample reserves regime they are not a binding policy tool.

The textbook ratio of broad money to the monetary base, implying banks lend out a fixed multiple of reserves. In practice banks lend when creditworthy demand exists and reserves do not constrain lending under ample reserves.
nodes.f: M = m x base

nodes.t: The view, now stated by central banks such as the Bank of England, that bank lending creates deposits and that money supply responds to loan demand and rates rather than being set mechanically by reserves.
Currency in circulation plus bank reserves held at the central bank, the liabilities the central bank directly controls. QE expands it mainly through reserves.
nodes.f: base = currency + reserves

nodes.t: The rate at which money turns over in spending, measured as nominal GDP divided by a money aggregate. Its instability weakened the link between money growth and inflation in recent decades.
nodes.f: V = nominal GDP / M

nodes.t: The identity that money times velocity equals the price level times real output, used by monetarists to argue that sustained money growth beyond output growth causes inflation if velocity is stable.
nodes.f: M x V = P x Y

nodes.t: The school associated with Milton Friedman holding that inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon and that steady money growth rules beat discretionary policy.

A regime in which large government debts force the central bank to keep rates low or finance deficits, subordinating inflation control to debt sustainability. Fear of it raises inflation expectations and term premium.
Policies that hold interest rates below inflation and steer savings into government debt, such as yield caps, regulation and capital controls, eroding debt in real terms at savers' expense.
A central bank directly funding government deficits by creating money, prohibited in many jurisdictions. Persistent use is associated with high inflation; helicopter money is a variant.
Friedman's thought experiment of money dropped from the sky, now meaning permanent money-financed fiscal transfers to households. It aims to raise spending when interest rate tools are exhausted.
The market belief that the Fed will ease policy to cushion large asset price declines, acting like a put option on risk assets. It can encourage risk-taking and moral hazard.
The tendency to take more risk when protected from its costs, such as banks expecting bailouts or investors expecting central bank support.
The belief that some financial firms are so large and interconnected that authorities cannot let them fail, giving them a funding subsidy. G-SIB surcharges and resolution plans aim to end it.
The trading maxim, associated with Martin Zweig, that investors should align positions with the direction of monetary policy because easing supports and tightening pressures asset prices.
The central bank for euro area countries, with a primary mandate of price stability, defined as 2 percent HICP inflation over the medium term. Its Governing Council sets three key rates.
The rate the ECB pays on banks' overnight deposits with the Eurosystem, its effective policy rate under excess liquidity. It sits below the main refinancing and marginal lending rates.
The euro short-term rate, a daily measure of euro area banks' overnight unsecured borrowing costs published by the ECB. It replaced EONIA and anchors euro OIS.
The ECB's Targeted Longer-Term Refinancing Operations, multi-year loans to banks at rates tied to their lending to firms and households, aimed at supporting credit supply.

An ECB tool from 2022 allowing potentially unlimited purchases of a member's bonds if spreads widen in a disorderly way unrelated to fundamentals, subject to policy conditions. It follows the earlier OMT program.
Japan's central bank, notable for decades of near-zero and negative rates, large purchases of JGBs and ETFs, and yield curve control, which it began exiting in 2024.
The UK central bank, whose Monetary Policy Committee sets Bank Rate to meet a 2 percent CPI target. It intervened in long gilts during the 2022 LDI crisis.
The Sterling Overnight Index Average, the Bank of England-administered overnight unsecured rate that replaced sterling LIBOR as the main reference rate.
China's central bank, which uses a mix of policy rates such as the 7-day reverse repo, loan prime rate guidance, reserve requirement ratio cuts, window guidance and the daily yuan fixing.
Switzerland's central bank, notable for heavy FX intervention to restrain franc appreciation, a large foreign asset portfolio including equities, and its abrupt 2015 removal of the EUR/CHF floor.
The ratio of nominal to real GDP, a price index covering all domestically produced goods and services. Unlike CPI it excludes imports and has weights that shift with spending patterns.
nodes.f: deflator = nominal GDP / real GDP x 100

nodes.t: Total income earned in producing domestic output, such as wages and profits, which in theory equals GDP. Gaps between GDP and GDI, the statistical discrepancy, can flag future revisions to growth.

The output an economy can sustain at full employment of labor and capital without rising inflation, estimated from labor force growth and productivity trends. It is unobservable and frequently revised.
nodes.f: potential growth approx labor force growth + productivity growth

nodes.t: Estimating current-quarter GDP or other variables in real time from incoming high-frequency data before official releases, as in the Atlanta Fed GDPNow and New York Fed Staff Nowcast models.
The empirical relationship, from Okun (1962), that output growth above potential lowers unemployment, roughly half a point of unemployment for each point of extra growth in recent US estimates.
nodes.f: change in u approx -b x (g - g_potential)

nodes.t: The inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation, first documented by Phillips (1958) for wages. The modern expectations-augmented version links inflation to expected inflation and slack; it was flat for years before 2021.
nodes.f: inflation = expected inflation - b x (u - u*) + supply shocks

nodes.t: The non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment: the unemployment rate below which inflation tends to rise. Estimates are uncertain and move over time with labor market structure.
The inverse relationship between job vacancies and unemployment. Movements along it reflect the cycle; shifts outward suggest worse matching between workers and jobs.
The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey from the BLS, measuring job openings, hires, quits and layoffs. It is released with a lag and has a small sample, so it is revised and noisy.
a: job openings and labor turnover survey

nodes.t: Job openings divided by the number of unemployed, a measure of labor market tightness. A high ratio means employers compete for workers, supporting wage growth.
nodes.f: V/U = job openings / unemployed

nodes.t: Voluntary separations as a share of employment, from JOLTS. High quits signal worker confidence and tend to lead wage growth.
The share of the working-age population employed or seeking work. Aging pulls it down over time, so the prime-age employment-population ratio is often used to judge cyclical slack.
nodes.f: LFPR = labor force / civilian noninstitutional population

nodes.t: The share of people aged 25 to 54 who are employed. It avoids aging effects and the ambiguity of who counts as unemployed, making it a clean gauge of labor market health.
nodes.f: employed 25-54 / population 25-54

nodes.t: The BLS's broadest underutilization measure, adding discouraged and marginally attached workers and those working part time for economic reasons to the unemployed.
The Current Population Survey of about 60,000 households, source of the unemployment rate and participation. It counts people, not jobs, and is noisier month to month than the payroll survey.

Weekly new filings for state unemployment insurance, the most timely US labor indicator. Sustained rises in the four-week average have preceded recessions; continuing claims track how long people stay out of work.
Later changes to released statistics as more complete data arrive, such as monthly payroll revisions and annual benchmark revisions. First prints can mislead, especially near turning points.
The monthly job gain needed to keep the unemployment rate stable given population growth and participation trends. It falls when immigration and labor force growth slow.
A quarterly BLS measure of changes in total compensation, wages plus benefits, for a fixed mix of jobs. It avoids the composition effects that distort average hourly earnings.
Labor compensation per unit of output, equal to wage growth minus productivity growth. Rising unit labor costs pressure margins or prices.
nodes.f: ULC growth = compensation growth - productivity growth

nodes.t: A feedback loop in which higher prices prompt workers to demand higher wages, which firms pass on as higher prices. It needs expectations to drift and is the main fear behind central bank responses to supply shocks.

A monthly diffusion index from business surveys on orders, output, employment, deliveries and prices, where 50 separates expansion from contraction. Key versions include ISM manufacturing and services and S&P Global flash PMIs.
nodes.f: index = % reporting better + 0.5 x % unchanged

nodes.t: The ISM manufacturing new orders index minus its inventories index, a leading indicator of production because strong demand against lean stocks forces output increases.
nodes.f: spread = ISM new orders - ISM inventories

nodes.t: Monthly manufacturing and services surveys from regional Reserve Banks, such as the Empire State, Philadelphia, Richmond, Kansas City and Dallas surveys, which preview the ISM indices.
A monthly Fed index of real output in manufacturing, mining and utilities. It is one of the coincident indicators used to date business cycles.
Industrial output as a share of estimated sustainable capacity. High utilization signals limited slack and potential price pressure; low readings accompany recessions.
nodes.f: utilization = output / capacity

nodes.t: A monthly Census estimate of nominal sales at retailers and food services. The control group, excluding autos, gasoline, building materials and food services, feeds directly into GDP estimates of goods spending.
A monthly Census report on new orders for goods meant to last three years or more. Core capital goods orders, excluding defense and aircraft, are a leading indicator of business investment.
Monthly counts of new residential construction begun and building permits issued. Permits lead starts, and housing is among the most rate-sensitive and cycle-leading sectors.

Monthly closings of previously owned homes, reported by the National Association of Realtors. Sales volume reflects affordability and mortgage rate lock-in; pending home sales lead it by a month or two.

Repeat-sales measures of home price changes, such as the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller and FHFA indices. Housing wealth affects consumption and collateral, and home prices feed shelter inflation with a lag.

Survey measures of household attitudes such as the University of Michigan sentiment index and the Conference Board confidence index. They are partisan and price-sensitive and predict spending only loosely.
What households, firms and markets expect inflation to be, measured by surveys and market breakevens. Anchored long-run expectations let central banks look through temporary shocks.

The Conference Board's composite of ten indicators, including claims, permits, orders, the yield spread and stock prices, designed to turn before the business cycle. It has given false recession signals.

Coincident indicators such as payrolls, real income, industrial production and real sales move with the cycle and are used to date it; lagging indicators such as unemployment duration and unit labor costs confirm turns after they occur.

The NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee declares US peaks and troughs based on depth, diffusion and duration of declines across activity measures, usually months after the fact. Two negative GDP quarters is not its rule.
An index of how data releases compare with consensus forecasts, such as the Citi Economic Surprise Index. It mean-reverts as forecasters adjust, so it measures expectations more than growth.
A BLS index of prices received by domestic producers for goods and services. Some PPI components, such as airfares, portfolio management and medical services, feed directly into core PCE estimates.
The Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, the euro area's standard inflation measure and the ECB's target variable. It excludes owner-occupied housing costs.
Core services inflation excluding housing, watched as the component most tied to wages and labor market tightness.
The housing component of CPI, mostly rent and owners' equivalent rent, the largest single CPI category. It lags market rents by about a year because existing leases reset slowly.
Underlying inflation measures that drop the most extreme price changes each month, such as the Dallas Fed trimmed mean PCE and the Cleveland Fed median CPI, avoiding arbitrary category exclusions.
The split of inflation into goods, driven by supply chains, commodities and the dollar, and services, driven by wages and rents. Services inflation is more persistent.
Swings in year-over-year growth rates caused by unusual moves in the comparison period a year earlier, not by current momentum. Month-over-month annualized rates avoid them.
Statistical removal of regular calendar patterns from economic data, such as holiday hiring, using methods like X-13ARIMA-SEATS. Shocks can distort seasonal factors and create residual seasonality.
A slowdown in the rate of inflation while prices still rise, distinct from deflation. The pace and cost of disinflation in output and jobs is the sacrifice ratio.
The cumulative loss of output, as a percent of GDP, needed to lower trend inflation by one percentage point. Credible policy and anchored expectations reduce it.
nodes.f: cumulative output loss / reduction in inflation

nodes.t: A sustained fall in the general price level. It raises real debt burdens and can make consumers delay purchases, and it binds when nominal rates hit zero, as in Japan for long stretches.
Irving Fisher's (1933) mechanism in which falling prices raise real debt burdens, forcing distress selling that pushes prices down further, deepening depressions.
Extremely rapid inflation, conventionally above 50 percent per month (Cagan), usually from money-financed deficits and collapsed confidence, as in Weimar Germany, Zimbabwe and Venezuela.
The relationship that the nominal interest rate approximately equals the real rate plus expected inflation (Fisher, 1930). It underlies breakeven inflation and real yield analysis.
nodes.f: (1+i) = (1+r)(1+expected inflation); i approx r + expected inflation

nodes.t: The change in output from a one-unit change in government spending or taxes. It is larger in recessions and at the zero lower bound and smaller when the central bank offsets fiscal moves.
nodes.f: multiplier = change in GDP / change in fiscal stance

nodes.t: The change in the fiscal deficit's contribution to growth from one period to the next, usually measured by the change in the cyclically adjusted deficit. A shrinking deficit is a drag even if it remains large.
nodes.f: impulse = change in cyclically adjusted primary deficit / GDP

nodes.t: Taxes and transfers that move against the cycle without new legislation, such as falling tax receipts and rising unemployment benefits in recessions, cushioning income.
The budget deficit adjusted for the business cycle, the part that would persist at full employment. It reveals the underlying fiscal stance hidden by automatic stabilizers.
The fiscal deficit excluding net interest payments. Whether a country needs a primary surplus to stabilize its debt depends on the gap between interest rates and growth.
nodes.f: primary deficit = total deficit - net interest

nodes.t: The gap between the average interest rate on government debt and nominal GDP growth. When it is negative, debt ratios can stabilize even with primary deficits; when positive, primary surpluses are needed.
nodes.f: change in debt/GDP approx (r - g)/(1+g) x debt/GDP + primary deficit/GDP

nodes.t: Government net interest outlays as a share of GDP or revenue. It rises with debt levels and with refinancing at higher rates, faster when debt maturity is short.
nodes.f: net interest / GDP

nodes.t: Higher government borrowing raising interest rates and displacing private investment. It is strongest at full employment and weakest when savings are idle and rates are pinned at zero.

The proposition, formalized by Barro (1974), that debt-financed tax cuts do not raise spending because rational households save to pay expected future taxes. Liquidity constraints and myopia make it fail in practice.

A government's failure to pay its debt on time or a distressed exchange on its bonds. Foreign-currency default is far more common than local-currency default, since governments can print their own currency.

The change in new credit flow as a share of GDP, popularized by Biggs, Mayer and Pick. Since growth relates to credit flows, the impulse leads demand; China's credit impulse is watched for commodity demand.
nodes.f: impulse = change in (new credit / GDP)

nodes.t: The Fed's quarterly survey of banks on lending standards and loan demand. Net tightening of standards for commercial and industrial loans has reliably preceded rising defaults and recessions.
The transmission of monetary policy through banks' willingness and ability to lend: tighter policy and weaker bank capital or funding reduce credit supply to bank-dependent borrowers.
A sharp reduction in credit availability not explained by rates alone, as lenders tighten standards and ration loans after losses or funding shocks, amplifying downturns.
The change in consumer spending from changes in household wealth, such as stock and home prices. Estimates put it at a few cents per dollar of wealth per year.
Personal saving as a share of disposable income, from the BEA. A low rate leaves less cushion for spending if income slows; it is heavily revised.
nodes.f: saving rate = (disposable income - outlays) / disposable income

nodes.t: After-tax personal income adjusted for inflation, the main driver of consumer spending capacity. It is one of the coincident indicators in recession dating.
Short cycles of a few years driven by firms building and running down inventories as sales expectations change. Inventory swings cause much of quarterly GDP volatility.

A persistent shortfall of demand relative to saving that keeps the neutral rate very low and growth weak, revived by Summers (2013) from Alvin Hansen's late-1930s idea, citing demographics and weak investment demand.

Richard Koo's term for a downturn in which firms or households focus on paying down debt after an asset bust rather than maximizing profit, so low rates fail to revive borrowing and fiscal support is needed.
Output growth not explained by growth in labor and capital inputs, the Solow residual. It captures technology, efficiency and measurement error and drives long-run living standards.
nodes.f: TFP growth = output growth - a x capital growth - (1-a) x labor growth

nodes.t: A New York Fed composite of shipping costs and PMI delivery times and backlogs, measured in standard deviations from average. It tracks supply-side pressure on goods inflation.
A heterodox view that a government issuing its own currency faces no solvency constraint, only an inflation constraint, so deficits should be judged by their effect on inflation and employment.
A country's trade balance plus net primary income and transfers with the rest of the world. A deficit means the country spends more than it earns and must be financed by capital inflows.
nodes.f: current account = savings - investment

nodes.t: The record of all transactions between a country and the world: the current account and the capital and financial accounts, which must sum to zero apart from errors and reserve changes.
nodes.f: current account + capital account + financial account = 0

nodes.t: A country's foreign assets minus foreign liabilities, the stock counterpart of cumulative current account flows plus valuation changes. The US position is deeply negative.
nodes.f: NIIP = foreign assets - foreign liabilities

nodes.t: The tendency for fiscal and current account deficits to coexist, since lower public saving, without offsetting private saving, must be funded from abroad.
nodes.f: (S - I) + (T - G) = current account

nodes.t: The ratio of a country's export prices to import prices. Improving terms of trade, such as rising commodity prices for an exporter, raise national income and tend to strengthen the currency.
nodes.f: ToT = export price index / import price index

nodes.t: Bernanke's (2005) hypothesis that high saving in emerging Asia and oil exporters, invested in US safe assets, held down long-term US yields and financed US current account deficits.

FX rates are quoted as the price of one unit of the base currency in the quote currency, so EUR/USD at 1.10 means one euro costs 1.10 dollars. A pip is usually the fourth decimal place, or the second for yen pairs.
A contract to exchange currencies at a set rate on a future date. The forward rate differs from spot by forward points that reflect the interest rate differential, not an expected move.
nodes.f: F = S x (1 + i_quote x t)/(1 + i_base x t)

nodes.t: A simultaneous spot and forward exchange in opposite directions, effectively a collateralized loan in one currency against another. It is the largest FX instrument by turnover and the main way to fund dollars offshore.

The spread added to one leg of a cross-currency swap that measures deviations from covered interest parity. A negative basis against the dollar means borrowing dollars through FX swaps costs more than direct dollar rates, signaling dollar funding scarcity.
A cash-settled FX forward in a currency with capital controls or limited convertibility, such as the Indian rupee or Korean won, settled in dollars against an official fixing.

The no-arbitrage condition that the forward premium equals the interest rate differential, so hedged returns are equal across currencies. It held tightly before 2008 but has shown persistent deviations since due to balance sheet costs.
nodes.f: F/S = (1 + i_domestic)/(1 + i_foreign)

nodes.t: The theory that the expected change in an exchange rate offsets the interest rate differential, so high-yielding currencies should depreciate. It fails over short horizons, which is why carry trades earn returns.
nodes.f: E[%change in S] = i_domestic - i_foreign

nodes.t: The finding, documented by Fama (1984), that high interest rate currencies tend not to depreciate as UIP predicts and often appreciate, so forward rates are biased predictors of future spot rates.
The theory that exchange rates move to equalize the price of a common basket across countries. Deviations are large and persist for years, but PPP gaps help explain long-horizon currency moves.
nodes.f: S = P_domestic / P_foreign (absolute); %dS = inflation differential (relative)

nodes.t: Faster productivity growth in traded goods in richer or fast-growing economies raises wages and nontraded prices, so their real exchange rates appear overvalued relative to PPP.

A trade-weighted average of a currency's value against partners' currencies, adjusted for relative inflation. It measures competitiveness better than any bilateral rate; the nominal version omits the inflation adjustment.

An ICE index of the dollar against six currencies, dominated by the euro at about 58 percent, with yen, sterling, Canadian dollar, krona and Swiss franc. The Fed's broad trade-weighted index covers far more trading partners.
A framework attributed to Stephen Jen in which the dollar strengthens both when the US outperforms and in global risk-off episodes, and weakens when global growth is broad and calm.

Currencies that tend to appreciate in global stress, mainly the dollar, yen and Swiss franc, because of deep markets, net foreign asset positions and carry trade unwinds that buy back funding currencies.
Currencies of developing economies, often higher yielding and more volatile, sensitive to dollar funding conditions, risk appetite and capital flows, and prone to sharp sell-offs in sudden stops.

The yield on a foreign bond after hedging currency risk with rolling forwards, approximately the foreign yield plus the interest rate differential plus cross-currency basis. It often reverses the apparent advantage of higher foreign yields.
nodes.f: hedged yield approx y_foreign + (i_domestic - i_foreign) + basis

nodes.t: A central bank or finance ministry buying or selling foreign currency to influence the exchange rate. Sterilized intervention offsets the effect on domestic money supply, which limits its lasting impact.

Foreign currency assets held by a central bank, mostly government bonds of reserve currencies plus gold. They fund intervention and provide insurance against sudden stops; the dollar is the dominant reserve currency.

Treasuries held by foreign central banks and governments, tracked in Treasury TIC data and Fed custody holdings. Changes reflect reserve management, intervention and diversification rather than return seeking.

A fixed exchange rate against an anchor currency or basket, defended with reserves, rates or capital controls. Currency boards back the money base fully with reserves; pegs break in devaluations when reserves or political will run out.

An exchange rate regime in which the currency floats but the central bank intervenes to smooth moves or lean against trends, without a declared target. Many emerging markets and some advanced economies operate this way.
The Mundell-Fleming result that a country cannot simultaneously have a fixed exchange rate, free capital movement and independent monetary policy; it must give up one.

Restrictions on cross-border flows of capital, such as limits on foreign purchases, taxes on inflows or bans on outflows. They protect pegs or policy autonomy but deter investment and spawn offshore markets.

The PBOC's daily central parity for the onshore yuan against the dollar, around which the onshore rate may trade within a band. Deviations from model estimates signal official tolerance for moves; offshore CNH trades freely.

The benchmark FX rate set over a five-minute window around 4pm London time, used to value index funds and portfolios. Concentrated benchmark orders make the fix a liquidity event; manipulation scandals led to reforms.

Eichengreen and Hausmann's term for emerging economies' inability to borrow abroad in their own currency. Foreign-currency debt makes depreciation raise debt burdens, turning currency falls into solvency crises.
An abrupt reversal of foreign capital inflows to a country, forcing a sharp current account adjustment through falling imports, currency depreciation and output loss, a concept developed by Calvo.
A sharp, sudden depreciation or forced abandonment of a peg, often triggered by a speculative attack when reserves look insufficient. Examples include sterling in 1992 and the Asian crisis of 1997.
The loss of manufacturing competitiveness when a resource boom drives up the real exchange rate, named after the Netherlands after its natural gas discoveries.

The advantages the US gains from issuing the main reserve currency: cheap borrowing in its own currency, seigniorage and higher returns on foreign assets than on foreign liabilities. The phrase is attributed to Valery Giscard d'Estaing.
Robert Triffin's observation that the reserve currency issuer must run external deficits to supply the world with reserves, which eventually undermines confidence in that currency.

The offshore market for dollar deposits and loans held outside the US banking system. Non-US banks and firms borrow dollars heavily, creating dollar funding needs that spike in stress and require Fed swap lines.

The postwar fixed exchange rate system agreed in 1944, with currencies pegged to the dollar and the dollar convertible to gold at 35 dollars an ounce. It ended when Nixon suspended convertibility in 1971.
The 1985 agreement among the G5 to coordinate intervention to weaken the dollar, followed by the 1987 Louvre Accord to stabilize it. It is the reference case for a coordinated currency agreement.

A chain of currency collapses starting with the Thai baht's devaluation in July 1997 and spreading to Indonesia, Korea and others, driven by dollar debts, pegs and sudden capital outflows. It spurred Asian reserve accumulation.
On January 15, 2015 the Swiss National Bank abandoned its 1.20 floor on EUR/CHF without warning, sending the franc up sharply in minutes and bankrupting some leveraged FX brokers.

The Fed's sharp tightening under Paul Volcker from 1979, targeting money growth and letting fed funds exceed 19 percent, which broke the Great Inflation at the cost of back-to-back recessions in the early 1980s.

The period from the mid 1960s to the early 1980s when US inflation repeatedly rose to double digits, attributed to loose policy, oil shocks and drifting expectations, ended by the Volcker disinflation.

The 2010 to 2013 sovereign debt crisis in Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, Italy and Cyprus, with surging spreads, bailouts and a Greek restructuring. Markets calmed after Draghi pledged whatever it takes in July 2012, though the Cyprus bailout came in March 2013.

A September 2022 sell-off in long gilts after an unfunded UK fiscal package, which triggered collateral calls on leveraged pension LDI strategies, forced selling and emergency Bank of England purchases.

The COVID shock in March 2020 when investors sold even Treasuries to raise cash, overwhelming dealers and unwinding basis trades, until the Fed bought Treasuries at record pace and opened emergency facilities.

A jump in overnight repo rates far above the fed funds range in September 2019 as tax payments and Treasury settlements drained reserves below banks' comfortable level, prompting Fed repo operations and bill purchases.

The yield gap between a government's bonds and a benchmark safe sovereign, such as Italy over Germany or an emerging market dollar bond over Treasuries. It prices default, redenomination and liquidity risk.
The 10-year Italian government bond yield minus the German Bund yield, the main gauge of euro area fragmentation risk and of Italy's fiscal credibility.
nodes.f: spread = y10 Italy - y10 Germany

nodes.t: German federal government bonds, the euro area's benchmark safe asset. The 10-year Bund yield anchors euro rates, and Bund futures are among the most traded rate contracts.
UK government bonds, notable for a very long maturity profile and large index-linked share, heavily held by pension funds and insurers through LDI strategies.
