Bonds issued by Japan's government, a market dominated by domestic holders and the Bank of Japan after years of QE and yield curve control. Rising JGB yields can pull Japanese capital home from foreign bonds.

A ratio of a price or value measure to a fundamental such as earnings, sales or book value, used to compare companies quickly. Every multiple embeds assumptions about growth, risk and return on capital.

Enterprise value divided by operating profit after depreciation and amortization. Fairer than EV/EBITDA when capital intensity differs across peers, because it charges for the cost of using up assets.
nodes.f: EV/EBIT = enterprise value / EBIT

nodes.t: Enterprise value divided by EBITDA less capital expenditure, a rough proxy for unlevered pre-tax cash flow. Useful for capital-heavy businesses where EBITDA overstates the cash available to capital providers.
nodes.f: EV / (EBITDA - capex)

nodes.n: EV to unlevered free cash flow
nodes.t: Enterprise value divided by free cash flow to the firm. The inverse is an unlevered cash yield that can be compared with the cost of capital less expected growth.
nodes.f: EV/FCFF

nodes.t: Market capitalization divided by revenue. Usable for loss-making firms, but it ignores margins and capital structure, so EV/sales is usually the cleaner comparison across companies with different debt levels.
nodes.f: P/S = market cap / revenue

nodes.t: Market capitalization divided by free cash flow to equity. Less exposed to accrual choices than P/E, though lumpy capex and working capital swings can distort a single year.
nodes.f: P/FCF = market cap / free cash flow

nodes.t: Share price divided by operating cash flow per share, or net income plus non-cash charges. Popular for cyclicals and banks in some markets; it ignores capital spending.
nodes.f: P/CF = price / operating cash flow per share

nodes.t: Market value divided by book equity less goodwill and other intangibles. The standard multiple for banks, because tangible equity is what absorbs losses.
nodes.f: P/TBV = market cap / (equity - goodwill - intangibles)

nodes.t: Price divided by earnings per share over the last twelve reported months. Based on actual results rather than forecasts, but backward-looking and distorted by one-off items.
nodes.f: price / LTM EPS

nodes.t: A figure summed over the four most recent reported quarters, computed as the last fiscal year plus year-to-date minus the prior year-to-date. Standard basis for trailing multiples and credit metrics.
nodes.f: LTM = FY + current YTD - prior YTD

nodes.t: A forward estimate covering the coming twelve months, usually a time-weighted blend of the current and next fiscal year consensus. Avoids comparing firms whose fiscal years end at different times.
Enterprise value divided by gross profit. Used for growth firms with heavy reinvestment in operating expenses, and to compare companies whose revenue mixes carry very different gross margins.
nodes.f: EV / gross profit

nodes.t: Enterprise value divided by annual recurring revenue, a common software and subscription multiple. Must be read beside growth, net revenue retention and margins to mean anything.
nodes.f: EV / ARR

nodes.t: Enterprise value divided by subscribers or users, used for telecom, media and early internet companies. Only meaningful when ARPU, churn and margin per user are comparable across firms.
nodes.f: EV / subscribers

nodes.t: Enterprise value of an oil and gas producer divided by its proved or proved plus probable reserves in barrels of oil equivalent. Ignores cost to extract, timing and fiscal terms.
nodes.f: EV / reserves (boe)

nodes.t: Share price divided by net asset value per share, where NAV marks assets at estimated market value less liabilities. Standard for REITs, resource companies, closed-end funds and holding companies.
nodes.f: P/NAV = price / NAV per share

nodes.t: REIT share price divided by funds from operations per share, the property sector's analogue of P/E. Price to AFFO is stricter because it deducts recurring capital spending.
nodes.f: P/FFO = price / FFO per share

nodes.t: Lease-adjusted enterprise value divided by EBITDA before rent. Puts asset-owning and asset-leasing firms such as airlines, retailers and restaurants on the same footing.
nodes.f: (EV + capitalized leases) / EBITDAR

nodes.t: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization and rent. Removes lease cost so that companies that lease and companies that own their assets can be compared.
nodes.f: EBITDAR = EBITDA + rent expense

nodes.t: Life insurer market value divided by embedded value, the present value of future profits on in-force policies plus adjusted net assets. A discount often signals doubts about assumptions or capital fungibility.
nodes.f: P/EV = market cap / embedded value

nodes.t: Enterprise value divided by invested capital. Plotted against ROIC across peers, it shows which firms are cheap or expensive for their returns, since value should rise with ROIC above the cost of capital.
nodes.f: EV/IC

nodes.t: A company's P/E divided by the market or sector P/E. Tracking it over time shows whether a stock's premium or discount to its benchmark is wide or narrow versus history.
nodes.f: relative P/E = stock P/E / index P/E

nodes.t: The reciprocal of the average of inverse multiples, the correct way to average ratios such as P/E across a peer set. It limits the pull of outliers and handles near-zero earnings better than a simple mean.
nodes.f: H = n / sum(1/m_i)

nodes.t: The P/E implied by a company's payout, growth and cost of equity under a constant-growth model. Compares the multiple the fundamentals support with the one the market pays.
nodes.f: leading P/E = payout ratio / (r - g)

nodes.t: The price to book implied by return on equity, growth and cost of equity. A firm earning exactly its cost of equity deserves a multiple of one; higher ROE justifies a premium.
nodes.f: P/B = (ROE - g) / (r - g)

nodes.t: Valuing a firm by applying multiples observed on similar listed companies. Quick and market-based, but it imports any mispricing in the peer group and depends heavily on peer selection.
Valuing a firm from multiples paid in past acquisitions of similar businesses. Includes a control premium, so values usually exceed trading comps, and older deals reflect different market conditions.

Pricing an asset by reference to how the market prices similar assets, rather than from its own cash flows. Answers whether something is cheap versus peers, not whether the whole group is fairly priced.
The amount an acquirer pays above the pre-announcement market price to gain control. It reflects expected synergies, the right to change strategy and payout, and competition among bidders.
nodes.f: premium = offer price / unaffected price - 1

nodes.t: A reduction applied to a non-controlling stake because its holder cannot set strategy, dividends or a sale. Used mainly in private company and estate valuations.
A reduction in value for an interest that cannot be sold quickly or cheaply, such as private shares or restricted stock. Often estimated with put option models or restricted stock studies.
The tendency of diversified firms to trade below the sum of their parts' standalone values. Attributed to cross-subsidies, weak capital allocation, opacity and investors' preference for pure plays.
nodes.f: discount = 1 - market value / SOTP value

nodes.t: The gap between a holding company's market value and the value of its stakes. Drivers include holding costs, tax leakage on disposal, governance concerns and limited ability for outsiders to access the assets.
nodes.f: discount = 1 - market cap / NAV

nodes.t: Values a share as the present value of expected future dividends discounted at the cost of equity. Fits stable payers such as utilities and banks; poor for firms that retain or buy back most earnings.
nodes.f: P0 = sum D_t / (1 + r)^t

nodes.t: The constant-growth dividend discount model of Gordon (1959): price equals next year's dividend divided by the cost of equity less a perpetual growth rate. Highly sensitive as growth approaches the discount rate.
A dividend model in which growth declines linearly from a high initial rate to a stable rate over a set period. Gives a closed-form approximation without a full multi-stage forecast.
nodes.f: P0 = D0(1 + gL)/(r - gL) + D0 x H x (gS - gL)/(r - gL), H = half-life of high growth

nodes.t: A DCF with distinct phases, typically high growth, a fade period and a stable terminal phase. Lets growth, margins and reinvestment converge toward mature levels instead of jumping to them.

Greenwald's value of a firm assuming no growth: normalized after-tax operating earnings divided by the cost of capital. Comparing it with asset value and market value separates franchise value from growth value.
nodes.f: EPV = adjusted EBIT x (1 - t) / WACC

nodes.t: A rough upper bound on a defensive stock's price from Benjamin Graham's rule that P/E times P/B should not exceed 22.5. A screening heuristic, not a valuation.
nodes.f: Graham number = sqrt(22.5 x EPS x BVPS)

nodes.t: Graham's deep value screen for stocks priced below net current asset value: current assets minus all liabilities. Buyers effectively get fixed assets and the business for free, though many such firms burn cash.
nodes.f: NCAV = current assets - total liabilities

nodes.t: What owners would receive if assets were sold off and liabilities paid. Assets are haircut by how quickly and cheaply they can be sold; a floor value for distressed or asset-heavy companies.
What it would cost a new entrant to rebuild a firm's assets today. A market value far above it invites entry unless a moat protects returns; a value below it discourages new supply.
Valuing a company from the market or replacement value of its assets less liabilities, rather than from earnings. Fits holding companies, resource firms, real estate and liquidations.

Values a firm as if all-equity financed, then adds the present value of financing side effects such as interest tax shields, minus expected distress costs. Handy when leverage changes over time, as in LBOs.
nodes.f: APV = unlevered value + PV(tax shields) - PV(distress costs)

nodes.n: Free cash flow to the firm
nodes.t: Cash generated after taxes and reinvestment but before any payments to lenders or shareholders. Discounted at WACC to give enterprise value.
nodes.f: FCFF = EBIT(1 - t) + D&A - capex - change in NWC

nodes.t: Cash available to shareholders after reinvestment and net debt flows. Discounted at the cost of equity to value equity directly; consistent leverage assumptions are essential.
nodes.f: FCFE = FCFF - interest x (1 - t) + net borrowing

nodes.t: Net operating profit after tax: operating income taxed as if the firm had no debt. The earnings measure behind ROIC and economic profit.
nodes.f: NOPAT = EBIT x (1 - tax rate)

nodes.t: Discounting each year's cash flow as if received at mid-year rather than year-end, reflecting that cash arrives through the year. Raises DCF value modestly relative to end-of-year discounting.
A partial year between the valuation date and the next fiscal year-end. Its cash flow and discount factor are scaled to the fraction of the year remaining.
The years in a DCF where revenue, margins and reinvestment are forecast line by line before the terminal value takes over. It should run until the business reaches a steady state.
Estimating terminal value by applying a multiple, usually EV/EBITDA, to final-year metrics. Common in banking and LBOs, but it smuggles relative valuation into an intrinsic model.
nodes.f: TV = terminal EBITDA x exit multiple

nodes.t: Estimating terminal value as next year's cash flow divided by the discount rate less a perpetual growth rate. The growth rate should not exceed long-run nominal economic growth.
nodes.f: TV = FCF_(n+1) / (WACC - g)

nodes.t: How long a firm can earn returns above its cost of capital before competition erodes them. Its length, more than near-term growth, drives the value of strong businesses.
Expresses continuing value through growth, return on new capital and the cost of capital, as popularized by McKinsey's Valuation. Shows that growth adds value only when RONIC exceeds WACC.
nodes.f: CV = NOPAT_(t+1) x (1 - g/RONIC) / (WACC - g)

nodes.t: The return earned on incremental capital invested, as distinct from the average ROIC on existing capital. In a terminal value it is often set near WACC, assuming competition removes excess returns on new projects.
nodes.f: RONIC = change in NOPAT / change in invested capital

nodes.t: The share of after-tax operating profit put back into the business through net capex, acquisitions and working capital. Growth equals the reinvestment rate times the return on that reinvestment.
nodes.f: reinvestment rate = (net capex + change in NWC) / NOPAT

nodes.t: The growth rate implied by how much a firm reinvests and how well. Ties growth assumptions in a DCF to reinvestment so that they stay internally consistent.
nodes.f: g = reinvestment rate x ROIC

nodes.t: The growth a firm can fund from retained earnings without changing leverage or issuing equity. The equity analogue of fundamental growth.
nodes.f: g = ROE x retention ratio

nodes.t: The share of net income kept in the business rather than paid as dividends. Equal to one minus the payout ratio.
nodes.f: b = 1 - dividends / net income

nodes.t: Operating profit after tax minus a charge for all capital employed at the cost of capital. Positive economic profit means the firm creates value; accounting profit alone cannot say that.
nodes.f: EP = (ROIC - WACC) x invested capital

nodes.t: Stern Stewart's branded version of economic profit, with accounting adjustments such as capitalizing R&D. Used for valuation and to link executive pay to returns above the cost of capital.
nodes.f: EVA = NOPAT - WACC x capital

nodes.t: The market value of a firm's debt and equity minus the capital invested in it. In theory it equals the present value of future economic profits.
nodes.f: MVA = market value - invested capital

nodes.t: Values equity as book value plus the present value of future earnings in excess of a charge for the cost of equity on book value. Anchors value on the balance sheet and pulls less of it into the terminal value.
nodes.f: V0 = B0 + sum (E_t - r x B_(t-1)) / (1 + r)^t

nodes.t: The condition that all changes in book equity, other than transactions with owners, pass through earnings. Residual income models rely on it; items booked straight to equity break it.
nodes.f: B_t = B_(t-1) + E_t - D_t

nodes.t: Cash flow return on investment: an inflation-adjusted internal rate of return on a firm's gross investment, developed by HOLT. Compared with a real discount rate to judge value creation.
Steps from enterprise value to equity value: subtract debt, preferred stock, noncontrolling interests and debt-like items, add cash and non-operating assets, then divide by diluted shares.
nodes.f: equity value = EV - debt + cash - preferred - NCI + non-operating assets

nodes.t: Basic shares plus the shares that options, warrants, RSUs and convertibles would add if exercised or converted. Using basic shares overstates per-share value, especially for firms with heavy stock pay.
Counts in-the-money options and warrants as dilutive, assuming exercise proceeds buy back shares at the current price. Only the net new shares are added.
nodes.f: net shares = options x (1 - strike / price)

nodes.t: Treats convertible securities as converted into common shares for diluted EPS, adding back the related after-tax interest or preferred dividends. Applied only when dilutive.

Obligations that behave like debt but sit outside it: unfunded pensions, lease liabilities, earnouts, litigation provisions, deferred consideration and some deferred revenue. Deducted in the equity bridge and negotiated in M&A.
Cash beyond what operations need, which can be added to enterprise value as a non-operating asset. Trapped overseas cash or cash needed for working capital should be treated differently.
A horizontal bar chart showing value ranges from several methods such as comps, precedents, DCF and 52-week trading range. Common in fairness opinions and pitch books.
A grid showing how a valuation output changes across two inputs, typically discount rate against terminal growth or exit multiple. Reveals how much of a conclusion rests on assumptions.
The perpetual growth rate consistent with a terminal value computed from an exit multiple. A cross-check: an implied rate above nominal GDP growth signals an aggressive multiple.
nodes.f: g = (TV x WACC - FCF_n) / (TV + FCF_n)

nodes.t: The EBITDA multiple consistent with a terminal value computed from perpetuity growth. Compared against current trading multiples as a reality check.
nodes.f: implied multiple = TV / terminal EBITDA

nodes.t: Earnings adjusted to a sustainable level by removing one-off items and smoothing cyclical swings in volume, price and margin. The base to which a multiple or capitalization rate should be applied.
Earnings a cyclical company would make at an average point in its industry cycle, often estimated from average margins across past cycles applied to current capacity.
nodes.f: mid-cycle EPS = revenue x average through-cycle margin / shares

nodes.t: For cyclicals, a low P/E often marks peak earnings and a good time to sell, while a high P/E on depressed earnings can mark the bottom. Applying normal multiples to peak earnings overvalues them.
a: buy high pe sell low pe

nodes.t: A stock that looks cheap on multiples but stays cheap or falls further because its earnings, assets or competitive position are deteriorating. Low price reflects a real problem rather than mispricing.

Merton's (1974) view that shareholders of a levered firm hold a call on its assets struck at the face value of debt. Explains why distressed equity keeps value and why volatility can help shareholders at lenders' expense.
nodes.f: E = call(assets, face value of debt, maturity, asset volatility)

nodes.t: Valuing flexibility in investment decisions, such as the right to expand, delay or abandon a project, with option-pricing logic. Most relevant where uncertainty is high and decisions can be staged.
Valuing an asset as the probability-weighted average of values in distinct scenarios, rather than from a single base case. Exposes skew between upside and downside that one point estimate hides.
nodes.f: value = sum p_i x V_i

nodes.t: The fraction of DCF enterprise value coming from the terminal value. For growth companies it often dominates, which means the valuation rests mainly on long-run assumptions rather than the forecast years.
nodes.f: share = PV(TV) / EV

nodes.t: The rule that nominal cash flows be discounted at nominal rates and real cash flows at real rates. Mixing them, such as real growth with a nominal discount rate, biases value.
nodes.f: (1 + nominal) = (1 + real) x (1 + inflation)

nodes.t: Cash flows and discount rate must be in the same currency, with the risk-free rate and expected inflation of that currency. Value should not change merely because the currency of analysis changes.
The perpetual growth rate assumed in a terminal value. It should be at or below long-run nominal economic growth, and must be backed by enough reinvestment to fund it.
A forecast where results stay flat or weak in the near term and then accelerate sharply later. Common in management plans and pitch decks; base rates show few such forecasts are met.

The tendency of companies and analysts to underestimate time and cost and overestimate benefits of plans, documented by Kahneman and Tversky. Shows up in synergy targets, project budgets and launch timing.
The tendency of returns on capital to drift toward the cost of capital as competitors enter. Strong moats slow the fade; modeling it explicitly keeps terminal values honest.
A company creates value only when it earns a return on invested capital above its cost of capital; growth at returns below it destroys value. The foundation of corporate finance valuation.
nodes.f: value created if ROIC > WACC

nodes.t: Value is created only by changing cash flows or risk, not by relabeling claims on them. Financial engineering, accounting changes and pure share swaps do not create value on their own.
The present value of a project's expected cash inflows minus the present value of its costs, discounted at the required return. A positive NPV means the project adds value.
nodes.f: NPV = sum CF_t / (1 + r)^t - initial investment

nodes.t: NPV in which each stage's cash flows are multiplied by the probability of reaching that stage, used for drug pipelines and other milestone-driven assets.
nodes.f: rNPV = sum p_t x CF_t / (1 + r)^t

nodes.t: An analyst's estimate of where a share should trade, usually over twelve months, from a multiple or DCF. Sell-side targets cluster near the current price and tend to follow it.
A three-scenario framing of a stock's value with explicit assumptions for each case. Weighting them and comparing the upside with the downside gives a risk-reward view.
nodes.f: skew = (bull - price) / (price - bear)

nodes.t: An identifiable event expected to close the gap between price and estimated value, such as earnings, a spin-off, asset sale, management change or regulatory decision.
Steinhardt's term for a well-founded view that differs from consensus. A stock idea needs one to have an edge; agreeing with the market only earns the market return.

Exploiting investors' focus on near-term results by owning assets whose value depends on longer-term outcomes the market discounts too heavily. Requires patient capital and tolerance for interim losses.
Share price change plus dividends reinvested, over a period, as a percentage of the starting price. The return an investor actually earned and a common basis for executive pay.
nodes.f: TSR = (P1 - P0 + dividends) / P0

nodes.t: Splitting shareholder return into earnings growth, change in the valuation multiple, dividend yield and change in share count. Separates operating performance from rerating.
nodes.f: TSR ~ EPS growth + multiple change + dividend yield

nodes.t: Extra return demanded for exposure to a country's political, economic and currency risks, added to the cost of equity. Often estimated from sovereign default spreads scaled by relative equity to bond volatility.
nodes.f: CRP = sovereign default spread x (equity vol / bond vol)

nodes.t: An extra return sometimes added to the cost of equity for small companies, based on the historical outperformance of small caps. The evidence is weak and unstable after its publication, so many practitioners avoid it.

An ad hoc addition to the discount rate for risks unique to one firm, common in private company valuation. Theory says diversifiable risk should be handled in cash flows instead, so it is easily abused.
Estimating cost of equity by stacking premia on the risk-free rate: equity risk premium, size, industry and company-specific premia. Used for private firms without a traded beta.
nodes.f: Ke = Rf + ERP + size premium + specific premium

nodes.t: Equity beta reflecting both business risk and financial leverage. Hamada's equation relevers an asset beta for a target debt to equity ratio.
nodes.f: beta_L = beta_U x (1 + (1 - t) x D/E)

nodes.t: Beta of a firm's assets as if it had no debt, isolating business risk. Computed from peers' equity betas and leverage, then relevered for the target's capital structure.
nodes.f: beta_U = beta_L / (1 + (1 - t) x D/E)

nodes.t: A beta built from the average unlevered beta of comparable firms in the same businesses, weighted by the target's mix and relevered. More stable than one firm's regression beta, which has large standard error.
A regression beta shrunk toward one, reflecting Blume's (1971) finding that betas mean-revert over time. Used by common data terminals as the default adjusted beta.
nodes.f: adjusted beta = 0.67 x raw beta + 0.33

nodes.t: The required return on preferred shares, approximated for perpetual preferred as the dividend divided by price. Enters WACC as a separate weight; preferred dividends are not tax-deductible.
nodes.f: Kp = preferred dividend / preferred price

nodes.t: A rating estimated from a firm's interest coverage or leverage by mapping it to typical ratios of rated companies. Provides a default spread and pre-tax cost of debt when no rating exists.
nodes.f: pre-tax Kd = risk-free rate + spread for synthetic rating

nodes.t: Income tax expense divided by pretax income. It differs from the statutory rate because of foreign rates, credits, deferred items and permanent differences; reconciliation appears in the tax note.
nodes.f: ETR = tax expense / pretax income

nodes.t: The tax rate on the next unit of income. It determines the value of interest deductions and is the right rate for interest tax shields, while the effective rate may suit near-term operating taxes.
The mix of debt and equity a firm aims to maintain over time. WACC weights should reflect it rather than a temporary current mix.
Weighting debt and equity in WACC by market values rather than book values, because investors' required returns apply to what their claims are worth now.
nodes.f: w_E = E / (D + E)

nodes.t: The discount rate that equates current price to the present value of forecast cash flows or earnings. A forward-looking expected-return estimate, sensitive to analyst forecast bias.
nodes.f: solve P0 = sum CF_t / (1 + r)^t for r

nodes.t: Tax saved because interest expense is deductible. Its present value is the main gain from debt in Modigliani-Miller with taxes and is captured in WACC through the after-tax cost of debt.
nodes.f: shield = interest x tax rate

nodes.t: Using a discount rate matched to each business line's risk instead of one corporate WACC. A single rate over-funds risky units and under-funds safe ones.
Deciding which long-term investments to make by estimating incremental cash flows and comparing their value with cost using NPV, IRR or payback.
Time for a project's cumulative cash flows to recover its initial cost. Easy to explain but ignores the time value of money and cash flows after payback.
Present value of future cash flows divided by initial investment. Above one means positive NPV; useful for ranking projects when capital is limited.
nodes.f: PI = PV(future cash flows) / investment

nodes.t: A limit on investment funds that forces a firm to choose among positive-NPV projects. Projects are then ranked by value per unit of scarce capital.
Management's choice of how to deploy cash among reinvestment, acquisitions, debt reduction, dividends and buybacks. Over long periods it shapes per-share value as much as operations do.

Modigliani and Miller (1958) showed that, without taxes, distress costs or frictions, firm value does not depend on capital structure. Its value lies in pointing to which frictions do make financing matter.
nodes.f: V_L = V_U

nodes.t: Cost of equity rises linearly with leverage because shareholders bear more risk. With corporate taxes, firm value rises by the present value of the interest tax shield.
nodes.f: Ke = Ku + (Ku - Kd) x (1 - t) x D/E; V_L = V_U + t x D

nodes.t: Firms choose leverage by balancing the tax benefit of debt against expected financial distress and agency costs. Predicts that stable, tangible-asset firms carry more debt.
Myers and Majluf (1984): because managers know more than investors, firms fund first with internal cash, then debt, and issue equity last. Explains why profitable firms often carry little debt.
Baker and Wurgler (2002): firms issue equity when their shares are richly valued and repurchase when cheap, so capital structure reflects the history of past timing attempts.
Costs of being near default: legal fees, lost customers and suppliers, fire sales and forgone investment. They offset the tax benefit of debt and are higher for firms with intangible assets.
Myers (1977): when debt is heavy, much of the payoff from new investment goes to creditors, so shareholders pass up positive-NPV projects. A reason distressed firms underinvest.
Shareholders of a levered firm gain from shifting into riskier projects, since they keep the upside while creditors bear more of the downside. A core agency cost of debt that covenants try to limit.
Jensen (1986): managers with cash beyond profitable investment tend to waste it. Debt, dividends and buybacks discipline them by forcing payouts.
a: agency cost of free cash flow

nodes.t: Conflict that arises when managers act for owners but have their own interests, or when shareholders and creditors want different things. Monitoring, incentives and contracts reduce but never remove it.
The debt to equity mix that minimizes WACC and maximizes firm value given taxes, distress costs and agency effects. In practice it is a range, not a point.
How much a firm can borrow while keeping acceptable credit metrics and covenant headroom through a downturn. Driven by cash flow stability, asset collateral value and rating targets.
A firm's approach to how much and how regularly it pays out cash to shareholders. Most firms smooth dividends and treat cuts as a last resort.
Miller and Modigliani (1961): with no taxes or frictions, payout policy does not change firm value, since investors can create homemade dividends by selling shares.
Dividend changes convey management's view of future earnings because cutting is costly. Increases tend to lift prices and cuts to drop them sharply.
Different investors prefer different payout policies due to taxes, income needs or mandates, so firms attract a clientele matching their policy and changing it can trigger turnover.
Lintner (1956) found firms set a target payout and adjust dividends only partially toward it each year, producing smooth dividends that lag earnings.
nodes.f: change in D = speed x (target payout x E - D_prior)

nodes.t: A one-off cash distribution outside the regular dividend, often after an asset sale or a cash buildup. Signals excess cash without committing to a higher recurring payout.

Issuing more shares per existing share, such as two for one, reducing the price per share without changing total value. Sometimes followed by positive returns, attributed to signaling or retail access.
Combining shares, such as one for ten, to raise the share price, often to meet exchange listing minimums. Usually associated with weak firms and followed by poor returns.
A distribution of additional shares instead of cash. It moves amounts within equity accounts but does not change firm value or any holder's proportional stake.
The first trading day a share trades without the right to the next dividend. The price typically drops by roughly the dividend amount at the open, adjusted for taxes.
The date on which a holder must be on the company's books to receive a dividend or vote. With T+1 settlement the ex-date generally falls on the record date.
A reduction or suspension of a regular dividend, typically after earnings or cash flow fall or leverage rises. Because firms resist cuts, they carry strong negative signaling.
How many times earnings or free cash flow cover the dividend. Coverage near or below one warns that the payout depends on borrowing or asset sales.
nodes.f: coverage = EPS / DPS or FCF / dividends

nodes.t: Index constituents that have raised dividends every year for a long run, twenty-five years for the S&P 500 version. A screen for durable payers, not a guarantee of future returns.

A reduction in existing holders' ownership share or per-share value from new share issuance through equity raises, stock pay, convertibles or stock-funded deals. Value-neutral only if new shares are sold at fair value.
A buyback in which a bank delivers most shares to the company upfront, borrows them, and covers by buying in the market over months, with a final price adjustment to the average price.
A buyback in which shareholders tender at prices within a stated range and the company pays the lowest single price that fills its target. Quick and large, usually at a premium.
Buying back shares gradually on the exchange under an authorization, within volume and timing safe harbors. The most common and flexible buyback form; authorizations need not be completed.
A prearranged trading plan, adopted when the insider lacks material nonpublic information, that lets insiders or companies buy or sell on a schedule while defending against insider trading claims.
Buybacks lift EPS mechanically by shrinking share count, but create value only if shares are bought below intrinsic value. Debt-funded buybacks also raise risk, which a higher P/E should not ignore.
Seasoned equity offerings tend to be followed by a price drop at announcement and weak long-run returns, consistent with managers issuing when they think shares are overvalued.
A sale of shares by a company that is already public, either newly issued primary shares that dilute holders or secondary shares sold by existing holders.
New shares offered first to existing holders in proportion to their stakes, usually at a discount, with tradable rights. Lets holders avoid dilution if they take up or sell their rights.
nodes.f: theoretical ex-rights price = (N x P + n x S) / (N + n)

nodes.t: A program that lets a listed company sell new shares gradually into the market through a broker at prevailing prices. Common for REITs, utilities and cash-hungry growth firms.
Private investment in public equity: a listed company sells shares or convertibles directly to selected investors, often at a discount. Fast, but can signal weak access to ordinary markets.
The difference between the price paid by the public and the proceeds to the issuer, kept by underwriting banks. Larger for IPOs and smaller deals.
nodes.f: gross spread = offer price - price paid to issuer

nodes.t: An overallotment option allowing underwriters to sell up to an extra share of the offering, usually fifteen percent, then cover by buying in the market if the price falls or exercising if it rises. Supports post-offering trading.

New issues on average close their first day above the offer price, leaving money on the table for issuers. Explanations include information asymmetry, winner's curse among investors and banker incentives.
nodes.f: first day return = first close / offer price - 1

nodes.t: The end of a contractual period, often 180 days after an IPO, during which insiders cannot sell. Expected supply around expiry has been associated with price weakness.
Going public by listing existing shares on an exchange without underwriters selling a new issue. Avoids underwriting fees and lockups but historically raised no new capital.
Contract terms in loans and bonds that restrict borrower actions or require financial ratios to stay within limits. Breaches give lenders rights to renegotiate, raise pricing or accelerate.
Debt with first claim on specified collateral and top payment priority. Lower yields and higher recoveries in default than unsecured or subordinated debt.
Subordinated debt or preferred equity between senior debt and common equity, often with PIK interest and warrants. Fills a financing gap in buyouts at a high cost.
A single loan combining senior and junior debt at one blended rate, provided mainly by direct lenders. Faster and simpler than a syndicated capital structure.
A provision giving bondholders or lenders the right to be repaid, often at 101 percent of par, if the company is acquired. Protects creditors against leveraged takeovers.
The risk that maturing debt cannot be rolled over, or only at much higher cost. Highest for weak credits with near-term maturities and for floating-rate borrowers.
Creditors cancel debt in exchange for equity in the restructured company. Cuts leverage and usually wipes out or heavily dilutes existing shareholders.
US bankruptcy liquidation: a trustee sells the debtor's assets and distributes proceeds to creditors by priority. Operations normally cease.
Borrowing heavily to pay a large dividend or buy back shares, sharply raising leverage without a change of control. Historically used as a takeover defense or to return cash.
A sponsor-owned company raises new debt to pay a dividend to its private equity owner. Returns capital early and boosts IRR, at the cost of higher leverage.
Trading mispricing between different securities of the same issuer, such as long bonds and short equity, or CDS against stock, on the view that their prices imply inconsistent default risk.
Equity with priority over common for dividends and liquidation, usually without voting rights and with fixed dividends that may be cumulative. Treated like debt in the equity bridge.

Ratios agencies weigh for corporate ratings, chiefly debt to EBITDA, funds from operations to debt and interest coverage, adjusted for leases and pensions. Ratings also reflect business risk and scale.
The combination of two companies, either by one buying the other or both forming a new entity. Value is created for the buyer only if synergies exceed the premium paid plus integration costs.
nodes.f: buyer value created = PV(synergies) - premium - integration costs

nodes.t: Extra value from combining two firms beyond their standalone values, from cost savings, revenue gains, tax or financing benefits. Usually overestimated and slower to arrive than planned.
nodes.f: synergy = V(A+B) - V(A) - V(B)

nodes.t: Savings from eliminating overlapping functions, facilities and procurement after a merger. More reliably achieved than revenue synergies, though they carry one-time costs to realize.
Extra sales from cross-selling, wider distribution or pricing power after a merger. Hard to realize and often offset by customer losses, so investors heavily discount them.
Buying a takeover target after announcement, and shorting the acquirer in stock deals, to earn the spread to the deal price. Returns resemble selling insurance against deal failure.
The gap between the offer value and the target's market price after announcement. It reflects time to close, financing and regulatory risk, and the downside if the deal breaks.
nodes.f: implied p(close) = (price - fallback) / (offer - fallback)

nodes.t: An acquisition paid in acquirer shares. Target holders share in the combined firm's risk and synergies; announcement returns for acquirers tend to be worse than in cash deals.
The number of acquirer shares given per target share in a stock deal. A fixed ratio shifts price risk to target holders; a fixed value with a floating ratio shifts it to the acquirer.
nodes.f: exchange ratio = offer price per target share / acquirer share price

nodes.t: The choice of paying for an acquisition in cash or shares. Cash signals confidence and gives target holders certainty; stock shares risk and can signal the acquirer views its shares as rich.
Part of an acquisition price paid later only if the target meets agreed milestones. Bridges valuation gaps between buyer and seller but often leads to disputes.
A fee the target pays the buyer if the target walks away, typically for a superior offer. Compensates the first bidder and deters interlopers.
A fee the buyer pays the target if the deal fails due to the buyer, such as a financing failure or regulatory block. Signals how much regulatory risk the buyer accepts.
A period after signing in which the target may solicit competing bids, with a reduced breakup fee. Common in private equity take-privates to support the board's fiduciary duty.
A merger term barring the target from soliciting other offers after signing, usually with a fiduciary out allowing it to accept a clearly superior unsolicited bid.
A material adverse change condition letting a buyer abandon a deal if the target suffers a severe, durable deterioration. Courts set a high bar, and broad industry events are usually carved out.
An acquisition pursued against the target board's wishes, by a tender offer directly to holders or a proxy fight to replace the board.
A public offer to buy shares directly from holders at a stated price, usually a premium, within a set period and subject to a minimum acceptance condition.
A shareholder rights plan that lets all holders except a hostile bidder buy discounted shares once the bidder crosses an ownership threshold, making an unapproved acquisition prohibitively dilutive.
A board divided into classes with only one elected each year, so a challenger needs two annual meetings to win control. A strong takeover defense often opposed by governance advocates.
A friendlier acquirer invited by a target's board to outbid a hostile bidder.
A contest in which a shareholder solicits votes to elect its own director nominees or pass proposals against management's recommendations.
A bank's letter to a board stating that a deal price is fair from a financial point of view, backed by comps, precedents and DCF. Fees contingent on closing create conflicts.
Investigation of a target's financials, operations, legal exposure and commercial position before committing capital. Confirms the thesis and surfaces issues to price or protect against.
Government review of whether a merger would substantially lessen competition, such as under the US Hart-Scott-Rodino process or by the European Commission. Can delay, condition or block deals.
The right of dissenting shareholders in certain mergers to ask a court to determine fair value and pay that instead of the deal price.
A private company becomes public by merging into an existing listed shell, skipping a traditional IPO. Faster, but historically associated with weaker disclosure and fraud risk.
A smaller acquisition added to an existing platform company, usually at a lower multiple. Lets a sponsor blend down its entry multiple and add synergies.
Consolidating a fragmented industry by acquiring many small firms into one platform. Value can come from scale and multiple arbitrage, but rapid acquisition can hide weak organic growth.
The initial acquisition in a sponsor's buy-and-build strategy, with the management and systems to absorb further add-on acquisitions.

A company whose strategy is a steady stream of acquisitions, often of small private firms at modest multiples, with capital redeployed under decentralized management. Success depends on price discipline and returns on capital.
Managers growing the firm through acquisitions or investment for size, status or pay rather than returns. A central agency cost that buybacks, debt and activists try to curb.
Roll (1986): acquirers overpay because overconfident managers believe their valuations beat the market's. Helps explain why target holders gain while acquirer holders often lose.
Studies find target shareholders capture most M&A gains while acquirer returns around announcement average near zero, worse for large public stock deals and better for small private cash deals.
Testing whether a deal raises or lowers the acquirer's EPS. Paying with cash or cheap debt is easily accretive, so EPS accretion says little about whether value is created.
nodes.f: accretive if acquirer P/E > target P/E paid, for all-stock deals

nodes.t: Financial statements restated as if a transaction such as an acquisition, disposal or refinancing had occurred earlier. Required in some filings; also a common vehicle for flattering adjustments.
Assigning an acquisition's price to the fair value of identifiable assets and liabilities, with any excess recorded as goodwill. Creates amortizable intangibles and a step-up in asset bases.
nodes.f: goodwill = price - fair value of net identifiable assets

nodes.t: A parent sells a minority stake in a subsidiary through an IPO, keeping control. Raises cash and sets a market value for the unit, often ahead of a full spin-off.
A parent distributes shares of a subsidiary to its own holders, creating a separate listed company. Often tax-free; aims to close a conglomerate discount and sharpen management focus.
Spun-off companies have historically outperformed after separation, partly because index and mandate holders sell shares they did not choose. Popularized by Greenblatt; the effect varies by period.
A parent offers its holders subsidiary shares in exchange for their parent shares, which shrinks the parent's share count. Usually done at a small premium to entice tendering.
A US structure in which a parent spins off a unit that then merges with a third party, with the parent's holders owning the majority of the combined company, allowing a tax-free disposal.
A class of a company's shares meant to follow the performance of one division, without separate legal ownership of its assets. Usually trades at a discount to the economics it tracks.
Selling a business unit or assets for cash or securities. Proceeds and the price received reveal what the market will pay for a part of the company.
A company running many unrelated businesses under one owner. Can allocate capital internally well, but often trades at a discount for opacity and cross-subsidy.
A table showing where transaction money comes from, such as debt tranches, sponsor equity and rollover, and where it goes, such as purchase equity, refinanced debt and fees. Both sides must balance.
nodes.f: total sources = total uses

nodes.t: The share of an LBO's price funded by the sponsor's equity rather than debt. A larger contribution lowers risk and returns; lenders often require a minimum.
nodes.f: equity % = sponsor equity / total sources

nodes.t: Breaking a buyout's equity return into EBITDA growth, multiple expansion and debt paydown from free cash flow. Shows how much came from operations versus leverage and market timing.
nodes.f: equity gain = EBITDA growth x entry multiple + multiple change x exit EBITDA + net debt reduction

nodes.t: Gaining value by buying businesses at a low multiple and selling or valuing the combination at a higher one, typically because size and quality command higher multiples.
Existing managers or founders reinvesting part of their sale proceeds in the new company's equity. Aligns incentives and reduces the cash a sponsor must pay.
An equity pool granted to managers in a sponsor-backed company, often a set percentage of shares vesting on time and return hurdles. Pays out heavily when the sponsor hits its target return.
A loan provision requiring a share of excess free cash flow to repay debt early. Speeds deleveraging and is modeled in LBOs to show debt falling over the hold.
The cash a company must keep for operations, which cannot be swept to lenders or counted as excess in valuation.
Senior leverage is secured or senior debt divided by EBITDA; total leverage includes all debt. Lenders set limits on each by tranche at entry and in covenants.
nodes.f: senior leverage = senior debt / EBITDA

nodes.t: How far a covenant ratio sits from its limit, often expressed as the percentage EBITDA decline before a breach. Thin headroom signals renegotiation or equity cures ahead.
nodes.f: EBITDA cushion = 1 - (debt / max leverage multiple) / current EBITDA

nodes.t: A buyer, usually a sponsor or controlling holder, acquires all public shares and delists the company. Requires a premium and board process protecting minority holders.
A buyout led by a company's own managers, usually with sponsor and debt funding. Raises conflicts because managers are both sellers' agents and buyers.
A simplified buyout model done by hand: entry price, debt, cash generation and exit multiple to estimate IRR and MOIC. A common interview test and quick screening tool.
nodes.f: IRR = MOIC^(1/years) - 1, with no interim cash flows

nodes.t: The EV/EBITDA multiple paid to acquire a company. The main driver of buyout risk, because a high entry leaves returns dependent on growth and a high exit multiple.
Investors buying stakes to push for changes in strategy, capital allocation, governance or a sale. Tactics range from private letters to public campaigns and proxy fights.

An SEC filing required within a short period after an investor acquires more than five percent of a voting class with intent to influence control. Discloses the holder's purpose and plans; passive holders file 13G instead.
A ballot listing both management and dissident nominees so holders can mix candidates from each side. Mandatory in US contested elections, it makes partial board wins for activists easier.
A shareholder advisory vote on executive compensation. Not binding, but low support pressures boards to redesign pay.
Share structures where one class carries more votes per share, letting founders keep control with a minority economic stake. Shields long-term plans but weakens accountability.
The rules and practices by which boards oversee managers and protect shareholder interests: board independence, voting rights, pay design and disclosure.
Firms such as ISS and Glass Lewis that recommend how institutions should vote at shareholder meetings. Their support often decides close votes and contests.
Several investors building positions in the same target around an activist campaign, adding voting power without forming a formal group that triggers joint disclosure.
The filing sent before a shareholder meeting describing matters to be voted on, director nominees, executive pay and related party dealings. In the US it is form DEF 14A.
Salary, bonus and equity awards for top managers. The metrics it rewards, such as EPS, revenue, TSR or ROIC, shape decisions and are worth reading before a thesis.
The share of a company owned by its officers and directors. Meaningful personal stakes align interests, though very high control can entrench management.
A company run by a founder or large holder whose wealth is concentrated in its shares. Often associated with long-term capital allocation and lower agency costs.
When a product becomes more valuable to each user as more users join, directly or through a second side of a market. Can produce winner-take-most outcomes and a strong moat.
The money, time, risk and retraining a customer bears to move to a competitor. High switching costs let incumbents raise prices and retain customers; enterprise software is a classic case.
Protection from brands, patents, licenses or regulatory approvals that competitors cannot easily copy. Brands matter as a moat only if they raise willingness to pay or lower acquisition costs.
Producing at durably lower cost than rivals through process, location, scale or unique resources. Most valuable in commodity-like industries where price is set by the marginal producer.
Producers ranked from lowest to highest unit cost against cumulative capacity. Price tends toward the cost of the marginal producer needed to meet demand, so low-cost producers earn rents.
A market only large enough to support one or a few profitable firms, such as a regional airport or pipeline, so new entry would make returns inadequate for everyone.
Unit costs falling as volume rises because fixed costs are spread over more units. A moat when the scale needed is large relative to the market.

Hamilton Helmer's framework for durable advantage: scale economies, network economies, counter-positioning, switching costs, branding, cornered resource and process power. Each needs both a benefit and a barrier.
A newcomer adopts a business model the incumbent could copy but will not, because doing so would damage its existing business. Index funds versus active managers are a standard example.
Preferential access to a valuable asset on attractive terms, such as a patent, unique talent, licence or low-cost deposit. One of Helmer's seven powers.
Embedded organizational know-how that lowers cost or improves quality and takes rivals years to replicate, such as a lean manufacturing system. The rarest of Helmer's powers.
The ability of a brand to command a price premium or lower customer acquisition cost through trust and reputation built over time.

Porter's (1979) framework for industry profitability: rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, buyer power and supplier power. Explains why some industries earn high returns on capital and others do not.
Customers' ability to push down prices or demand more, highest when buyers are concentrated, purchase in volume, face low switching costs or can integrate backward.
Suppliers' ability to raise prices or cut quality, strongest when they are concentrated, their input is critical and unique, or switching costs are high.
Products from other industries that meet the same need cap what an industry can charge. Substitutes are often missed because they do not look like competitors.
Obstacles that make it hard for new firms to enter profitably: scale, capital needs, regulation, brands, switching costs or network effects. Without them, excess returns attract entry.
The sequence of activities from raw inputs to end customer. Analyzing where profit pools sit along it shows which links have power and which are commoditized.
The ability to raise prices without losing much volume. Buffett called it the single most important factor in evaluating a business; visible in stable or rising gross margins through inflation.
The total revenue available if a product won every possible customer. Useful for bounding growth, but routinely overstated; serviceable and obtainable market are narrower estimates.
A firm's sales as a percentage of total industry sales. Gains in share signal competitive advantage only if they come without sacrificing margins or returns.
nodes.f: share = firm sales / industry sales

nodes.t: The progression from introduction through growth, shakeout and maturity to decline. Appropriate valuation methods, margins and capital needs differ at each stage.
A product becoming undifferentiated so buyers choose mainly on price, compressing margins toward cost of capital. Driven by standardization, new entrants and transparent pricing.
Christensen's term for a cheaper, simpler product that starts in overlooked low-end or new markets and improves until it displaces incumbents, who rationally focus on their best customers.
A market where network effects, scale or data advantages let the leader capture most profits. Valuation then depends heavily on the probability of becoming the leader.
A model, associated with Costco and described by Nick Sleep, in which a firm passes scale savings to customers through lower prices, driving more volume and further savings.
Marathon's framework: high returns attract capital and new supply, which drives returns down, and vice versa. Investors watch industry capex and consolidation rather than demand forecasts.
How well executives allocate capital, execute, communicate and treat shareholders. Judged from track record, incentives, candor about mistakes and per-share results over full cycles.
Philip Fisher's method of learning about a company by talking to customers, suppliers, competitors and former employees. The forerunner of modern channel checks.
Buffett's idea that an investor should stay within businesses they understand well enough to judge. Knowing the boundary matters more than its size.
A business able to reinvest large amounts at high returns on capital for many years, compounding intrinsic value. Its value depends on the length and size of the reinvestment runway.
A troubled company with a plan to restore profitability through new management, restructuring or refinancing. Outcomes are binary and base rates of success are modest.
Investments driven by corporate events such as spin-offs, mergers, restructurings, rights issues or index changes, where value depends more on the event than on the market.
Buying stocks at very low prices relative to assets or normalized earnings, often troubled or unloved. Returns come from mean reversion, with high exposure to value traps.
A style combining growth and value screens, seeking above-average earnings growth at moderate multiples, often using the PEG ratio.
Selling a base product cheaply to lock in high-margin recurring sales of consumables or services. Value rests on the installed base and its attachment rate.
Digital goods such as software and content cost little to serve an extra user once built, so incremental margins can be very high. Competition can push prices toward that low cost.
Expenses are recognized in the same period as the revenues they help produce, which is why assets are depreciated and costs are accrued rather than booked when cash moves.
Accounting's asymmetric tendency to recognize losses when probable but gains only when realized. Leaves book values below economic values for firms with internally built intangibles.

An item is material if omitting or misstating it could change a reasonable investor's decision. Auditors and preparers use it to decide what to disclose and correct; small items can still be material qualitatively.
International Financial Reporting Standards, issued by the IASB and used for listed companies in the EU and many other countries. More principles-based than US GAAP.

Key differences that affect comparisons: IFRS bans LIFO, allows capitalizing development costs, lets impairments reverse, treats nearly all leases as finance leases, and allows interest paid in financing cash flow.
The ASC 606 and IFRS 15 framework: identify the contract, identify performance obligations, set the transaction price, allocate it to obligations, and recognize revenue as each is satisfied.
A distinct promise in a customer contract to transfer a good or service. Revenue is recognized as each obligation is satisfied, at a point in time or over time.
The price at which an entity would sell a good or service separately, used to allocate a bundled contract's price among its performance obligations. Estimates shift revenue between periods.
Parts of a contract price that depend on future events, such as rebates, returns, bonuses or usage fees. Included in revenue only to the extent a significant reversal is unlikely.

Whether a company controls a good before transfer and reports gross revenue as principal, or arranges it for others and reports only its net fee as agent. Changes revenue and margins without changing profit.
Billing a customer and recognizing revenue while the seller keeps physical goods. Allowed only under strict conditions; a recurring red flag in revenue manipulation cases.
Pushing excess inventory onto distributors near period end, often with discounts or return rights, to pull revenue forward. Tends to show up as rising receivables and weaker sales later.

Recognizing revenue progressively as work is performed, measured by inputs such as costs incurred or outputs delivered. Used in construction, defense and services; estimates of total cost drive reported profit.
nodes.f: revenue to date = contract price x costs incurred / total estimated costs

nodes.t: A right to payment for work already performed that is conditional on something other than time, such as further delivery. Rising contract assets relative to revenue warrant scrutiny.
Contracted revenue not yet recognized, including both deferred revenue and unbilled amounts. Current RPO, due within twelve months, is a leading indicator for subscription firms.
Revenue plus the change in deferred revenue, a proxy for amounts invoiced in a period. Popular in software, though shifts in billing terms can distort it.
nodes.f: billings = revenue + change in deferred revenue

nodes.t: The value of orders received but not yet delivered or recognized. Common for industrials and defense; definitions vary and cancellable orders can inflate it.
Orders received divided by revenue billed in a period. Above one means backlog is growing; watched closely in semiconductors, equipment and defense.
nodes.f: book-to-bill = orders / billings

nodes.t: Incremental costs of obtaining a contract, mainly sales commissions, capitalized and amortized over the expected customer life under ASC 340-40. Inflates near-term margins for fast-growing subscription firms.
The US lease standard putting most leases on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and lease liability. Operating leases still show a single straight-line rent expense in the income statement.

The IFRS lease standard treating nearly all leases like financing: depreciation of the asset plus interest on the liability. Raises EBITDA versus US GAAP operating leases and moves the principal part of lease payments into financing cash flow.
The balance sheet asset representing a lessee's right to use a leased item over the lease term, initially equal to the lease liability plus direct costs and prepayments.

The present value of remaining lease payments, discounted at the rate implicit in the lease or the lessee's incremental borrowing rate. Treated as debt by rating agencies and in lease-adjusted leverage.
Selling an owned asset, usually real estate, and leasing it back. Raises cash and can book a gain, but replaces ownership with a long-term rent obligation that behaves like debt.
Debt plus lease liabilities divided by EBITDAR. Lets analysts compare firms that lease assets with firms that own and borrow to fund them.
nodes.f: (debt + lease liabilities) / EBITDAR

nodes.t: A promise to deliver shares once vesting conditions, usually continued service, are met. Expensed at grant-date fair value over the vesting period; always has value unlike an option.
The grant-date fair value of employee options, estimated with Black-Scholes or a lattice model, recognized over the vesting period. Required under ASC 718 and IFRS 2.
An equity award whose payout depends on hitting targets such as TSR, EPS or revenue over several years. The chosen metrics reveal what management is paid to optimize.
Withholding some vesting shares to pay employees' taxes, with the company paying cash to tax authorities. That cash is a real cost of stock pay often reported in financing cash flow.
Outstanding options and unvested awards plus shares available for future grants, as a share of shares outstanding. Measures potential dilution from equity plans.
nodes.f: overhang = (awards outstanding + available for grant) / shares outstanding

nodes.t: Shares granted under equity plans in a year as a percentage of weighted shares outstanding. Shows how fast stock pay dilutes holders absent buybacks.
nodes.f: burn rate = shares granted / weighted average shares

nodes.t: Adding stock-based compensation back to non-GAAP earnings or free cash flow because it is non-cash. It is still a real cost paid in dilution or buyback cash, so add-backs can greatly overstate owner economics.
Disclosure of revenue, profit and assets by operating segment, as defined by how the chief operating decision maker reviews results (ASC 280, IFRS 8). The raw material for sum-of-the-parts work.

Adjustments added to EBITDA for items deemed non-recurring or non-cash, such as restructuring, synergies not yet achieved and stock pay. Aggressive add-backs inflate deal leverage capacity and valuation.
Earnings per share excluding items management labels non-recurring or non-cash, often amortization of acquired intangibles, restructuring and stock pay. Consensus forecasts are usually on this basis.
Growth recomputed at prior-period exchange rates to remove currency translation effects. Helps isolate underlying demand but hides real economic currency exposure.
Revenue growth excluding acquisitions, divestitures and currency effects. Shows whether the existing business is gaining, especially for serial acquirers and roll-ups.
Sales growth from stores open at least a year, excluding new and closed units. Separates demand at existing locations from footprint expansion in retail and restaurants.
Average receivables divided by revenue, times days in the period: how long customers take to pay. Rising DSO can mean looser credit terms or aggressive revenue recognition.
nodes.f: DSO = receivables / revenue x 365

nodes.t: Inventory divided by cost of goods sold, times days: how long stock sits before being sold. A rising figure can warn of slowing demand or obsolete goods.
nodes.f: DIO = inventory / COGS x 365

nodes.t: Payables divided by cost of goods sold, times days: how long the firm takes to pay suppliers. Stretching payables boosts operating cash flow temporarily.
nodes.f: DPO = payables / COGS x 365

nodes.t: Days from paying suppliers to collecting from customers. A shorter or negative cycle means the business funds growth with suppliers' and customers' money.
nodes.f: CCC = DSO + DIO - DPO

nodes.t: A business that collects from customers before paying suppliers, such as many retailers, subscription firms and marketplaces. Growth then releases cash, but a slowdown reverses the effect.

A target level of net working capital agreed in an acquisition; the price is adjusted up or down at closing by the difference from the actual level. Stops sellers draining working capital before closing.
nodes.f: price adjustment = closing NWC - peg

nodes.t: Money owed by customers for goods or services delivered on credit, reported net of an allowance for expected non-payment.
A reserve against receivables that will not be collected. Cutting it relative to receivables lifts earnings and is a classic quiet lever.
a: allowance for credit losses on receivables

nodes.t: Selling receivables to a third party at a discount for immediate cash. Lowers DSO and lifts operating cash flow, so disclosure of its use matters for cash-flow quality.
A bank pays a firm's suppliers early and the firm repays the bank later, letting the firm extend payables. Can make bank debt look like trade payables and flatter operating cash flow.
Reducing inventory's carrying value when it falls below net realizable value due to obsolescence or price declines. Hits gross margin and often follows a demand slowdown.
First-in, first-out: the oldest inventory costs flow to cost of goods sold first. In rising prices it shows higher profits and a balance sheet nearer current cost.
Last-in, first-out: the newest inventory costs flow to cost of goods sold first. Allowed under US GAAP but not IFRS; in rising prices it lowers reported profit and taxes.
The difference between inventory at FIFO and at LIFO cost, disclosed by LIFO users. Adding it back puts LIFO and FIFO firms on a comparable basis; a shrinking reserve can boost margins.
nodes.f: FIFO COGS = LIFO COGS - change in LIFO reserve

nodes.t: Cost of goods sold divided by average inventory: how many times stock is sold and replaced a year. Low or falling turnover can warn of obsolete inventory.
nodes.f: turnover = COGS / average inventory

nodes.t: Gross margin return on inventory investment: gross profit divided by average inventory at cost. Tells a retailer how much margin each unit of inventory earns.
nodes.f: GMROI = gross profit / average inventory cost

nodes.t: Revenue divided by average total assets: how efficiently a firm uses assets to generate sales. A DuPont component that varies widely by industry.
nodes.f: asset turnover = revenue / average total assets

nodes.t: Long-lived tangible assets used in operations, carried at cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment. Gross PP&E versus net PP&E shows how old the asset base is.
Non-physical assets such as patents, customer relationships, software and brands. Mostly recognized only when acquired; internally built ones are expensed and missing from the balance sheet.

Allocating the cost of a finite-lived intangible asset over its useful life, the intangible counterpart of depreciation. Goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles are not amortized under US GAAP for public firms or IFRS.
Amortization of intangibles recognized in acquisitions. Usually excluded from adjusted EPS, defensibly when no reinvestment is needed to maintain them, less so when acquisitions are recurring.

Development costs for internal-use or sale software recorded as an asset once technical feasibility or the application stage is reached, then amortized. Rising capitalization rates flatter operating margins.
Interest on borrowing used to build long-lived assets, added to the asset's cost rather than expensed. It lowers reported interest expense, so coverage ratios should add it back.
An analyst adjustment treating research spending as an investment: capitalizing past R&D as an asset and amortizing it. Raises invested capital and often changes ROIC for intangible-heavy firms.
nodes.f: research asset = sum of unamortized past R&D

nodes.t: An acquisition where the fair value of net identifiable assets exceeds the price paid, producing an immediate gain instead of goodwill. Rare and worth checking for optimistic fair values.
Future tax savings from deductible temporary differences and loss carryforwards. Recognized only to the extent future taxable profit is probable.
Taxes owed in the future because book income currently exceeds taxable income, often from accelerated tax depreciation. A growing firm can defer it for a long time, so it partly behaves like equity.
A reserve reducing deferred tax assets that are unlikely to be used. Releasing it boosts earnings in one period, which analysts usually exclude from run-rate profit.
Past tax losses that can offset future taxable income, lowering cash taxes. Worth valuing separately; ownership changes can limit their use under US Section 382.
Income taxes actually paid in a period, disclosed in the cash flow statement or notes. Differs from book tax expense because of deferrals, credits and timing.
A contract, common in Up-C IPOs, requiring the company to pay pre-IPO owners most of the tax savings it realizes from a basis step-up. A real liability that belongs in the equity bridge.
Possible obligations from lawsuits, guarantees or environmental claims that depend on future events. Accrued if probable and estimable, otherwise disclosed in notes.
The present value of legally required costs to dismantle and restore sites at the end of an asset's life, such as wells, mines and nuclear plants. A debt-like item for energy and utility valuation.
Costs of layoffs, closures and reorganizations, typically excluded from adjusted results. When they recur every year they are part of the normal cost of running the business.
Taking unusually large write-offs and reserves in one period, often after a CEO change or in a bad year, so that later periods look better as charges reverse or costs disappear.
Over-reserving in good times, then releasing reserves to smooth earnings in weak periods. Hard to see except through reserve trends relative to the underlying exposure.

Reporting defined benefit plans: the funded status sits on the balance sheet, while service cost, interest cost and expected asset returns run through income. Assumption changes can move earnings and equity materially.
nodes.f: funded status = plan assets - DBO

nodes.t: The present value of pension benefits employees have earned, discounted at high-grade corporate bond yields. Rising rates shrink it, so funded status depends heavily on rates.

Gains and losses that bypass net income and go straight to equity, such as currency translation, some securities, hedge results and pension remeasurements. Accumulated OCI can hide large unrealized losses.
Cumulative net income kept in the business after dividends since inception. Large deficits signal a history of losses, while large balances show the capacity to pay.
nodes.f: RE_end = RE_begin + net income - dividends

nodes.t: Shares a company has repurchased and holds rather than retiring, shown as a reduction of equity at cost. Large buybacks can push book equity negative.
The share of a consolidated subsidiary owned by outsiders. Because 100 percent of the subsidiary's EBITDA is consolidated, its value must be subtracted when bridging from EV to the parent's equity.

Accounting for a stake typically of 20 to 50 percent: the investment is carried at cost plus the share of profits, with no revenue or EBITDA consolidated. Such stakes are added separately in the equity bridge.
Statements combining a parent and all entities it controls as one economic unit, line by line, with intercompany items eliminated and outside owners shown as noncontrolling interest.

An entity controlled through contracts rather than voting equity, which must be consolidated by its primary beneficiary. Used in structured finance and in offshore structures for some Chinese listings.
The three-level ranking of fair value inputs: Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 model-based unobservable inputs. Level 3 marks deserve the most skepticism.
Debt securities a bank intends to hold to maturity, carried at amortized cost so price changes do not hit earnings or equity. Large unrealized losses can be invisible until assets must be sold.
Debt securities carried at fair value with unrealized gains and losses in other comprehensive income rather than net income. Hits book equity but not reported earnings.
Converting foreign subsidiaries' results into the reporting currency, which changes reported figures without changing local performance. Translation gains and losses on net assets go to OCI.

Rules that let a company match the timing of gains and losses on a hedge with the item hedged, so derivative swings do not create artificial earnings volatility. Requires documentation and effectiveness.
A component disposed of or held for sale that represents a strategic shift, reported separately below continuing operations. Results of continuing operations are the run-rate base.
Assets expected to be sold within a year, carried at the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell, and no longer depreciated.
The assumption that a company will keep operating for the foreseeable future. An auditor's going concern warning signals substantial doubt about survival over the next year.
The auditor's conclusion on whether statements are fairly presented: unqualified, qualified, adverse or disclaimer. Critical audit matters in the report flag the areas of most judgment.
A deficiency in internal control over financial reporting with a reasonable possibility of a material misstatement. Disclosed under Sarbanes-Oxley and often precedes restatements.
Revising previously issued financial statements to correct a material error. Usually damages credibility and is followed by weak returns, regulatory scrutiny and management turnover.
Replacing the external auditor, especially abruptly, with a smaller firm, or after disagreements. A red flag requiring an 8-K disclosure in the US.
Dealings between a company and its insiders, their families or affiliated entities. Must be disclosed; large or recurring ones can transfer value away from outside shareholders.
Cash held for a specific purpose, such as collateral, escrow or regulatory reserves, that cannot fund operations or be distributed. Excluded from net debt calculations by careful analysts.

Warning signs that reported earnings overstate economics: receivables or inventory outgrowing sales, profits without cash, rising capitalization, frequent one-offs, auditor changes, late filings and complex related-party dealings. Each warrants questions, not conclusions.

Using accounting judgment or timing of real decisions to steer reported results toward targets, from reserve timing to cutting R&D at quarter end. Within GAAP it is legal but reduces earnings quality.
Receivables rising much faster than sales, lifting DSO. Can mean extended terms, weaker customers or revenue booked before it is earned; inventory outgrowing sales is the parallel warning.
nodes.f: gap = receivables growth - revenue growth

nodes.t: Recording ordinary expenses as assets so they hit earnings slowly through amortization and leave operating cash flow for investing cash flow. A rising capitalized share of spending lifts both margins and reported operating cash flow.

How items are split among operating, investing and financing cash flows. Choices such as factoring, supply chain finance, capitalized costs and IFRS interest placement can flatter operating cash flow without changing total cash.
The gap between earnings and operating cash flow scaled by average net operating assets. High accruals suggest earnings that are less likely to persist.
nodes.f: accrual ratio = (net income - CFO - CFI) / average net operating assets

nodes.t: Sloan (1996) found that firms with high accruals subsequently underperform those with low accruals, because investors fail to see that accrual-driven earnings persist less than cash earnings.
The difference between adjusted and GAAP earnings. A wide or widening gap, especially from recurring items like stock pay, restructuring or acquired amortization, points to lower earnings quality.
nodes.f: gap = adjusted earnings / GAAP earnings - 1

nodes.t: Booking revenue from transactions where cash flows back to the customer through offsetting purchases, investments or loans, so no real economic sale occurs. Inflates revenue and growth.
Ohlson's (1980) logit model of bankruptcy probability using size, leverage, working capital, liquidity, profitability, funds from operations and recent losses. A complement to the Altman Z-score.

A public research report by an investor short a stock, alleging fraud, accounting problems or overvaluation. Can move prices sharply; claims need independent checking since authors profit from declines.
Current assets divided by current liabilities, a basic liquidity test. The stricter quick ratio drops inventory and prepaid items; very high values can also mean idle capital.
nodes.f: current ratio = current assets / current liabilities; quick ratio = (cash + securities + receivables) / current liabilities

nodes.t: Total debt divided by shareholders' equity, in book or market value terms. Book values become meaningless when buybacks or losses push equity near zero, so market values or debt to EBITDA often work better.
nodes.f: D/E = total debt / equity

nodes.t: Earnings before fixed charges divided by interest plus lease payments and sometimes required principal. Stricter than interest coverage for lease-heavy firms; also a common loan covenant.
nodes.f: FCCR = (EBITDA - capex - cash taxes) / (interest + scheduled principal)

nodes.t: Funds from operations, roughly operating cash flow before working capital, divided by adjusted debt. A core rating agency leverage metric; higher is stronger.
nodes.f: FFO / debt

nodes.t: How many months a loss-making company can operate before cash runs out, given its current burn. A short runway forces a raise, often on poor terms.
nodes.f: runway = cash / monthly net burn

nodes.t: Net income divided by average total assets. The core profitability measure for banks, where small differences in ROA translate into large differences in ROE because of leverage.
nodes.f: ROA = net income / average total assets

nodes.t: EBIT divided by capital employed, usually total assets less current liabilities. A pre-tax cousin of ROIC widely used in Europe and in capital-intensive industries.
nodes.f: ROCE = EBIT / (total assets - current liabilities)

nodes.t: Cash return on capital invested: cash flow divided by gross capital invested, a Deutsche Bank method that treats intangibles and leases consistently across firms.
Gross profit divided by total assets. Novy-Marx (2013) showed it predicts returns about as well as book to market does, and is cleaner than net income because it sits high in the income statement.
nodes.f: GP/A = (revenue - COGS) / total assets

nodes.t: Revenue minus cost of goods sold. Shows what remains to cover operating expenses and reflects pricing power and production costs.
nodes.f: gross profit = revenue - COGS

nodes.t: Earnings before interest and taxes, usually operating income adjusted for non-operating items. Captures operating performance after depreciation and amortization, independent of financing.
nodes.f: EBIT = revenue - COGS - opex - D&A
