nodes.t: The residual Brinson term from overweighting segments where the manager also selected well, or underweighting where selection was strong. Often folded into selection in practice.
nodes.f: (w_p - w_b) x (R_p,segment - R_b,segment)

nodes.t: A refinement of Brinson attribution that measures allocation relative to total benchmark return, so overweighting a segment that rose less than the overall benchmark counts as negative allocation.
Attributing returns to exposures to risk model factors times factor returns, plus a specific return. It separates style bets from stock selection better than sector-based methods.
nodes.f: R = sum of x_k x f_k + specific return

nodes.t: Methods that combine single-period arithmetic attribution effects into multi-period totals that add up to compounded active return, such as Carino or Menchero smoothing.
Separating the return effects of currency exposure and hedging decisions from local market allocation and selection in global portfolios, as in the Karnosky-Singer framework.
Sharpe's (1992) method of regressing a fund's returns on style index returns with weights constrained to be positive and sum to one, inferring the fund's effective style mix without holdings.
Classifying a portfolio's style from the characteristics of its actual holdings, such as size and valuation. More accurate than returns-based analysis but needs timely holdings data.
Jensen's (1968) intercept from regressing a portfolio's excess returns on the market's excess return: the return beyond what CAPM predicts for its beta. Multi-factor versions use more factors.
nodes.f: alpha = R_p - [rf + beta x (R_m - rf)]

nodes.t: Excess return per unit of beta, suitable for judging a portfolio that is one part of a larger diversified holding, since it ignores diversifiable risk.
nodes.f: Treynor = (R_p - rf) / beta_p

nodes.t: Modigliani and Modigliani's (1997) risk-adjusted return: the return a portfolio would have earned if levered or delevered to the benchmark's volatility. Same ranking as Sharpe but in return units.
nodes.f: M2 = rf + Sharpe_p x sigma_benchmark

nodes.t: Jensen's alpha divided by residual volatility, the risk-adjusted value of a manager's stock selection. It guides how much to allocate to an active manager in the Treynor-Black model.
nodes.f: AR = alpha / sigma(residual)

nodes.t: Keating and Shadwick's (2002) ratio of probability-weighted gains above a threshold to probability-weighted losses below it. It uses the whole return distribution rather than mean and variance.
nodes.f: Omega(L) = integral above L of (1 - F(r)) dr / integral below L of F(r) dr

nodes.t: The ratio of a fund's return to its benchmark's return in periods when the benchmark rose (upside capture) or fell (downside capture). Low downside with decent upside capture signals defensive skill or style.
nodes.f: upside capture = fund return in up periods / benchmark return in up periods

nodes.t: The share of trades, positions or periods that are profitable or beat the benchmark. Meaningful only with the payoff ratio, since a low hit rate with large winners can be highly profitable.
nodes.f: hit rate = winning trades / total trades

nodes.t: Average gain on winning trades divided by average loss on losing trades. Together with hit rate it determines expectancy and characterizes a manager's style.
nodes.f: expectancy = hit rate x avg win - (1 - hit rate) x avg loss

nodes.t: A return that removes the effect of the timing and size of external cash flows by compounding sub-period returns between flows. The GIPS standard for judging manager skill.
nodes.f: TWR = product of (1 + r_i) - 1

nodes.t: The internal rate of return on a portfolio's actual cash flows, reflecting both investment performance and the investor's timing of contributions and withdrawals.
An approximation of time-weighted return over a period that weights each cash flow by the fraction of the period it was invested, avoiding daily valuations.
nodes.f: R = (EMV - BMV - CF) / (BMV + sum of w_i x CF_i)

nodes.t: The shortfall of investors' money-weighted returns in a fund versus the fund's time-weighted return, caused by buying after strong performance and selling after weak performance.
nodes.f: gap = MWR - TWR

nodes.t: The CFA Institute's Global Investment Performance Standards for calculating and presenting investment performance fairly, requiring composites of all similar portfolios and time-weighted returns.

Cremers and Petajisto's (2009) measure of how much a portfolio's holdings differ from its benchmark: half the sum of absolute weight differences. Low active share with high fees signals closet indexing.
nodes.f: Active share = 0.5 x sum of |w_p,i - w_b,i|

nodes.t: Whether past winners keep winning. For mutual funds, persistence is weak and mostly among the worst performers; Carhart (1997) found momentum explains much of the rest.
Choosing external managers through investment and operational due diligence, judging process, people, edge, capacity and fees rather than chasing recent returns.

Reviewing a fund's non-investment infrastructure: valuation, custody, administration, trade processing, compliance, cybersecurity and service providers. Many hedge fund failures are operational rather than investment losses.
The inflation of hedge fund database returns because managers report voluntarily and often add their track record only after good early performance, importing a flattering history.
An average of reporting hedge funds' returns by strategy. Survivorship, backfill and smoothing make such indices overstate returns and understate risk compared with investable experience.
Gross returns are before management and performance fees; net returns are what investors keep. With hedge fund fees, a large share of gross alpha can go to the manager.
A commission charged on buying (front-end) or selling (back-end) mutual fund shares, used to pay intermediaries. Breakpoints reduce it for larger purchases.
An annual fee paid from US mutual fund assets for distribution and marketing, included in the expense ratio.
Engle's (1982) autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity model, in which today's variance depends on past squared shocks. It formalized volatility clustering and led to GARCH.
nodes.f: sigma_t^2 = omega + sum of alpha_i x e_(t-i)^2

nodes.t: Nelson's (1991) exponential GARCH, which models log variance so it stays positive and lets negative shocks raise volatility more than positive ones.
nodes.f: ln sigma_t^2 = omega + beta ln sigma_(t-1)^2 + alpha |z| + gamma z

nodes.t: Glosten, Jagannathan and Runkle's (1993) GARCH variant that adds an extra term for negative shocks, capturing the asymmetric response of volatility to bad news.
nodes.f: sigma_t^2 = omega + (alpha + gamma x I[e<0]) e_(t-1)^2 + beta sigma_(t-1)^2

nodes.t: Corsi's (2009) heterogeneous autoregressive model that forecasts realized volatility from its daily, weekly and monthly averages. Simple, hard to beat, and widely used with intraday data.
nodes.f: RV_(t+1) = b0 + b_d RV_t + b_w RV_week + b_m RV_month + e

nodes.t: Engle's (2002) dynamic conditional correlation model: fit univariate GARCH to each asset, then model time-varying correlations of the standardized residuals with a small number of parameters.
A model with an unobserved state that evolves over time and observations that depend on it, estimated by the Kalman filter for linear Gaussian cases. Used for time-varying betas and trend extraction.
nodes.f: x_t = F x_(t-1) + w_t; y_t = H x_t + v_t

nodes.t: A time series in which the current value is a linear function of its own past values plus noise. An AR(1) is stationary if the coefficient's absolute value is below one.
nodes.f: AR(1): y_t = c + phi y_(t-1) + e_t

nodes.t: A time series modeled as a linear combination of current and past noise terms. Its autocorrelation cuts off after the order q, a signature used in model identification.
nodes.f: MA(1): y_t = mu + e_t + theta e_(t-1)

nodes.t: A model combining autoregressive and moving average terms for a stationary series. Box and Jenkins popularized identifying the orders from autocorrelation patterns.
nodes.f: y_t = c + sum phi_i y_(t-i) + e_t + sum theta_j e_(t-j)

nodes.t: An ARMA model applied to a series after differencing d times to remove a unit root. Prices are often modeled as ARIMA(0,1,0), a random walk.
The correlation of a series with its own lagged values. Return autocorrelation signals predictability or stale prices; autocorrelated residuals invalidate standard errors.
nodes.f: rho_k = cov(y_t, y_(t-k)) / var(y_t)

nodes.t: The correlation between a series and a lag after removing the effect of shorter lags. Its cutoff identifies the order of an autoregressive model.
A test of whether a group of autocorrelations up to a chosen lag are jointly zero, used to check residuals for leftover structure or returns for predictability.
nodes.f: Q = T(T+2) x sum over k of rho_k^2 / (T - k), chi-square with h df

nodes.t: A test for first-order autocorrelation in regression residuals. Values near 2 suggest none; values well below 2 suggest positive autocorrelation, a sign of misspecification or spurious regression.
nodes.f: DW approx 2 x (1 - rho_1)

nodes.t: A series of uncorrelated random shocks with zero mean and constant variance. A well-specified model should leave white noise residuals.

A process in which each value equals the previous one plus an unpredictable shock, so changes are unforecastable and variance grows with time. A benchmark model for asset prices and a hard-to-beat forecast.
nodes.f: p_t = p_(t-1) + e_t

nodes.t: Fama's (1970) proposition that prices fully reflect available information, in weak, semi-strong and strong forms. Any test is joint with an asset pricing model, so anomalies may reflect mispricing or a bad model.

Granger and Newbold (1974) showed that regressing one trending, nonstationary series on another often yields high R squared and significant t-statistics even when they are unrelated. Difference the series or test for cointegration.
A sudden change in a model's parameters, such as a mean, volatility or beta, at some date. Ignoring breaks biases estimates and can make a series look nonstationary.
An F-test of whether regression coefficients differ before and after a specified break date. It requires the date to be chosen in advance; unknown dates need sup-F style tests.
A test that tracks the cumulative sum of recursive residuals and flags parameter instability when it crosses boundaries. Used for monitoring models and strategies for breaks.
A stationarity test whose null hypothesis is that the series is stationary, the reverse of the ADF test. Using both helps distinguish stationary, unit root and inconclusive cases.
A VAR in differences for cointegrated series that adds an error correction term, so variables pull back toward their long-run equilibrium after deviations.
nodes.f: dY_t = alpha beta' Y_(t-1) + sum Gamma_i dY_(t-i) + e_t

nodes.t: A maximum likelihood test for the number of cointegrating relationships among several series, using trace and maximum eigenvalue statistics.
A two-step cointegration test: regress one series on another, then apply a unit root test to the residuals with adjusted critical values. Simple but handles only one relationship.
A continuous-time mean-reverting process in which the drift pulls the variable toward a long-run mean at a speed theta. The standard model for spreads in pairs trading and for short rates in Vasicek.
nodes.f: dx = theta (mu - x) dt + sigma dW

nodes.t: The expected time for a deviation from equilibrium to shrink by half, estimated from an AR(1) or OU fit. Guides holding periods and stop rules for spread trades.
nodes.f: half-life = -ln(2) / ln(phi) for AR(1); ln(2) / theta for OU

nodes.t: A measure of long-range dependence: 0.5 indicates a random walk, above 0.5 persistence or trending, below 0.5 anti-persistence. Estimates are noisy and biased in short samples.
Autocorrelations that decay slowly, hyperbolically rather than exponentially, as seen in volatility. Modeled with fractional integration such as ARFIMA or FIGARCH.
Differencing a series by a non-integer order d to make it stationary while keeping as much memory of levels as possible. Lopez de Prado promotes it for machine learning features.
nodes.f: (1 - L)^d x_t with 0 < d < 1

nodes.t: Non-constant variance of regression errors. It leaves OLS coefficients unbiased but makes standard errors wrong, so robust errors or weighted least squares are needed.
White's (1980) heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors, which remain valid when error variance differs across observations but assume no autocorrelation.
Standard errors that allow correlation of errors within groups, such as by firm or by time. Petersen (2009) showed finance panels often need clustering by both, or t-statistics are badly overstated.

Fama and MacBeth's (1973) two-step method: run a cross-sectional regression of returns on characteristics or betas each period, then average the coefficients and use their time-series variation for standard errors.
nodes.f: t = mean(lambda_t) / (sd(lambda_t) / sqrt(T))

nodes.t: High correlation among regressors, which makes individual coefficients unstable and imprecise even when the overall fit is good. Common with overlapping factor definitions.
A diagnostic for multicollinearity: how much a coefficient's variance is inflated because its regressor is explained by the others. Values above about 5 to 10 are often flagged.
Bias in a regression coefficient when a left-out variable both affects the outcome and is correlated with an included regressor, so the included one absorbs its effect.
nodes.f: bias = beta_omitted x cov(x, z) / var(x)

nodes.t: Correlation between a regressor and the error term, from omitted variables, reverse causality or measurement error, which makes OLS estimates biased and inconsistent for causal effects.
Estimating a causal effect using a variable that moves the regressor but affects the outcome only through it. Weak instruments give biased, imprecise estimates.
nodes.f: IV estimate = cov(z, y) / cov(z, x); 2SLS in general

nodes.t: The causal effect that an instrumental variables estimate identifies: the effect for units whose treatment status is changed by the instrument, which may differ from the population average.
Measurement error in a regressor, which biases its coefficient toward zero. In Fama-MacBeth tests using estimated betas this attenuates risk premia, one reason to use portfolios.
nodes.f: plim beta_hat = beta x var(x) / (var(x) + var(error))

nodes.t: Bias from analyzing a sample that is not representative because of how units entered it, such as surviving funds, listed firms or chosen backtests. Survivorship bias is one form.
Capping extreme values of a variable at chosen percentiles, such as 1% and 99%, to limit outliers' influence on means and regressions. Trimming drops them instead.
Estimators that stay reliable when data contain outliers or depart from assumptions, such as the median, median absolute deviation and Huber regression.
nodes.f: MAD = median(|x - median(x)|)

nodes.t: Using multi-period returns that share periods, such as monthly samples of annual returns, which creates strong autocorrelation and makes naive t-statistics far too large.
Regressing future returns on a current predictor such as dividend yield or the term spread. Persistent predictors and overlapping horizons create bias and inflated significance.
Stambaugh's (1999) finite-sample bias in predictive regressions when the predictor is persistent and its shocks correlate with return shocks, as with valuation ratios. It overstates predictability.
Bias when prices are recorded at different times or are stale, which induces spurious autocorrelation and lead-lag effects and understates betas and correlations of illiquid assets.
Dimson's (1979) beta estimate for thinly traded assets that sums coefficients on lagged, current and leading market returns, correcting the downward bias from stale prices.
nodes.f: beta = sum over k of b_k from regressing r_t on r_m,t-k

nodes.t: A beta forecast shrunk toward one, because estimated betas mean-revert. The Blume adjustment is the widely quoted version; Vasicek shrinkage weights by estimation precision.
nodes.f: Blume: adjusted beta = 0.67 x raw beta + 0.33

nodes.t: Tibshirani's (1996) regression with an L1 penalty on coefficients, which shrinks many exactly to zero and so selects variables. Selection is unstable with correlated predictors.
nodes.f: min sum (y - Xb)^2 + lambda x sum |b_j|

nodes.t: Rotating correlated variables into uncorrelated components ordered by the variance they explain. In rates, the first three components resemble level, slope and curvature.
nodes.f: eigen-decomposition: Sigma = V Lambda V'

nodes.t: Distance of an observation from the mean scaled by the covariance matrix, so unusual combinations of moves count as extreme even if each move alone is modest.
nodes.f: d^2 = (x - mu)' Sigma^-1 (x - mu)

nodes.t: Koenker and Bassett's (1978) method of estimating how predictors shift chosen quantiles of the outcome, not just its mean. Used to model tail risk and conditional VaR directly.
nodes.f: minimize sum of rho_tau(y - Xb), the check loss

nodes.t: Giving observations weights that decay geometrically with age, set by a half-life or decay factor, so estimates adapt to recent data. The half-life trades responsiveness against noise.
nodes.f: weight_k = lambda^k; half-life = ln(0.5) / ln(lambda)

nodes.t: Re-estimating a model on a fixed-length window that moves forward through time, letting parameters change. Expanding windows instead keep all history and adapt more slowly.
The gap between arithmetic and geometric average returns caused by volatility: compounding means a loss requires a larger gain to recover. Leverage and high volatility magnify it.
nodes.f: geometric mean approx arithmetic mean - sigma^2 / 2

nodes.t: The arithmetic mean averages period returns; the geometric mean is the constant rate that compounds to the realized ending value. The geometric is lower whenever returns vary and is what investors actually earn.
nodes.f: G = [product of (1 + r_i)]^(1/n) - 1

nodes.t: Stein's (1956) and James and Stein's (1961) result that, when estimating three or more means, shrinking each sample mean toward a common value lowers total squared error. The basis of Bayes-Stein return estimates.
nodes.f: mu_JS = mean_bar + (1 - c) x (mu_i - mean_bar)

nodes.t: Resampling contiguous blocks of observations rather than single points, which preserves short-range dependence such as autocorrelation and volatility clustering. Block length is a key tuning choice.
A bootstrap for regressions with heteroskedastic errors that keeps each observation's regressors and multiplies its residual by a random sign or weight, preserving the variance pattern.

An interval built from the distribution of a statistic across bootstrap resamples, using percentiles or bias-corrected versions such as BCa. Useful for Sharpe ratios and other statistics without simple formulas.
White's (2000) bootstrap test of whether the best of many tested strategies truly beats a benchmark once the search across all of them is accounted for.
Hansen's (2005) test for superior predictive ability, a refinement of White's reality check that is less affected by including poor or irrelevant strategies in the comparison set.

A bootstrap multiple-testing procedure that controls the family-wise error rate while accounting for dependence among test statistics, identifying which of many strategies are individually significant.
Estimating the bias and variance of a statistic by recomputing it with each observation, or block, left out in turn. A precursor to the bootstrap.

A test that builds the null distribution by randomly shuffling labels or timing, such as signal dates against returns, and comparing the actual statistic with the shuffled ones. Few distributional assumptions.
The updated probability distribution of a parameter after combining the prior with the likelihood of observed data via Bayes' rule. It expresses all remaining uncertainty.
nodes.f: posterior proportional to likelihood x prior

nodes.t: A prior that, combined with a given likelihood, yields a posterior in the same family, such as beta with binomial or normal with normal, so updating has a closed form.
The conjugate model for success rates: a beta prior on the probability updated by counts of hits and misses. A natural way to estimate a trader's or signal's true hit rate from short records.
nodes.f: Beta(a, b) prior + k hits in n gives Beta(a + k, b + n - k)

nodes.t: A Bayesian interval containing a parameter with a stated posterior probability. Unlike a frequentist confidence interval, it supports the direct statement that the parameter lies inside with that probability.

Algorithms such as Metropolis-Hastings and Gibbs sampling that draw from a posterior distribution by constructing a Markov chain whose long-run distribution is the target, used when posteriors lack closed forms.
A Bayesian model in which group-level parameters, such as each fund's alpha, are drawn from a common distribution, so estimates borrow strength across groups through partial pooling.
Estimating the prior from the data itself, such as the cross-sectional spread of fund alphas, then shrinking each estimate toward the group. Practical shrinkage without a fully specified prior.
Weighting forecasts from several models by their posterior probabilities instead of choosing one, which accounts for model uncertainty and usually improves out-of-sample accuracy.
nodes.f: p(y | data) = sum of p(y | M_k) x p(M_k | data)

nodes.t: The ratio of the probability of the data under two competing models, which multiplies prior odds into posterior odds. A Bayesian alternative to p-values for model comparison.
nodes.f: BF = p(data | M1) / p(data | M2)

nodes.t: The distribution of future observations after integrating over parameter uncertainty in the posterior. It is wider than plugging in point estimates, which matters for portfolio choice.
The default claim a test tries to reject, such as zero alpha or no predictability. Failing to reject it is not evidence that it is true, especially with low power.
Rejecting a true null hypothesis, a false positive such as declaring a worthless strategy profitable. Its rate is the significance level, which inflates when many tests are run.
Failing to reject a false null hypothesis, a false negative such as discarding a genuinely skilled manager. Its probability is one minus statistical power.
The probability that a test detects a true effect of a given size. Return data are so noisy that confirming a modest Sharpe ratio requires many years, so most track records have low power.
nodes.f: power = 1 - P(type II error)

nodes.t: The magnitude of an effect, such as an alpha or Sharpe ratio, as distinct from its statistical significance. Large samples can make trivial effects significant; small ones can hide large effects.
A range constructed so that, across repeated samples, a stated share of such ranges would contain the true parameter. Wide intervals around estimated returns warn against precise conclusions.
nodes.f: estimate +/- z x standard error

nodes.t: Controlling the family-wise error rate by testing each of m hypotheses at significance level alpha divided by m. Simple but conservative, especially with correlated tests.
nodes.f: per-test level = alpha / m

nodes.t: Trying many specifications, samples, filters or variable definitions and reporting those that reach significance, which makes p-values meaningless. Backtest tuning is a common form.
Lo's (2002) result on the sampling uncertainty of an estimated Sharpe ratio, which is large for typical track records and grows with autocorrelation, skewness and fat tails.
nodes.f: SE(SR) approx sqrt((1 + 0.5 x SR^2) / T) for iid returns

nodes.t: Bailey and Lopez de Prado's (2012) probability that a strategy's true Sharpe ratio exceeds a benchmark, given the observed Sharpe, track length, skewness and kurtosis.
nodes.f: PSR = Phi[(SR - SR*) sqrt(T - 1) / sqrt(1 - g3 SR + (g4 - 1)/4 SR^2)]

nodes.t: Bailey and Lopez de Prado's estimate of how many observations are needed to be confident at a given level that a strategy's true Sharpe exceeds a threshold. Negative skew and fat tails lengthen it.
A test of normality based on sample skewness and kurtosis. Daily asset returns reject normality almost always, mainly through excess kurtosis.
nodes.f: JB = (n/6) x [S^2 + (K - 3)^2 / 4], chi-square with 2 df

nodes.t: A nonparametric test comparing a sample's empirical distribution with a reference distribution, or two samples with each other, using the largest gap between cumulative distribution functions.
nodes.f: D = sup |F_n(x) - F(x)|

nodes.t: Comparing nested models by twice the difference in their maximized log-likelihoods, which is approximately chi-square distributed with degrees of freedom equal to the number of restrictions.
nodes.f: LR = 2 x (lnL_unrestricted - lnL_restricted)

nodes.t: Testing restrictions on parameters using only the unrestricted estimates and their covariance, such as whether several coefficients are jointly zero. The GRS test of zero alphas is a finite-sample relative.
nodes.f: W = (R b - r)' [R V R']^-1 (R b - r)

nodes.t: Gibbons, Ross and Shanken's (1989) test of whether the alphas of a set of test portfolios are jointly zero under a factor model, used to judge whether a model prices the cross-section.
A test of whether a group of regression coefficients are jointly zero, or whether one model fits significantly better than a nested one, comparing residual sums of squares.
nodes.f: F = [(RSS_r - RSS_u)/q] / [RSS_u/(n - k)]

nodes.t: A model selection score that rewards fit and penalizes parameters, estimating relative out-of-sample prediction error. Lower is better; it tends to pick larger models than BIC.
nodes.f: AIC = 2k - 2 lnL

nodes.t: Schwarz's model selection score with a heavier parameter penalty that grows with sample size, so it favors more parsimonious models and is consistent for the true model when it is among the candidates.
nodes.f: BIC = k ln(n) - 2 lnL

nodes.t: Choosing parameter values that make the observed data most probable under the model. Efficient when the model is correct; misspecified distributions can still give consistent estimates via quasi-likelihood.
nodes.f: theta_hat = argmax sum ln f(x_i | theta)

nodes.t: Hansen's (1982) estimation method that chooses parameters to make sample moment conditions, such as pricing errors, as close to zero as possible. Standard for testing asset pricing models with a stochastic discount factor.
nodes.f: min g(theta)' W g(theta), with g the sample moments

nodes.t: Estimating a causal effect by comparing the change in outcomes for a treated group before and after an event with the change for an untreated group. Relies on parallel trends without treatment.
nodes.f: DiD = (Y_treat,after - Y_treat,before) - (Y_control,after - Y_control,before)

nodes.t: Estimating a causal effect by comparing units just above and just below a threshold that determines treatment, such as index inclusion cutoffs, where units near the line are otherwise similar.

Abadie's method of building a weighted combination of untreated units that tracks the treated unit before an event, then using it as the counterfactual afterward. Suited to single treated units such as a country.

Matching or weighting treated and untreated units by their estimated probability of treatment given observed characteristics, to mimic a randomized comparison. It cannot fix bias from unobserved confounders.
An event or rule that assigns treatment as if at random, such as a regulatory change or index reconstitution, letting researchers estimate causal effects without a designed experiment.
A directed acyclic graph whose arrows encode assumed causal links among variables. It shows which variables to control for and which to leave alone to estimate a causal effect.

Pearl's rule for choosing control variables: adjust for a set that blocks every non-causal path from treatment to outcome that enters the treatment through an arrow, without including descendants of the treatment.
Spurious association created by conditioning on a variable caused by both the treatment and the outcome, such as studying only funds that survived. Controlling for more variables can make bias worse.
Rerunning a causal or event analysis on fake event dates, untreated groups or outcomes that should not respond. Finding effects there suggests the main result is spurious.
A relationship that holds within every subgroup reversing or vanishing when the groups are combined, because group sizes differ. Common in aggregated performance and attribution data.
Extreme observations tend to be followed by less extreme ones because part of any extreme result is luck. Explains why top-ranked funds and estimated betas tend to drift toward average.
The symmetric bell-shaped distribution fully described by mean and variance. Convenient for risk models, but daily asset returns show far more extreme moves than it implies.
nodes.f: f(x) = exp(-(x - mu)^2 / (2 sigma^2)) / (sigma sqrt(2 pi))

nodes.t: The distribution of a variable whose logarithm is normal. Black-Scholes assumes prices are lognormal, which keeps them positive and makes compounded returns normal.
nodes.f: E(X) = exp(mu + sigma^2 / 2)

nodes.t: A symmetric distribution with heavier tails than the normal, controlled by degrees of freedom. Often used in VaR and GARCH models to capture fat-tailed returns.
nodes.f: excess kurtosis = 6 / (v - 4) for v > 4

nodes.t: Sums or averages of many independent finite-variance variables approach a normal distribution. Convergence is slow with fat tails and fails with infinite variance, which matters for aggregated returns.
Sample averages converge to the expected value as the sample grows. It applies across many independent bets, not necessarily to one investor's path through time, which is where ergodicity matters.

The number of independent observations a dependent dataset is worth. Autocorrelation, overlapping returns and few independent regimes make long histories far less informative than their length suggests.
nodes.f: AR(1) case: n_eff approx n x (1 - rho) / (1 + rho)

nodes.t: Learning a mapping from inputs to known targets using labeled examples, then predicting targets for new inputs. Return forecasting and default prediction are supervised problems.

Finding structure in unlabeled data, such as clusters, latent factors or anomalies, without a target variable. Used in finance for regime detection, stock clustering and statistical factor extraction.
Learning representations by predicting parts of the data from other parts, such as the next token or a masked value, so the labels come from the data itself. The basis of language model pretraining.
The portion of data a model's parameters are fitted on. In time series it must precede the validation and test periods to avoid leakage.
Data held out from training and used to tune hyperparameters and choose among models. Repeated use makes it partly in-sample.
Data kept untouched until final evaluation. It gives an unbiased estimate of performance only if it is used once, after all modeling choices are fixed.
Partitioning data into training, validation and test sets. For market data the split should be chronological, with gaps between segments so overlapping labels do not leak.
A setting chosen before training rather than learned from the data, such as tree depth, learning rate or penalty strength.
Searching over hyperparameter values to maximize validation performance. Extensive tuning on financial data is a form of multiple testing and inflates backtest results.
Evaluating every combination from a predefined grid of hyperparameter values. Simple but expensive, and wasteful when only a few hyperparameters matter.
Sampling hyperparameter combinations at random from specified ranges. Bergstra and Bengio (2012) showed it usually finds good settings faster than grid search.
Hyperparameter search that fits a surrogate model, often a Gaussian process, to past trials and picks the next trial with an acquisition function that balances exploration and exploitation.
A function scoring how far predictions are from targets; training minimizes it. The choice encodes what errors cost, for example squared versus absolute error.
The quantity an optimizer minimizes or maximizes, typically the loss plus regularization penalties. In trading research it may be a utility or risk-adjusted return target.
Average of squared prediction errors. Penalizes large misses heavily, and its minimizer is the conditional mean.
nodes.f: MSE = (1/n) x sum of (y - yhat)^2

nodes.t: Square root of mean squared error, expressed in the units of the target, so it reads as a typical error size.
nodes.f: RMSE = sqrt(MSE)

nodes.t: Average absolute prediction error. Less sensitive to outliers than squared error, and its minimizer is the conditional median.
nodes.f: MAE = (1/n) x sum of abs(y - yhat)

nodes.t: Classification loss equal to the negative log probability assigned to the true class. Rewards confident correct probabilities and punishes confident mistakes severely.
nodes.f: L = -sum of y x ln(p)

nodes.t: Loss that is quadratic for small errors and linear for large ones, combining squared-error efficiency near zero with absolute-error robustness to outliers such as bad ticks.
Asymmetric absolute loss whose minimizer is a chosen quantile of the target distribution. Used to forecast value at risk and prediction intervals.
nodes.f: L = max(q x e, (q - 1) x e), where e = y - yhat

nodes.t: Classification loss used by support vector machines that is zero once a point is classified correctly with enough margin and grows linearly otherwise.
nodes.f: L = max(0, 1 - y x f(x))

nodes.t: Iterative optimization that moves parameters against the gradient of the loss, scaled by a learning rate, until the loss stops falling.
nodes.f: theta_new = theta - learning rate x gradient of loss

nodes.t: Gradient descent using gradients from small random batches instead of the full dataset. Each step is cheap, and the noise can help escape poor regions of the loss surface.
Step size for each gradient update. Too high and training diverges; too low and it crawls or stalls. Usually decayed during training.
Adaptive optimizer of Kingma and Ba (2014) that scales each parameter's step using running averages of its gradients and squared gradients. The default for most neural networks.
The subset of training examples used for one gradient update. Batch size trades gradient noise against hardware efficiency.
Halting training when validation performance stops improving, a cheap regularizer that limits the effective complexity of the model.
When a model is too simple or constrained to capture real structure, giving high error on both training and test data. The high-bias side of the bias-variance trade-off.
Expected prediction error on new data from the same distribution. Training error underestimates it; out-of-sample tests estimate it.
Difference between training performance and out-of-sample performance. A large gap is the signature of overfitting.
Assumptions built into a model that let it generalize beyond its data, such as linearity, smoothness, locality in convolutional networks or sequence order in recurrent networks.
Wolpert's result that, averaged over all possible problems, no learning algorithm outperforms any other. Gains come from matching a model's inductive bias to the problem at hand.
As features multiply, data become sparse in feature space, distances lose meaning and the sample size needed explodes. Severe in finance, where many candidate features face short histories.
Pattern where test error falls, rises near the point where a model can fit the training data exactly, then falls again as model size keeps growing.
Plot of training and validation performance against sample size or training time, used to diagnose whether more data or more capacity would help.
The range of functions a model can represent. Higher capacity fits more patterns, including noise.
Linear model for binary outcomes that maps a weighted sum of features to a probability through the logistic function. A strong, interpretable baseline for default or direction prediction.
Regression family linking a linear predictor to the mean of a response from an exponential-family distribution, covering linear, logistic and Poisson regression.
Regression in which the response is a sum of smooth nonlinear functions of individual features, keeping per-feature interpretability while allowing curvature.
Linear regression with an L1 penalty on coefficients that shrinks many exactly to zero and so selects features (Tibshirani 1996).
nodes.f: minimize sum of squared residuals + lambda x sum of abs(b)

nodes.t: Penalized regression combining L1 and L2 penalties (Zou and Hastie 2005). Selects features like lasso while handling groups of correlated predictors like ridge.
nodes.f: minimize RSS + lambda1 x sum of abs(b) + lambda2 x sum of b^2

nodes.t: Regressing the target on the first few principal components of the features rather than the raw features, which reduces dimension and multicollinearity.
Dimension reduction that builds components to maximize covariance with the target, unlike PCA, which ignores the target. Used in return prediction with many correlated predictors.
Classifier that finds the boundary with the widest margin between classes and handles nonlinear boundaries through kernels. Support vector regression applies the idea to continuous targets.
Computing inner products in a high-dimensional feature space through a kernel function without building that space explicitly, letting linear methods fit nonlinear patterns.
Bayesian nonparametric model placing a prior over functions defined by a covariance kernel, giving predictions with uncertainty bands. Cost grows with the cube of sample size.
Model that splits data recursively on feature thresholds into leaves with simple predictions. Captures nonlinearity and interactions, but a single tree overfits and is unstable.
Bootstrap aggregating (Breiman 1996): training models on bootstrap resamples and averaging them, which cuts the variance of unstable learners such as deep trees.
Ensemble method that fits weak learners in sequence, each focusing on the errors left by the ones before, mainly to reduce bias.
Widely used gradient boosting library (Chen and Guestrin 2016) with regularized tree objectives, second-order gradients and efficient split finding. A default for tabular financial data.
Gradient boosting library from Microsoft that uses histogram-based splits and leaf-wise tree growth for speed on large tabular datasets.
Gradient boosting library from Yandex with ordered boosting and native handling of categorical features, designed to reduce target leakage from category encoding.
Anomaly detector that isolates points with random splits; anomalies need fewer splits to isolate than normal points. Used for bad-tick and fraud detection.
Partitions observations into k clusters by minimizing squared distance to cluster centroids. Requires choosing k and favors round clusters of similar size.
Builds a tree of nested clusters by merging or splitting groups according to a linkage rule. Underpins hierarchical risk parity.
Models data as a weighted mix of Gaussian distributions fitted by expectation-maximization, giving soft cluster probabilities. Used to describe return regimes.
Iterative maximum likelihood method for models with hidden variables: estimate the hidden assignments, then refit the parameters, and repeat until convergence.
Model in which an unobserved state follows a Markov chain and each state emits observations from its own distribution. Applied to inferring bull, bear and crisis regimes.
Neural network trained to reconstruct its input through a narrow bottleneck, learning a compressed representation. Used for denoising, anomaly detection and latent factor models.
Autoencoder that learns a probabilistic latent space (Kingma and Welling 2013), so new samples, such as synthetic return paths, can be generated.
Optimization inspired by evolution that mutates and recombines candidate solutions and keeps the fittest. Applied to trading rule discovery, where it overfits backtests easily.
Model of Kelly, Pruitt and Su (2019) with latent factors whose loadings vary with observable stock characteristics, tying statistical factors to traits such as value and momentum.

nodes.n: Empirical asset pricing via machine learning
nodes.t: Gu, Kelly and Xiu (2020) compared machine learning methods for predicting US stock returns from many characteristics. Trees and neural networks beat linear models, mainly by capturing nonlinear interactions, with momentum, liquidity and volatility signals dominant.
Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016) argued that, given extensive factor mining, a new factor should clear a t-statistic of about 3 rather than the conventional 2.
Penalty that shrinks neural network weights toward zero at each update; equivalent to an L2 penalty under plain stochastic gradient descent.
Regularization that randomly zeroes a fraction of neural network units during training (Srivastava et al. 2014), preventing co-adaptation and acting like an implicit ensemble.
Expanding training data with transformed copies, such as noise-added or resampled return paths, to make models more robust. Augmentation that breaks time order can leak information.
Limiting decision tree complexity by cutting branches with little validation benefit, or by capping depth and minimum leaf size.
Maximum a posteriori estimation: choosing the parameters that maximize likelihood times prior. A Gaussian prior gives ridge regression and a Laplace prior gives lasso.
Model property in which most coefficients or weights are zero, improving interpretability and often robustness. Encouraged by L1 penalties.
Splitting data into k folds and training on k-1 while testing on the remaining one, in turn. Standard k-fold assumes independent observations and leaks badly in financial time series.
Validation in which each test fold comes after its training data in time, with expanding or rolling training windows, so the model never trains on the future.
Training window anchored at the start of the sample that grows with each step, using all available history.
An inner loop tunes hyperparameters and an outer loop scores performance on folds the tuning never saw, avoiding the optimistic bias of selecting and scoring on the same data.
Simulating a strategy on historical data to estimate how it would have performed, including signals, costs and constraints. A backtest is a hypothesis test with many hidden trials, not proof.
Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado and Zhu (2014): the more strategy variants tried, the longer the backtest must be before a high Sharpe ratio is unlikely to have arisen by chance.
Running a strategy live on real-time data without capital, testing pipelines, latency and signal stability out of sample before money is at risk.
A simple reference model, such as the historical mean, a random walk or a linear regression, that a complex model must beat to justify its cost.
Forecast equal to the last observed value or a long-run average. For returns, the historical mean is the standard benchmark behind out-of-sample R squared.
Table of predicted versus actual classes counting true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives; the basis of most classification metrics.
Share of predicted positives that are truly positive. Matters when acting on a false signal is costly.
nodes.f: Precision = TP / (TP + FP)

nodes.t: Share of actual positives the model catches, also called sensitivity or true positive rate. Matters when missing an event, such as a default, is costly.
nodes.f: Recall = TP / (TP + FN)

nodes.t: Harmonic mean of precision and recall, a single number balancing the two.
nodes.f: F1 = 2 x precision x recall / (precision + recall)

nodes.t: Share of predictions that are correct. Misleading with imbalanced classes and for return direction, where a few large moves matter more than many small ones.
nodes.f: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / N

nodes.t: Plot of true positive rate against false positive rate across decision thresholds; the area under it is AUC.
Plot of precision against recall across thresholds. More informative than the ROC curve for rare events such as defaults or crashes.
When one class is rare, such as defaults or fraud, so naive models predict the majority and accuracy misleads. Addressed by reweighting, resampling or threshold choice.
Synthetic minority oversampling technique (Chawla et al. 2002), which creates synthetic minority examples by interpolating between neighbors. Must be applied only inside training folds.
The probability cutoff that turns a classifier's score into an action. It should be set from the costs and payoffs of each error, not left at 0.5.
Mean information coefficient divided by its standard deviation over time, measuring how consistent a signal's skill is.
nodes.f: ICIR = mean(IC) / std(IC)

nodes.t: Plot of predicted probabilities against observed frequencies by bin. A calibrated model lies on the diagonal.
Recalibrating classifier scores by fitting a logistic regression on held-out data (Platt 1999).
Including a feature that carries information about the target that was not available at prediction time, such as a field updated after the event. Produces spectacular backtests that fail live.
Fitting scalers, imputers, PCA or feature selection on the full dataset before splitting, so test-period statistics shape the training data.
When label horizons overlap, such as 20-day forward returns sampled daily, adjacent observations share outcomes. This inflates the apparent sample size and leaks across train and test splits.
Evaluating many models on the same holdout until one looks good, which turns the test set into training data through selection.
Using revised fundamentals in a backtest when only the originally reported figures were known at the time.
Delay between a period's end and the public release of its data, such as weeks for quarterly filings or macro statistics. Features must be lagged to match.
Change over time in the relationship between features and target, so a once-valid model degrades. Common in markets as participants adapt to known patterns.
Change in the distribution of the target, such as the default rate, while the feature distribution within each class stays fixed.
Loss of predictive performance after deployment from drift, crowding or regime change; requires monitoring and a retraining policy.
Erosion of a signal's predictive power, either over the holding horizon after the signal forms or over calendar time as others discover and trade it.
Time for a signal's predictive power or expected return contribution to fall by half, guiding rebalance frequency and acceptable turnover.
Correlation arising from chance, common trends or confounders rather than a real link. Abundant whenever many series are searched.
Gelman and Loken's term for analysis choices made after seeing the data, which create many implicit tests even without conscious fishing.
Tuning methods to a shared public benchmark until reported gains reflect the test set's quirks rather than general skill.
Labeling each observation by the sign or size of its return over a fixed future window. Simple, but ignores the path taken and changing volatility.
Labeling method that fits trend regressions over several forward windows and takes the sign of the most significant t-statistic as the label (Lopez de Prado).
The degree to which an observation's label horizon does not overlap those of other observations; used to down-weight redundant samples (Lopez de Prado 2018).
Bootstrap that draws observations with probability tied to their uniqueness, reducing redundancy among overlapping labels.
Differencing a series by a non-integer order to make it stationary while keeping more memory of price levels than ordinary returns do.
Event sampler that triggers when cumulative deviations from a reference level exceed a threshold, so sampling concentrates around large moves.
Sampling market data by activity, such as trades, volume or dollar value, instead of clock time. Returns become closer to normal and better synchronized with information arrival.
Bars formed after a fixed number of trades rather than a fixed time interval.
Bars formed each time a fixed number of shares or contracts trades.
Bars formed each time a fixed notional value trades, which stays robust to price level changes and share count changes.
Bars sampled at fixed clock intervals, such as one minute or one day. They oversample quiet periods and undersample busy ones.
Bars formed when signed order flow imbalance exceeds its expected level, aiming to sample when informed trading appears.
Shapley additive explanations (Lundberg and Lee 2017): attribute each prediction to features using Shapley values from cooperative game theory, giving consistent local and global importance.
Shapley (1953): a fair split of a coalition's payoff that averages each player's marginal contribution over all orders in which players could join.
Tree-based importance that sums the impurity reduction from splits on each feature. Fast, but computed in-sample and biased toward features with many distinct values.
Computing importance for clusters of correlated features together, avoiding the dilution that occurs when substitute features split the credit.
Plot of a model's average prediction as one feature varies, averaging over the observed values of the others. Hides effects that differ across observations.
The degree to which people can understand why a model makes a prediction. Matters for risk sign-off, regulation and spotting nonsense relationships.
When one feature's effect depends on another's value, such as momentum behaving differently in high-volatility regimes. Trees capture interactions automatically; linear models need explicit terms.
Cleaning a sample correlation matrix by replacing eigenvalues consistent with pure noise, as judged by random matrix theory, to stabilize portfolio optimization.
Distribution of eigenvalues of a purely random correlation matrix given the ratio of variables to observations. Eigenvalues inside its bounds cannot be told apart from noise.
Running a candidate model beside the production model and promoting it only after it beats the incumbent on live data.
The ability to rerun a research result and get the same outputs, which requires fixed data versions, code, random seeds and environment.
Initial value for a pseudorandom number generator. Fixing it makes runs reproducible; varying it shows how much a result depends on luck.
Forecasting which assets will beat others at a point in time, rather than whether the market will rise. Offers more breadth and observations than time-series prediction.
Forecasting one asset's or market's future values from its own history and other variables. Few independent observations make it harder than cross-sectional prediction.
The length of time a prediction targets. Shorter horizons give more observations but higher cost drag; longer ones give fewer independent samples.
Forecast giving a full distribution or event probabilities rather than a single point, scored by proper scoring rules such as log loss or CRPS.
Scoring rule whose expected score is optimized by reporting one's true probabilities, such as the log score or the Brier score.
Range expected to contain a future observation with a stated probability. It is wider than a confidence interval for the mean because it includes the noise of the outcome itself.
Choosing a subset of candidate features to cut noise, cost and overfitting, using filters, wrapper searches or embedded methods such as lasso. Must be done inside training folds.
Inputs unlike anything in the training data, where model outputs are unreliable. Markets produce these in crises.
Training a classifier to tell training rows from test rows. If it succeeds, the distributions differ and validation results may not carry over.
Data organized as rows and feature columns, such as stock-month panels. Gradient-boosted trees often match or beat deep learning on it.
Data observing many entities over many periods, such as stocks by month. Inference needs care with cross-sectional and time dependence, for example clustered standard errors.
Model of layered units, each taking a weighted sum of inputs passed through a nonlinear activation, with weights learned by backpropagation. A flexible function approximator that needs much data.
Feedforward neural network with one or more hidden layers of fully connected units; the standard deep model for tabular inputs.
Nonlinear function applied to a unit's weighted input, such as ReLU, sigmoid or tanh, which lets networks represent nonlinear relationships.
Rectified linear unit, the default hidden-layer activation: cheap to compute and resistant to vanishing gradients.
nodes.f: ReLU(x) = max(0, x)

nodes.t: Function turning a vector of scores into probabilities that sum to one; used for multi-class outputs and attention weights.
nodes.f: softmax(z_i) = exp(z_i) / sum of exp(z_j)

nodes.t: Algorithm computing the gradient of the loss with respect to every network weight by applying the chain rule backward through the layers (Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams 1986).
Gradients shrinking exponentially as they pass backward through many layers or time steps, stalling learning in early layers. Addressed by ReLU, gated recurrent units and residual connections.
Shortcut that adds a layer's input to its output (He et al. 2015), easing gradient flow and making very deep networks trainable.
Machine learning with many-layered neural networks that learn hierarchical representations from raw data; dominant for images, audio and language.
Learning useful features automatically from raw data instead of engineering them by hand.
Dense vector representing an item such as a word, document, company or asset, learned so that similar items sit close together. Used for peer identification and semantic search.

Result (Cybenko 1989; Hornik 1991) that a network with one hidden layer and enough units can approximate any continuous function on a bounded domain. It says nothing about learning that function from finite data.
Network applying learned filters across local windows with shared weights; efficient for images and also applied to price charts and limit order book snapshots.
Network that processes sequences step by step with a hidden state carrying memory of past inputs. Plain versions struggle with long-range dependencies.
Long short-term memory (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997): recurrent unit with gates controlling what to store, forget and output, which eases vanishing gradients over long sequences.
Deep model of Zhang, Zohren and Roberts (2019) combining convolutions and an LSTM to predict short-term mid-price moves from limit order book data.

Framework of Buehler, Gonon, Teichmann and Wood (2019) that trains neural networks to hedge derivatives under transaction costs and frictions by directly optimizing a risk measure over simulated paths.
Attention-based multi-horizon forecasting model (Lim et al. 2021) combining recurrent layers, variable selection and interpretable attention over time.
Large model pretrained on many time series to forecast unseen series without task-specific training. Its value for financial returns is unproven given their low signal to noise.
Network that passes messages along graph edges, learning from relationships such as supply chains, ownership links or co-movement networks.
Reusing a model trained on one task or dataset as the starting point for another, saving data and compute.
Continuing the training of a pretrained model on a smaller task-specific dataset to adapt it.
Initial large-scale training of a model on broad data, usually self-supervised, to learn general representations before adapting it to tasks.
Large model pretrained on broad data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks, such as a large language model. Term from Bommasani et al. (2021).
Transformer trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next token, which yields broad abilities in writing, reasoning, coding and information extraction.
Training objective of predicting each token from the ones before it; the core pretraining task for GPT-style language models.

Architecture of Vaswani et al. (2017), "Attention Is All You Need", built on self-attention instead of recurrence, which allows parallel training on long sequences. The basis of modern language models.
Method that lets a model weight parts of its input by relevance when producing each output, computed from query, key and value vectors.
Attention in which every position in a sequence attends to every other position, with cost growing with the square of sequence length.
nodes.f: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q x K^T / sqrt(d)) x V

nodes.t: Information added to token representations to convey order, since attention alone ignores position; includes sinusoidal and rotary schemes.
Architecture in which an encoder maps the input to representations and a decoder generates output from them; the original transformer design for translation.
Transformer that generates text left to right using causal self-attention, the design of GPT-style language models.
Encoder-only transformer (Devlin et al. 2018) pretrained by predicting masked words, widely fine-tuned for classification and extraction, including financial sentiment.
BERT variant further trained on financial text for tasks such as sentiment classification of news, filings and analyst reports.
Component that splits text into tokens from a fixed vocabulary, often subword pieces built by byte-pair encoding. Token counts drive model cost and context limits.
Maximum number of tokens a model can process in one call, covering prompt and output. Longer windows raise memory and compute cost per request.
Stored key and value vectors for past tokens so a transformer need not recompute them for each new token. It grows with context length and batch size and often binds inference memory.
Empirical power-law relationships between model loss and parameters, data and compute (Kaplan et al. 2020), used to plan the size of training runs.
Hoffmann et al. (2022) found that compute-optimal training grows parameters and training tokens in roughly equal proportion, implying many earlier models were undertrained.
A model performing a new task from instructions or examples in its prompt, without any change to its weights.
Including a few worked examples in a prompt to show the desired task and format; zero-shot prompting gives instructions only.
Designing instructions, context and examples so that a model produces reliable output.
Prompting or training a model to write intermediate reasoning steps before its answer, which improves multi-step problem solving (Wei et al. 2022).
Language model trained, often with reinforcement learning, to generate extended reasoning before answering, trading more inference tokens for accuracy on hard problems.
Spending more computation at inference, through longer reasoning, repeated sampling or search, to improve answers. Shifts compute demand from training toward inference.
Everything after pretraining that shapes a model's behavior: supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization and reinforcement learning.
Post-training a pretrained model on curated prompt and response pairs to teach it to follow instructions.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: train a reward model on human preference comparisons, then optimize the language model against that reward.
Model trained to score outputs by predicted human or rule-based preference, used as the optimization target in RLHF.
Training models with reinforcement learning on tasks whose answers can be checked automatically, such as math or code tests, avoiding a learned reward model.
Low-rank adaptation (Hu et al. 2021): fine-tuning by learning small low-rank update matrices while freezing the original weights, cutting memory and storage needs.
Representing weights and activations with fewer bits, such as 8 or 4, to cut memory use and speed up inference at some cost in accuracy.
Training a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher's outputs, keeping much of the capability at lower inference cost (Hinton et al. 2015).
Architecture that routes each token to a few of many expert subnetworks, so total parameters grow without a matching rise in compute per token.
Attention algorithm (Dao et al. 2022) that reorders the computation to minimize reads and writes to slow memory, speeding training and inference with exact results.
A language model stating false or fabricated information fluently, such as invented figures or citations. A core risk when using models for investment research.
Supplying a model with documents retrieved from a search index at query time so its answers are grounded in specific sources.
Store that indexes embeddings for fast nearest-neighbor similarity search; underlies retrieval-augmented generation.
Parameter scaling a model's output probabilities before sampling. Low values make output near-deterministic; high values make it more varied.
Exponential of the average negative log likelihood per token; lower values mean the model predicts the text better.
nodes.f: PPL = exp(average negative log likelihood per token)

nodes.t: Standardized test sets for comparing models on a capability such as coding or math. Contamination of training data and saturation limit what scores mean.
When top models score near the ceiling of a benchmark, so it no longer separates them and new tests are needed.
Model that takes in or produces several data types, such as text, images, audio and charts.
Generative model that learns to reverse a gradual noising process, producing images, audio or video by iterative denoising.
Treating documents such as filings, transcripts and news as quantitative inputs through word counts, dictionaries, embeddings or language models; surveyed by Gentzkow, Kelly and Taddy (2019).
Representing a document by its word counts, ignoring order. Simple and transparent; the basis of dictionary sentiment methods.
Term frequency times inverse document frequency: weights words that are frequent in a document but rare across the collection.
nodes.f: tfidf = tf x ln(N / df)

nodes.t: Finance-specific sentiment word lists of Loughran and McDonald (2011), built because general dictionaries misclassify words such as liability, tax or cost as negative in financial text.
Scoring the tone of financial text, such as news, filings or calls, with dictionaries, classifiers or language models to predict returns, volatility or flows.
Method of Mikolov et al. (2013) that learns word embeddings by predicting words from their neighbors, so related words get nearby vectors.
Unsupervised method, classically latent Dirichlet allocation (Blei, Ng and Jordan 2003), describing each document as a mixture of topics.
Extracting and classifying names of companies, people, places and amounts from text; a first step in mapping news to tickers.
Cohen, Malloy and Nguyen (2020): firms whose annual report text changes notably from the prior year subsequently underperform, as investors underreact to the changes.
Framework of states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards and a discount factor that formalizes sequential decisions; the foundation of reinforcement learning.
Recursive condition that a state's value equals the best immediate reward plus the discounted expected value of the next state; the basis of dynamic programming.
nodes.f: V(s) = max over a of [r(s, a) + gamma x E V(s')]

nodes.t: A rule mapping states to actions, deterministic or random, that a reinforcement learning agent learns in order to maximize expected cumulative reward.
Expected cumulative discounted reward from a state, or from a state-action pair, when following a given policy.
Off-policy algorithm (Watkins 1989) that learns the value of each state-action pair from experience through repeated Bellman updates.
Q-learning with a neural network approximating action values, stabilized by experience replay and target networks (Mnih et al. 2015).
Reinforcement learning methods that adjust policy parameters directly in the direction that raises expected reward.
Architecture in which an actor chooses actions and a critic estimates value, reducing the variance of policy updates.
Policy gradient method of Schulman et al. (2017) that limits the size of each update with a clipped objective; widely used, including in RLHF.
Balancing trying actions to learn their value against choosing the best-known action; central to bandits and reinforcement learning.
Problem of repeatedly choosing among options with unknown payoffs to maximize total reward; the simplest exploration-exploitation setting.
Bandit strategy that draws from each option's posterior payoff distribution and picks the option with the best draw (Thompson 1933).
An agent maximizing the measured reward in unintended ways, such as a trading agent exploiting simulator flaws or a model gaming its reward model.
Designing intermediate rewards to guide learning. For trading agents, choices such as risk penalties and cost charges largely determine behavior.
Weight between 0 and 1 applied to future rewards; lower values make an agent short-sighted.
Learning a policy from a fixed log of past data without interacting with the environment, the realistic setting for trading. Fails when the policy favors actions rarely seen in the data.
Synthetic environment, such as an order book model or agent-based model, used to train and test trading agents. Agents readily exploit unrealistic features such as missing market impact.
Simulation of many interacting agents following rules, used to study emergent market behavior such as bubbles, herding and crashes.
Performance lost when a policy trained in simulation meets the real market, because of unmodeled impact, latency and other traders' reactions.
Applying reinforcement learning to slice large orders over time to minimize implementation shortfall, an approach studied by Nevmyvaka, Feng and Kearns (2006).
Transforming raw data into predictive inputs, such as ratios, changes, ranks and interactions. In finance, domain-driven features usually matter more than the choice of model.
Natural log of the price relative. Log returns add up over time and roughly equal simple returns for small moves, but do not add across assets in a portfolio.
nodes.f: r = ln(P_t / P_t-1)

nodes.t: Converting a feature to its rank or percentile among assets each period, which removes scale, outliers and market-wide shifts.
Rescaling a feature to mean zero and unit variance using only statistics available at the time of each observation.
nodes.f: z = (x - mean) / standard deviation

nodes.t: Past values of a variable used as predictors, lagged far enough that they were truly available at decision time.
Statistics computed over trailing windows, such as 20-day volatility or 12-month momentum. Each window must end before the prediction time.
Returns divided by a recent volatility estimate, making signals and targets comparable across assets and regimes.
Removing sector averages from a feature or signal so predictions reflect differences within sectors rather than sector bets.
Regressing a signal on known factor exposures and keeping the residual, isolating information not already captured by common factors.
Returns left after removing exposure to the market and other factors; a common prediction target for stock selection models.
The future return over a chosen horizon used as the training label. Choices of horizon, price adjustment and benchmark shape what the model learns.
Inputs derived from dates, such as day of week, month-end, option expiry or holiday proximity.
Replacing a category with the average target value observed for that category. It leaks unless computed out-of-fold.
Filling gaps in data by forward fill, medians or models. It must use only past information and should flag that a value was missing.
Classifying trades as buyer- or seller-initiated, using exchange aggressor flags or rules such as Lee and Ready (1991) when flags are missing.
Sum of squared intraday returns over a period, a model-free estimate of variance. Microstructure noise biases it at very high sampling frequencies.
nodes.f: RV = sum of r_i^2

nodes.t: Panel of stock-level characteristics such as size, value, momentum, profitability and accruals, standardized each month; the standard input for cross-sectional return models.
How much a signal's implied portfolio changes each rebalance. High turnover needs a larger predictive edge to overcome trading costs.
A quantitative forecast of relative or absolute returns used to set positions.
Inputs describing the market state, such as volatility level, trend or credit spreads, which let models condition on the environment.
System that stores computed features with timestamps for reuse in training and live serving, keeping definitions identical and point-in-time correct in both.
Images from satellites used to count cars in parking lots, gauge crop health, read oil tank levels or track construction before official data appear.
Anonymized mobile device location data used to estimate foot traffic at stores, factories or venues.
Aggregated credit card, debit card or bank transaction data used to estimate company sales ahead of reported results.
Purchase data parsed from consumer email receipts by opted-in panels, giving item-level detail on online spending.
Automated collection of public web data, such as prices, product listings, job postings or reviews. Raises terms-of-service and legal questions.
Panel or clickstream estimates of site visits, downloads and active users, used as proxies for engagement and demand at internet companies.
Scraped or aggregated hiring listings that show where companies are expanding, cutting or shifting strategy.
Measures of attention and tone from social platforms and forums, linked to retail flows, meme stocks and short-term volatility.
Machine-readable news feeds tagged with entities, topics, novelty and sentiment, timestamped for trading use.
Automatic identification system (AIS) transponder data on vessel positions, used to track oil exports, commodity flows and port congestion.
Scraped online prices of goods across retailers, used to measure inflation in real time and to judge company pricing power.
Volume of internet search queries for chosen terms, a proxy for consumer interest, investor attention and labor market stress.
Data mapping customers, suppliers and shipments between firms. Cohen and Frazzini (2008) showed news propagates along customer-supplier links with a lag.
Environmental, social and governance scores and inputs from data vendors. Ratings for the same company often disagree widely across providers.
Observations and forecasts of temperature, precipitation and storms, which drive energy demand, crop yields and retail traffic.
Patent filings and citations used to measure innovation output and technology positioning.
Data on shares on loan, borrow fees and lendable supply utilization, signaling short-seller demand and squeeze risk.
Using alternative data to forecast company-reported operating metrics, such as revenue, subscribers or same-store sales, and trading the expected surprise versus consensus.
Distortion when an alternative data panel, such as card users or app installs, does not represent the target population or changes composition over time.
Information a reasonable investor would consider important that has not been publicly disclosed. Trading on it is illegal insider trading, so data vendors must show their data contain none.
Vetting a dataset's sourcing, consent, licensing, MNPI risk, history length, coverage and point-in-time integrity before buying or using it.
Record of where data came from and how they were collected and transformed; needed for legal compliance and for trusting a signal.
Contract terms governing who may use data, for which purposes, and whether redistribution, derived works or exclusivity are allowed.
Protection of personal information in datasets through consent, anonymization and aggregation, governed by laws such as GDPR and CCPA.
Licensing a dataset to one or a few buyers to preserve its edge. Widely sold data decay faster as their signal is traded away.
Loss of a dataset's predictive value as more buyers adopt it, its panel changes, or companies learn to manage the measured metric.
Total floating point operations used to train a model. For a dense transformer it is roughly six times parameters times training tokens.
nodes.f: C = 6 x N x D (N parameters, D tokens)

nodes.t: Floating point operations, the unit of compute work, and FLOP/s, the rate a chip performs them. A job's total FLOPs differs from a chip's peak FLOP/s, which real workloads rarely reach.
Share of a cluster's peak compute actually spent on useful model math. Communication, memory stalls and failures keep it well below 100 percent in large training runs.
nodes.f: MFU = achieved model FLOP/s / peak FLOP/s

nodes.t: Choosing model size and number of training tokens to minimize loss for a fixed compute budget.
Training a smaller model on more tokens than compute-optimal, spending more on training to cut the lifetime cost of serving it.
Splitting each batch across many devices that each hold a full model copy, then averaging their gradients. Gradient exchange makes network bandwidth critical.
Splitting one model across devices, by dividing layer matrices (tensor parallelism) or assigning layers to stages (pipeline parallelism). Tensor parallelism needs the fastest interconnects.

Artificially generated data from simulations or models, used to augment scarce real data or to train language models. Risks include mismatch with reality and degraded models when trained on their own output.
The concern that the stock of high-quality human text for pretraining is finite and being used up, shifting effort toward synthetic data, other modalities and reinforcement learning.
The most capable models at a given time, trained at the largest compute scale by a few labs.
Model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to run and modify, though training data and code may stay private. Puts pressure on the pricing of closed models.
Model available only through its provider's API or apps, with weights kept private.
Compact model, often distilled from a larger one, cheap enough to run on modest hardware or devices for narrower tasks.
Running models locally on phones, PCs or vehicles instead of in data centers, cutting latency and serving cost but limited by device memory and power.
Accelerator block for AI workloads built into phones and PCs, used for on-device inference.
Cost of serving model outputs, driven by model size, tokens processed, hardware price, utilization and batching. The main variable cost of AI products.
Inference phase that processes the whole prompt in parallel to build the KV cache; it is limited mainly by compute.
Inference phase that generates output tokens one at a time, each step reading the full weights and KV cache; it is limited mainly by memory bandwidth.
Latency from sending a request to receiving the first output token, dominated by queueing and prefill.
Throughput of generated tokens, per user or per system. Larger batches raise system throughput but slow each user.
Serving technique that adds and removes requests from a running batch at every decoding step, raising accelerator utilization.
Using a small draft model to propose several tokens that the large model checks in one pass, speeding generation without changing the output distribution.
Share of time or capacity that accelerators spend on useful work. Low utilization inflates the effective cost of each unit of compute.
Nvidia's CUDA programming platform, libraries and developer base, which raise switching costs for customers considering rival accelerators.
Google's custom AI accelerator built around large matrix multiply units, used internally and rented through its cloud.
Application-specific integrated circuit: a chip designed for one workload, trading flexibility for efficiency. Custom AI accelerators are ASICs.
Field-programmable gate array: chip whose logic can be reconfigured after manufacture; used for ultra-low-latency trading, networking and prototyping.
Specialized GPU circuitry for fast matrix multiply-accumulate at reduced precision; the source of most AI throughput on modern GPUs.
Bit width used to represent numbers, such as FP32, BF16, FP8 or FP4. Lower precision raises throughput and cuts memory at some risk to accuracy.
The widening gap between processor compute speed and memory bandwidth, which leaves many AI workloads waiting for data rather than doing math.
Rate at which data move between memory and processor, in bytes per second. It sets the ceiling on token generation speed for large models.
Operations performed per byte moved from memory. Low-intensity workloads are memory bound and high-intensity ones compute bound, as shown by the roofline model.
nodes.f: intensity = FLOPs / bytes moved

nodes.t: Servers designed as a whole rack, with many GPUs joined by a high-speed fabric into one large scale-up domain; requires liquid cooling and very high power per rack.
Scale-up links accelerators into one tightly coupled domain with very high bandwidth; scale-out joins many such domains over a network fabric with lower bandwidth per chip.
a: front end versus back end network

nodes.t: Nvidia's high-bandwidth GPU-to-GPU interconnect for scale-up domains, much faster than standard PCIe links.
Networks linking accelerators in AI clusters. Collective exchange of gradients and activations makes network bandwidth and latency a key determinant of cluster efficiency.
Low-latency, high-bandwidth network standard with native remote direct memory access, long dominant in AI training clusters.
Ethernet enhanced with congestion control and remote direct memory access for AI clusters, competing with InfiniBand for scale-out fabrics.
Module converting electrical signals to light and back for fiber links between switches and servers. Volumes scale with cluster size and link speed.
Placing optical engines in the same package as a switch or processor chip, cutting the power used to drive signals compared with pluggable transceivers.
Hourly price of renting accelerator capacity, on demand or under reserved contracts. Falling rates signal easing scarcity and pressure the value of GPU fleets.
The accounting useful life assigned to AI servers. Longer lives lift reported earnings, while rapid generational gains may shorten real economic life.
Debt secured by GPU fleets and their rental contracts, used by neoclouds. Credit risk depends on residual values and the quality of the customer contracts.
Multi-year agreement to buy cloud or GPU capacity, often take-or-pay, creating backlog for the provider and fixed commitments for the buyer.
Contract obliging the buyer to pay for a committed quantity whether or not it uses it; common in compute, power and energy deals.
Government restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips, chipmaking tools and related technology to certain countries, reshaping demand, supply chains and product design.
Dynamic random-access memory: the main working memory in computers, storing bits as charge that must be refreshed. A cyclical commodity market with few producers.
