Non-volatile memory that keeps data without power, used in solid-state drives; more commoditized and cyclical than DRAM.
Boom-bust swings in DRAM and NAND prices as capacity additions lag demand shifts, moving producers' margins sharply.

Stacking DRAM dies vertically, linked by through-silicon vias, and placing the stack beside the processor on an interposer for very wide bandwidth. HBM uses more wafer area per bit than standard DRAM.
Chip company that designs chips but outsources manufacturing to foundries, unlike an integrated device manufacturer, which designs and makes its own.
Extreme ultraviolet lithography, which uses very short wavelength light to print the finest chip features. The tools come from a single supplier, ASML.
Share of dies on a wafer that work. It falls with larger die size and immature processes, raising the cost per good chip.
Maximum die area a lithography tool can print in one exposure, which caps the size of a single chip and motivates chiplets and advanced packaging.
Small die combined with others in one package to form a larger processor, improving yield and allowing parts made on different nodes to be mixed.
Techniques that connect multiple dies densely within one package, such as 2.5D interposers and 3D stacking; a recurring bottleneck for AI accelerator supply.
Chip-on-wafer-on-substrate: TSMC's 2.5D packaging that places logic dies and HBM stacks side by side on a silicon interposer. Its capacity has constrained AI accelerator output.
Stacking dies on top of each other with vertical connections, increasingly made by hybrid copper bonding, to shorten wires and raise bandwidth.
Electronic design automation tools used to design and verify chips; a concentrated market with high switching costs.
Concentration of leading-edge chip fabrication in one company and one geography, a supply and geopolitical risk for the whole AI industry.
Data center model in which a provider leases space, power and cooling to tenants who install their own equipment, priced per kilowatt per month.
Power available to IT equipment, the standard measure of data center capacity in megawatts, excluding cooling and other overhead.
Total facility power divided by IT equipment power; a value of 1.0 would mean zero overhead for cooling and power conversion.
nodes.f: PUE = total facility energy / IT equipment energy

nodes.t: Power drawn per server rack in kilowatts. AI racks draw many times more than conventional racks, forcing liquid cooling and heavier electrical design.
Removing server heat with liquid instead of air, needed for dense AI racks. Direct-to-chip cold plates are the main form; immersion in fluid is an alternative.
Process and queue for connecting new loads or generators to the power grid. Long waits make power access the main constraint on data center timing.
Electricity generated on site, often by gas turbines or engines, and used directly without passing through the utility grid, letting data centers bypass interconnection delays.
Long-term contract to buy electricity from a specific generator at agreed prices, used by hyperscalers to secure clean or firm power.
Factory-built nuclear reactor of smaller size, proposed as firm carbon-free power for data centers; commercial deployment is still at an early stage.
Long lead times for transformers, switchgear and turbines as data center and grid demand outruns manufacturing capacity.
Data centers agreeing to cut consumption during grid stress in exchange for faster connection or lower costs; training jobs tolerate this better than live inference.
Sites with secured power capacity and zoning for data centers, valued for how quickly they can be energized.
Risk that data centers or GPU fleets lose value before paying back their cost because demand falls short or technology moves on.
Future depreciation expense created by heavy current capex, which weighs on margins over the useful life of the assets.
Risk that total AI infrastructure investment exceeds sustainable demand, as in past railway and telecom build-outs, leading to overcapacity, price collapse and write-downs.
Off-balance-sheet structures, such as joint ventures and special purpose vehicles funded by private capital, that build data centers leased back to a hyperscaler.
Jevons (1865): efficiency gains that cut the cost of using a resource can increase its total consumption. Applied to AI, cheaper tokens may raise total compute demand.
Layers of the AI industry: chips and equipment, infrastructure and cloud, models, and applications, each with different margins and sources of advantage.
Business whose product is a thin layer over a third-party model, exposed to its supplier's pricing and to rivals with the same access.
Investing in suppliers to a boom, such as chips, equipment and power, rather than betting on which end users will win.
Charging developers per token processed by a model, with separate rates for input and output and discounts for caching and batch jobs.
Price or cost for each unit of model input or output, usually quoted per million tokens.
Output tokens cost more than input tokens because generation is sequential and memory bound, while prompt tokens are processed in parallel.
Reusing the processed form of repeated prompt prefixes across requests at a discount, cutting cost and latency for long shared context.
Tokens a reasoning model generates while thinking before its answer, billed as output and raising the cost per task.
Rapid fall in the price per token for a given level of capability, driven by better hardware, software efficiency and competition.
Erosion of pricing power as many models reach similar capability, shifting value toward distribution, proprietary data and cost.
Charging per user per month, the traditional software model, which AI agents threaten if they reduce the number of human users needed.
Fall in the number of software licenses customers need when AI automates work, pressuring seat-based software revenue.
Gross margin of AI products after inference compute costs; typically below classic software margins because every use consumes compute.
Recent monthly or weekly revenue scaled to a yearly figure; common for fast-growing AI firms but flattering when usage is volatile or one-off.
nodes.f: run-rate = monthly revenue x 12

nodes.t: Directing each request to the cheapest model able to handle it, lowering cost and reducing dependence on any one provider.
Arrangement in which a model lab receives compute and investment from a cloud provider, which resells the lab's models and captures its compute spending.
System in which a language model plans, calls tools and takes multi-step actions toward a goal with limited human direction.
A model emitting structured calls to external functions, such as search, code execution or databases, and using the results in its answer.
Open protocol introduced by Anthropic in 2024 that standardizes how AI applications connect models to tools and data sources.
Agent that operates a computer through screenshots, clicks and typing, letting it use software that has no API.
Agent that reads, writes, runs and tests code in a repository; one of the first agent categories with heavy real usage.
Design requiring human review or approval at key steps, trading speed for control over errors and risk.
Attack in which instructions hidden in content an AI reads, such as a web page or document, hijack its behavior.
Length of task, measured in the time a person would need, that an agent can complete reliably. Longer horizons multiply the chances of compounding errors.
When each step of a multi-step task has some chance of failure, overall success falls geometrically with the number of steps.
nodes.f: P(success) = p^n for n independent steps each succeeding with probability p

nodes.t: Stream of quotes, trades and status messages from a venue or vendor. Feeds differ in depth, latency, normalization and cost.
Proprietary data feed from an exchange, faster and deeper than the consolidated feed, used by latency-sensitive traders.
Feed showing aggregate resting size at each price level on each side, without individual orders.
Full order-level feed of every add, modify, cancel and execution, allowing exact rebuilding of the book and queue positions.
Record of every individual trade and quote update, the most granular historical market data. Trade and quote (TAQ) datasets are the standard source for US equities research.
Open, high, low, close and volume aggregated over intervals. Compact, but discards the sequence of prices within each bar, so stop and limit fills inside a bar are ambiguous.
Software that receives raw venue messages, decodes the protocol, rebuilds the order book and passes normalized data to applications.
Compact binary message formats used by exchange feeds, such as Nasdaq ITCH, which feed handlers decode for speed.
Network method sending one stream to many subscribers at once. Exchanges broadcast feeds this way, so dropped packets must be recovered separately.
Detecting missing messages through sequence numbers and recovering them from retransmission or snapshot channels before the book is trusted again.
Feeds combine periodic full-book snapshots with incremental updates; a consumer starts from a snapshot and applies the changes in sequence.
Combining rapid updates into fewer messages that carry only the latest state per interval; saves bandwidth but hides intermediate prices.
Data from many venues converted into one common schema and symbology, easier to use at some cost in latency and venue-specific detail.
Charges by exchanges and vendors for real-time and historical data, with separate fees for display, non-display algorithmic use and redistribution.
Closing price set by a venue's closing auction, used for index levels, fund valuation and benchmarks; it can differ from the last trade.
All listed strikes and expiries for an underlying, with quotes, volume, open interest and implied volatilities.

Adjusting a continuous futures series at each roll by adding the price gap (back-adjusted) or multiplying by a ratio, removing artificial jumps between contracts. Roll timing follows calendar, volume or open interest rules.
Central database of each instrument's identifiers, attributes and history; the backbone that joins data across sources.
System of instrument identifiers, such as tickers, CUSIP, ISIN, SEDOL, FIGI and vendor codes, and the mapping among them over time.
Change in a security's trading symbol from a rename, merger or relisting. Tickers are reused over time, so they are unsafe as permanent keys.
Identifier that stays fixed for a security across name and ticker changes, such as CRSP's PERMNO, used to link price histories correctly.
Matching records that refer to the same company or instrument across datasets with differing names and identifiers.
Company events that change share count, price or security identity, such as splits, dividends, spin-offs, mergers, rights issues and name changes. Price histories must be adjusted for them.
Cumulative multiplier applied to historical prices and volumes to account for splits and distributions, making returns continuous.
nodes.f: adjusted price = raw price x cumulative adjustment factor

nodes.t: Historical prices rescaled for splits and often dividends. Adjusted levels change whenever new actions occur, so raw prices and factors should be stored separately.
Price series that assumes dividends and distributions are reinvested; the correct basis for comparing long-horizon performance.
Return on a stock's final delisting event. Shumway (1997) showed that omitting these returns biases backtests upward, especially for small stocks delisted for poor performance.
Dataset that includes securities that later delisted, merged or failed, so backtests see the universe as it actually was.
Dated record of which securities belonged to an index and when. Using today's members for past periods builds survivorship into the universe.
Choosing which assets a strategy may trade on each date using only information known then, such as past liquidity, price and size filters.
Data stored as they were known at each past moment, keeping original values before revisions and the time each became available. Essential for avoiding look-ahead bias.
Records carrying two timestamps: when a fact was true and when it was recorded or known, which allows queries of what was known as of any date.
Joining each record to the latest record from another table at or before its timestamp; the standard way to align asynchronous data without look-ahead.
Successive published versions of a statistic, such as each estimate of a quarter's GDP, kept so backtests use the value known at the time (as in the ALFRED database).
Center for Research in Security Prices: academic database of US stock prices, returns and delistings with permanent identifiers; the standard for survivorship-free equity research.
Database of standardized company fundamentals widely used in academic and quantitative research, with point-in-time versions available.
Institutional Brokers' Estimate System: database of analyst earnings forecasts and recommendations with their history.
Time an event happened at its source, such as the exchange matching engine.
Time a message reached the consumer's system. Its gap from the event timestamp measures feed latency, and realistic simulations should act on it.
Making sure data from different sources share a clock and time zone and reflect when each value was actually knowable.
Keeping system clocks aligned to a reference time using protocols such as NTP or PTP, often with hardware timestamping on network cards; regulators require tight sync for audit trails.
Storing times in UTC and converting carefully, since daylight saving shifts and differing exchange local times cause silent misalignment.
Schedule of each venue's trading days, holidays, early closes and session times, needed to compute returns and align markets.
Schedule of data releases and earnings dates with exact times, needed to timestamp when information became public.
Automated sequence that ingests, validates, transforms and stores data on a schedule to feed research and trading.
Scheduling and coordinating pipeline tasks as a dependency graph with retries and alerts, using tools such as Airflow or cron.
Property that rerunning a job gives the same result without duplicating data; essential for safe retries and backfills.
Storing data by column instead of by row, which allows heavy compression and fast scans of a few fields across many rows; Parquet is the common open format.
Database optimized for timestamped data, with fast range queries, as-of joins and compression; kdb+ is the classic one in trading.
Low-cost storage of raw data in native formats for later processing, in contrast to a warehouse of cleaned, modeled tables; a lakehouse adds table features on top of the lake.
Automated tests for completeness, valid ranges, duplicates, staleness and cross-source consistency, run before data reach models.
Rules removing erroneous prints, such as trades far from the prevailing quote or later-cancelled trades, from price data.
Missing intervals caused by outages, holidays or vendor problems, which must be told apart from genuine periods of no activity.
Unannounced change in a data source's fields, types or meanings that silently breaks downstream pipelines; data contracts guard against it.
Tracking how each dataset was derived from its sources through each transformation, for debugging and audit.
Keeping immutable snapshots of datasets so any result can be reproduced on the exact data used.
Ensuring the code and data path used in backtests matches live trading, so that differences in timing, fills or features do not create phantom performance.
Backtest engine that processes market events in time order through the same logic as live trading; more realistic than vectorized backtests for execution-sensitive strategies.
Modeling which orders would have executed in a backtest and at what price, accounting for queue position, spread and market impact.
Differences between vendors' values for the same field, arising from timing, adjustments or methodology; cross-checking sources catches errors.
A reference crude grade whose assessed or traded price anchors pricing of physical cargoes and derivatives, with other grades priced at a differential to it.
Medium sour crude benchmarks used to price Middle East exports to Asia, assessed from Dubai, Oman and related grades.
Price assessment of physical North Sea cargoes loading in a near forward window, drawn from a basket of North Sea grades plus WTI Midland; the base for pricing most of the world's physical crude.
American Petroleum Institute measure of liquid density relative to water; higher API means lighter crude that usually yields more gasoline and diesel per barrel.
nodes.f: API = 141.5 / specific gravity - 131.5

nodes.t: Classification of crude by sulfur content: sweet crude is low in sulfur, sour crude is high and costs more to refine, so it usually trades at a discount.
Premium or discount of a crude grade versus a benchmark, reflecting density, sulfur, acidity, location, freight and how many refineries can run it.
Price gap between light sweet and heavy sour crudes; it widens when heavy supply is plentiful or complex refining capacity is scarce, and narrows when heavy barrels are cut.
Heavy sour Canadian crude blend priced at a differential to WTI; the discount tracks pipeline and rail takeaway capacity out of Alberta and heavy refining demand on the US Gulf Coast.
Pipeline and storage hub in Cushing, Oklahoma that is the delivery point for NYMEX WTI futures; tank levels there strongly influence WTI time spreads.
Price difference between two delivery months of the same commodity futures; a positive near-minus-far spread signals backwardation and a negative one signals contango.
nodes.f: spread = near-month price - later-month price

nodes.t: Value of products a refinery makes from a barrel minus the crude cost and operating costs; the main driver of how hard refiners run.
nodes.f: margin = product revenue per barrel - crude cost - operating cost

nodes.t: Standard US refining margin proxy: the value of two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of distillate minus three barrels of crude, expressed per barrel.
nodes.f: (2 x gasoline + 1 x diesel - 3 x crude) / 3, all in dollars per barrel

nodes.t: Price of a single refined product minus the price of crude, such as the gasoline crack or the diesel crack; shows which product is driving refinery economics.
Measure of refinery sophistication that weights each secondary processing unit by its cost relative to crude distillation; complex refineries can turn cheap heavy sour crude into light products.
Crude processed as a share of operable distillation capacity; high utilization tightens product markets and leaves little slack for outages.
nodes.f: utilization = crude runs / operable capacity

nodes.t: Planned maintenance shutdown of refinery units, usually concentrated in spring and autumn, which temporarily cuts crude demand and product supply.
Refinery conversion process that uses a catalyst to break heavy gasoil into gasoline, propylene and lighter products; the core of gasoline-oriented refineries.
Conversion process that cracks heavy streams under hydrogen pressure, favoring high-quality diesel and jet fuel output.
Refinery unit that thermally cracks the heaviest residue into lighter products plus petroleum coke, letting refiners profit from running discounted heavy crude.
Share of each product, such as gasoline, distillates, jet and fuel oil, obtained from a barrel, set by crude quality and refinery configuration.
Diesel, gasoil, heating oil and jet fuel; the product group most tied to freight, industry, farming and aviation, and often the tightest part of the barrel.
NYMEX gasoline futures contract for a blendstock that becomes finished gasoline after ethanol is added, delivered in New York Harbor; the main US gasoline benchmark.
NYMEX ultra-low sulfur diesel futures, formerly the heating oil contract, delivered in New York Harbor; the main US distillate benchmark.
ICE Futures Europe diesel contract delivered in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp region; the benchmark for European and much of the world's middle distillates.
Heavy residual fuel left after distillation, burned by ships fitted with scrubbers and by some power plants; its discount to crude tracks residue supply and sulfur rules.

International Maritime Organization rule effective 2020 cutting the sulfur limit in marine fuel outside emission control areas to 0.5 percent from 3.5 percent, shifting demand from high sulfur fuel oil to compliant fuels and distillates.
Measure of gasoline volatility; regulators require lower RVP in summer to limit evaporation, so summer-grade gasoline costs more and gasoline futures shift grade between seasons.
Northern hemisphere summer period of peak gasoline demand, which tends to support gasoline cracks and refinery runs.
Responsiveness of oil consumption to price; very low in the short run because vehicles, planes and plants cannot switch quickly, so small supply gaps can move prices sharply.
Ability of US tight oil producers to raise output within months of higher prices because wells are short-cycle, which tends to cap prolonged price spikes.
Weekly count of active drilling rigs, most often cited from Baker Hughes; a lagging indicator of price and a leading indicator of production months later.
Number of active hydraulic fracturing crews; tracks well completions and therefore leads shale output more directly than the rig count.
Wells drilled but not yet fracked and brought online; an inventory that producers can complete to add output without new drilling.
Rate at which a well or field's output falls without new investment; shale wells decline steeply in their early years, so producers must keep drilling just to hold output flat.
Oil price a petrostate needs to balance its government budget; high fiscal breakevens push producers toward higher prices or higher volumes.
Years of production remaining if current output continues against current reserves.
nodes.f: R/P = reserves / annual production

nodes.t: Oil and gas value chain segments: exploration and production, transport and storage, and refining and marketing, each with different exposure to price and volume.
Realized value at the wellhead or plant after deducting royalties, transport, processing and production costs from the market price.
nodes.f: netback = market price - royalties - transport - production costs

nodes.t: Capacity to move oil or gas out of a producing basin; when output outgrows it, local prices fall to deep discounts versus coastal hubs until new pipes arrive.
Inventories divided by daily demand; normalizes stock levels for demand growth when comparing with history.
nodes.f: days of cover = stocks / daily consumption

nodes.t: Industry-held oil inventories in OECD countries, often compared with their five-year average as the headline gauge of oil market balance.
Convention of judging inventories against their seasonal five-year average; surpluses versus this norm tend to coincide with contango and deficits with backwardation.
Projection of supply minus demand over time; a surplus implies inventory builds and contango, while a deficit implies draws and backwardation.
Gap between the stock change implied by supply and demand estimates and the inventory change actually observed, signaling incomplete or wrong balance data.
Monthly International Energy Agency assessment of oil supply, demand and stocks, read alongside EIA and OPEC monthly reports to frame the balance.
Production targets agreed by OPEC+ members and how closely actual output matches them; overproduction by members weakens the credibility and effect of cuts.
Collective reduction in output targets to tighten balances; its effect depends on compliance, spare capacity and the response of producers outside the group.
Episode in which a major producer raises output or refuses to cut to defend market share and squeeze rivals, crashing prices; 1986, 2014 to 2016 and 2020 are standard examples.
Supplier with spare capacity able to raise or cut output quickly to balance the market; Saudi Arabia has historically played this role in oil.
World oil demand minus non-OPEC supply and OPEC natural gas liquids; the crude volume OPEC must supply to keep global inventories flat.
nodes.f: call = global demand - non-OPEC supply - OPEC NGLs

nodes.t: Cboe crude oil volatility index derived from options on the United States Oil Fund ETF; the oil market analog of the VIX.
April 2020 episode when the expiring May WTI futures contract settled below zero because Cushing storage was nearly full and longs had nowhere to take delivery.
Price spike near futures expiry when long holders stand for delivery and deliverable supply is scarce, forcing shorts to buy back at high prices.
Gaining control of enough deliverable supply and long futures to dictate settlement prices; the Hunt brothers in silver (1980) and Sumitomo in copper (1996) are classic cases.
Louisiana pipeline interconnect that is the delivery point for NYMEX natural gas futures and the main US gas price benchmark.
Title Transfer Facility, a virtual Dutch gas trading point that serves as Europe's main natural gas benchmark.
Platts spot price assessment for LNG cargoes delivered into Northeast Asia; the main Asian spot LNG benchmark.
Virtual trading point for UK natural gas, quoted in pence per therm and closely linked to TTF.
Price difference between a regional gas hub and Henry Hub, set by pipeline constraints, local supply and seasonal demand.
West Texas gas hub where Permian associated gas trades; prices there have at times gone negative when pipeline capacity fell short of supply.
Natural gas produced alongside oil, so its supply follows oil drilling economics rather than gas prices.
Weekly report of working gas in US underground storage, released Thursdays; the injection or withdrawal versus expectations is the most market-moving gas data point.
US gas storage convention: injection season runs roughly April through October as storage fills, withdrawal season November through March as heating demand draws it down.
Weather demand measures based on deviation of daily average temperature from 65 F; they drive short-term gas and power demand forecasts.
nodes.f: HDD = max(0, 65 - average temp F); CDD = max(0, average temp F - 65)

nodes.t: The March-April natural gas futures spread, which can explode when late-winter storage runs short; named for the traders it has ruined.
2006 failure of hedge fund Amaranth Advisors after concentrated natural gas calendar spread positions lost billions of dollars within weeks.
Cooling natural gas to about minus 162 Celsius so it shrinks roughly 600-fold for shipping; liquefaction plants are the costliest link in the LNG chain.
Warming LNG back into gas at import terminals or floating storage and regasification units for delivery into pipelines.
Long-term agreement underpinning an LNG project, often with take-or-pay terms; US contracts commonly price as a percentage of Henry Hub plus a fixed liquefaction fee.
Long-term LNG contracts priced as a slope times a lagged crude average, such as Brent or the Japan Crude Cocktail, plus a constant.
nodes.f: price = slope x lagged oil price + constant

nodes.t: Routing flexible cargoes to the destination with the highest netback; the JKM-TTF spread minus the shipping cost difference decides whether cargoes head to Asia or Europe.
Generators shifting between coal and gas as relative fuel and carbon prices change; a large price-sensitive source of gas demand.
Ethane, propane, butanes and natural gasoline separated from wet gas; prices follow petrochemical demand, crude and export capacity.
Leaving ethane in the gas stream to be sold as fuel instead of extracting it when its value as petrochemical feedstock is lower.
Crude price per barrel divided by gas price per MMBtu; a ratio far above the energy-equivalent level near 6 means gas is cheap relative to oil on an energy basis.
nodes.f: ratio = oil price per barrel / gas price per MMBtu

nodes.t: One million British thermal units, the energy unit for US natural gas pricing; roughly equal to one thousand cubic feet of gas.
Wholesale electricity price at a specific grid node, equal to the marginal cost of serving one more megawatt-hour there; it splits into energy, congestion and loss components.
nodes.f: LMP = energy component + congestion component + loss component

nodes.t: Ranking of generators from lowest to highest marginal cost; the costliest unit needed to meet demand sets the clearing price paid to all dispatched units.
Independent system operators and regional transmission organizations that run US wholesale power markets and dispatch the grid, such as PJM, ERCOT, CAISO and MISO.
Two-settlement design: a day-ahead auction sets hourly schedules and prices, and a real-time market settles deviations at spot prices, creating a tradable DA-RT spread.
Purely financial bids to buy or sell power day-ahead and reverse the position in real time, which helps converge the two prices.
Market paying generators and demand response to be available in future periods, separate from energy sales, to secure reliability; PJM's capacity auction is a prominent example.
Power market without capacity payments, where scarcity prices during tight hours must reward investment in new supply; ERCOT in Texas is the main US example.
Rules that lift power prices toward a cap when operating reserves run short, signaling the value of reliability and paying flexible supply.
Fuel energy a power plant burns per unit of electricity, in Btu per kWh; lower heat rates mean more efficient plants.
nodes.f: heat rate = fuel input Btu / electricity output kWh

nodes.t: Power price divided by gas price; it shows the efficiency of the marginal gas unit priced into the market and is traded as a view on power relative to gas.
nodes.f: implied heat rate = power price per MWh / gas price per MMBtu

nodes.t: Gross margin of a coal plant: power price minus coal cost adjusted for the plant's efficiency; the clean dark spread also deducts carbon cost.
nodes.f: dark spread = power price - coal price x coal heat rate

nodes.t: Spark spread net of the cost of carbon allowances needed per megawatt-hour; the relevant margin for gas plants in carbon-priced markets.
nodes.f: clean spark = power - gas price x heat rate - carbon price x emissions per MWh

nodes.t: Energy a generator actually produces over a period divided by what it would produce running at full nameplate capacity the whole time.
nodes.f: capacity factor = MWh generated / (MW capacity x hours in period)

nodes.t: Discounted lifetime cost of building and running a generator divided by discounted lifetime output; useful for comparing technologies but blind to when and where power is produced.
nodes.f: LCOE = PV(lifetime costs) / PV(lifetime MWh)

nodes.t: Shape of net load in solar-heavy grids: a midday trough and a steep evening ramp, which depresses midday prices and rewards batteries and fast-ramping plants.
Wholesale prices below zero when inflexible or subsidized generation exceeds demand, so producers pay to keep running rather than shut down.
Falling capture prices for wind and solar as more is built, because they produce in the same hours and depress prices in exactly those hours.
Risk that the hourly profile of a hedge or of generation does not match the load or exposure it covers, leaving residual exposure to intraday price patterns.
Instruments paying the congestion price difference between two grid nodes, letting holders hedge or speculate on locational price differences.
Backlog of generation and storage projects waiting for grid operator studies and approval to connect; long queues slow the arrival of new supply.
Charging batteries when power is cheap and discharging when it is expensive, plus selling ancillary services; returns depend on daily price spreads, efficiency losses and cycle limits.
Grid services beyond bulk energy, such as frequency regulation, spinning and non-spinning reserves and voltage support, procured by system operators.
Available generating capacity above expected peak demand, as a share of peak; a thin margin raises the risk of scarcity prices and blackouts.
nodes.f: reserve margin = (capacity - peak demand) / peak demand

nodes.t: Standard power trading blocks: baseload covers all hours, peak covers weekday daytime hours (often 16 per day), and peak usually trades at a premium.
Tradable permits to emit one tonne of CO2 under a cap-and-trade system such as the EU ETS; their price adds to fossil generation cost and shifts the merit order.
Tradable certificate representing one megawatt-hour of renewable generation, used to meet renewable mandates or support clean energy claims.
Credits generated by biofuel blending and used by refiners and importers to show compliance with the US Renewable Fuel Standard; their cost feeds into refining margins.
Contracts paying on weather indices such as heating or cooling degree days or rainfall, used by utilities and energy firms to hedge volume risk.
The main venue for industrial metals futures, with daily prompt dates out to three months and a global warehouse network for physical delivery.
March 2022 episode in which nickel prices more than doubled in a day on a short squeeze, after which the London Metal Exchange suspended trading and cancelled trades.
CME Group exchange division listing gold, silver and copper futures; its warehouse stocks and the spread to London prices are watched for physical tightness.
Twice-daily electronic auction benchmark for gold in London, successor to the historic London gold fix and used to settle many contracts.
Gold or silver held in London vaults, the standard basis for over-the-counter bullion trading and settlement.
Allocated metal is specific bars owned outright and held for the owner; unallocated metal is a claim on a dealer's general stock and carries the dealer's credit risk.
Interest rate for borrowing gold, approximated as the dollar interest rate minus the gold forward rate; spikes signal scarce lendable metal.
nodes.f: lease rate = USD rate - gold forward offered rate

nodes.t: Long-observed inverse relationship between gold and real interest rates, because gold pays no income; the link can weaken when central bank or geopolitical buying dominates.
Ounces of silver needed to buy one ounce of gold; traders use it as a relative value and risk appetite gauge.
nodes.f: ratio = gold price / silver price

nodes.t: Platinum, palladium, rhodium and related metals, used mainly in vehicle catalytic converters, with mine supply concentrated in South Africa and Russia.
Light metal made by energy-intensive smelting of alumina from bauxite; electricity cost is the key driver of the smelter cost curve.
Metal used mainly in stainless steel and increasingly in battery cathodes, with supply shifting toward Indonesian processing of laterite ore.
Battery metal produced from brines and hard rock spodumene and sold as carbonate or hydroxide; prone to boom-bust cycles as supply responds with long lags.
Battery metal mostly mined as a byproduct of copper and nickel, with supply heavily concentrated in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Nuclear fuel traded as U3O8 mostly through long-term utility contracts with a thin spot market; conversion and enrichment are separately priced steps in the fuel cycle.
Group of 17 elements used in magnets, electronics and defense; mining and especially processing are concentrated in China, making supply a policy lever.
Steel price minus raw material cost: iron ore and coking coal for blast furnaces or scrap for electric arc furnaces; the core steelmaker margin.
High-quality coal converted to coke for blast-furnace steelmaking, priced separately from and usually above thermal coal.
Coal burned for electricity, priced off benchmarks such as Newcastle for Asia and API2 for Europe.
Gold miner cost metric that adds sustaining capital, exploration, and corporate overhead to cash operating costs per ounce.
Revenue from secondary metals subtracted from a mine's primary-metal cost, which can make reported unit costs very low or negative.
Fees miners pay smelters to process concentrate into metal; falling TC/RCs signal tight concentrate supply relative to smelting capacity.
Falling metal content per tonne of ore as the best deposits are depleted, which raises unit costs and capital needs over time.
Unplanned output losses from strikes, accidents, weather, or politics; analysts often bake a disruption allowance into supply forecasts.
Metal recovered from scrap and recycled, which rises with price and supplements mine output, especially in copper, aluminium and steel.
Government moves to capture more mineral or energy rent through higher royalties, export bans, forced local processing or nationalization; a key political risk in resources.
LME warehouse stocks earmarked for withdrawal; a rising share of cancelled warrants signals physical demand and possible tightness ahead.
Exchange-traded funds holding allocated gold bars, giving brokerage access to bullion; their holdings are a gauge of Western investment demand.
Miner profits move by more than the gold price because costs are largely fixed, so miners amplify both gains and losses in the metal.
Firms that pay upfront for a share of a mine's future metal output or revenue, gaining commodity exposure without operating costs or most capex risk.
The largest US crop by volume, used for animal feed, ethanol and exports; CBOT corn futures are the global benchmark.
Oilseed crushed into meal for feed and oil for food and biofuel; prices depend on US and Brazilian crops and on Chinese import demand.
Food grain traded in several classes, including CBOT soft red winter, Kansas City hard red winter and Minneapolis spring wheat; exports come from many regions so weather risk is diversified.
Ethanol plant margin: value of ethanol and distillers grains produced minus the cost of corn and natural gas consumed.
Ending stocks divided by annual use; low ratios leave little buffer, so prices react sharply to supply shocks.
nodes.f: stocks-to-use = ending stocks / total use

nodes.t: Weekly USDA reports on planting, development, harvest and crop condition ratings during the season; changes in good-to-excellent ratings move grain futures.
USDA reports estimating planted area: Prospective Plantings in March and Acreage at the end of June; key early signals of new-crop supply.
Growing-season period when grain prices trade mostly on weather forecasts, with critical windows such as corn pollination in July, adding a risk premium that fades with good weather.
Local cash price minus nearby futures; it reflects transport, storage and local demand, and it is what farmers and elevators actually trade.
Calendar spread equal to storage plus financing cost, the widest contango that can persist before cash-and-carry arbitrage caps it; grain spreads near full carry signal ample supply.
nodes.f: full carry = storage cost + financing cost over the period

nodes.t: Live cattle, feeder cattle and lean hog futures, driven by herd cycles, feed costs, disease and meat demand.
Multi-year cycle in which ranchers expand or liquidate herds in response to prices and feed costs; because heifers are held back to rebuild, beef supply responds slowly.
Hog production margin: lean hog value minus the cost of corn and soybean meal fed to raise the animal.
Brazilian mills shift cane between sugar and ethanol depending on relative returns, linking world sugar prices to Brazilian fuel prices.
Nitrogen, phosphate and potash crop inputs; nitrogen products such as ammonia and urea are made from natural gas, so gas shocks pass through to farm costs.
Government ban, quota or tax on exports to protect domestic supply or prices, which tightens world markets; common in grains, fertilizer and critical minerals.
Pacific Ocean temperature cycles that shift rainfall worldwide, affecting crops such as Australian wheat, Southeast Asian palm oil and South American soybeans.
The most produced vegetable oil, grown mainly in Indonesia and Malaysia; it competes with soybean oil and is used for food and biodiesel.
Maximum price move allowed in a session for some futures contracts; a locked-limit market can halt trading and trap positions until prices reset.
Baltic Exchange composite of dry bulk freight rates across ship sizes and routes; it moves with both cargo demand and fleet supply.
Ways to hire ships: a voyage charter pays per cargo for one trip, a time charter pays a daily hire rate for a period while the charterer pays fuel and port costs.
Voyage revenue minus voyage costs such as fuel and port fees, divided by voyage days; puts spot voyages on a daily-rate basis comparable with time charters.
nodes.f: TCE = (voyage revenue - voyage costs) / voyage days

nodes.t: Tanker freight convention quoting rates as a percentage of a published flat rate for each route, updated annually.
Crude tanker sizes: VLCCs carry about two million barrels, Suezmaxes about one million and Aframaxes less; each suits different ports and routes.
Cash-settled derivative on future freight rates for a route or index, used by shipowners and charterers to hedge freight exposure.
Storing crude or products on tankers when contango exceeds chartering and financing costs; large floating storage signals severe oversupply.
Cargo tonnage multiplied by distance carried; rerouting and longer voyages raise effective demand for ships even when cargo volumes are flat.
nodes.f: ton-miles = tonnes carried x miles sailed

nodes.t: Ships on order as a share of the existing fleet; a central gauge of future supply growth in shipping cycles.
Boom-bust pattern in which high freight rates spur newbuild orders that arrive years later into softer demand, pushing rates down until scrapping restores balance.
Narrow sea routes such as Hormuz, Malacca, Suez, Bab el-Mandeb and Panama whose disruption forces rerouting and lifts freight, insurance and delivered prices.
Additional marine insurance charged for voyages through conflict zones, adding to delivered cost and sometimes diverting ships entirely.
Spot rate benchmarks for container shipping, such as the Shanghai Containerized Freight Index and the Drewry World Container Index.
Older tankers with opaque ownership and insurance used to move sanctioned oil outside Western shipping and insurance services.
Crude from sanctioned producers that trades at discounts through intermediaries; sanctions often redirect trade flows more than they cut total supply.
G7-led mechanism barring Western shipping, insurance and finance for Russian oil sold above a set price, aiming to cut revenue while keeping barrels flowing.
Fee paid to a shipowner when loading or discharging takes longer than the agreed laytime; port congestion turns it into a material cost.
Buying spot, selling forward and storing the commodity when the contango exceeds storage plus financing cost; this trade caps how wide contango can get.
nodes.f: profit = futures price - spot price - storage cost - financing cost

nodes.t: Condition where storage approaches full capacity, forcing spot prices down sharply until production or consumption adjusts; it produces super contango.
Valuing storage capacity as a strip of spread options between injection and withdrawal dates, with intrinsic value from the current curve and extrinsic value from volatility.
Price difference for the same commodity at two delivery points; when transport capacity is free, it is bounded by transport cost.
Trade between related commodities, such as crack, crush, spark or corn-wheat spreads, that exposes the trader to a processing or substitution margin rather than outright price.
Rules-based basket of commodity futures, such as the production-weighted S&P GSCI or the more diversified Bloomberg Commodity Index, rolled on a set schedule.
Monthly window when commodity index funds roll expiring futures into later months; predictable flows that other traders can position ahead of.
Total return on collateralized futures splits into spot price change, roll yield from curve shape and interest earned on the cash collateral.
nodes.f: total return = spot return + roll yield + collateral yield

nodes.t: Firms such as Vitol, Trafigura, Glencore and Cargill that buy, store, blend and ship physical commodities, earning on location, time and quality spreads.
Idea that net hedging demand by producers or consumers creates a risk premium paid to speculators who take the other side, shaping futures returns.
Option paying on the average price over a period rather than the price on one date; the standard form for commodity hedges because consumption is continuous.
OTC contract exchanging a fixed price for a floating average price over a period, used by producers and consumers to hedge without physical delivery.
Firms such as Platts and Argus whose assessments of physical deals set benchmark prices for cargoes and settle many derivatives; methodology details move money.
Physical or contract-backed assets with intrinsic use value, such as real estate, infrastructure, farmland, timber and commodities, often held for income and partial inflation protection.
Owning essential long-lived assets such as toll roads, airports, pipelines, utilities, towers and data centers, valued for contracted or regulated cash flows and high barriers to entry.

Real estate and infrastructure strategy ladder: core (stable income, low leverage), core-plus, value-add (repositioning) and opportunistic (development, distress, high leverage), with rising return targets.
Brownfield assets are existing and operating; greenfield assets are new builds that carry construction, permitting and ramp-up risk in exchange for higher expected returns.
Government grant to finance, build or operate an asset such as a toll road for a fixed term, after which it reverts to the grantor, so value runs down toward term end.
Long-term contract in which a private party finances, builds and operates public infrastructure, paid through user charges or government availability payments.
Government payment to an operator for keeping an asset available to agreed standards regardless of usage, removing demand risk from the investor.
Non-recourse lending to a single-asset special purpose vehicle, repaid only from the project's cash flows and secured by its contracts and assets.
Cash available for debt service divided by scheduled principal and interest; lenders set minimums and cash lockup triggers on it in project and real estate loans.
nodes.f: DSCR = cash flow available for debt service / (principal + interest)

nodes.t: Value of a regulated utility's invested capital on which regulators allow a return; earnings grow mainly as the rate base grows.
nodes.f: allowed earnings = rate base x equity share x allowed ROE

nodes.t: Return on equity a utility regulator lets the company earn on its rate base; the spread between earned and allowed ROE and the cost of equity drives utility valuation.
Publicly traded US partnership, common in midstream energy, that passes taxable income through to unitholders and pays large distributions.
Contract or tariff clause that raises revenue with a price index such as CPI, giving infrastructure and leases partial inflation protection.
Forest real asset earning harvest income plus biological growth; owners can delay harvests when prices are low, letting trees keep growing in volume and value.
Real asset earning cash rent or crop income plus land appreciation; values track crop prices, farm incomes and interest rates.
Cell towers, fiber networks and data centers held as infrastructure, earning long-term leases from carriers, cloud providers and other tech tenants.
Tower costs are mostly fixed, so each additional tenant on an existing tower adds revenue at very high margin; colocation drives returns.
Listed vehicle holding contracted renewable or infrastructure assets and paying out most cash flow as dividends, funded by issuing equity to buy more assets.
Exposure of an asset's revenue to spot market prices rather than fixed contracts, common in power plants and storage after contracts expire.
US structure in which investors with tax liability fund renewable projects in exchange for tax credits and depreciation benefits; credit transferability now offers an alternative route.
Cap rate minus the 10-year Treasury yield; a gauge of real estate's risk premium and relative value versus bonds.
nodes.f: spread = cap rate - 10-year Treasury yield

nodes.t: REIT holding mortgages or mortgage securities funded with leverage and earning the net interest spread; highly sensitive to rates, spreads and funding conditions.

nodes.n: REIT premium or discount to NAV
nodes.t: Gap between a REIT's share price and the estimated private-market value of its properties; persistent discounts can prompt buybacks, asset sales or take-privates.
Cap rate implied by a listed REIT's enterprise value and its NOI, compared with private appraisal cap rates to judge whether public or private markets look mispriced.
nodes.f: implied cap rate = NOI / (equity market value + debt + preferred - non-property assets)

nodes.t: Share of leasable space that is leased (occupancy) or empty (vacancy); the main volume driver of property NOI.
nodes.f: vacancy rate = vacant space / total space

nodes.t: Change in occupied space over a period: space newly leased minus space vacated; positive absorption signals growing demand.
Average remaining lease term weighted by rent; a longer WALT means more contracted income and less near-term re-leasing risk.
Lease in which the tenant pays property taxes, insurance and maintenance (triple net), making the landlord's income resemble a long bond tied to tenant credit.
Gap between in-place rents and current market rents, indicating income upside or downside as leases roll over.
Concentration of lease expiries that exposes income to re-leasing at market rents, downtime and leasing costs.
Landlord spending to fit out space and pay brokers when signing leases; large in office and often understated in headline earnings.
Free months or other incentives that make effective rent lower than headline rent, used to defend face rents in weak markets.
nodes.f: net effective rent = (total rent over term - concessions) / term

nodes.t: NOI divided by loan amount; a lender metric that does not depend on cap rates or interest rates.
nodes.f: debt yield = NOI / loan amount

nodes.t: Servicer that takes over a securitized commercial mortgage in default or at risk, deciding whether to modify, extend or foreclose.
Lenders extending maturing loans rather than foreclosing, hoping values recover; it delays loss recognition and can trap capital in weak assets.
Value loss in older office buildings as tenants favor newer space and use less of it, leaving owners facing heavy capex, conversion or writedowns.
Warehouses and distribution centers whose demand tracks e-commerce, inventory strategies and supply chains.
Apartment buildings with short leases that let rents reset quickly, giving inflation sensitivity and exposure to new supply waves.
Institutional ownership of detached homes for rent, a sector that scaled after the 2008 housing crash.
Ability of typical households to buy a home, measured by price-to-income or mortgage payment as a share of income; poor affordability depresses sales volumes.
Homeowners holding low fixed-rate mortgages are reluctant to sell and take on a higher rate, cutting existing-home supply and turnover.
Repeat-sales US home price index that tracks price changes of the same homes over time, published monthly with a lag.
Homes listed for sale divided by the monthly sales pace; low readings point to tight markets and rising prices.
nodes.f: months supply = inventory for sale / monthly sales

nodes.t: Home price divided by annual rent for comparable housing; high ratios suggest owning is expensive relative to renting.
nodes.f: ratio = home price / annual rent

nodes.t: Recurring sequence of recovery, expansion, oversupply and recession driven by long construction lags and credit availability.
Stabilized NOI divided by total development cost; it must exceed market cap rates by a margin to justify the risk of building.
nodes.f: yield on cost = stabilized NOI / total development cost

nodes.t: Private property values based on periodic appraisals adjust slowly to market moves, smoothing reported returns and understating volatility and correlation.
Index of open-end diversified core equity US real estate funds; the main benchmark for core private real estate.
REIT not listed on an exchange that offers limited periodic redemptions at a sponsor-set NAV; it can cap or prorate withdrawals when requests surge.
US tax rule letting real estate investors defer capital gains by reinvesting sale proceeds into like-kind property within set deadlines.
Leverage is positive when a property's cap rate exceeds the all-in cost of debt, lifting equity returns, and negative when debt costs more than the property yields.
Long-term lease of land to a building owner who pays ground rent and surrenders improvements at expiry; the landowner's position is senior and bond-like.
Hotel revenue per available room, the main hotel performance metric, combining occupancy and pricing.
nodes.f: RevPAR = occupancy rate x average daily rate

nodes.t: Private equity firm that buys and controls companies using equity from its funds plus acquisition debt, aiming to sell within several years.
Attribution of a buyout's equity gain to EBITDA growth, multiple expansion and debt paydown, showing whether returns came from operations or from market and leverage.
Strategy of acquiring a platform company and bolting on smaller add-on acquisitions at lower multiples, seeking scale, synergies and multiple arbitrage.
Share of a buyout's total price funded with sponsor equity rather than debt; a larger check lowers default risk but also lowers equity returns for a given outcome.
Equity that selling owners or managers reinvest into the new deal instead of taking cash, aligning them with the buyer's exit.
Purchase of a division from a larger company, requiring standalone functions and usually transitional service agreements with the former parent.
Sale of a sponsor-owned company to another private equity firm; common when IPO and strategic exits are scarce.
Floating-rate senior secured loan to a sub-investment-grade borrower, typically syndicated and held largely by CLOs and loan funds.
Maintenance covenants are tested regularly, such as quarterly leverage limits; incurrence covenants apply only when the borrower takes an action such as adding debt or paying dividends.
Ranking of secured claims on the same collateral; first-lien lenders are repaid first in default, while second-lien lenders accept lower recoveries for higher spreads.
Capital senior to common equity with a fixed or accruing return, used in buyouts, real estate and GP financing as a bridge between debt and equity.
Issuing a loan or bond below par, giving lenders upfront yield on top of the coupon spread.
nodes.f: yield pickup per year approx = OID / expected life of loan

nodes.t: Lending secured by pools of receivables, inventory, equipment or consumer loans rather than by enterprise value, a growing part of private credit.
Loans on which a lender has stopped recognizing interest income because full collection is doubtful; a key credit quality metric for BDCs.
Loan to a software company sized on annual recurring revenue rather than EBITDA, betting on retention and later profitability.
Open-ended private markets vehicle with continuous subscriptions and periodic, capped redemptions, rather than a fixed-life fund.
Standard private fund structure with an investment period of several years and a total term near ten years plus extensions, returning capital as assets are sold.
Amount an LP agrees to provide to a fund over its life, drawn through capital calls; the undrawn part remains a binding liability for the LP.
Committing more than the target private allocation on the expectation that calls and distributions will keep invested NAV near target; risky if distributions slow.
When public markets fall faster than lagging private marks, private allocations rise above target, pressuring LPs to slow new commitments or sell on the secondary market.
Planning yearly commitments across vintages so a portfolio reaches and holds a target private allocation, usually modeled with cash flow projections.
Contract governing a private fund: fees, carry, waterfall, investment limits, key person rules, GP removal and reporting.
LPA provision suspending the investment period if named senior professionals leave or stop devoting sufficient time to the fund.
LP rights to remove the GP or end the investment period by supermajority vote, either for cause or without cause.
Order in which fund proceeds are split: return of contributed capital, then the preferred return, then a GP catch-up, then the carried interest split.

A European (whole-fund) waterfall pays carry only after LPs recover all contributions and the preferred return; an American (deal-by-deal) waterfall pays carry per realized deal, earlier and with more clawback risk.
Waterfall tier after the preferred return in which the GP receives most or all distributions until it has received its full carry share of total profits.
The GP's own capital invested in its fund, commonly around 1 to 3 percent of commitments, intended to align its interests with LPs.
Crediting part or all of portfolio company monitoring and transaction fees against the management fee LPs pay.
Reduction in the management fee rate or switch of its basis from commitments to invested capital after the investment period ends.
IRR is sensitive to timing, can be lifted by early distributions or subscription lines without more profit, implicitly assumes reinvestment at the IRR, and can have multiple solutions.
Public market equivalent ratio from Kaplan and Schoar (2005) that discounts fund cash flows by public index returns; above 1 means the fund beat the index.
nodes.f: KS-PME = PV(distributions + NAV) / PV(contributions), discounted at index returns

nodes.t: Annualized excess return of a private fund over a public benchmark, computed as the IRR of cash flows compounded forward at index returns.
Placing a fund within peer vintage returns; many managers can claim top quartile by picking the metric, benchmark, or vintage definition, so claims need checking.
Spread of returns between top and bottom managers, much wider in venture and buyouts than in public equity, making manager selection the dominant decision.
LP investing directly alongside a fund in a specific deal, usually with low or no fees and carry, often offered when the GP needs a larger equity check.
Minority equity stakes in private markets firms, entitling holders to a share of management fees, carry and balance sheet returns.
Sale of an LP's interests in one or more funds to a secondary buyer, usually priced at a discount or premium to the latest reported NAV.
Transaction organized by the GP, such as a continuation vehicle or tender offer, that lets existing LPs sell or roll their exposure to selected assets.
Secondary trades are quoted as a percentage of the latest reported NAV; discounts reflect stale marks, unfunded obligations, asset quality and sellers' liquidity needs.
nodes.f: price as % of NAV = purchase price / reported NAV

nodes.t: Organized purchase of shares from employees and early investors of a private company, offering liquidity before an IPO or sale.
Private holdings are marked using comparable company multiples, recent transactions, DCF models or option pricing methods, typically calibrated to the last financing round.
Option pricing method that infers total equity value from the price of the latest preferred round, allocating value across share classes as call options with different strikes.
Independent valuation of a private US company's common stock used to set option strike prices without adverse tax consequences; usually below preferred round prices.
Right of preferred shareholders to receive a set multiple of their investment before common holders in a sale; participating preferred also shares in what remains.
Adjustment to preferred stock conversion price after a down round; full ratchet resets to the new price, while broad-based weighted average adjusts only partly.
Investor right to buy into future rounds to maintain its ownership percentage, valuable in breakout companies.
Simple agreement for future equity, introduced by Y Combinator: an early-stage instrument converting into equity at the next priced round, usually subject to a valuation cap or discount.
Early-stage debt that converts into equity at the next financing round, usually at a discount or capped valuation, accruing interest until conversion.
Pre-money is a company's value before a new investment; post-money adds the new cash, and the investor's ownership equals the investment divided by post-money.
nodes.f: post-money = pre-money + new investment; ownership = investment / post-money

nodes.t: Requiring an enlarged option pool inside the pre-money valuation, shifting its dilution entirely onto existing holders and lowering the effective pre-money price.
Ledger of a company's securities and holders, including preferred classes, options, warrants and convertibles; the basis for any payout analysis.
Sequence of pre-seed, seed, Series A, B, C and later rounds, each typically tied to milestones, larger checks and new lead investors.
Interim financing, often from existing investors via notes or an extension, to extend runway until a larger round or exit.
Venture round that preserves a headline valuation by giving new investors senior preferences, ratchets or guaranteed returns instead of a lower price.
Choosing the number of companies, initial check sizes and follow-on reserves so a fund can own meaningful stakes in the rare outliers that drive returns.
Capital held back to invest in later rounds of existing portfolio companies, ideally concentrated in the winners.
Venture heuristic that each initial investment should have a plausible path to returning the entire fund on its own, given power-law outcomes.
Loans to venture-backed startups, usually with warrants, sized against equity already raised rather than against cash flow.
Program that gives startups a small investment, mentorship and a demo day in exchange for equity; Y Combinator is the best-known example.
Venture investing by operating companies pursuing both strategic and financial goals, often with different incentives from traditional VCs.
Fund past its intended life holding residual assets with weak exit prospects while still charging fees, often resolved through secondaries.
Time a sponsor owns a portfolio company before exit; longer holds lower IRR for the same multiple of money, which is why IRR and MOIC must be read together.
Running an IPO process and a sale process in parallel to increase price tension and certainty of exit.
Strategic acquirers can pay for synergies with their existing businesses; financial buyers price on standalone cash flow and leverage capacity.
Banker-run sale with staged non-binding and binding bids designed to maximize price and terms for the seller.
Pre-arranged debt package offered to bidders by the seller's advisor to speed an auction and set a leverage floor.
Policy covering losses from breaches of seller representations in an acquisition, reducing escrow and indemnity needs.
Locked box fixes the price from a historical balance sheet with protection against value leakage; completion accounts adjust the price after closing to actual figures.
Vehicle in which an entrepreneur raises capital to find, buy and run one small company, with investors funding the search and holding rights to invest in the deal.
Dealmaker without a committed fund who sources a deal and then raises equity deal by deal, earning fees and a promote.
US government-guaranteed small business loan program widely used to finance acquisitions of small companies, with personal guarantee and equity injection requirements.
Part of a purchase price financed by the seller and usually subordinated to senior debt, keeping the seller invested in a smooth handover.
Small-business earnings measure that adds back one owner's compensation and discretionary expenses to pre-tax profit; used to value owner-operated firms.
nodes.f: SDE = pre-tax profit + owner compensation + interest + D&A + discretionary expenses

nodes.t: Statistical reversal of appraisal smoothing, such as the Geltner method, to estimate the true volatility and correlation of private asset returns.
nodes.f: true return r_t = (observed r_t - a x observed r_t-1) / (1 - a)

nodes.t: Correlation of an asset's returns with its own past returns; high positive autocorrelation in reported returns is a sign of smoothed or stale pricing.
View that much of buyout performance can be matched by leveraged portfolios of small, cheap public stocks, which questions the size of private equity alpha.
Capital without a redemption or fund-term clock, such as holding companies, insurance float or perpetual vehicles, allowing indefinite holds.
Structure owning controlling stakes in several operating businesses indefinitely and reallocating their cash centrally; Berkshire Hathaway and Constellation Software are well-known examples.
Private firm managing a wealthy family's capital, often investing directly in companies and real assets with long horizons.
State-owned investment fund, often funded by commodity revenue or reserves, investing long-term across public and private assets.
Alternative asset managers owning or partnering with insurers and investing policyholder reserves in private credit to earn a spread over liabilities.
Bank sale of the credit risk on a slice of a loan portfolio to investors, typically via a synthetic securitization, to reduce regulatory capital.
Companies too large for small business lending but too small for broadly syndicated loans and bonds; the main arena for direct lenders.
Buyout or loan undertaken jointly by several sponsors or lenders to share a large check and its risk.
Underwritten loan or bond that banks cannot sell to investors at expected terms, leaving them holding the risk or selling at a loss.
Separating a company's real estate into a property company and its operations into an operating company, often to raise cash; rent obligations raise operating risk.
LPA clause letting a GP reinvest early proceeds or amounts equal to fees, raising total invested capital above commitments.
Institutional Limited Partners Association guidance on fund terms, governance and standardized fee and performance reporting.
Trading in shares of venture-backed companies via brokers, platforms or tender offers, subject to transfer restrictions and company rights of first refusal.
US Section 1202 exclusion of capital gains on qualifying small company stock held for a minimum period, up to set limits; a major tax benefit for founders and early investors.
Drag-along rights let majority holders force minorities to join a sale; tag-along rights let minorities join a sale on the same terms as the majority.
Append-only ledger of transaction blocks, each linked to the previous by a cryptographic hash and replicated across many nodes that agree on its state through a consensus mechanism.
Consensus mechanism in which miners compete to find a block hash below a target, making it very costly to rewrite history; Bitcoin uses it.
Consensus mechanism in which validators lock tokens as collateral to propose and attest blocks, and lose part of that stake if they misbehave.
Total computing power securing a proof-of-work network, measured in hashes per second; a gauge of security and of miner investment.
Automatic retargeting of mining difficulty so blocks keep arriving near the target interval; Bitcoin adjusts every 2,016 blocks.
Expected miner revenue per unit of hashrate per day, combining coin price, block subsidy, fees and difficulty; the core bitcoin mining profitability metric.
Revenue for miners or validators from newly issued coins plus transaction fees; in Bitcoin the subsidy halves on schedule, so fees must eventually carry more of security spending.
Bitcoin's accounting model in which balances are sets of unspent transaction outputs that each transaction consumes and creates; it enables coin-age metrics.
Pool of valid but unconfirmed transactions waiting to be included in a block; congestion there pushes fees up.
Unit measuring computational work on Ethereum; users pay gas used times a price made of a base fee plus an optional priority tip.
nodes.f: fee = gas used x (base fee + priority fee)

nodes.t: Ethereum fee mechanism adopted in 2021 that sets an algorithmic base fee per block, which is burned, plus an optional tip to the block producer.
Ethereum's 2022 switch from proof of work to proof of stake, sharply cutting new ETH issuance and energy use.
Point after which a transaction cannot be reversed; probabilistic and growing with confirmations under proof of work, explicit after checkpoints in many proof-of-stake systems.
Control of a majority of hashrate or stake that lets an attacker reorder, censor or double-spend recent transactions; cheapest against small networks.
Program deployed on a blockchain that executes deterministically when called and can hold and move assets according to its code.
Execution environment for Ethereum smart contracts, also adopted by many other chains so that contracts and tools carry over.
Base blockchain that provides its own consensus, data and security, such as Bitcoin, Ethereum or Solana.
Network that executes transactions off the main chain and posts data or proofs back to it, inheriting much of its security while cutting costs.
Layer 2 that treats posted batches as valid unless challenged with a fraud proof during a dispute window, which delays native withdrawals.
Layer 2 that posts a validity proof showing each batch of transactions is correct, allowing faster settlement on the base chain.
Guarantee that the transaction data behind a block or rollup batch is published so anyone can verify state; a main cost driver for rollups.
High-throughput proof-of-stake layer 1 with a single global state, favored for trading and consumer applications; it has suffered several network outages.
Protocol that moves assets between blockchains by locking them on one chain and minting representations on another; bridges have been among the largest hack targets.
Token representing another asset on a different chain, backed by custodied collateral, such as wrapped bitcoin on Ethereum; it adds custodian or bridge risk.
Service that feeds off-chain data such as asset prices into smart contracts; manipulated or stale oracle prices are a major source of DeFi losses.
Decentralized exchange design in which a liquidity pool quotes prices from a formula instead of an order book; the constant product rule is the classic form.
nodes.f: constant product: x x y = k

nodes.t: Shortfall of an AMM liquidity provider's position versus simply holding the two assets, caused by price divergence; providers profit only if fees exceed it.
nodes.f: constant product IL = 2 x sqrt(r) / (1 + r) - 1, where r = new price ratio / old price ratio

nodes.t: AMM design, introduced by Uniswap v3, in which providers supply liquidity only within chosen price ranges, raising capital efficiency and fee income but also impermanent loss.
Exchange where trades settle on-chain through smart contracts without a custodian, using AMMs or on-chain order books.
Router that splits an order across decentralized venues and paths to get the best net execution after fees and price impact.
Profit block producers and searchers capture by ordering, inserting or censoring transactions, such as arbitrage, liquidations and sandwich attacks.
MEV tactic that places a buy just before and a sell just after a victim's DEX trade to profit from the price impact the victim causes.
Ethereum arrangement in which specialized builders assemble blocks and bid for inclusion by validators, mostly through relays such as MEV-Boost.
Uncollateralized loan that is borrowed and repaid within one transaction or the whole transaction reverts; used for arbitrage and in oracle manipulation attacks.
Pool-based lending in which borrowers post overcollateralized crypto and rates adjust algorithmically with utilization; Aave and Compound are standard examples.
Automatic sale of a borrower's collateral when its value falls below the required ratio, executed by keepers or bots for a liquidation bonus.
nodes.f: health factor = collateral value x liquidation threshold / debt value

nodes.t: Forced selling from liquidations pushes prices lower and triggers further liquidations; a recurring cause of sharp crypto crashes.
Moving capital across protocols to earn fees and token incentives; headline yields often come from emissions that dilute token holders.
Protocol yield paid from actual fee revenue rather than newly emitted tokens, which makes it more sustainable than incentive-driven yield.
Scheduled issuance of new tokens to users, stakers or teams; emissions dilute holders and can make reported yields illusory.
Value of assets deposited in a protocol or chain; a rough usage gauge inflated by double counting of reused collateral and by token price moves.
Token giving voting rights over protocol parameters and treasury, sometimes with a claim on fees; low turnout and whale concentration often weaken governance.
Entity governed by token holder votes executed through smart contracts, often controlling a protocol treasury.
Fees a protocol keeps for itself or its token holders after paying liquidity providers or validators; the base for fundamental crypto valuation.
Crypto analogs of equity multiples, such as market cap or fully diluted value divided by annualized fees or protocol revenue.
nodes.f: price to fees = market cap / annualized fees

nodes.t: Token price times the maximum or eventual total supply; a large gap between FDV and circulating market cap signals future dilution from unlocks.
nodes.f: FDV = price x total eventual supply

nodes.t: Tokens currently tradable in the market, excluding locked, vested and treasury holdings; market cap uses this supply.
Scheduled release of vested tokens to insiders and early investors, which adds sellable supply and often pressures price.
Design of a token's supply, issuance, distribution, utility and value accrual, which determines who gets value and when.
Return to stakers from new issuance plus fees and MEV; the issuance part is largely a transfer from non-stakers through dilution rather than new income.
Staking through a protocol that issues a tradable receipt token representing staked assets plus rewards, such as Lido's stETH.
Reusing staked ETH to secure additional services in exchange for extra yield and extra slashing risk; EigenLayer popularized the model.
Penalty that destroys part of a validator's stake for provable misbehavior such as double signing; the enforcement tool of proof of stake.
Free distribution of tokens to users or holders, used to reward early activity and spread ownership; recipients often sell quickly.
Public sale of newly created tokens to fund a project; the 2017 boom led US regulators to treat many such sales as unregistered securities offerings.
US Supreme Court (1946) test for an investment contract: an investment of money in a common enterprise with an expectation of profits from others' efforts; central to whether tokens are securities.
Rules governing token issuance, trading venues, custody and stablecoins; the split of authority between securities and commodities regulators shapes market structure.
Token without cash flow claims whose value rests on attention and community; marked by extreme volatility and heavy insider concentration at launch.
Any cryptocurrency other than bitcoin; altcoins usually have higher beta to crypto market moves and higher failure rates.
Bitcoin's share of total crypto market capitalization; it tends to rise in risk-off phases and fall during speculative altcoin rallies.
nodes.f: dominance = bitcoin market cap / total crypto market cap

nodes.t: Pattern of bitcoin bull and bear phases loosely aligned with halvings; it rests on very few cycles and may reflect global liquidity as much as supply.
Stablecoin backed by cash and short-term government securities held by an issuer and redeemable at par, such as USDT and USDC.
Stablecoin minted against overcollateralized crypto deposits with automatic liquidations, such as DAI.
Stablecoin that relies on minting and burning a companion token rather than full reserves to hold its peg; prone to death spirals once confidence breaks.
May 2022 depeg of the algorithmic stablecoin UST and hyperinflation of its sister token LUNA, erasing tens of billions of dollars of value within days.
A stablecoin or pegged token trading away from its target value due to reserve doubts, redemption frictions or collateral failure; USDC briefly depegged in March 2023 when SVB failed.
Mix of cash, Treasury bills, repo and other assets backing a stablecoin; reserve quality, custody and attestation determine run risk.
Issuers earn interest on reserves while holders usually receive no yield, so issuer profits depend heavily on short-term rates and outstanding supply.
Change in outstanding stablecoins, watched as a gauge of dollar liquidity available to crypto markets.
US federal law enacted in 2025 creating a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins, including licensing, reserve and redemption requirements.
The EU Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, a comprehensive framework for crypto issuers, service providers and stablecoins across member states.
On-chain tokens representing shares in funds holding US Treasury bills, used as yield-bearing cash and collateral in crypto markets.
Off-chain assets such as bonds, private credit, funds or real estate represented by tokens on a blockchain, relying on legal wrappers and custodians.
Digital money issued directly by a central bank, for retail or wholesale use, distinct from privately issued stablecoins.
Safekeeping of private keys on behalf of clients by custodians using cold storage, multi-party computation and asset segregation.
Secret number that authorizes spending from a crypto address; whoever controls it controls the funds, and lost keys mean lost assets.
Holding one's own private keys in a hardware or software wallet, removing intermediary risk but taking on loss, theft and inheritance risk.
Hot wallets keep keys online for operational liquidity; cold wallets keep keys offline for most holdings, trading convenience for security.
Key security schemes requiring several parties to approve a transaction, either through multiple on-chain signatures or through split-key cryptography off-chain.
Exchange disclosure showing assets held on-chain, ideally paired with a Merkle-tree proof of liabilities; without liabilities it does not prove solvency.
November 2022 failure of crypto exchange FTX after it emerged that customer funds had been used by affiliated trading firm Alameda Research; a lesson in custody and commingling risk.
Early dominant bitcoin exchange that failed in 2014 after losing a very large amount of customer bitcoin; the first major custodial failure in crypto.
Venue combining brokerage, matching, custody, clearing and often lending in one entity, unlike traditional markets where these roles are separated.
