Futures contract with no expiry that stays near spot through periodic funding payments between longs and shorts; the dominant crypto derivative.
Periodic payment between perpetual futures longs and shorts based on the perp's premium or discount to spot; persistently high positive funding signals crowded leveraged longs.
Buying spot crypto and shorting dated futures or perpetuals to earn the basis or funding; a carry trade exposed to exchange, margin and liquidation risk.
Exchange futures open interest divided by the exchange's coin reserves; a rough gauge of leverage building in crypto derivatives.
nodes.f: ELR = open interest / exchange reserves

nodes.t: Exchange mechanism that forcibly closes profitable opposing positions when liquidation losses exceed the exchange's insurance fund.
Cash-settled, regulated bitcoin and ether futures on CME, used by institutions for hedging and as the short leg of ETF basis trades.
Crypto liquidity is split across many exchanges and chains with different fees, collateral and access, creating price gaps that arbitrageurs close imperfectly.
Premium of crypto prices on South Korean exchanges over global prices, sustained at times by capital controls; a textbook case of limits to arbitrage.
Analysis of public blockchain data, such as holder behavior, flows, fees and cost bases, to infer supply, demand and positioning.
Sum of every coin valued at the price when it last moved on-chain; approximates the aggregate cost basis of holders.
nodes.f: realized cap = sum over coins of price at last movement

nodes.t: Market value divided by realized value; high readings mean holders sit on large unrealized gains, low readings suggest capitulation.
nodes.f: MVRV = market cap / realized cap

nodes.t: Value of coins when spent divided by their value when last moved; readings above 1 mean coins are being sold at a profit on average.
nodes.f: SOPR = value at spend / value at creation

nodes.t: Network value divided by daily on-chain transaction volume; a crypto analog of a price-to-sales ratio.
nodes.f: NVT = market cap / daily transaction volume

nodes.t: Net movement of coins onto exchanges, read as potential selling, or off them, read as holding; noisy because of internal wallet reshuffles.
Coin holders split by how long coins have sat unmoved, commonly about 155 days; long-term holders tend to distribute into bull markets.
Unique addresses transacting in a period; a rough usage proxy distorted by address reuse, exchanges and bots.
Distribution of coin supply by age since last movement, showing how holder behavior shifts across cycles.
Coins moved multiplied by days since they last moved; spikes reveal long-dormant coins being spent.
nodes.f: CDD = sum of coins moved x days since last moved

nodes.t: Co-movement of bitcoin with technology stocks and liquidity conditions, which rose as institutions entered; it undercuts the hedge narrative in risk-off periods.
Listed company that raises equity and debt to hold crypto on its balance sheet, with Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy) the main example; shares trade at a premium or discount to holdings.
nodes.f: mNAV = enterprise value / value of crypto held

nodes.t: Total miner or validator revenue that pays for network security; the debate over whether fees can replace shrinking bitcoin subsidies.
Layer 2 network of bitcoin payment channels that enables fast, cheap payments off-chain, settling net balances on-chain.
Unique on-chain token representing ownership of a specific digital item; NFT markets are thin, illiquid and highly speculative.
Ethereum standard interface for fungible tokens, which lets any wallet or protocol handle any compliant token.
Protocol change that is not backward compatible, splitting the chain when some nodes refuse to upgrade, as with Bitcoin Cash in 2017.
Anti-money-laundering requirement, extended to crypto by the FATF, that service providers pass originator and beneficiary information with transfers.
Service converting bank money into crypto and back (the off-ramp); usually the main regulatory and banking chokepoint for the sector.
Risk of loss from code bugs, economic exploits or abuse of upgrade keys in a protocol; audits reduce it but do not eliminate it.
Privileged keys letting a team upgrade, pause or change contracts, adding centralization and governance risk to nominally decentralized protocols.
Scam in which developers drain pool liquidity or dump their tokens after attracting investors.
Firms that took crypto deposits promising yield and lent them on, often to leveraged traders; Celsius and BlockFi failed in 2022.
Bitcoin's fixed maximum supply of 21 million coins, approached gradually as the block subsidy halves.
Model valuing bitcoin by the ratio of existing supply to annual new issuance; criticized as spurious because issuance is preset and the fit rests on a short sample.
nodes.f: S2F = existing stock / annual new supply

nodes.t: Claim that a network's value scales with the square of its users, applied loosely to value crypto networks from active addresses.
nodes.f: value proportional to n^2

nodes.t: Permanent removal of tokens from supply, through fee burns or buy-and-burn programs; the crypto analog of share buybacks.
Decentralized exchange for perpetual futures using on-chain or hybrid order books or pooled liquidity, letting traders keep custody of collateral.
Market trading contracts that pay on event outcomes, so prices can be read as crowd probabilities; examples include Polymarket and Kalshi.
Light refinery and condensate stream used as petrochemical cracker feedstock and gasoline blendstock; it competes with ethane and LPG as feed, so its crack tracks chemical demand.
Losses suffered by funds that hold near-month futures and roll them in contango, so the fund lags the spot price over time; oil ETFs in 2020 were a stark case.
February 2021 winter storm that froze gas wells and knocked out generation across ERCOT, holding power prices at the price cap for days and bankrupting several retailers and a cooperative.
Collapse of Russian pipeline gas deliveries to Europe in 2022 that drove TTF to record highs, forced industrial demand destruction and set off a scramble for LNG import capacity.

Minerals deemed essential to economic and national security with concentrated supply, such as lithium, cobalt, rare earths and graphite; governments respond with stockpiles, subsidies and trade controls.
New-crop soybean futures price divided by new-crop corn price; it guides farmers' planting mix, with high ratios favoring more soybean acres.
nodes.f: ratio = November soybeans / December corn

nodes.t: Price difference between LME cash metal and the three-month contract; backwardation in this spread signals scarce nearby metal.
US law requiring cargo moved between US ports to travel on US-built, US-owned and US-crewed ships, which raises domestic shipping costs and shapes regional fuel prices.
Daily hire rates for LNG tankers, which spike when long-haul arbitrage or floating storage ties up the fleet and fall when new ships flood the market.
Two-way contract paying a generator the difference between a strike price and the market price, and collecting it back when prices exceed the strike; used in renewable auctions such as the UK's.
nodes.f: payment = (strike - reference price) x MWh generated

nodes.t: Secondary sale of an equal percentage slice of every asset in a fund portfolio, so buyers cannot cherry-pick and the seller keeps proportional exposure.
Increase in a portfolio company's carrying value after a higher-priced financing round; markups from insider-led or structured rounds are weaker evidence of value.
Financing term requiring existing investors to buy their pro rata share of a new round or lose preferred rights, often by conversion to common stock.
Lease in which the tenant pays a single rent and the landlord covers property taxes, insurance and operating costs, leaving the landlord exposed to expense inflation.
Converting obsolete buildings, most often offices, to other uses such as housing; feasibility depends on floorplate depth, plumbing, windows and the purchase basis.
Buying property for less than it would cost to build today, which offers a margin of safety because new competing supply is uneconomic until rents rise.
Short-term floating-rate loan funding development in draws against completed work, repaid by permanent financing or sale once the property stabilizes.
Short-term floating-rate loan on a transitional property being leased up or repositioned, refinanced into permanent debt once cash flow stabilizes.
Data centers lease space by megawatts of critical IT load, often to hyperscalers on long pre-signed leases; access to power and grid connections is the binding constraint on supply.
Bitcoin miners selling reserves and switching off rigs when hashprice falls below operating costs, often after a halving; hashrate dips and difficulty then adjusts down.
Change in ether supply equal to new staking issuance minus base fees burned; it turns negative when network usage is heavy enough.
nodes.f: net issuance = issuance to validators - fees burned

nodes.t: Options on bitcoin and ether traded mainly on Deribit, with CME and spot ETF options growing; implied volatility indices such as DVOL track their pricing.
Government holding of bitcoin as a reserve asset; the US established one in 2025 from forfeited coins, and the idea fuels debate about official sector demand.
Commercial bank deposits represented on a blockchain; unlike stablecoins they remain bank liabilities within deposit regulation.

Field explaining asset prices and investor choices through psychology and market frictions. Its two pillars are systematic cognitive biases and limits to arbitrage that let mispricing persist. Key figures include Kahneman, Tversky, Thaler, Shiller and Shleifer.

Kahneman and Tversky's research program showing that judgment under uncertainty relies on mental shortcuts such as representativeness, availability and anchoring, which are often useful but produce predictable, systematic errors.

Model of two modes of thought: System 1 is fast, intuitive and automatic; System 2 is slow, deliberate and effortful. Most biases arise when System 1 answers and System 2 fails to check. Popularized by Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011).

Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, so vivid, recent or heavily reported events such as crashes, frauds and big winners are overweighted relative to their true frequency. Tversky and Kahneman (1973).

Judging likelihood by resemblance to a stereotype instead of by base rates, for example assuming a company with a great story or fast recent growth must be a great investment. Drives base-rate neglect and the law of small numbers.

Letting feelings about an asset drive judgments of both its risk and its return, so liked assets are seen as safer and higher returning at once, contrary to the usual risk-return tradeoff. Studied by Slovic and coauthors.
Unknowingly answering an easier question in place of a hard one, such as replacing 'is this stock undervalued' with 'do I like this company'. Kahneman and Frederick's account of how heuristics work.
Preference for the current state of affairs, so investors keep existing holdings, allocations and default options even when switching would be better. Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988).

Valuing something more once you own it: owners demand more to sell than they would pay to buy the same item. Thaler (1980); linked to loss aversion. Makes investors reluctant to sell inherited or long-held positions.

Avoiding choices that could later cause regret, for example holding losers to avoid confirming a mistake or following the crowd so a loss is shared. Regret from action usually stings more than regret from inaction.
Preferring known risks over unknown probabilities, as shown in the Ellsberg paradox. Investors pay up for familiar assets and avoid ones whose odds feel unknowable, even at similar expected outcomes.

Heath and Tversky (1991): people prefer to bet on uncertain events in areas where they feel knowledgeable, even over equally likely known chances. Feeling competent, not actual odds, drives willingness to take the bet.
Favoring investments one knows, such as employer stock, local firms or famous brands, and mistaking familiarity for lower risk. A main driver of home bias and concentrated employee holdings.

Evaluating each risk in isolation instead of as part of total wealth, so a small positive expected value bet is rejected because its standalone loss looks painful. Kahneman and Lovallo; Barberis, Huang and Thaler.

Loss aversion combined with frequent evaluation: checking a portfolio often makes losses more visible and pushes investors toward overly safe allocations. Benartzi and Thaler (1995) used it to explain the equity premium puzzle.
Taking more risk after gains because profits feel like someone else's money. Thaler and Johnson (1990). Can feed escalating speculation late in rallies.
After losses, taking extra risk for a chance to get back to even. Thaler and Johnson (1990). Behind doubling down, revenge trading and loss chasing.
The benchmark against which outcomes are coded as gains or losses, often purchase price, a recent high or expectations. Moving the reference point changes risk taking even when wealth is unchanged.

Value function over gains and losses relative to a reference point: concave for gains, convex for losses and steeper for losses. Tversky and Kahneman (1992) estimated curvature about 0.88 and a loss aversion coefficient about 2.25.
nodes.f: v(x) = x^0.88 for gains; v(x) = -2.25 * (-x)^0.88 for losses

nodes.t: Tversky and Kahneman's 1992 version of prospect theory that applies probability weights to cumulative distributions of outcomes, respecting stochastic dominance and handling many outcomes.
In prospect theory people overweight small probabilities and underweight moderate to large ones, which explains demand for both lottery tickets and insurance.
Overweighting outcomes that are certain relative to ones that are merely probable, so a sure gain is valued well above a slightly risky larger gain. Central to the Allais paradox.
Risk attitudes flip with the sign of outcomes: people are risk averse over gains and risk seeking over losses. A core prospect theory finding behind the disposition effect.
Ignoring components shared by all options and focusing on differences, so the same choice presented in stages can produce a different decision. Kahneman and Tversky (1979).
Investors get utility from realizing gains and losses on individual positions, not only from total wealth, which helps explain the disposition effect and heavy trading. Barberis and Xiong.
Loomes and Sugden (1982) and Bell (1982): choices account for anticipated regret from comparing the outcome received with what the rejected option would have paid.
Prices moving too far on news or past performance, then reversing. De Bondt and Thaler (1985) found long-term past losers outperformed past winners over the following years.
Prices adjusting too slowly to news, producing drift in the direction of the surprise. A leading explanation for medium-term momentum and post-earnings drift.
Updating beliefs too little when new evidence arrives, staying anchored on prior views. Edwards (1968). Contributes to underreaction to earnings news.
Crediting successes to skill and blaming failures on bad luck, which inflates confidence after wins and blocks learning after losses.
Most people rate their own skill above average, in driving, investing and much else, which cannot be true for most of them.
Excessive certainty in one's estimates, shown by confidence intervals far too narrow to contain the truth as often as claimed. The most robust form of overconfidence in forecasting.
Believing you rank higher relative to others than you do, for example that you will beat the market after costs when most participants cannot.
Kruger and Dunning (1999): low-skill people tend to overestimate their competence because they lack the skill to see their own errors. The size of the effect is debated.
Confidence that comes from a coherent story rather than from evidence of predictive accuracy. Kahneman found stock pickers and interviewers stayed confident despite records no better than chance.

nodes.n: What you see is all there is
nodes.t: Kahneman's term for building a confident judgment from only the information at hand, without asking what is missing. Leads to neglect of unknowns and of the other side's case.
Overestimating the chance of good outcomes for oneself or one's project. Shows up in analyst forecasts, management guidance and startup projections.

Believing a streak of success makes the next success more likely, such as chasing a fund after a few great years. Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky (1985); later work found a modest real hot hand in sports, but investors still overweight streaks.
Expecting small samples to mirror the population, so a few years of returns or a handful of trades are taken as proof of skill. Tversky and Kahneman (1971).
Seeing meaningful streaks or clusters in random data, such as runs of up days, that are expected by chance alone.
General tendency to perceive meaningful patterns and connections in unrelated data; in markets, finding chart shapes or causal stories in noise.
Perceiving a relationship between variables that does not exist or is weaker than believed, often because a few memorable co-occurrences stand out.
Overweighting information that is prominent or striking, such as a headline price move, over information that matters more but is dull, such as a footnote change.
Sims's framework in which agents with finite processing capacity optimally choose what to attend to, explaining sluggish and selective reactions to information.

Retail investors are net buyers of attention-grabbing stocks after news, extreme moves or high volume, because buying means searching thousands of names while selling only covers what they own. Barber and Odean (2008).
Earnings released on Fridays get a weaker immediate price response and more later drift than other days, consistent with investor inattention. DellaVigna and Pollet (2009).

Prices reacting to information already public, as when a years-old United Airlines bankruptcy story resurfaced online in September 2008 and the stock briefly collapsed. Tetlock (2011) found stale news predicts reversals.
Investors trading the wrong security because of similar names or tickers, such as buying an obscure firm instead of a famous one in the news. Rashes (2001) documented comovement from such confusion.
More information beyond a point raises confidence without raising accuracy, and pushes analysts to fixate on noise.
Larger menus can reduce decision quality and participation; retirement plans offering many funds see lower enrollment and more naive allocation rules. Iyengar and coauthors.
People disproportionately stay with preset options; automatic enrollment raises retirement plan participation sharply. Madrian and Shea (2001).
Changing how choices are presented to steer behavior without restricting options or changing incentives much, such as automatic savings escalation. Thaler and Sunstein (2008).
Thaler and Benartzi's program in which employees commit in advance to raise their savings rate out of future pay raises, turning inertia and present bias into allies.
Discomfort from holding beliefs that conflict with evidence or actions, often resolved by dismissing the evidence instead of updating. Festinger (1957).
Holding a belief after the evidence behind it has been discredited. Keeps investors in broken theses long after the original reason is gone.
Reasoning toward the conclusion one wants, applying harsh scrutiny to unwelcome evidence and little to welcome evidence. Talking one's own book is a market version.
Continuing to invest in a failing course of action because of what has already been invested, often adding capital to defend an earlier decision. Staw (1976).
Avoiding information that may be bad; investors log in to check portfolios less often when markets fall. Karlsson, Loewenstein and Seppi (2009).

Splitting money equally across whatever options are offered, so allocations depend on the menu rather than on risk. Benartzi and Thaler (2001). DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal (2009) found 1/N hard to beat out of sample.
nodes.f: w_i = 1/N

nodes.t: Thinking in nominal instead of real terms, such as comparing earnings yields with nominal bond yields or feeling richer from inflationary gains. Modigliani and Cohn (1979) argued it misprices stocks under inflation.
Treating low-priced shares as cheaper or having more upside than high-priced ones, although price per share is arbitrary and changes with splits.
Investors anchor on a stock's 52-week high and are reluctant to bid above it, so stocks near their highs keep drifting up as news is absorbed. George and Hwang (2004).

Why investors prize cash dividends when, without taxes and costs, selling shares produces equivalent cash (Miller and Modigliani). Behavioral answers include self-control and mental accounting rules to spend income but not capital. Black (1976).
Failing to act on long-term goals because of short-term temptation, leading to undersaving and to rules such as spending only dividends.
Discounting the near future much more steeply than the distant future, so preferences reverse as a reward draws closer, producing time-inconsistent choices.
nodes.f: V = A / (1 + kD)

nodes.t: Overweighting immediate payoffs relative to all later ones, as in Laibson's (1997) beta-delta model; causes procrastination on saving, rebalancing and hard decisions.
nodes.f: U = u0 + beta x sum(delta^t x ut)

nodes.t: Overweighting near-term results such as quarterly earnings or monthly performance at the expense of long-term value, encouraged by career incentives and frequent evaluation.
Bad news and losses weigh more heavily in attention and memory than equivalent good news, so fear tends to spread faster than optimism.
Preferring to do something over doing nothing even when inaction has better expected value, such as trading in response to every headline. Goalkeepers diving on penalties are the classic example.
Judging harmful actions as worse than equally harmful inactions, so losses from holding feel more acceptable than losses from trading.
When outcomes are emotionally vivid, people react to whether something could happen rather than how likely it is. Sunstein's term; drives overpayment for protection against salient tail events.
Focusing on the count of bad outcomes and ignoring the size of the base, so 10 failures out of 1,000 can feel riskier than 1 out of 10.
Preferring to eliminate a small risk completely over a larger reduction of a bigger risk, even when the latter cuts more expected loss.
Personal experience of returns shapes lifelong risk taking: Malmendier and Nagel (2011) found people who lived through poor stock returns hold fewer stocks decades later.
Caring about wealth compared with peers, not only about absolute wealth, which pushes investors to chase whatever their neighbors and colleagues own. Keeping up with the Joneses.

Market returns that track investor mood rather than news, such as weaker returns after national sports losses and stronger ones on sunny days. Hirshleifer and Shumway (2003); Edmans, Garcia and Norli (2007).

People rationally ignore their own information and copy predecessors, so early choices can lock in a herd even when wrong. Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch (1992). Cascades are fragile and can reverse sharply on small news.
Cohesive groups suppressing dissent to reach consensus, producing overconfident decisions. Janis (1972). Investment committees counter it by collecting written views before discussion.
Overweighting the views of perceived authorities, such as famous investors or officials, regardless of the evidence offered.
Using others' behavior as evidence of the correct action; in markets, crowded ownership and rising prices become reasons to buy in themselves. One of Cialdini's influence principles.
Idea, from Mackay's Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds (1841), that people go mad in herds and recover slowly one by one; the book recounts tulip mania and the 1720 bubbles.

Averages of many independent estimates often beat individual experts, provided judgments are diverse, independent and decentralized. Fails when herding destroys independence. Galton's ox weight contest; Surowiecki (2004).

Deliberately positioning against prevailing sentiment, buying what is unloved and selling what is popular when the crowd's view looks fully priced. Works only when the contrarian is also right on fundamentals.
Selling driven by fear rather than analysis, usually after sharp declines, which locks in losses at depressed prices and widens the gap between fund and investor returns.
Late bubble stage in which investors believe prices can only rise, risk feels absent and skeptics are mocked as not getting it.
Market saying that bull markets climb despite persistent doubts; skepticism keeps positioning light, leaving sidelined buyers to push prices higher.
Unjustified enthusiasm that lifts prices above fundamentals. Greenspan used the phrase in a December 1996 speech, and Shiller used it as the title of his 2000 book on stock market valuation.
Keynes's term in the General Theory (1936) for spontaneous optimism that drives investment more than calculated expected values; swings in animal spirits help explain booms and slumps.
Shiller's (2019) idea that popular stories spread like epidemics and drive spending, investing and market events, somewhat independently of fundamentals.

Gartner's model of how expectations for a new technology evolve: trigger, peak of inflated expectations, trough of disillusionment, slope of enlightenment, plateau of productivity. A frame for story-driven tech stocks.

Belief that old valuation and leverage limits no longer apply because of a new era. Reinhart and Rogoff (2009) documented the pattern across centuries of crises; Templeton called it among the most dangerous phrases in investing.
Minsky-Kindleberger sequence for manias: displacement, boom, euphoria, distress and revulsion. Set out in Kindleberger's Manias, Panics, and Crashes (1978).
Minsky's theory that stability breeds instability: calm periods encourage a shift from hedge to speculative to Ponzi finance until a shock forces deleveraging.

Minsky's term for borrowers whose cash flows cover neither interest nor principal, so they rely on rising asset prices or new borrowing. Hedge finance covers both; speculative finance covers interest only.
Buying an asset not for its cash flows but because someone should pay more later. Works until buyers run out.

A price above fundamental value that rational investors still hold because the bubble component is expected to grow at the required return. Blanchard and Watson (1982). Requires an infinite horizon, ruling it out for finite-lived assets.

Knowingly buying overpriced assets expecting to sell before the collapse. Brunnermeier and Nagel (2004) found hedge funds were overweight tech stocks in 1999 and 2000 and cut exposure before the peak.
Arbitrageurs may know a bubble exists but not when others will act, so each rides it instead of attacking alone, and the bubble persists. Abreu and Brunnermeier (2003).
Risk that irrational traders push a mispricing further before it corrects, which deters arbitrageurs with short horizons or outside capital. De Long, Shleifer, Summers and Waldmann (1990).
Pairs such as Royal Dutch and Shell with fixed claims on the same cash flows that traded at persistent deviations from parity, a textbook case of limits to arbitrage. Froot and Dabora (1999).
Any test of market efficiency is also a test of some asset pricing model, so an anomaly could be mispricing or a missing risk factor; efficiency cannot be tested alone. Fama.
Lo's (2004) view that efficiency varies over time as participants adapt, compete and exit, so strategies work in some environments and fail in others.
Shiller (1981) showed stock prices move far more than later realized dividends can justify, contradicting simple present-value efficient market models.
Mehra and Prescott (1985): historical US stock returns exceeded safe returns by far more than standard consumption models can explain without implausibly high risk aversion.
Popular, high-multiple stocks with strong past growth that investors extrapolate. Lakonishok, Shleifer and Vishny (1994) argued value beats glamour because investors overextrapolate past growth.
Stocks with little analyst coverage or institutional ownership have historically earned higher returns, partly as pay for information costs and illiquidity.
Investors pay up for positively skewed, lottery-like payoffs, so such assets earn low average returns. Barberis and Huang (2008) tied it to probability weighting.
In betting markets longshots are overpriced and favorites underpriced, so bets on longshots lose far more per dollar. Mirrors overpriced lottery stocks and out-of-the-money options.
Trading more than one's information justifies, so costs erode returns. Barber and Odean (2000) found the most active retail accounts earned the lowest net returns.
a: trading is hazardous to your wealth

nodes.t: App features such as confetti, streaks, push alerts and one-tap options that raise retail trading frequency and risk taking.

Risk to a professional manager of trailing peers or the benchmark, which encourages index hugging and herding and discourages unconventional bets even with positive expected value. Keynes noted it is better to fail conventionally.
Moving money into funds or assets after strong returns and out after weak ones, which tends to buy high and sell low and makes investor returns trail fund returns.
Folklore separating informed professional flows from late retail flows; gauges built on the split are used as contrarian or confirming signals, with mixed evidence.
Weekly American Association of Individual Investors poll of members' six-month outlook as bullish, neutral or bearish. Used as a contrarian indicator at extremes.
Total borrowing against securities in brokerage accounts. Rapid growth signals leveraged speculation and raises forced selling risk when prices fall.

Composite investor sentiment measure built from proxies such as IPO volume and first-day returns, closed-end fund discounts, equity share of issuance and the dividend premium. High readings predict weak future returns on speculative, hard-to-value stocks.
In 1998 and 1999 firms that added .com to their names earned large abnormal returns regardless of any change in business. Cooper, Dimitrov and Rau (2001). A clean measure of mania mispricing.

Letting one positive trait shape judgment of unrelated ones, such as assuming a great product or celebrated CEO implies a great stock at any price. Rosenzweig showed it distorts business success studies.
Experts struggle to imagine not knowing what they know, so they misjudge how others will read information and how fast it will be priced.
Raising bet size or risk to recover losses quickly; in trading it leads to revenge trades and blowups.
Buying more of a position after it falls to lower the average cost. Sound when the thesis still holds and sizing allows; dangerous when it is escalation of commitment in disguise.
Fraud that targets members of a group, such as a religious, ethnic or professional community, exploiting trust within it. Madoff's scheme spread largely through social and charitable networks.
Adding an option that is clearly worse than one alternative shifts choice toward that alternative. Used in pricing tiers and in presenting negotiation packages.

Von Neumann and Morgenstern (1944) showed that choices satisfying a few axioms maximize the probability-weighted average of utility of outcomes rather than of the outcomes themselves; risk aversion is concave utility.
nodes.f: EU = sum of p_i x u(x_i)

nodes.t: Preferring a sure outcome to a gamble with the same expected value; in utility terms, a concave utility function. Measured by Arrow-Pratt coefficients.
nodes.f: ARA = -u''(w)/u'(w); RRA = -w x u''(w)/u'(w)

nodes.t: Constant relative risk aversion utility, under which an investor keeps the same fraction of wealth in risky assets at any wealth level; log utility is the case gamma equals 1.
nodes.f: u(w) = w^(1-gamma) / (1-gamma)

nodes.t: Utility equal to the natural log of wealth. Maximizing expected log wealth is the Kelly criterion and maximizes the long-run growth rate. Bernoulli (1738) proposed it to resolve the St. Petersburg paradox.
nodes.f: u(w) = ln(w)

nodes.t: Each extra unit of wealth adds less satisfaction than the last, which implies risk aversion and explains why ruinous bets are bad even at positive expected value.
A coin-flip game with infinite expected payout that people will pay only a small sum to play. Resolved by diminishing marginal utility (Bernoulli) or by the finite wealth of any counterparty.
nodes.f: EV = sum over n of (1/2)^n x 2^n = infinity

nodes.t: Allais (1953) showed people choose in ways that violate the independence axiom of expected utility, typically by overweighting certainty.
Ellsberg (1961) showed people prefer bets on urns with known odds over unknown odds even when that is inconsistent with any single subjective probability, demonstrating ambiguity aversion.
Option A first-order dominates B if A's chance of exceeding every outcome level is at least as high; any investor preferring more wealth picks A. Second-order dominance adds risk aversion.
Choose the option whose worst outcome is best; a rule for deep uncertainty. Gilboa and Schmeidler's maxmin expected utility applies it over a set of plausible probability models.
Choose the option that minimizes the largest regret, the gap between its payoff and the best payoff in each state. Savage (1951). Less conservative than maximin.
Simon's idea that real decision makers have limited information, time and computing power, so they use rules and satisfice instead of optimizing.
Choosing the first option that meets an acceptability threshold instead of searching for the best. Simon (1956). Sensible when search is costly.
Gigerenzer's view that a heuristic is rational when matched to its environment; simple rules can beat complex models in uncertain, data-poor settings.
Simple rules that use little information, such as take-the-best, and often predict as well as regression out of sample because they cannot overfit. Gigerenzer and Goldstein (1996).
If one of two options is recognized and the other is not, infer the recognized one scores higher on the criterion. Tested for stock picking with mixed results. Goldstein and Gigerenzer.

Unwanted variability in judgments that should be identical, such as different underwriters pricing the same risk differently. Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein (2021) argue it rivals bias as a source of error.
nodes.f: MSE = bias^2 + noise^2

nodes.t: Procedures that reduce error without knowing its direction: independent judgments before discussion, structured criteria, averaging several estimates and delaying intuition until the facts are in.

Judging a decision by its process: framing, alternatives considered, information, clear values, sound reasoning and commitment to act, separately from how it turned out. Decision analysis school of Howard.
Considering the consequences of consequences and how others will respond, not only the first effect of an action.
The value of the best alternative given up. Every holding should be compared with the next best use of capital, not with zero; Buffett and Munger use it as the bar for any new idea.
A bet where the potential gain greatly exceeds the potential loss, so it can be attractive even with a low chance of success. Central to options, venture capital and Pabrai's heads-I-win approach.
Separating reversible decisions, which should be made quickly, from irreversible ones, which deserve care. Bezos's one-way and two-way doors.
Structured list of questions and known failure modes reviewed before committing capital, borrowed from aviation and surgery. Pabrai and Munger popularized checklists to catch predictable errors.
A person assigned to argue against the prevailing view so dissent is legitimate and assumptions get tested.
Before buying, state the consensus view, your differing view, why you are right and what will make the market see it; if you cannot, there is no edge.
Structured debrief asking what was planned, what happened, why, and what to sustain or improve. US Army practice adapted to trade and deal postmortems.

Tetlock and Gardner's (2015) findings from the Good Judgment Project: some forecasters beat others reliably by starting from base rates, breaking problems down, updating often in small steps and tracking accuracy.
Tetlock's (2005) distinction: hedgehogs know one big idea and forecast confidently but poorly; foxes draw on many ideas, hedge and forecast better.
Breaking an unknown quantity into factors that can be estimated and multiplying them, to reach an order-of-magnitude answer fast; used for market sizing and sanity checks.
Pushing an average of forecasters' probabilities away from 50% because each forecaster holds only part of the shared information; improves aggregate accuracy in forecasting tournaments.
Combining many judgmental forecasts by mean, median or track-record weights to cut noise. Distinct from statistical combination of model forecasts.
Structured, anonymous, multi-round expert survey in which panelists revise estimates after seeing a summary of others' views, limiting dominance and groupthink. Developed at RAND in the 1950s.
Choosing when to stop searching to maximize expected payoff. In the secretary problem the best rule rejects the first n/e (about 37%) of candidates, then takes the next one better than all seen.
nodes.f: look phase = n / e

nodes.t: Balancing gathering information on uncertain options against using the best known one, formalized as multi-armed bandit problems. Applies to strategy allocation and research time.

Judging a specific combination of conditions as more likely than one of its parts, which breaks probability rules. Tversky and Kahneman's Linda problem (1983). Detailed scenarios feel more plausible but are less probable.
Confusing P(evidence given innocence) with P(innocence given evidence). In markets, mistaking how unlikely a backtest is under pure chance for the probability the strategy is real.
Crediting an intervention for what was simple regression toward the mean, such as praising a new manager for recovery after an unusually bad year.
Drawing the target after shooting: finding clusters in data and presenting them as if predicted. The backtest version is postdiction.
A spurious negative correlation created by selecting on an outcome that depends on both variables, such as looking only at funded startups or listed firms.
Boyd's cycle of observe, orient, decide, act; the side that cycles faster and orients better gains the advantage. Applied to trading and competitive strategy.
Binding yourself in advance to a course of action to resist later temptation, such as written sell rules or automatic contributions; a Ulysses contract.

nodes.n: Type I and Type II errors
nodes.t: A Type I error is a false positive, acting on an edge that is not real; a Type II error is a false negative, missing a real edge. Tightening one usually loosens the other.
Forecasting from the specifics of the case at hand, its plan and its story, which tends toward optimism; the outside view starts instead from base rates of similar cases.

The claim that stocks get less risky with a longer horizon because annualized return volatility falls. Samuelson (1963) showed the spread of terminal wealth still widens, so horizon alone does not justify more risk.
Holding mostly very safe assets plus a small allocation to highly convex, high-risk bets, while avoiding the middle; Taleb's recipe for robustness under uncertainty.
Taleb's term for systems that gain from volatility and stress rather than merely surviving it; convex exposures are antifragile and concave ones fragile.
Rule of thumb that roughly 80% of effects come from 20% of causes, as when a few holdings drive most portfolio returns. Reflects skewed, power-law-like distributions.
Earning returns on prior returns so wealth grows geometrically; the rule of 72 gives the approximate doubling time. Buffett's snowball: long runway plus time.
nodes.f: FV = PV x (1 + r)^n; doubling time about 72 / r%

nodes.t: A strategy that pays at least as well as any other no matter what opponents do. In the prisoner's dilemma, defecting is dominant for both players.
Repeatedly removing dominated strategies to narrow likely play; deeper rounds assume common knowledge of rationality.
The strategy that maximizes a player's payoff given others' strategies; a Nash equilibrium is a set of mutual best responses.
An outcome where no one can be made better off without making someone worse off. Nash equilibria need not be Pareto efficient, as the prisoner's dilemma shows.
A game where one side's gains equal the other's losses, such as poker before rake. Active management against the market is zero sum before costs and negative sum after.
An interaction where total value can grow, such as trade, long-run business ownership and integrative negotiation.
Von Neumann (1928): in finite two-player zero-sum games a mixed strategy guarantees each player the value of the game; maximizing one's worst case equals minimizing the opponent's best case.
A game where players move in turn and later movers see earlier moves; drawn as a game tree in extensive form and solved by backward induction.
A game where players choose without seeing each other's choices, shown as a payoff matrix in normal form.
Solving a sequential game from the last move backward, choosing the best action at each point given best play afterward.
A Nash equilibrium that is also an equilibrium in every subgame, which rules out threats that would not be carried out. Selten (1965).
A game of incomplete information in which players have private types drawn from known distributions and update beliefs with Bayes' rule. Harsanyi; Bayesian Nash equilibrium extends Nash to it.
The same stage game played many times, where the threat of future retaliation can sustain cooperation that a one-shot game would not.
In infinitely repeated games with patient players, almost any outcome giving each player more than their minimum guaranteed payoff can be sustained as an equilibrium, including cooperation.
Cooperate first, then copy the opponent's last move. Won Axelrod's iterated prisoner's dilemma tournaments by being nice, retaliatory, forgiving and easy to read.
Cooperate until the opponent defects once, then defect forever; the harshest punishment, which sustains cooperation if players are patient enough.
In repeated play with uncertainty about types, a player acts tough or reliable early to shape beliefs and gain later. Kreps, Wilson, Milgrom and Roberts (1982).

Selten (1978): backward induction says an incumbent should never fight entrants in a finite sequence of markets, yet fighting early seems sensible; resolved by reputation models with uncertainty about type.
A game where players gain by choosing the same action and there are several equilibria, so outcomes depend on expectations, as in bank runs and currency pegs.
Coordination game where joint cooperation pays most but is risky, so playing safe is the risk-dominant equilibrium. Models trust, liquidity provision and rescue consortiums.
Two players head toward disaster; the one who swerves loses face, but if neither does both lose badly. Models debt-ceiling standoffs, price wars and brinkmanship.
A solution people converge on without communicating because it seems natural or salient, such as a round number or precedent. Schelling (1960).
A move that changes your own future incentives so a threat or promise becomes believable, such as burning bridges, public pledges or contracts with penalties. Schelling.
A threat the threatener would actually want to carry out when the time comes; rational opponents ignore threats that are not credible.

Costless, non-binding, unverifiable communication; it conveys information only when sender and receiver interests are close enough. Crawford and Sobel (1982). Applies to guidance and management commentary.
A signal is credible when it costs low-quality types more to send, as in Spence's (1973) education model; insider buying, buybacks and dividends can signal management confidence.
In a signaling game, an equilibrium where different types send different signals so receivers can infer type; in a pooling equilibrium all types send the same signal and nothing is learned.
The uninformed side offers a menu of choices that leads informed parties to reveal their type, such as deductible choices or loan terms. Rothschild and Stiglitz (1976).

Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011): a sender who commits in advance to how information will be revealed can shift a rational receiver's actions, the logic behind disclosure policy and forward guidance design.
Deliberately creating a risk of mutual disaster that neither side fully controls in order to force the other side to back down. Schelling.
A contest where players pay ongoing costs until one quits and the survivor takes the prize, as in price wars and standoffs; expected costs can eat most of the prize.
Arthur's (1994) puzzle: people go to a bar only if they expect it not to be crowded, so any widely shared forecast defeats itself. A model of crowded trades and the minority game.
Competitors repeatedly cutting prices to win share, often destroying industry profits; commodity, airline and retail sectors are prone to them.
Gains from moving first, such as scale, customer lock-in or preempting capacity; can be offset by second-mover advantages like learning from the leader's mistakes.
Leader-follower quantity competition in which the leader commits to output first and earns more than under simultaneous Cournot competition.
Firms choose quantities at the same time; equilibrium price falls between monopoly and competitive levels and approaches marginal cost as the number of firms grows. Cournot (1838).
Firms choose prices at the same time; with identical products and costs, even two firms drive price to marginal cost, the Bertrand paradox. Differentiation and capacity limits soften it.
An incumbent's moves to make entry unprofitable, such as excess capacity, limit pricing or a reputation for fighting; credible only if the incumbent would follow through after entry.
Firms keeping prices high without an explicit agreement, through repeated interaction and threat of retaliation; easier with few players, transparent prices and stable demand.
Members of a cartel secretly producing above quota because each gains individually while the group loses, a prisoner's dilemma that makes cartels unstable without monitoring and punishment.
Shared resources get overused because each user captures the full benefit while costs are spread across all. Hardin (1968). Fits crowded trades and exits in a stampede.
People enjoy a shared benefit without paying for it, so it is underprovided; dispersed shareholders free ride on monitoring, which is why blockholders and activists matter.
Experiment where players contribute to a pot that is multiplied and shared equally; contributions fall over rounds unless free riders can be punished.

Designing the rules of a game so self-interested players produce a desired outcome, sometimes called reverse game theory. Hurwicz, Maskin and Myerson shared the 2007 Nobel. The basis of auction and market design.
Any outcome achievable by some mechanism can also be achieved by one in which players truthfully report their private information, which simplifies mechanism design.
A mechanism is incentive compatible when each participant does best by acting on its true preferences, as in a second-price auction.
Akerlof (1970): when sellers know quality and buyers do not, buyers pay average prices, good sellers withdraw and the market can unravel. Applies to used cars, small private companies and new issues.
Everyone knows a fact, knows that everyone knows it, and so on without end. A public announcement can change behavior even when everyone already knew privately.
Keynes's analogy in which investors pick not what they think is best but what they think others will think is best, adding layers of expectation; formalized in guess-two-thirds-of-the-average games.
A model where a level-0 player acts naively and each level-k player best responds to level k-1; experiments show most people reason only one or two steps deep.
Shubik's (1971) auction for a dollar in which the second-highest bidder also pays, so bidders escalate past the prize's value to avoid losing their bid. A model of escalation.
When a deal needs every holder's consent, individuals can demand more by refusing, as in sovereign debt restructurings and land assembly; collective action clauses limit it.

After one party makes an investment specific to a relationship, the other can renegotiate to capture its value, so parties underinvest without protective contracts. Williamson; Klein, Crawford and Alchian.

Coase (1960): if property rights are clear and bargaining costs are low, parties negotiate to the efficient outcome whoever holds the rights; real transaction costs explain why allocation still matters.
The set of payoff splits no subgroup could beat by breaking off on its own; if it is empty, any deal is unstable because some coalition always wants to defect.

Milgrom and Stokey (1982): if all traders are rational with common priors and this is common knowledge, private information alone cannot generate trade, since any offer reveals information. Real trading needs noise, hedging or differing priors.
Aumann (1976): rational agents with a common prior whose posteriors are common knowledge cannot hold different posteriors. Persistent disagreement implies different priors or irrationality.
Grossman and Stiglitz (1980): if prices fully reflected information, no one would pay to collect it, so markets must stay inefficient enough to reward the cost of research.
Pay based on relative rank drives effort but also risk shifting: fund managers behind at midyear tend to raise risk to catch up. Lazear and Rosen (1981); Brown, Harlow and Starks (1996).
Distressed firms or traders with limited liability take big risks because owners keep the upside while creditors bear the downside. Seen in late-1980s US savings and loan failures.
Competition forcing constant improvement just to keep a relative position; trading edges decay as rivals copy them.
Traders who know another investor must sell first sell ahead and then buy back cheaper, worsening the distressed party's losses. Brunnermeier and Pedersen (2005); seen around LTCM and Amaranth.
Diamond and Dybvig (1983): banks turn illiquid loans into demand deposits, creating two equilibria, one normal and one a self-fulfilling run; deposit insurance removes the run equilibrium.
Fehr and Schmidt (1999): people dislike unequal outcomes, especially being behind, which explains rejections in ultimatum games and punishment of free riders.
Open ascending auction where the price rises until one bidder remains; with private values, bidders stay in until the price reaches their value.
Open descending auction where the price falls until a bidder accepts; strategically the same as a first-price sealed bid. Google used a Dutch-auction format for its 2004 IPO.
Each bidder submits one sealed bid; the highest wins and pays its own bid, so bidders shade below their values.
Sealed-bid second-price auction: the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid, which makes bidding your true value a dominant strategy. Vickrey (1961).
With independent private values, risk-neutral bidders and symmetric equilibrium, standard auction formats give the seller the same expected revenue. Myerson (1981); Riley and Samuelson (1981).
The minimum price a seller will accept in an auction; Myerson showed a well-set reserve raises expected revenue even though it risks no sale.
Bidding below your true value in a first-price auction to keep some profit if you win; the fewer the rivals, the more you shade.
Every bidder pays its bid but only the highest wins; models lobbying, patent races and contests for talent.
An auction where the item is worth about the same to all bidders but that value is uncertain, such as an oil lease or a company; the winner tends to be whoever overestimated most.
Each bidder knows its own value, which differs across bidders and does not depend on what others know; no winner's curse arises.

Milgrom and Weber (1982): when values are affiliated, revealing more information about the item raises expected revenue, which is why sellers publish data rooms and appraisals and why open ascending auctions beat sealed bids.
Multi-unit auction where all winning bidders pay the same market-clearing price; the US Treasury uses this format.
Multi-unit auction where each winner pays its own bid; bidders shade more than in uniform price formats.
Placing a bid in the final seconds of a fixed-end online auction, as on eBay, to avoid bidding wars and to hide information from rivals; less useful against proxy bidding with true values.
Bidders colluding to suppress competition, by rotating winners or submitting cover bids, so prices fall below competitive levels; illegal in most markets.

IPO process in which underwriters gather indications of interest from institutions to set the offer price and allocate shares; allocations reward investors who reveal demand, which helps explain underpricing.
Bulow and Klemperer (1996): a simple auction with one extra serious bidder beats the best negotiation with fewer bidders, so for sellers competition is worth more than bargaining skill.

A gambler with finite capital who keeps betting at fair or unfavorable odds against a far richer opponent will eventually go broke. At fair odds, the chance of ruin starting with a against b is b/(a+b).
nodes.f: P(ruin) = b / (a + b) at fair odds

nodes.t: Doubling the stake after each loss so one win recovers everything plus one unit; fails because losing streaks, table limits and finite capital eventually cause ruin.
Raising size after wins and cutting after losses, as in pyramiding into winners, which caps damage during losing streaks.
The casino's expected profit as a share of each bet, such as about 5.26% on double-zero roulette; over many bets the law of large numbers makes it near certain.
nodes.f: house edge = -EV per unit staked

nodes.t: The probability embedded in odds or prices: decimal odds d imply 1/d, and a binary contract priced at p cents implies about p%. Across all outcomes the total exceeds 100% by the bookmaker's margin.
nodes.f: implied p = 1 / decimal odds

nodes.t: The bookmaker's margin built into odds so implied probabilities sum to more than 100%; standard minus 110 on both sides implies about 4.5% hold.
nodes.f: overround = sum(1 / decimal odds) - 1

nodes.t: Comparing the odds a bet was placed at with the final pre-event line; consistently beating the close is the best evidence of betting skill because closing lines are efficient.
Bets from sophisticated, winning bettors whose action moves lines; books limit them and follow their flow, while recreational bettors are called squares.
Sudden, broad line movement across books caused by coordinated sharp betting; chasing it late usually captures little value.
Comparing odds across books and placing each bet at the best available price; small price gains compound into large differences in long-run return.
Betting both sides of a game at different lines after the line moves, so a result landing between them wins both bets, while other results lose only the margin.

Backing every outcome across books or platforms when combined implied probabilities sum below 100%, locking a profit if all bets settle as expected; risks include limits, voided bets and mismatched rules.
nodes.f: arb exists if sum(1 / best decimal odds) < 1

nodes.t: A bet combining several selections that pays only if all win; payouts multiply but so does the book's edge, making parlays some of the worst-value bets offered.
Pool betting where all stakes on an event are pooled, the house takes a cut and winners share the rest, so odds are set by the crowd; used in horse racing.
Tracking cards dealt in blackjack to know when the remaining deck favors the player, then betting more. Thorp's Beat the Dealer (1962) proved the edge and applied Kelly sizing.
Results measured in big blinds won per 100 hands; because hand outcomes are noisy, tens of thousands of hands are needed before a win rate is statistically meaningful.
nodes.f: bb/100 = 100 x big blinds won / hands played

nodes.t: Betting a hand that is probably behind but has outs to improve, winning either through fold equity now or by hitting later.
Betting a hand that is likely best so that worse hands call; a thin value bet targets hands only slightly worse.
A betting range made of very strong hands and bluffs with few medium hands; a linear or merged range bets from the strongest hands down to medium ones.
A range that mixes value hands and bluffs in proportions that leave opponents indifferent between calling and folding, so they cannot exploit it.
A bet larger than the pot, used with a polarized range and nut advantage to apply maximum pressure on capped ranges.
The share of a range a player must continue with against a bet so that the bettor's bluffs do not profit automatically.
nodes.f: MDF = pot / (pot + bet)

nodes.t: How often a bluff must succeed to break even, which depends only on bet size relative to the pot.
nodes.f: alpha = bet / (bet + pot)

nodes.t: Cards in your hand that remove combinations of strong hands from an opponent's range, which guides bluffing and calling choices.
Tournament model converting chip stacks into shares of prize money; near pay jumps chips lost are worth more than chips won, so players must tighten.
Expected future losses when you make a hand that is still second best, which reduce the true value of calling.
Effective stack divided by the pot on the flop; a low ratio favors committing with top pair, a high one favors drawing to nut hands.
nodes.f: SPR = effective stack / pot

nodes.t: When so much of a stack is already in the pot that folding is worse than calling; planning commitment in advance avoids getting stuck by accident.
Poker term for thinking about what the opponent thinks you hold, and what they think you think; going one level beyond the opponent wins, going two can lose.
The share of a hand's raw equity it actually captures given position and playability; hands played out of position realize less.
Choosing where to compete based on your edge over the opposition; for investors, picking markets with weak competition and forced or uninformed counterparties.
The house's fee on each pot or tournament; it makes poker negative sum, so a small edge can still lose money, much as fees do in active management.
Bargaining that creates value by trading across issues the sides value differently, so both can gain; also called expanding the pie.
Bargaining over a fixed amount where one side's gain is the other's loss, such as price alone; anchors, concessions and reservation prices dominate.
Positions are what parties demand; interests are why they demand it. Fisher and Ury's Getting to Yes (1981) argues that probing interests uncovers trades positional bargaining misses.
Fisher and Ury's method: separate the people from the problem, focus on interests, invent options for mutual gain and insist on objective criteria, backed by a strong BATNA.
Independent standards such as market comparables, appraisals or precedent used to justify terms, which makes concessions easier to accept and resists pressure tactics.
Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers: presenting several packages of equal value to you to learn the other side's priorities and look flexible.
The ambitious target a negotiator aims for; setting high, justifiable aspirations predicts better outcomes than focusing on the walk-away point.
Making offers so the midpoint between yours and theirs lands on your target, anticipating a split-the-difference close.
Settling at the midpoint of current offers; it feels fair but rewards whoever anchored more aggressively.
Giving something only in exchange for something, phrased as if you do X, I can do Y, so concessions are traded rather than gifted.
Making a second concession before the other side has answered the first, which signals weakness and moves the deal with no return.
Asking for a small extra concession after the main deal is agreed, when the other side does not want to reopen talks; countered by asking for something back.
Claiming that a higher authority must approve terms, which slows concessions and lets a negotiator decline without confrontation.
a: need to check with my boss

nodes.t: Aggressive moves such as extreme opening demands, threats, take-it-or-leave-it offers and fake deadlines; effective in one-off deals but costly to trust and reputation.
An offer with a very short expiry meant to stop the other side from shopping alternatives; often met by asking for time or testing the deadline.
Opening with a firm, final offer and refusing to concede, named for GE's Lemuel Boulware; can backfire because the other side sees it as unfair.
Voss's term for showing you understand the counterpart's emotions and perspective to build trust and draw out information, without conceding anything.
Repeating the last few words a counterpart said, as a question, to prompt them to keep talking and reveal more.
Naming the counterpart's emotion or concern, as in it seems like you are worried about timing, to defuse it or confirm it.
Open how and what questions, such as how am I supposed to do that, that get the other side solving your problem and revealing its constraints.
Price model taught by Voss: open at 65% of your target, then move to 85%, 95% and 100% with shrinking steps, end on a precise number and add a non-monetary item.
Precise first offers such as 4,985 instead of 5,000 are seen as better researched and draw smaller counteroffers. Mason, Lee, Wiley and Ames (2013).
A reply that proposes new terms and implicitly rejects the original; a firm, reasoned counter re-anchors quickly so the first offer does not set the frame.
Pausing after an offer or question so the other side fills the gap, often revealing information or improving their own offer.
The tendency to return favors and concessions; it powers concession trading and the door-in-the-face tactic. One of Cialdini's influence principles.
Making a large request you expect to be refused, then a smaller one that looks like a concession and is more likely accepted.
Getting agreement to a small request first, making a larger later request more likely to succeed through the wish to stay consistent.
People act to stay consistent with what they have said or done, especially publicly; small written commitments make later agreement more likely. A Cialdini principle.
Options seem more valuable when limited or about to disappear; competing bids and deadlines exploit it. A Cialdini principle.
Terms that depend on a future outcome, letting parties bet on their disagreement instead of deadlocking; earnouts and performance fees are examples.
A mostly non-binding document setting price, structure and key deal terms, usually with binding exclusivity and confidentiality clauses; it frames the rest of the negotiation.
Part of the purchase price held back for a period to cover breaches of representations and indemnity claims, shifting risk from buyer to seller.
Seller's statements of fact about the business, such as financials, liabilities and compliance, backed by indemnities if they prove false; the scope is heavily negotiated.
Exhaustion late in a long negotiation that makes parties concede to get done, or walk away from a deal that still makes sense; time and sunk effort shift bargaining power.
Each side submits a final offer and the arbitrator must pick one without compromise, which pushes both toward reasonable numbers; used in Major League Baseball salary disputes.
A neutral third party helps the sides reach a voluntary agreement without imposing one; useful when emotions or information gaps block a deal.
Lax and Sebenius: sharing information to create value leaves you exposed to value claiming, while claiming tactics block value creation, so negotiators must manage the tension.
Discounting a proposal because the adversary made it; the same terms look worse coming from the other side. Ross and Stillinger.
Assuming the other side's interests directly oppose yours, which hides trades that would create value.
After reaching a deal, the parties look for improvements that leave both better off, keeping the signed deal as a fallback. Raiffa.
Controlling which issues are discussed and in what order; settling easy issues first builds momentum, while the order of votes can decide outcomes.
Forming alliances with parties who share interests to gain bargaining power in multiparty settings such as creditor committees and proxy contests.
Putnam (1988): negotiators bargain with the other side and with their own constituents at once; a narrow set of terms acceptable at home can be a source of bargaining power.
Lax and Sebenius's framework: beyond tactics at the table, shape deal design and set up the right parties, sequence and alternatives before talks begin.

In bargaining models an outside option raises a player's share only if it is credible enough to be taken; otherwise the split is set by patience and the threat of delay. Binmore, Shaked and Sutton (1989).
The payoffs each side gets if talks fail; in Nash bargaining, gains are split from this point, so improving yours raises your share.
Graham's rough value for a growth stock: earnings times 8.5 plus twice the expected growth rate, where 8.5 is his P/E for a no-growth firm; he later scaled it by 4.4 over the current AAA bond yield.
nodes.f: V = EPS x (8.5 + 2g); revised V = EPS x (8.5 + 2g) x 4.4 / Y

nodes.t: Graham's investor who wants safety and freedom from effort: a diversified portfolio of large, financially strong, consistent dividend payers at moderate multiples, with a stock-bond mix between 25% and 75%. The enterprising investor does more work for more return.
Graham's test: an investment operation, after thorough analysis, promises safety of principal and an adequate return; anything else is speculation. Price paid relative to value decides which it is.
Buying very cheap, mediocre businesses for one last free puff of value; Buffett's early Graham style, later replaced by buying great businesses at fair prices.

nodes.n: Wonderful business at a fair price
nodes.t: Buffett's shift, under Munger's influence, from fair businesses at wonderful prices to great, high-return businesses at fair prices, since time is the friend of the wonderful business and the enemy of the mediocre one.
Munger's bin for decisions too difficult to judge well, which are simply passed over; good results need only a few sound decisions, not an opinion on everything.
Buffett's thought experiment of a lifetime card with 20 investment slots, forcing extreme selectivity and conviction-weighted concentration.
Buffett's baseball analogy: investing has no called strikes, so an investor can wait as long as needed for an obvious bargain inside their competence and then swing hard.
Buffett's measure that adds a holder's share of investees' retained earnings, less the tax due if distributed, to its reported earnings, since dividends understate the economics of minority stakes.
Buffett's one-dollar test: every dollar of earnings a company retains should, over time, create at least one dollar of market value; otherwise it should be paid out.
Buffett's term for the pressure that makes companies resist change, absorb all available cash, feed leaders' pet projects and copy peers, regardless of shareholder value.

Buffett's structure: permanent ownership of whole businesses, decentralized operations, central allocation of all spare cash, insurance float as cheap funding and a stated aim of compounding per-share value.
Munger's call to learn the big ideas of the main disciplines, such as math, psychology, economics, physics and biology, and use them together instead of relying on one narrow specialty.
Solving a problem backward by asking what would guarantee failure and then avoiding it. Munger borrowed Jacobi's advice to invert, always invert.
Munger's term for extreme outcomes when several psychological tendencies act in the same direction at once, as in auctions, cults and manias.
Munger's 1995 talk listing about two dozen standard causes of misjudgment, such as incentives, social proof, consistency, envy and denial, meant as a checklist against error.
Judgment bends toward what pays the judge, often unconsciously; Munger's never ask a barber whether you need a haircut. Check how advisers, managers and sell-side analysts are paid.
Munger's warning that to a man with a hammer every problem looks like a nail; investors with one model force it on situations it does not fit.
Munger's view that the money is made in the waiting, not in the trading: buy great businesses and refrain from activity. Livermore said much the same about sitting tight.

Soros's sequence in which a prevailing bias and an underlying trend reinforce each other, accelerate past reality, survive tests, reach a moment of truth and then reverse into a self-reinforcing bust.
Soros's premise that participants' views are always incomplete or distorted, so markets are always somewhat wrong and those errors shape the fundamentals they are meant to reflect.
Soros's practice of taking a small position on a hypothesis to focus attention, then adding or exiting quickly as evidence comes in.
Dalio's framework that sorts environments by whether growth and inflation are rising or falling relative to expectations; each asset class does best in particular quadrants, so balance across them.
Dalio's cycle, lasting roughly 50 to 75 years, of debt rising faster than income until rates can fall no further, ending in deleveraging; the short-term debt cycle is the 5 to 10 year business cycle.

Dalio's term for a deleveraging that balances austerity, debt restructuring, wealth transfers and money printing so nominal growth stays above nominal interest rates and debt burdens fall without depression.
Dalio's observation that combining about 15 good, uncorrelated return streams can cut portfolio risk by roughly 80% without lowering expected return.
Bridgewater practice of weighting opinions by each person's track record and ability to explain their reasoning, not by seniority or a simple vote.
Bridgewater principle of recording meetings and making blunt feedback normal so ideas are judged on merit rather than politics.
Dalio's principle that losses and mistakes are the best teachers if examined honestly, so each failure should produce a written rule for next time.
Marks's term for going past the obvious first-level conclusion to ask what the consensus expects, what is priced in and why your view differs; a good company is not the same as a good investment.
Marks's image of sentiment swinging between greed and fear, credulity and skepticism, rarely resting at the reasonable midpoint.
Marks and Buffett define risk as the chance of losing money for good, not price volatility; volatility only becomes loss for those forced to sell.
Marks's approach: you cannot predict, but you can prepare by judging where the cycle stands from valuations, credit terms and investor behavior, then adjusting aggressiveness.
a: where are we in the cycle
you cant predict you can prepare

nodes.t: Marks's emphasis on winning by avoiding big losers: limiting downside capture matters more than chasing upside, and risk control is the mark of a great investor.
Concentrate when conviction is high, watch liquidity and central bank policy above earnings, look about 18 months ahead, and cut quickly when wrong; preserve capital first, then go for big wins.

Renaissance's style: many weak, short-horizon signals combined statistically, high turnover, leverage on low-volatility returns and strict adherence to models. Edge comes from breadth and the law of large numbers.
Simons and Thorp style of making money from thousands of small, nearly independent bets each slightly better than even, so results depend on breadth and costs, not on any single call.
Lynch's term for a stock that rises tenfold; he argued a few big winners drive a portfolio's results, so selling winners too early is costly.
Lynch's six types: slow growers, stalwarts, fast growers, cyclicals, turnarounds and asset plays, each with different expectations, valuation yardsticks and sell rules.
Lynch's advice that everyday observation of products and stores can spot winners early, as a starting point for research rather than a replacement for it.
Lynch's word for acquisitions outside a company's core that destroy value; also used for spreading a portfolio across too many mediocre ideas.
Lynch's test: explain in about two minutes why you own a stock, what has to happen for it to work and what could go wrong.
Lynch's sentiment gauge: when people at a party avoid talking stocks, the market is near a low; when they give you tips, it is near a high.
Templeton's rule to buy when pessimism is greatest and sell when optimism peaks; at the outbreak of war in 1939 he bought a basket of cheap US stocks, many near bankruptcy.
Templeton's practice of searching every country for the cheapest stocks against long-run earnings power, an early form of global value investing.
Bogle's argument that investors as a group earn the market return minus costs, so the lowest-cost funds must, on average, deliver the best net returns.
Sharpe (1991): before costs the average actively managed dollar must earn the passive market return, so after costs it must earn less.
Philip Fisher's checklist for growth stocks from Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits (1958), covering sales growth potential, R&D, margins, management depth and integrity.
Adding to a winning position only after the market confirms the trade, usually in smaller increments, and never adding to losers. Associated with Livermore.
Livermore's idea that prices trend in the direction of least resistance, so a trader should wait for price action to confirm it and then trade with it.
Paul Tudor Jones's emphasis on what could go wrong: use stops, cut losers, and seek trades with about five-to-one reward to risk; he also used the 200-day moving average as an exit rule.
Julian Robertson's Tiger approach: own the best companies and short the worst, often in the same industry, based on fundamental research.
Pabrai's framework: invest in simple, distressed businesses with durable moats, place few bets with favorable odds, and seek setups where heads I win, tails I don't lose much.
a: heads i win tails i dont lose much

nodes.t: Copying high-conviction ideas of investors with strong records, often found in 13F filings, then doing your own work; Pabrai advocates it openly.
Chuck Akre's test for a compounder: an extraordinary business with high returns on capital, talented and honest management, and ample room to reinvest at high returns.
Walter Schloss's simple value method: buy statistically cheap stocks, often near lows, diversify widely, avoid debt-laden firms and hold patiently, with little contact with management.
John Neff's low P/E screen comparing earnings growth plus dividend yield with the P/E; ratios well above one flagged neglected value.
nodes.f: (EPS growth % + dividend yield %) / P/E

nodes.t: Nicolas Darvas's method of buying stocks that break above a trading range of new highs on rising volume, with stops just below the box.
Jeremy Grantham's definition of a bubble as a two standard deviation departure from an asset's long-run price trend; he found nearly all such episodes eventually reverted.
Fundsmith's three steps: buy good companies, do not overpay, do nothing; focus on high return, cash-generative businesses held for long periods.
a: buy good companies dont overpay do nothing

nodes.t: Seth Klarman's value investing as risk aversion: demand a margin of safety, hold cash when bargains are scarce, favor catalysts and complexity others avoid, and judge results on an absolute basis.

Jeremy Siegel's case that over long periods US equities have beaten bonds and cash in real terms, with lower real risk over very long horizons than commonly assumed. Critics stress survivorship of the US market.
Treating cash as a call option on future bargains rather than a drag; its value rises with volatility and the chance of dislocations. Buffett and Klarman hold it when opportunities are scarce.
Owning assets for long periods regardless of short-term moves, which cuts costs, taxes and timing errors but requires tolerating deep drawdowns.

Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, buying more units when prices are low. Lump sum investing usually wins on expected return since markets tend to rise, but DCA reduces regret and timing risk.

Moving in and out of markets based on forecasts. Because a few large up days drive long-run returns and often follow sharp drops, missing them hurts badly; few investors time markets profitably after costs.
Keynes moved from macro-driven timing, which failed for him, to concentrated holdings of a few businesses he understood well, held through volatility; he managed King's College's endowment this way.

Dutch speculation in rare tulip bulbs, traded largely through informal forward contracts, that peaked and collapsed in early 1637. Historians debate its economic scale, but it remains the archetype of a speculative mania.
The VOC, founded in 1602, issued transferable shares that traded in Amsterdam, creating an early permanent joint-stock company and one of the first active secondary stock markets.

John Law merged a note-issuing royal bank with the Mississippi Company in France, used new paper money to inflate its shares, and saw both collapse in 1720, discrediting paper money in France for decades.
South Sea Company shares soared in 1720 on a plan to swap UK government debt for its stock, then crashed; many other bubble companies floated alongside. Newton reportedly lost heavily.

Panic that began in London when banker Alexander Fordyce fled after speculative losses, bringing down Scottish banks such as Ayr Bank and spreading to Amsterdam and the American colonies through credit chains.

First US financial panic, set off by William Duer's failed leveraged speculation in government debt and bank stock; Treasury Secretary Hamilton bought securities and supported lending to calm markets.
British banking panic after a boom in Latin American bonds and mining shares, including a fictitious country, Poyais; dozens of banks failed before the Bank of England lent freely.
US panic and long depression after land speculation, the Specie Circular requiring hard money for land and tighter British credit; many banks suspended specie payments.
British railway share boom of the 1840s that peaked around 1845 and 1846, then collapsed; many lines were built and investors lost heavily, a template for technology capex booms.
Triggered by the failure of the Ohio Life Insurance and Trust Company amid falling grain and railroad values; spread through telegraph-linked markets to Europe, an early global crisis.
