Collapse of London discount house Overend, Gurney and Company in May 1866 set off a panic; Bank of England lending during it shaped Bagehot's Lombard Street.
Jay Gould and Jim Fisk tried to corner the New York gold market; gold collapsed on September 24, 1869 when the Treasury sold gold, ruining many speculators.
Jay Cooke and Company failed in September 1873 over railroad financing; the NYSE closed for ten days and a long depression followed in the US and Europe.
Barings nearly failed after losses on Argentine securities; the Bank of England organized a guarantee fund with other banks to prevent a wider panic.

A central bank, treasury or leading banker organizes private institutions to jointly guarantee or recapitalize a failing firm to prevent contagion, as the Bank of England did for Barings in 1890, J.P. Morgan did in 1907 and the New York Fed did for LTCM in 1998.
Railroad failures and bank runs amid doubts about US gold reserves led to a severe depression; J.P. Morgan helped the Treasury restore gold reserves in 1895.
A control fight between Harriman and the Hill-Morgan group cornered Northern Pacific stock in May 1901, squeezing short sellers and briefly crashing the wider market.
A failed copper corner triggered runs on trust companies such as Knickerbocker Trust; J.P. Morgan organized private rescues. Its lessons led to the Federal Reserve Act of 1913.
The NYSE closed from July 31, 1914 until December 1914 at the start of World War I to stop European selling of US securities from draining gold.

International system from about the 1870s to 1914 in which major currencies were convertible into gold at fixed rates; it gave price stability over decades but transmitted deflation and limited crisis lending.

German hyperinflation that peaked in 1923 as money-financed deficits and reparations pressure destroyed the mark; holders of real assets and foreign currency survived while savers and bondholders were wiped out.
Mid-1920s Florida real estate frenzy driven by trading of purchase binders and easy credit, which collapsed by 1926 and foreshadowed 1929.
Fraud that pays earlier investors with money from new ones rather than from profits, named for Charles Ponzi's 1920 postal coupon scheme; it collapses when new money slows.

Worldwide depression from 1929 through the 1930s in which US output and prices fell sharply, thousands of banks failed and unemployment soared. Friedman and Schwartz blamed monetary contraction; Bernanke stressed credit disruption.
Failure of the large New York Bank of United States in December 1930 after merger talks collapsed; one of the biggest bank failures of the early Depression and a blow to confidence.
US tariff act of June 1930 that raised duties on many imports; trading partners retaliated and world trade shrank, though economists debate its share in the Depression.
Britain suspended gold convertibility in September 1931 after reserve losses; Eichengreen showed countries that left gold earlier recovered sooner from the Depression.
Ivar Kreuger's match empire collapsed after his death in March 1932, revealing large-scale fraud and fake assets; it fed demands for US securities disclosure laws.
Roosevelt closed all US banks in March 1933 and reopened those judged sound with federal backing, ending the run wave; deposits flowed back.
The Banking Act of 1933 separated commercial from investment banking and created federal deposit insurance through the FDIC; the separation was largely repealed in 1999.
Executive Order 6102 in April 1933 required Americans to sell most gold to the government; the Gold Reserve Act of 1934 then raised the official price to 35 dollars an ounce, devaluing the dollar.
A sharp relapse within the Depression after fiscal tightening and higher bank reserve requirements; the standard warning about withdrawing support too early.
March 1951 agreement ending the Fed's wartime commitment to cap Treasury yields, restoring independent monetary policy after a period of rising inflation.
After traders cornered onion futures in the mid-1950s, Congress banned onion futures trading in 1958; the ban still stands.
Sharp US stock decline in the first half of 1962, worst in late May, that ended an overvalued growth stock boom.
Tino De Angelis borrowed against warehouse receipts for vegetable oil that largely did not exist; the 1963 collapse hit American Express and brokerages. Lesson: verify collateral yourself.
Late-1960s boom in concept stocks, conglomerates and aggressive performance funds, which ended in the 1969 to 1970 bear market.
1960s wave of unrelated acquisitions, often by high-P/E acquirers buying low-P/E firms with stock to manufacture EPS growth; it reversed when acquirer multiples fell.
Late-1960s back-office breakdown when Wall Street volume overwhelmed manual settlement, forcing shortened trading days and broker failures; it led to SIPC in 1970 and central securities depositories.
The Penn Central railroad's June 1970 bankruptcy left it in default on commercial paper and froze that market; the Fed opened the discount window so banks could replace issuers' funding.
On August 15, 1971 Nixon suspended dollar convertibility into gold and imposed wage and price controls and an import surcharge, effectively ending the Bretton Woods system.
Early-1970s large growth stocks treated as one-decision buys at very high P/Es; they fell hard in 1973 and 1974, though some later earned their prices. Lesson: quality at any price fails.
Severe US bear market in which the S&P 500 fell by nearly half amid the oil shock, rising inflation, Watergate and tight policy; real losses were among the worst since the 1930s.

German regulators closed Bankhaus Herstatt in June 1974 after it had received Deutsche marks but before it paid dollars to counterparties, giving FX settlement risk its name and prompting the Basel Committee.
Franklin National Bank of New York failed in October 1974 after FX losses and fraud, then the largest US bank failure; the Fed lent heavily to manage the wind-down.
On May 1, 1975 the SEC ended fixed brokerage commissions, cutting trading costs and opening the way for discount brokers.
The Hunt brothers built huge leveraged silver positions; exchange margin rule changes and Fed pressure forced liquidation, and silver crashed on Silver Thursday, March 27, 1980.
Mexico said in August 1982 it could not service its foreign debt, setting off a decade of defaults and restructurings across Latin America, resolved largely through Brady bonds from 1989.
Oklahoma's Penn Square Bank failed in July 1982 after reckless energy lending, much of which it had sold to larger banks such as Continental Illinois.
A wholesale funding run on Continental Illinois in May 1984 led regulators to protect all depositors and creditors, giving rise to the phrase too big to fail.
Deregulation of the London Stock Exchange on October 27, 1986, ending fixed commissions and allowing outside ownership of member firms, which moved trading onto screens.

Failure of hundreds of US thrifts in the 1980s and early 1990s after rate mismatches, deregulation and risky lending, with deposit insurance encouraging gambling for resurrection; the Resolution Trust Corporation sold off assets.
KKR won a 1988 bidding war for RJR Nabisco, the largest LBO of its era, epitomizing the 1980s leverage boom and the winner's curse risk in auctions; chronicled in Barbarians at the Gate.
US stock drop on Friday, October 13, 1989 after financing for a UAL buyout fell through, marking the end of the junk-financed LBO wave.
Drexel Burnham Lambert, the dominant junk bond underwriter under Michael Milken, filed for bankruptcy in February 1990 after legal penalties and losses in a weakening junk market.
Japanese stock and land bubble fed by easy money after the Plaza Accord; the Nikkei peaked at the end of 1989 and did not regain that level for over three decades, followed by years of deflation.
Early-1990s banking crises in Sweden, Finland and Norway after credit and property booms; Sweden's blanket guarantees, recapitalizations and bad banks became a model response.
Regulators in several countries shut the Bank of Credit and Commerce International in July 1991 after uncovering massive fraud, money laundering and hidden losses across its global network.
On Black Wednesday, September 16, 1992, the UK left the European Exchange Rate Mechanism after failing to defend sterling; Soros's Quantum Fund profited heavily from shorting the pound.
Orange County, California filed for bankruptcy in December 1994 after its treasurer's leveraged bet on falling rates through reverse repos and inverse floaters failed as the Fed raised rates.
Mexico devalued the peso in December 1994 amid a run on dollar-linked short-term debt; a US-led rescue followed. It showed the danger of short-term foreign currency borrowing.
Barings Bank failed in February 1995 after trader Nick Leeson hid huge losses on Nikkei futures and options in Singapore; he controlled both trading and settlement.
Sumitomo trader Yasuo Hamanaka's years-long manipulation of copper prices and hidden losses came to light in 1996, costing the firm billions.
Canadian miner Bre-X's claimed giant Indonesian gold deposit was exposed in 1997 as salted core samples, wiping out investors. Lesson: verify primary data independently.
In August 1998 Russia devalued the ruble, defaulted on domestic debt and froze some foreign payments, causing a global flight to quality that helped sink LTCM.
In August 1998 the Hong Kong government bought large amounts of local stocks to defeat speculators who were shorting equities while attacking the currency peg.

After 3Com sold part of Palm in a March 2000 IPO, Palm's market value implied 3Com's remaining businesses had large negative value, yet shorting Palm was hard. Lamont and Thaler's limits-to-arbitrage case.
Collapse in 2000 to 2002 of telecom carriers and equipment makers after debt and vendor-financed overbuilding of fiber networks; much capacity sat unused for years.
After the September 11, 2001 attacks, US stock markets stayed closed until September 17; the Fed supplied heavy liquidity and stocks fell sharply in the week after reopening.
Enron used off-balance-sheet partnerships and mark-to-market accounting to hide debt and inflate earnings; it filed for bankruptcy in December 2001 and its auditor Arthur Andersen collapsed.
Argentina defaulted at the end of 2001 as its one-to-one dollar peg collapsed; litigation by holdout creditors dragged on until 2016.
WorldCom booked ordinary line costs as capital expenditure to inflate profits, then filed for bankruptcy in July 2002, the largest US filing to that date.
Italian dairy group Parmalat collapsed in December 2003 when a bank account supposedly holding billions in cash turned out not to exist. Lesson: confirm cash balances directly.
Mid-2000s US home price boom fed by loose lending, securitization and the belief that national prices never fall; its bust set off the 2008 crisis.
John Paulson's 2006 and 2007 bet against subprime mortgages through credit default swaps, one of the most profitable trades on record; cheap, asymmetric protection on fragile credit.
On August 9, 2007 BNP Paribas froze three funds holding US subprime assets, saying they could not be valued; often marked as the start of the global financial crisis.
UK lender reliant on wholesale funding suffered the first British bank run in over a century in September 2007 after it sought Bank of England support; it was nationalized in 2008.
Societe Generale disclosed in January 2008 that trader Jerome Kerviel had built huge unauthorized futures positions; unwinding them cost billions of euros.
In March 2008 Bear Stearns lost its repo funding within days and was sold to JPMorgan with Fed support, showing how fast a wholesale-funded dealer can fail.
Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on September 15, 2008 without a rescue, freezing funding markets worldwide and turning a crisis into a panic.

nodes.n: Reserve Primary Fund breaks the buck (2008)
nodes.t: The Reserve Primary Fund fell below one dollar per share in September 2008 because of Lehman paper, sparking a run on money funds that the Treasury stopped with a guarantee.
AIG had sold vast CDS protection on mortgage securities; collateral calls it could not meet led to a government rescue in September 2008 that also protected its counterparties.
The Troubled Asset Relief Program, enacted in October 2008, was used mainly to inject capital into banks and later automakers, a fiscal backstop for the financial system.
In September 2008 the SEC temporarily banned short selling in hundreds of financial stocks; studies found it widened spreads and hurt liquidity without stopping the declines.

In October 2008 Porsche revealed it controlled most of Volkswagen's shares through stock and options, leaving little free float; shorts scrambled to cover and VW briefly became the world's most valuable company.
Bernard Madoff's decades-long Ponzi scheme was exposed in December 2008 as redemptions surged; red flags included unusually smooth returns, a tiny auditor and self-custody.
Iceland's three main banks, grown to many times GDP on foreign funding, collapsed in October 2008, leading to capital controls and an IMF program.
Futures broker MF Global filed for bankruptcy in October 2011 after a large leveraged bet on European sovereign bonds; customer funds that should have been segregated were found missing.
S&P cut the US credit rating below AAA in August 2011 after a debt ceiling standoff; stocks fell but Treasuries rallied as a safe haven anyway.
ECB President Mario Draghi's July 2012 pledge to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro, backed by the OMT program, compressed periphery bond spreads without OMT ever being used.
The March 2013 Cyprus rescue imposed losses on uninsured depositors and capital controls, a template for bail-ins.
On October 15, 2014 the 10-year Treasury yield swung sharply within minutes without major news, exposing fragile liquidity in a market dominated by automated trading.
Chinese stocks surged on margin financing, then crashed from June 2015 despite state buying; a surprise yuan devaluation in August spread turmoil to global markets.
The UK's June 23, 2016 vote to leave the EU sent sterling sharply lower and caused a brief risk-off move; global equities recovered within weeks.
In late 2017 small firms that added blockchain to their names, such as Long Island Iced Tea becoming Long Blockchain, saw sharp share jumps, a replay of the dot-com name effect.
Neil Woodford's flagship UK fund suspended redemptions in June 2019 after illiquid and unlisted holdings collided with outflows, then was wound up.
After a sharp late-2018 selloff, the Fed signaled patience in January 2019 and paused rate hikes, reinforcing beliefs that the Fed would respond to market stress.
Shares of bankrupt Hertz surged on retail buying in June 2020 and the company tried to sell new stock into the rally until the SEC objected; equity in bankruptcy is usually wiped out.
German payments firm Wirecard admitted in June 2020 that a large share of its reported cash likely did not exist and filed for insolvency; short sellers and journalists had flagged it for years.
From 2021 Evergrande and other Chinese developers defaulted after regulators capped leverage with the three red lines, exposing a model funded by presales and rising prices.
In March 2023 Credit Suisse was pushed into a takeover by UBS; its AT1 bonds were written to zero while shareholders received something, upending expectations about the creditor hierarchy.

In late January 2025 Chinese lab DeepSeek's low-cost reasoning model raised doubts about AI compute demand; Nvidia suffered one of the largest single-day market value losses on record and AI infrastructure stocks sold off.
Momentum oscillator by Larry Williams that places the close within the recent high-low range on a scale from 0 to -100; readings near 0 are overbought and near -100 oversold.
nodes.f: %R = (highest high - close) / (highest high - lowest low) x -100

nodes.t: Oscillator by Donald Lambert measuring how far the typical price sits from its moving average in units of mean absolute deviation; moves beyond plus or minus 100 flag unusual strength or weakness.
nodes.f: CCI = (typical price - SMA of typical price) / (0.015 x mean deviation)

nodes.t: The average of a bar's high, low and close, used as the input price in CCI, money flow index, pivot points and some VWAP calculations.
nodes.f: typical price = (high + low + close) / 3

nodes.t: Momentum indicator giving the percentage change in price over a fixed lookback; crossing zero marks a shift from falling to rising momentum over that window.
nodes.f: ROC = (close / close n periods ago - 1) x 100

nodes.t: Volume-weighted measure by Marc Chaikin of where closes fall within each bar's range, summed over a window; positive values suggest accumulation, negative values distribution.
nodes.f: CMF = sum(money flow multiplier x volume, n) / sum(volume, n)

nodes.t: Ratio from -1 to +1 locating the close within the bar's high-low range; +1 means a close at the high. It is the building block of Chaikin's volume indicators.
nodes.f: MFM = ((close - low) - (high - close)) / (high - low)

nodes.t: Cumulative running total of money flow volume developed by Marc Chaikin; divergence between the line and price is read as hidden buying or selling.
nodes.f: ADL = prior ADL + money flow multiplier x volume

nodes.t: A mathematical transformation of price, volume or open interest plotted with or below a chart to summarize trend, momentum, volatility or participation.
Indicator that fluctuates within a band or around a centre line, used to judge momentum and stretched conditions; most useful in ranges and prone to staying extreme in strong trends.

Volatility envelope around an exponential moving average set at a multiple of average true range; closes outside the channel signal strong momentum, and Bollinger bands inside Keltner signal a squeeze.
nodes.f: bands = EMA(n) plus or minus k x ATR(n)

nodes.t: Bands drawn at the highest high and lowest low of the last n periods, from Richard Donchian; a new channel high or low is the classic breakout entry used by trend followers.
nodes.f: upper = max(high, n); lower = min(low, n)

nodes.t: Pair of lines bounding price action, either parallel trendlines, highest-high and lowest-low bands, or volatility envelopes, used to define trend and breakout levels.
Tushar Chande's indicator measuring how many periods have passed since the latest n-period high and low; Aroon up near 100 with Aroon down near 0 marks a strong uptrend.
nodes.f: Aroon up = (n - periods since n-period high) / n x 100

nodes.t: Welles Wilder's system of +DI and -DI lines comparing upward and downward range expansion to true range; their crossovers give direction and ADX gives trend strength.
nodes.f: +DI = 100 x smoothed +DM / ATR; -DI = 100 x smoothed -DM / ATR

nodes.t: Alexander Elder's indicator combining price change and volume to measure the force behind a move; usually smoothed with a short EMA.
nodes.f: force index = (close - prior close) x volume

nodes.t: Long-term momentum indicator by Edwin Coppock: a weighted moving average of the sum of two long rates of change on monthly index data, traditionally used to spot major bear market bottoms.
nodes.f: Coppock = WMA10(ROC14 + ROC11) on monthly data

nodes.t: Indicator by E.W. Dreiss comparing the sum of true ranges with the overall high-low range over n bars; high values mean sideways chop, low values mean directional trending.
nodes.f: CHOP = 100 x log10(sum TR(n) / (max high - min low)) / log10(n)

nodes.t: Moving average that gives linearly larger weights to more recent prices, reacting faster than a simple average of the same length.
nodes.f: WMA = sum(w_i x P_i) / sum(w_i), with w = 1..n

nodes.t: Moving average whose smoothing constant rises in trending markets and falls in noisy ones, set by the efficiency ratio, so it follows trends and flattens in chop.
nodes.f: SC = (ER x (fast - slow) + slow)^2; KAMA_t = KAMA_t-1 + SC x (P - KAMA_t-1)

nodes.t: Least squares trendline fitted to price over a window with parallel lines at a multiple of the residual standard deviation, framing trend and dispersion around it.
Floor-trader levels computed from the prior period's high, low and close that mark likely intraday support and resistance; widely watched, which partly explains why they matter.
Volume-weighted average price computed from a chosen event, such as an earnings gap or a major low, showing the average cost of everyone who traded since then.
nodes.f: AVWAP = sum(P x V since anchor) / sum(V since anchor)

nodes.t: Histogram of traded volume at each price level over a period, plotted sideways, showing where the market accepted value and where it moved through quickly.
The price level with the most traded volume or time in a profile; it acts as a magnet and as a reference for fair value during the session.
The price range around the point of control that contains a set share of volume or time, conventionally about 70 percent; trading outside it suggests initiative activity.
J. Peter Steidlmayer's chart format, developed at the CBOT, that stacks time-price opportunities by half-hour to show the distribution of activity across prices within a session.
View that markets move to facilitate trade, auctioning up until buyers stop and down until sellers stop, alternating between balance around value and imbalance toward new value.
Bandwidth measures the width of Bollinger bands relative to the middle band and flags volatility contractions; %B locates price within the bands, with 1 at the upper band.
nodes.f: BW = (upper - lower) / middle; %B = (price - lower) / (upper - lower)

nodes.t: Setup where volatility contracts so far that Bollinger bands move inside Keltner channels, on the idea that compressed volatility tends to be followed by expansion and a directional move.
Trailing stop placed a multiple of ATR below the highest high since entry for longs, or above the lowest low for shorts, letting stops adapt to volatility.
nodes.f: long stop = highest high(n) - k x ATR(n)

nodes.t: Candlestick variant built from averaged prices that smooths noise so trends show as runs of same-coloured candles; its plotted prices are not actual traded prices.
nodes.f: HA close = (O + H + L + C) / 4; HA open = (prior HA open + prior HA close) / 2

nodes.t: Chart that shows each period's open, high, low and close as a vertical range with left and right ticks; the Western equivalent of a candlestick.
Japanese charting form, popularized in the West by Steve Nison, that shows each period's open-to-close range as a body and its extremes as shadows, making buyer-seller balance easy to see.
Chart made of fixed-size bricks added only when price moves by the box size, ignoring time and small fluctuations to isolate trend.
Time-independent chart of X columns for rising prices and O columns for falling prices, with a new column only after a reversal of a set number of boxes.
Chart axis where equal distances represent equal percentage changes; essential for long histories, and trendlines drawn on it can differ from arithmetic ones.
Line joining swing highs and lows that exceed a set percentage move, filtering minor noise; its last leg repaints, so it describes the past rather than signalling.
Signal generated when a faster moving average crosses a slower one, or price crosses an average; simple and robust in trends, costly in sideways markets through whipsaws.
Bars showing MACD minus its signal line; shrinking bars show momentum slowing before the lines actually cross.
nodes.f: histogram = MACD - signal line

nodes.t: Pattern where price makes a higher low while an oscillator makes a lower low (or the mirror for downtrends), read as a sign the trend will continue rather than reverse.
When an indicator's past values change after new data arrives, as with zigzag or centred averages; backtests on repainted values show signals no trader could have acted on.
A signal that reverses soon after it is taken, producing a small loss; frequent in range-bound markets and the main cost of trend-following systems.
Move through support or resistance that quickly reverses back inside the range, trapping breakout traders; the trapped positions can fuel a sharp move the other way.
Return of price to a broken level after a breakout, where former resistance should act as support (or vice versa); a hold confirms the breakout.
Principle that broken support tends to become resistance and broken resistance becomes support, because traders who missed or lost on the level act around it.
A temporary counter-trend move within an established trend, often toward a moving average or prior breakout level, used as a lower-risk entry point.
Straight line joining successive higher lows in an uptrend or lower highs in a downtrend; more touches and a gentler slope make it more significant.
Local price peaks and troughs that stand above or below neighbouring bars; their sequence defines trend structure and common stop placement.
Sequence of swing points: higher highs and higher lows define an uptrend, lower highs and lower lows a downtrend; a break of the last swing is a change of structure.
A change in the direction of the prevailing trend, signalled by broken structure, reversal patterns or divergence; distinct from a pullback, which resumes the trend.
Trading from raw price bars, swings and levels with few or no indicators, on the view that indicators only repackage price.
Reading the same market on several chart periods so that trades follow the higher time frame trend and use the lower time frame for timing.
Rule that switches a strategy on or off based on a market condition, such as price above its 200-day average or volatility below a threshold, to avoid trading in hostile regimes.
Entry when price moves more than a multiple of recent volatility from a reference, such as the open or prior close; aims to catch range expansion early.
Recurring geometric shape in price, classed as reversal or continuation, from which traders infer the likely next move and a measured target; evidence of reliability is mixed.
Reversal pattern of three peaks with the middle highest; a close below the neckline joining the troughs completes the top, with a target equal to head-to-neckline height.
nodes.f: target = neckline - (head - neckline)

nodes.t: Bottoming version of head and shoulders with three troughs, the middle lowest; a break above the neckline, ideally on rising volume, completes the reversal.
nodes.f: target = neckline + (neckline - head)

nodes.t: Line joining the reaction lows (or highs) of a head and shoulders or double top or bottom; its break is the trigger that completes the pattern.
Reversal patterns where price fails twice near the same high (an M) or holds twice near the same low (a W); confirmed only when the intervening trough or peak breaks.
Bullish continuation base popularized by William O'Neil: a U-shaped cup followed by a small, shallow pullback (the handle) near the old high, with entry on a breakout above the handle.

Converging patterns where swings narrow between two trendlines: ascending (flat top, rising lows), descending (flat bottom, falling highs) and symmetrical; usually continuation, with breakouts in either direction possible.
Converging pattern where both trendlines slope the same way; a rising wedge is usually bearish and a falling wedge bullish, because momentum fades within the move.
Short, rectangular counter-trend consolidation after a sharp move (the pole), on declining volume; a breakout in the trend direction projects a move similar to the pole.
nodes.f: target = breakout point + pole length

nodes.t: Small symmetrical triangle forming after a sharp move, read the same way as a flag: brief pause, then continuation by roughly the length of the prior move.
Sideways range bounded by horizontal support and resistance; a close outside it signals the direction of the next move, often by about the range height.
Price target method assuming the next leg will roughly equal a prior leg or pattern height, used with flags, ranges and head and shoulders.
Abrupt trend reversal with no base or topping process, hard to anticipate because no pattern forms first; common after capitulation.
Final stage of a decline when remaining holders sell in panic regardless of price, often on extreme volume and breadth; frequently marks or precedes a low.
Range on a chart with no trading because a bar opened beyond the prior bar's high or low, usually after news; classed as common, breakaway, runaway or exhaustion.
Gap that launches price out of a base or range on heavy volume, marking the start of a new trend; it often stays unfilled.
Gap in the middle of a strong trend, signalling continued urgency; it is said to occur near the halfway point of the move.
Late-trend gap on climactic volume that is soon reversed and filled, marking the final burst of buying or selling.
Cluster of bars isolated by a gap on each side, an exhaustion gap then a breakaway gap in the opposite direction; a sharp reversal signal.
Large opening gap on an earnings or news release; follow-through in the gap direction is related to post-earnings drift and is the basis of several momentum setups.
Bar that makes a new high (or low) in the trend direction and then closes beyond the prior close in the opposite direction, hinting at exhaustion.
An inside day has its range wholly within the prior bar's range, showing contraction; an outside day engulfs the prior range, showing expansion.
Toby Crabel's setup flagging the narrowest daily range of the last seven days, on the idea that range contraction precedes range expansion.
Intraday strategy entering when price breaks the high or low set in the first minutes of the session, associated with Toby Crabel.
Rule-based trend system taught by Richard Dennis and William Eckhardt in the 1980s: Donchian channel breakouts, ATR-based position sizing and fixed exits, showing trading could be taught.
Stan Weinstein's framework that every stock cycles through basing, advancing, topping and declining stages, identified mainly with a 30-week moving average; buy stage 2, avoid stage 4.
Mark Minervini's base in which successive pullbacks get shallower and volume dries up, showing supply being absorbed before a breakout.
William O'Neil's growth stock method combining strong current and annual earnings, new products or highs, supply and demand, leadership, institutional sponsorship and a confirmed market uptrend.
O'Neil's signal of a new market uptrend: a strong gain in a major index on higher volume, a few days or more after a rally attempt begins from a low.
Session where a major index falls meaningfully on higher volume than the prior day, read as institutional selling; a cluster of them warns of a top.
The thick part of a candlestick between the open and the close; filled or red when the close is below the open, hollow or green when above.
Thin lines above and below a candlestick body marking the high and low; long shadows show prices that were rejected during the period.
One- to three-candle formation named in Japanese charting tradition that signals indecision, reversal or continuation; meaningful mainly in context, at trends and levels.
Candle where open and close are nearly equal, signalling indecision; after a strong trend it can warn of exhaustion.

Doji variants: a dragonfly opens and closes at the high after a long lower shadow, showing rejection of lows; a gravestone opens and closes at the low after a long upper shadow, showing rejection of highs.
Small body near the top of the range with a long lower shadow; called a hammer after a decline (bullish) and a hanging man after an advance (bearish warning).
Small body near the low of the range with a long upper shadow; a shooting star after an advance is bearish, an inverted hammer after a decline is a possible bottom.
Two-candle reversal where the second body fully covers the first and has the opposite colour; bullish after declines, bearish after advances.
Two-candle pattern where a small body sits inside the prior large body, signalling a loss of momentum; a harami cross uses a doji as the second candle.

nodes.n: Piercing line and dark cloud cover
nodes.t: Two-candle reversals: a piercing line opens below the prior low and closes above the midpoint of a down candle; dark cloud cover is the bearish mirror.
Three-candle reversals: a large candle, a small-bodied star gapped away from it, then a strong candle in the opposite direction closing well into the first body.

nodes.n: Three white soldiers and three black crows
nodes.t: Three consecutive long candles in the same direction, each closing near its extreme; soldiers signal strong buying after a decline, crows strong selling after an advance.

Studies on liquid US stocks generally find little standalone predictive value in candlestick patterns after costs, while some find modest effects in specific markets; context and confirmation matter more than the shape.

Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron (1992) found moving average and range breakout rules had predictive power on the Dow, but later work using White's Reality Check showed much of such evidence weakens after correcting for data snooping and costs.
Paper "Foundations of Technical Analysis" that used kernel regression to detect chart patterns automatically and found several patterns carried incremental information about returns in US stocks.
Argument that widely watched levels and signals work partly because enough traders act on them at the same time; the effect is fragile and fades when it becomes crowded.
Tendency of limit orders, stops and price targets to cluster at round numbers, which creates support, resistance and overshoots near them.
Price pushing briefly through an obvious level where stop orders cluster, triggering them and then reversing; the result of liquidity seeking, whether deliberate or not.
George and Hwang (2004) found that stocks trading near their 52-week high outperform those far from it, consistent with investors anchoring to that level and underreacting to news.
Breadth momentum indicator by Sherman and Marian McClellan equal to a fast minus a slow exponential average of daily net advances; extremes flag overbought or oversold breadth.
nodes.f: McClellan = EMA19(advances - declines) - EMA39(advances - declines)

nodes.t: Running total of the McClellan oscillator, used as a slower gauge of the breadth trend; its direction and level frame the intermediate market cycle.
nodes.f: summation_t = summation_t-1 + McClellan_t

nodes.t: Richard Arms' ratio of the advance-decline ratio to the up-down volume ratio; values above 1 mean volume is concentrated in falling stocks, and very high readings mark short-term selling extremes.
nodes.f: TRIN = (advancers / decliners) / (up volume / down volume)

nodes.t: Volume in advancing issues divided by volume in declining issues; lopsided days such as 9-to-1 up or down are read as signs of thrusts or capitulation.
nodes.f: ratio = up volume / down volume

nodes.t: Daily count of stocks at 52-week highs less those at 52-week lows; expanding new highs confirm an advance, while a rising index with shrinking highs warns of narrowing participation.
nodes.f: net = new highs - new lows

nodes.t: Breadth warning attributed to Jim Miekka that fires when unusually many stocks make new highs and new lows at once in a rising market, signalling internal disagreement; it gives many false alarms.

Rapid shift from very weak to very strong breadth over a short window; Martin Zweig's version uses a 10-day average of the advancing share of issues and has historically appeared near the start of new bull phases.
nodes.f: Zweig: EMA10(advances / (advances + declines)) rises from below 0.40 to above 0.615 within 10 days

nodes.t: Number of NYSE stocks whose last trade was an uptick minus those on a downtick, updated through the day; extreme readings mark intraday buying or selling programs.
nodes.f: TICK = upticking issues - downticking issues

nodes.t: Share of stocks in an index that are on point and figure buy signals; readings above 70 are considered overbought and below 30 oversold.
Relative performance of an equal-weight index against its cap-weighted version; when cap-weight leads, gains are concentrated in the largest stocks.
Market advance driven by a small number of large stocks while most constituents lag; often cited as a late-cycle warning, though it can persist for long periods.
Movement of leadership between sectors as the cycle evolves, for example from early-cycle financials and discretionary toward late-cycle energy and defensives; also a strategy that follows it.
Julius de Kempenaer's chart plotting a set of assets by relative strength and its momentum, so they rotate through leading, weakening, lagging and improving quadrants.
Chart of one price divided by another, such as a stock over its index or copper over gold, used to see relative trend independent of overall market direction.
Current volume divided by typical volume at the same point in the day or over recent sessions; high values show unusual interest that makes moves more meaningful.
nodes.f: RVOL = volume / average volume

nodes.t: Exceptionally high volume at the end of an extended move, signalling that the last eager buyers or sellers have acted; it often marks an exhaustion point.
Wyckoff term for panic selling on very high volume and wide ranges after a long decline, absorbed by strong hands and followed by an automatic rally.
Wyckoff term for a burst of heavy, eager buying at the top of an advance that is met by professional supply, followed by an automatic reaction lower.
Richard Wyckoff's approach to reading supply and demand through price, volume and time, based on laws of supply and demand, cause and effect, and effort versus result.
Schematic of a trading range in which large operators absorb supply after a decline, typically including a selling climax, a spring and a sign of strength before markup.
Schematic of a trading range in which large operators sell into demand after an advance, typically with a buying climax and an upthrust before markdown.
Brief break below trading range support that quickly reverses back inside, shaking out weak holders and testing remaining supply before markup.
Brief push above trading range resistance that fails and returns inside the range, trapping buyers; the distribution counterpart of the spring.
Wyckoff principle comparing volume (effort) with price movement (result); heavy volume with little progress suggests absorption and a possible turn.
Method developed from Wyckoff by Tom Williams that reads each bar's range, close location and relative volume to infer professional buying or selling.
Running total of volume traded at the ask minus volume traded at the bid; it shows whether aggressive buyers or sellers dominate and can diverge from price.
nodes.f: delta = buy-initiated volume - sell-initiated volume

nodes.t: Order flow chart showing, inside each bar, the volume traded at the bid and at the ask at every price, exposing imbalances and absorption.
Watching the stream of trades and quotes (time and sales) to judge who is aggressive, how size is being worked and whether levels are holding.
Large resting orders soaking up aggressive buying or selling so that price stops moving despite heavy volume; often a sign of a hidden large participant.
Options volume far above open interest or normal levels in a name, often in short-dated out-of-the-money contracts, watched as a possible sign of informed positioning.

nodes.n: Price, volume and open interest reading
nodes.t: Classic futures rule set: rising price with rising open interest confirms a trend, rising price with falling open interest suggests short covering, and so on.
Share of lendable supply of a security that is currently on loan; high utilization with rising fees signals crowded shorts and hard-to-borrow conditions.
nodes.f: utilization = shares on loan / lendable shares

nodes.t: Poll of investors or advisors about their market outlook; useful mainly at extremes and as a contrarian input, since stated views and positioning can differ.
Measure of crowd sentiment or positioning used against the crowd: extreme optimism is read as bearish and extreme pessimism as bullish.

Framework built from Charles Dow's editorials and formalized by William Hamilton and Robert Rhea: the market has three trends, primary trends have three phases, and the industrial and transport averages must confirm each other.
In Dow theory, the major bull or bear trend lasting a year or more, within which secondary reactions and minor moves occur.
In Dow theory, a counter-trend move within the primary trend lasting weeks to months and typically retracing a third to two-thirds of the prior swing.

nodes.n: Three phases of a Dow trend
nodes.t: Dow theory's stages of a primary trend: accumulation by informed investors, public participation as news improves, and distribution or excess as the crowd piles in.
Dow theory rule that a trend signal requires both the industrial and transport averages to make new highs or lows; when one fails, the divergence is a warning.
R.N. Elliott's theory that crowd psychology moves prices in fractal patterns, five waves with the trend followed by three corrective waves, popularized by Frost and Prechter; labelling is subjective.
Five-wave move in the direction of the larger trend, labelled 1 to 5, in which waves 1, 3 and 5 advance and waves 2 and 4 correct.
Counter-trend Elliott pattern labelled A, B, C, taking forms such as zigzags (5-3-5), flats (3-3-5) and triangles (3-3-3-3-3).
Three hard rules for impulses: wave 2 never retraces all of wave 1, wave 3 is never the shortest of waves 1, 3 and 5, and wave 4 does not overlap wave 1's price territory.
An impulse wave, most often wave 3, that is much longer than the others and subdivides visibly into its own five waves.
Wedge-shaped Elliott pattern in which waves overlap; an ending diagonal appears in wave 5 or C and often precedes a sharp reversal.
Price targets set at Fibonacci multiples of a prior swing projected beyond it, commonly 1.272, 1.618 and 2.618, used for profit targets in trends and Elliott wave counts.
nodes.f: target = swing end + ratio x swing length

nodes.t: John Murphy's approach of reading stocks, bonds, commodities and currencies together, on the view that their relationships shift through the business cycle.
Copper price divided by gold price, used as a growth versus safety gauge; it has tended to track long-term Treasury yields.
nodes.f: ratio = copper price / gold price

nodes.t: Observation that high-yield spreads often widen before equity prices fall, because bondholders are more sensitive to default risk; a divergence between them is a warning.
Ratios of cyclical to defensive assets, such as discretionary to staples, small caps to large caps, or high beta to low volatility, used to read risk-on or risk-off behaviour.
Return pattern tied to the calendar rather than to fundamentals, such as month turns, holidays or weekdays; many are small, unstable and vulnerable to data mining.
Saying popularized by the Stock Trader's Almanac that the direction of the S&P 500 in January predicts the full year; the evidence is weak once the market's general upward drift is accounted for.
Tendency, noted by Yale Hirsch, for stocks to rise over the last five trading days of the year and the first two of the next.
Predictable flows as balanced funds, pensions and target-date funds trade back to policy weights after stocks and bonds diverge, watched by desks as a short-term price pressure.
Pattern, also from Hirsch, in which US stocks have done better in the third year of a presidential term than in the first two; sample sizes are small.
Historic finding that returns differed by weekday, notably weak Mondays documented by French (1980); much of it has faded in recent decades.
Decomposition of returns into close-to-open and open-to-close; for many US stocks and indexes a large share of long-run gains has accrued overnight.
nodes.f: overnight = open_t / close_t-1 - 1; intraday = close_t / open_t - 1

nodes.t: Selling of losing positions before the tax year ends to realize capital losses, which depresses prices of recent losers and can lead to a rebound afterwards.
Fund managers buying recent winners and selling losers before reporting dates so holdings look better; it creates small predictable trading pressures near quarter ends.
Price behaviour around monthly and quarterly option expiry, including pinning near large open interest strikes and changes in dealer hedging flows afterwards.
The SEC's Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis and Retrieval system where public company, fund and insider filings are submitted and published free of charge.
SEC tool that searches the text of filings, including exhibits, over recent years; useful for finding mentions of customers, suppliers, risks or terms across all filers.

Tagging standard that labels each financial statement number in a filing with a defined element, making SEC financial data machine-readable; inline XBRL embeds the tags in the human-readable document.
Quarterly report for the first three fiscal quarters with unaudited, reviewed financial statements, MD&A and updates to risks; filed 40 or 45 days after quarter end depending on filer size.
8-K items that often signal trouble: 4.01 change of auditor, 4.02 non-reliance on prior financial statements, 5.02 sudden officer departures, and 3.01 delisting notices.
Form 12b-25 notice that a company cannot file its periodic report on time; late filings frequently precede restatements, control failures or negative news.
Reading the proxy to see which metrics drive management bonuses and equity awards, since pay design shapes behaviour, for example EPS targets encouraging buybacks or adjusted metrics.
Section of SEC filings listing material risks to the business; mostly boilerplate, so the useful signal is in additions, deletions and wording changes between filings.
Disclosure of the judgments with the largest effect on reported results, such as reserves, impairments and revenue estimates, and how sensitive results are to them.
Notes to the financial statements that detail accounting policies, debt terms, leases, contingencies, segments and related parties; often where the real risks and adjustments are found.
The independent auditor's opinion on whether financial statements fairly present the company's position under the applicable framework; qualified or adverse opinions are rare and serious.
Correspondence in which SEC staff question a company's disclosures and the company responds; published on EDGAR after reviews close, they reveal where regulators see weak accounting.
Short-form beneficial ownership report for holders above 5 percent who are passive or qualified institutions; switching from 13G to 13D signals a change toward activism.
Registration statement for an IPO or other registered offering by companies that cannot use short forms, containing the prospectus, financials, risk factors and use of proceeds.
Short-form registration available to seasoned issuers that lets them register securities in advance and sell them from the shelf over time, enabling fast follow-ons and at-the-market programs.
Annual report (20-F) and current reports (6-K) filed by foreign private issuers; less frequent and less detailed interim reporting than US domestic filers.
Notice filed by affiliates intending to sell restricted or control securities under Rule 144; a leading indicator of insider selling before the trade itself is reported.
Notice filed after an exempt private offering under Regulation D, giving the amount raised and investor types; used to track private fundraising by companies and funds.
Monthly portfolio holdings report filed by registered funds, with quarter-end data made public after a lag; more detailed than 13F, covering bonds and derivatives.
Using dictionaries or language models to score tone, uncertainty and readability in filings and calls; Loughran and McDonald (2011) showed general dictionaries misclassify many finance words.
Press release reporting quarterly results, usually with GAAP and non-GAAP figures and guidance, furnished to the SEC on Form 8-K under Item 2.02, often shortly before the call.
Management's forecast of future revenue, earnings or other metrics; changes in guidance often move stocks more than the reported quarter.
Unofficial expectation for earnings circulating among traders that differs from published consensus; beating consensus but missing the whisper can still disappoint.
Quarter in which a company beats consensus and raises guidance, usually the best reaction case; a beat without a raise can disappoint when expectations already price in more.
Management setting guidance low enough to beat it reliably; investors learn the pattern and adjust expectations, so the beat itself carries less information.
Pattern in which analyst estimates start optimistic and drift down toward a level the company can beat by reporting day, documented by Richardson, Teoh and Wysocki.
Quarter in which management, often new, takes every possible charge and write-down at once to reset the base and make later results look better.
Company disclosing results or a guidance change ahead of the scheduled release, more often for negative news to avoid a surprise.
Weeks before results when companies limit communication with investors and analysts to avoid selective disclosure of the quarter's results.
Schedule of expected earnings release dates; confirmed dates come from company announcements, and a late or changed date can itself carry information.
Price move the options market prices for an earnings release, approximated by the at-the-money straddle for the nearest expiry divided by the stock price.
nodes.f: implied move = ATM straddle price / stock price

nodes.t: Spread of analyst forecasts for the same metric; high dispersion signals uncertainty, and Diether, Malloy and Scherbina (2002) found high-dispersion stocks subsequently underperform.
nodes.f: dispersion = std dev of estimates / abs(mean estimate)

nodes.t: Inferring news about one company from results or comments of a peer, supplier or customer; markets often move peers on an early reporter's numbers.
Recording management's past guidance, targets and claims against outcomes to calibrate how much weight to give new statements.
Schedule of upcoming data releases, central bank meetings and auctions with release times and consensus forecasts; essential for knowing when event risk is concentrated.
How official data are produced and published: fixed schedules announced in advance, strict pre-release access rules, and release at set times so all users get data at once.
Archive of what each statistic showed on each past date before revisions, such as ALFRED, needed so backtests use only information known at the time.
Median of surveyed economist forecasts for a data release; markets react to the surprise against this number rather than to the level.
nodes.f: surprise = actual - consensus median

nodes.t: Period around each FOMC meeting during which Fed officials refrain from public comment on policy, so markets get no new signals before the decision.
First published report by an analyst on a company, usually a long piece with model, thesis, rating and target; initiations after IPO quiet periods often skew positive.
Recommendation such as buy, hold or sell, or overweight and underweight relative to a coverage group; buy ratings far outnumber sells, so downgrades carry more information.
Analyst's projected price, usually over twelve months, derived from multiples or DCF; targets tend to follow price rather than lead it and are on average optimistic.
Stock price reaction to analyst upgrades and downgrades; Womack (1996) found significant drift after changes, larger after downgrades.
Systematic upward bias in analyst forecasts and ratings, linked to investment banking ties and the need for management access; it is larger for long-horizon forecasts.
Tendency of analysts to keep forecasts near consensus to limit career risk; it compresses dispersion and delays the incorporation of new information.
2003 settlement between regulators and major banks over research conflicts, requiring separation of research from investment banking and funding of independent research.
FINRA rule on equity research conflicts, restricting investment banking influence over analysts, requiring disclosures and setting quiet periods around offerings.
European rules that required asset managers to pay for research separately from trading commissions, which cut research budgets and analyst coverage of smaller companies; later partly relaxed.
Paying for research and services with trading commissions rather than direct fees, permitted in the US within Section 28(e) limits; criticized for hiding costs from clients.
Broker-arranged meetings between investors and company management at conferences, roadshows and site visits; a large part of what institutions pay brokers for.
Management visiting investors without an offering attached, to explain strategy; Reg FD forbids sharing material nonpublic information in these meetings.
Investor who buys a stake and pushes management for changes such as asset sales, buybacks or board seats, often signalled by a 13D filing.
Tracking component orders, supplier commentary and production schedules to infer a company's volumes, such as supplier capacity bookings ahead of a product launch.
Original information gathered directly by the investor, through surveys, interviews, site visits or data collection, rather than read from published sources.
Controls on expert network use: screening out current employees with confidential duties, pre-call disclaimers, chaperones and logs, to avoid receiving MNPI.
Data collected from websites, such as prices, inventory counts, reviews or job listings; terms of service, legal limits and site changes create compliance and continuity risk.
Aggregated, anonymized transaction data from card or bank account panels used to estimate company sales before reporting; panel composition biases must be corrected.
Imagery of parking lots, oil tanks, ships or crops, and phone location data on store visits, used to estimate activity at assets and retailers.
Counts of visits to physical locations estimated from phone location panels, used for retailers, restaurants and real estate; panel changes can create false trends.
Companies releasing bad news when attention is low, such as Friday evenings or busy days; DellaVigna and Pollet (2009) found weaker immediate reactions to Friday announcements.
Investors can process only so much information, so news released when attention is scarce is incorporated slowly, contributing to drifts and underreaction.
SEC rule adopted in 2000 requiring issuers that disclose material nonpublic information to analysts or investors to disclose it publicly at the same time, or promptly if unintentional.
Giving material information to some investors or analysts before the public; prohibited for issuers by Reg FD and a historic source of sell-side edge.
Doctrine that an analyst may combine public and non-material nonpublic information into a conclusion that would itself be material, without violating insider trading law.
Mostly judge-made doctrine under Rule 10b-5: liability requires trading on MNPI in breach of a duty, under the classical theory for insiders or the misappropriation theory for outsiders.
SEC anti-fraud rule under the Exchange Act prohibiting material misstatements, omissions and deceptive practices in connection with buying or selling securities.
Insider trading theory, upheld in United States v. O'Hagan (1997), that an outsider who trades on confidential information taken in breach of a duty to its source commits fraud.
Rule from Dirks v. SEC (1983) that a person who receives a tip is liable if the insider breached a duty for personal benefit and the tippee knew or should have known.
Trading a different but economically linked company's securities using MNPI about one's own employer; SEC v. Panuwat applied the misappropriation theory to it.
Company policy barring insiders from trading in the weeks before earnings until shortly after release, to reduce the risk of trading on MNPI.
Exchange Act provision requiring officers, directors and 10 percent holders to give the company any profit from buying and selling its stock within six months, regardless of intent.
Policies and physical or system separation that keep MNPI held by one part of a firm, such as banking, away from trading and research.
Compliance lists of securities in which a firm limits trading or research because it may hold MNPI; the watch list is confidential, the restricted list is broadly communicated.
Bringing an investor over the wall by sharing confidential information, such as a pending offering, with consent; the investor is then restricted until the information is cleansed.
Difference between what the price implies about future fundamentals and what the investor expects; the source of return when the gap closes.
Claim that known information is already reflected in the price; testing it requires estimating what expectations the price implies, not assuming them.
Record written at the time of each decision of the reasoning, expectations, confidence and emotional state, so later reviews can separate skill from luck.
Written case for a position covering thesis, valuation, risks, catalysts and sizing, reviewed by others before capital is committed.
Writing the strongest version of the opposing argument and the downside scenario before committing, to counter confirmation bias.
Assigning someone to attack a thesis or model as an adversary would, to find weaknesses the author cannot see.
Confirming a fact with independent sources that do not share the same origin; three reports from one original source are one source.
How fast the value of a piece of information decays as it spreads into prices, from milliseconds for headlines to months for slow-moving fundamentals.
Process for finding candidate investments, such as screens, new highs and lows, spin-offs, insider buying, conferences and peer reads; sources shape which biases enter the pipeline.
Filter applied to a universe on quantitative criteria such as valuation, quality or momentum to narrow research candidates; point-in-time data are needed to backtest screens honestly.

nodes.n: Sample selection bias in research data
nodes.t: When the panel, survey or alt-data sample differs systematically from the population of interest, such as card users skewing young, so naive extrapolation misestimates the total.
Manipulation in which promoters hype a thinly traded security with misleading claims, then sell into the buying they create.
Gaining control of enough supply of a security or commodity, often alongside large long derivatives positions, to dictate prices to shorts who must deliver or cover.

US federal agency that regulates securities markets, issuers, broker-dealers, exchanges, investment advisers and funds, with a mission of investor protection, fair and orderly markets and capital formation.
Self-regulatory organization overseen by the SEC that writes and enforces rules for US broker-dealers, licenses registered representatives and runs market surveillance.
US agency regulating futures, options on futures and most swaps, including exchanges, clearing houses and intermediaries, under the Commodity Exchange Act.
Industry body given authority to set and enforce rules for its members under government oversight, such as exchanges, FINRA and the NFA.
US law requiring registration and full disclosure for public offerings of securities, with liability for misstatements in registration statements, unless an exemption applies.
US law that created the SEC and governs secondary trading, exchanges, broker-dealers, periodic reporting, proxy solicitation and anti-fraud rules.
US law regulating mutual funds, ETFs and other registered investment companies, covering disclosure, leverage limits, custody, governance and conflicts.
US law requiring registration of investment advisers and imposing a fiduciary duty of care and loyalty toward clients.
2002 US law passed after Enron and WorldCom that requires CEO and CFO certification of financial reports, internal control assessments and created the PCAOB to oversee auditors.
Processes that give reasonable assurance financial statements are reliable; a material weakness disclosure signals higher risk of misstatement.
2010 US financial reform law that moved most swaps to clearing and reporting, created the CFPB and FSOC, imposed the Volcker Rule and expanded systemic risk oversight.
Dodd-Frank provision limiting proprietary trading by banks and their investments in hedge funds and private equity funds, with exemptions for market making and hedging.
2012 US law easing capital raising, including confidential IPO filings and lighter disclosure for emerging growth companies, general solicitation in some private offerings, and crowdfunding.
Reg NMS rule requiring trading centers to prevent trade-throughs of protected, automatically accessible quotes at better prices on other venues.
Reg NMS limit on the fee a venue may charge to execute against its displayed quotes, which shapes the economics of maker-taker pricing.
Reg NMS rule setting minimum quoting increments for stocks, historically one cent for prices of a dollar or more, which also determines queue and spread dynamics.
Under Reg SHO, a broker must have reasonable grounds to believe shares can be borrowed for delivery before accepting a short sale.
Reg SHO list of securities with large, persistent fails to deliver, published daily, triggering mandatory close-out requirements.
SEC circuit breaker that, after a stock falls 10 percent in a day, allows short sales only above the national best bid for the rest of that day and the next.
SEC framework under which alternative trading systems, including dark pools, operate as broker-dealers rather than exchanges, with Form ATS-N disclosures for NMS stock ATSs.
SEC rule requiring exchanges, clearing agencies and large ATSs to keep systems capacity, integrity and resilience, test them and report outages.
SEC rule requiring brokers that provide market access to have pre-trade risk controls, such as credit and fat-finger limits, so no client trades unfiltered.
SEC rule requiring broker-dealers to hold minimum liquid net capital, after haircuts on securities positions, so they can wind down without harming customers.
Federal Reserve rule governing credit brokers may extend for securities purchases, setting initial margin for stocks at 50 percent of purchase value.
Regulated venue where buyers and sellers trade listed securities under published rules, providing price discovery, listings, auctions and market data.
Exchange fee model that pays rebates to orders adding liquidity and charges fees to orders removing it; inverted venues do the reverse.
SEC-mandated database tracking the full lifecycle of orders across US equity and options markets for surveillance; its cost and privacy terms have been contested.
Exchange requirements to list and stay listed, such as minimum price, market value, shareholders and governance; breaches lead to deficiency notices and possible delisting.
Removal of a security from an exchange, voluntarily or for failing standards; it usually cuts liquidity and many holders must sell, and delisting returns must be in backtests.
US-traded certificate representing shares of a foreign company held by a depositary bank; prices track local shares via conversion arbitrage, with FX and fees added.
SEC safe harbour for public resale of restricted and control securities, with holding periods, volume limits for affiliates and Form 144 notice.
SEC rule allowing resale of privately placed securities to qualified institutional buyers, creating a large institutional market for high-yield and other bonds without registration.
SEC exemptions for private offerings, chiefly Rule 506, allowing unlimited capital raises from accredited investors without registration; 506(c) permits general solicitation if buyers are verified.
Agreement barring insiders and pre-IPO holders from selling for a period after an IPO, commonly 180 days; expirations can weigh on prices as supply arrives.
Restrictions on issuer communications during registration and on research by underwriting banks for a period after an IPO.
Offsetting each member's trades against all others through the clearing house so only net obligations settle, sharply reducing the securities and cash that must move.
Firm admitted to a clearing house that clears its own and clients' trades, posts margin and contributes to the default fund.
Concern that central clearing concentrates systemic risk in a few CCPs, whose failure or procyclical margin calls could spread stress.
Margin and haircut models that raise requirements when volatility rises, forcing collateral calls and selling at the worst time and amplifying stress.
Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation, the US post-trade utility that owns NSCC, DTC and FICC, clearing and settling most US securities trades.
National Securities Clearing Corporation, DTCC's CCP for US equities and corporate bonds, which nets trades through continuous net settlement and requires member margin.
Depository Trust Company, the US central securities depository that holds securities in book-entry form and settles transfers between participants.
Fixed Income Clearing Corporation, DTCC's clearing house for US Treasuries, agency securities and repo, central to Treasury clearing reform.
Settlement method that transfers securities only if the matching cash payment is made at the same time, removing principal risk.
Bank that holds and safekeeps assets for funds and institutions, settles their trades, collects income and handles corporate actions.
SEC rule requiring most cash Treasury and Treasury repo trades by direct participants to be centrally cleared, phased in over several years.
Firm that designs, calculates and licenses benchmarks, such as S&P Dow Jones Indices, MSCI and FTSE Russell; its rules decide which stocks passive money must buy.
Published rules for an index: eligibility, weighting, float adjustment, caps, rebalancing schedule and treatment of corporate actions.
Weighting index constituents by shares available to public investors, excluding strategic, government and insider holdings.
nodes.f: float mcap = price x shares outstanding x float factor

nodes.t: Index giving every constituent the same weight at rebalance, tilting toward smaller stocks and requiring regular trading back to equal weights.
Index weighting stocks by share price, as the Dow Jones Industrial Average does, so a high-priced stock moves it more regardless of company size.
nodes.f: DJIA = sum of prices / Dow divisor

nodes.t: S&P criteria for addition, including US domicile, size, liquidity, float and positive GAAP earnings in the latest quarter and the sum of the last four, with a committee making final choices.
Periodic rebuilding of the Russell US indexes by market cap ranking on a rank day, historically annual in June, generating some of the heaviest closing auction volume of the year.
MSCI's quarterly and semi-annual reviews that add, delete and reweight constituents, plus annual market classification reviews that can move a country between categories.
Index providers' grouping of countries into developed, emerging and frontier based on economic development, size and market accessibility; reclassification shifts large passive flows.
Price rise of stocks added to major indexes from announcement to inclusion, documented by Shleifer (1986) and Harris and Gurel (1986); evidence suggests it has shrunk as it became anticipated.
Traders buying expected additions and selling deletions ahead of index funds, earning the price pressure that funds pay; it raises passive investors' hidden costs.
Limits on single-stock or group weights in an index, often to meet fund diversification rules; caps force selling of the largest names at rebalances.
Global Industry Classification Standard developed by MSCI and S&P, which assigns companies to sectors, industry groups, industries and sub-industries; reclassifications shift sector fund holdings.
Trading a basket of many stocks at once, for index arbitrage, portfolio transitions or rebalancing; historically defined by NYSE as baskets of fifteen or more stocks.
Framework of policies, inventory, tiering, validation, monitoring and governance that controls losses from model errors or misuse across an organization.
Complete register of models in use, with owners, purpose, inputs, dependencies, risk tier and validation status; missing models are unmanaged risk.
Ranking models by materiality, complexity and uncertainty to set the depth and frequency of validation and monitoring.
Validation step assessing whether a model's theory, design, assumptions and data are appropriate for its purpose, judged against literature and industry practice.
Comparing model outputs with actual outcomes, including backtesting, to judge accuracy and detect deterioration.
Periodic checks that a model still performs as validated, tracking input drift, output stability, overrides and errors against thresholds that trigger review.
Alternative models built to compare against a production model; large disagreements flag specification or implementation problems.
Documented conditions where a model is unreliable, such as untested regimes, extrapolated inputs or simplified mechanics; users must know them to avoid misuse.
Applying a model outside the purpose, population or range it was built and validated for, a major source of model risk even when the model itself is sound.
Written description of a model's purpose, theory, data, assumptions, limitations, testing and change history, detailed enough for an independent party to understand and reproduce it.
Process requiring versioning, testing and approval of model changes before production, so silent edits do not alter results.
Judgemental adjustment applied to model output to cover known weaknesses or unusual conditions; it should be documented, justified and tracked for performance.
Outputs of one model feeding another, so an error propagates and compounds; aggregate model risk can exceed the sum of individual model risks.
Risk from many models sharing data, assumptions or vendors, so they fail together; SR 11-7 asks firms to consider it across the portfolio of models.
Errors, gaps, staleness or bias in model inputs that corrupt outputs regardless of model quality; garbage in, garbage out.
Errors from manual, untested spreadsheet models, such as wrong ranges or copy-paste mistakes; audits have repeatedly found errors in a large share of operational spreadsheets.
Gap between the model as designed and the model as coded or deployed, from bugs, unit errors, wrong data mappings or deployment mistakes.
Second person checking model code for errors, hidden look-ahead and divergence from documentation; finds implementation bugs that output testing can miss.
Error in model outputs from estimating parameters with finite, noisy data; ignoring it makes forecasts and optimized portfolios look more precise than they are.
Whether estimated coefficients stay similar across subperiods and samples; unstable parameters suggest overfitting or structural change.
Error from choosing the wrong functional form, omitting relevant variables or including irrelevant ones, so estimates are biased whatever the sample size.
Uncertainty about which model is correct, beyond parameter error within a model; often larger than parameter uncertainty and ignored when one model is chosen.
Frank Knight's distinction between risk, where probabilities are known, and uncertainty, where they cannot be meaningfully assigned; models handle the first and fail silently on the second.
Combining predictions from several models weighted by evidence or performance, as in Bayesian model averaging, to hedge model uncertainty.
Feeding a model extreme, boundary and inconsistent inputs to see where outputs become unstable, unrealistic or break, rather than only stressing the portfolio it values.
Checking model behaviour at the edges of its input range, such as zero or negative rates, zero volatility or empty data, where hidden assumptions fail.
FRTB requirement comparing risk-model P&L with front-office P&L for each trading desk; desks failing it lose internal model approval.
Valuing positions with a model when no reliable market price exists; the inputs and assumptions are unobservable, so valuations can drift from realizable prices.
Accounting classification of fair value inputs: Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 unobservable model inputs; Level 3 valuations carry the most model risk.
Reserve deducted from model-based valuations to reflect model uncertainty or known limitations, so reported values are prudent.
Measure of how much a variable's distribution has shifted between a reference sample and current data, used to monitor input drift in credit and other models.
nodes.f: PSI = sum((actual% - expected%) x ln(actual% / expected%))

nodes.t: Running a new model in production on live inputs without acting on its outputs, to compare it with expectations before it controls capital.
Rules that cut risk or trigger review when a strategy's drawdown exceeds what its backtest says is plausible, separating bad luck from a broken model.
Rules fixed before testing: hypothesis, universe, data, costs, sample splits, metrics and the number of variants allowed, to limit researcher degrees of freedom.
Recording a hypothesis and test plan before seeing the results, so findings cannot be reframed after the fact.
Record of every backtest variant tried, including failures, needed to count trials for deflated Sharpe ratios and multiple testing corrections.
Keeping a final test sample untouched until the model is fixed and using it once; every peek turns it into training data.
Hypothesizing after the results are known: presenting a post hoc finding as if it had been predicted, which hides how many alternatives were explored.
Overstated backtest returns from dropping stocks when they delist without recording the often large final loss; Shumway (1997) showed missing delisting returns bias results.
Adjusting historical prices and volumes for splits, dividends, spin-offs and mergers; wrong adjustments create false signals and returns in backtests.
Backtests that assume zero or fixed costs overstate returns, especially for high-turnover and small-cap strategies; costs should scale with size, volatility and liquidity.
Robert Lucas's (1976) argument that relationships estimated under one policy regime break when policy changes, because agents change behaviour; models must be structural to survive policy shifts.
When a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure, because people optimize the measure instead of the goal; applies to KPIs, risk limits and model metrics.
When a widely used model changes the market it describes, as portfolio insurance did in 1987 or common risk models do when many funds sell together.
George Box's maxim that all models are wrong but some are useful; the question is whether a model is wrong in ways that matter for its use.
Models assuming normally distributed returns understate the frequency of large moves; many crisis losses followed from treating fat-tailed outcomes as near impossible.
Models assuming positions can be sold at marked prices within a fixed horizon break when liquidity vanishes and forced sellers move prices.
David Li's (2000) Gaussian copula let banks and rating agencies price CDO tranches with a single correlation input; it understated joint default risk in housing and contributed to the 2008 losses.
Before 2008, structured finance rating models assumed modest correlation of mortgage defaults and relied on short histories of rising house prices, so many AAA tranches were later downgraded.
JPMorgan trading losses in a large synthetic credit portfolio; investigations found a new VaR model with spreadsheet errors that understated risk, alongside weak oversight.
Herndon, Ash and Pollin (2013) found coding errors and exclusions in an influential spreadsheet linking high public debt to lower growth, a cautionary case about unreviewed analysis.
a: growth in a time of debt

nodes.t: Oil marketing unit hedged long-dated fixed-price supply contracts with rolled short-dated futures; contango and margin calls created funding losses, showing hedge models must include liquidity.
Interest rate models and systems that assumed rates could not fall below zero, such as lognormal models, failed when rates went negative, forcing shifts to normal or shifted models.
Black-Scholes assumes constant volatility and lognormal prices; the observed smile and skew, steepest after 1987, show the market rejects that assumption and prices crash risk.
Macro models widely used by central banks before 2008 largely lacked a financial sector and so offered little warning of the crisis; later versions added financial frictions.

Combining two grids of numbers so each output entry is a weighted sum of a row of the first against a column of the second. A neural network's layer, a graph walk and a portfolio's return across scenarios are all matrix products, which is why GPUs, built to do many of them at once, run AI.
nodes.f: C_ij = sum_k A_ik B_kj

nodes.t: Computing every running total (or running product) of a sequence in about log2 of its length rounds by combining partial results that double in span each round, possible whenever the operation is associative. Matrix products are, so a step-by-step recursion such as a filter can be run as a scan of matrix multiplications.
nodes.f: P_t = M_1 M_2 ... M_t for every t, in log2(T) rounds

nodes.t: A random walk on a graph that restarts at chosen seed nodes with a fixed probability each step; how often it visits each node ranks the nodes by their connection to the seeds. Each step is one sparse matrix-vector product, and many seed sets can be walked at once as one matrix product.
nodes.f: r = (1 - a) s + a P r

nodes.t: A blockchain consensus design in which the computation miners must do to add blocks is itself useful, such as the matrix multiplications of AI inference, instead of hashing done only to secure the chain. Its claims rest on cheap verification of the work and on whether the useful output finds paying buyers.

Credentials and reachability for every data source, with fallbacks per ticker.

The engine's latest research: the out-of-sample TLT hedge line and its band, the stock-bond regime, data checks, the reasoner's scenario probabilities and the brain's readings, each with its date and evidence label.
