Run YOUR holdings (for example from Robinhood's MCP) through the same lens as the model book: weights, limit checks, concentration, which names are the same bet, sensitivity to each root cause, the gap to the model book, and the portfolio vector to score with evaluate_trade. For this call only: nothing is stored; cannot trade.

The engine's decision loop: what the data says (observe), what it means and what each price requires (orient), the solver, the hedge book and an action per position with its frameworks (decide), and proposals, what to watch and when to look again (act).

One holding's accounting quality, the 10-year growth its price requires (reverse DCF), how often companies that size achieved it (base rates), and the case the price is right and wrong. Override market value or beta to test.

Switch the prebuilt hedges (TLT, put spread, collar, gold, VIX calls, index short, semis short, trend cut, de-gross) on or off at chosen sizes: the book in every scenario, growth, worst case, cost, and the advisor's sets.

Ask the mind (one graph of about 2,600 nodes joining the brain, the engine, about 400 checked facts and papers, 267 verified quotes, 213 economies, the S&P 500 companies, the ML models and the tested assumptions) a question or claim. Returns what it recalled, the claim it weighed, the probability with a leave-one-family-out range, the evidence for and against with weights and sources (one row is t

The labs' tested trading claims on the longest data the engine reads: the 10-month trend rule with a bootstrap, max test and deflated Sharpe; RSI, MACD, Bollinger and golden-cross tests; CAPE and P/E against future returns out of sample; Markov regimes; GARCH; Brent-WTI cointegration; variance ratios; Sell in May; every p-value with Holm and BH corrections.

Exact decision math from the card room: poker equity (seeded Monte Carlo over a seven-card evaluator) and pot odds, Kelly sizing, risk of ruin, Rubinstein and Nash bargaining, the expected-surplus haggling offer, IRR, TVPI/DPI/RVPI, Kaplan-Schoar PME, the Takahashi-Alexander J-curve, and the convenience yield a commodity curve implies.

Machine learning on 155 years of data, judged the honest way: purged walk-forward skill against the historical mean (with a Diebold-Mariano test), the chance that picking the in-sample winner misleads (CPCV), conformal intervals with their realized coverage, permutation importance, calibration, today's forecasts, the nearest historical analogs and how unfamiliar today is.

Where the engine's models meet the real world: each model's assumptions with a live test (fat tails, dependence, structural breaks, the stock-bond correlation by regime, crisis correlation), the breakpoint at which each conclusion flips (trend costs and delay, Kelly across windows, the TLT hedge's correlation limit), Taleb's kappa, the fragility heuristic and 400 resampled worlds.

What a quant's backtested Sharpe is worth live: after trading costs, the out-of-sample or post-publication decay McLean and Pontiff measured, the deflated Sharpe ratio for the number of variants tried, and the minimum backtest length.

Damodaran's two tools: the implied equity risk premium (kind erp: level, cash_yield, growth, rf) and the narrative-to-numbers DCF (kind dcf: revenue, growth_high, margin_now, margin_target, sales_to_capital, wacc_start, wacc_mature, rf, p_fail...).

Technical analysis for one ticker: every indicator (moving averages, RSI, MACD, Bollinger, ATR, ADX, stochastic, Ichimoku, Supertrend, parabolic SAR, OBV, money flow), today's signals, support and resistance, Fibonacci, pivots, divergences, the trend template, relative strength, and an event study of each signal on the ticker's own history with false-discovery control.

A company's annual statements from its SEC filings, ratios (margins, ROIC, cash conversion, accruals, capex to depreciation, stock pay, leverage, growth and its acceleration, Rule of 40), Piotroski F, Altman Z'' and Beneish M scores, and flags.

The reinforcement-learning sizing agent (fitted Q iteration over trend, volatility, valuation and drawdown states): its out-of-sample record against holding and the trend rule, the deflated chance its edge is real, and today's exposure. Research only.

The decision engine for the MODEL book: today's stock exposure and hedge with the evidence gate that decides how far to trust the engine, regime probabilities (hidden Markov), changepoint odds, model-averaging weights, stacked forecasts including a neural-network ensemble, what drives and what would flip the decision, and its walk-forward record since 1940. Research only; never places orders.

The mind's verdict on every claim it weighs, computed at once by spreading all of them through the graph as one matrix: the odds each claim is true, its range, its number of signals and what it hinges on. With related: a node id, the nodes nearest it in the mind's 64-number spectral map instead.

The portfolio engine for the MODEL book: today's mix of stocks, 10-year Treasuries, gold and cash; the regimes of the three assets together with each one's stock-bond correlation; eight policies walked forward since 1940 and a learner over them; ten years simulated from today's regime odds; and today's mixes replayed through eight drawdowns. Research only; never places orders.

Every Treasury ETF (SHY, IEI, IEF, TLH, TLT, EDV, ZROZ) repriced bond by bond at a 10-year and 30-year yield you set, on today's Treasury par curve: price, instant change, 12-month total return with income and roll, and the break-even yield rise. Research only.

The chronicle: any month since 1871, any year, a named episode or 'months like now', with valuation, rates, inflation, drawdown, what the next 12 months returned and the most similar months in history.
Which data sources (Databento, Yahoo, Stooq, SEC, Treasury, CFTC, FRED, GitHub mirrors) and credentials the engine can reach.

What legendary and current investors actually said about a question or claim, arranged from extreme bear (-2) to extreme bull (+2): verbatim quotes with speaker, date and source link from a verified library. Never generates a quote.

The whole brain: every monthly series the engine reads (equities, rates, inflation, energy, metals, grains, softs, currencies, and in the daily run credit, activity and money), links learned by graphical lasso with stability selection and LiNGAM orientation, joined with the judged concepts and the holdings. Trace a shock month by month to any node, or read a node.

How far to trust the brain: out-of-sample coverage of its 90% error bars (textbook against adaptive conformal), the stacked weights on five rival world models, and each measured link's robustness value to an unseen common cause.
Run the TLT hedge policy hedge.tlt.v2 on a stock-bond correlation path and a 36-month inflation reading.

Score a candidate portfolio (equity, TLT hedge, put spread, gold) on the reasoner's seven 3-month scenarios: certainty-equivalent growth, worst case, the loss limit, regret against the alternatives, and the best portfolio on the grid.
Write a structured, hashed order PROPOSAL against the model book and check it against the limits. Never executes: a person reviews it and acts elsewhere.

Score one decision's process (logged before, sized by rule, kill respected, two sources) and its luck quadrant, or a whole journal export: calibration, hit rate, alpha after beta and the process-outcome grid.

Compare competing explanations of one observation by Bayes' rule and rank the unchecked evidence by how much doubt it would remove (bits). Use a field case (leadtime, pipeline, credit) or supply your own.

What the data says about the brain's own assumptions: the causal order learned by DirectLiNGAM against the assumed order, and each measured link's path over time (Kalman smoother): latest value, 90% band, drift and sign changes.

Reason over the brain (34 nodes, about 110 links): which root causes explain the readings, what that implies for each holding and the book, which link is most to blame for the misfit, what to observe next, and doing versus seeing a value.

nodes.t: A deterministic cash-flow model for illiquid funds: capital calls are a time-varying fraction of uncalled commitments, distributions a time-varying fraction of the fund's asset value, and returns are constant. nodes.t: Because passive investors hold the market and earn its return, active investors as a group must also earn the market return before costs. After their higher costs, the average actively managed dollar must therefore trail the average passively managed dollar. Contrary evidence reflects measurement errors.
nodes.source_title: The Arithmetic of Active Management (Financial Analysts Journal 47(1), 7-9)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Stanford reprint: Sharpe, FAJ 47(1) Jan/Feb 1991; arguments and 'improper measurement' match.

nodes.n: The Performance of Mutual Funds in the Period 1945-1964
nodes.t: Introduced Jensen's alpha, a CAPM-based measure of risk-adjusted performance. Across 115 funds from 1945 to 1964, funds on average could not beat a buy-and-hold strategy, even measured before management expenses, and few individual funds did better than chance would predict.
nodes.source_title: The Performance of Mutual Funds in the Period 1945-1964 (Journal of Finance 23(2), 389-416)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN abstract: derives CAPM-based risk-adjusted measure, 115 funds 1945-1964, gross of expenses, chance; Crossref JF 23(2) 1968 (SSRN lists 1967).

nodes.n: On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance
nodes.t: Using survivor-bias-free data, common factors in stock returns, including one-year momentum, plus fund expenses almost fully explain persistence in mutual fund returns. The only strong unexplained persistence is the underperformance of the worst funds, and the results do not support the existence of skilled or informed managers.
nodes.source_title: On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance (Journal of Finance 52(1), 57-82)
nodes.checked: corrected by a second checker: doi.org/Wiley page blocked; Crossref confirms Carhart, JF 52(1) 1997 and abstract; 'four-factor model became the standard benchmark' is not in the source.

nodes.n: Mutual Fund Flows and Performance in Rational Markets
nodes.t: A rational model in which skilled managers face decreasing returns to scale. Investors chase past performance, flows grow funds until expected excess returns vanish, so performance does not persist and average funds do not beat passive benchmarks, even though managers have real and varied skill.
nodes.source_title: Mutual Fund Flows and Performance in Rational Markets (Journal of Political Economy 112(6), 1269-1295)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: UChicago page and Crossref: Berk and Green, JPE 112(6) 2004; abstract consistent.

nodes.n: Luck versus Skill in the Cross-Section of Mutual Fund Returns
nodes.t: The aggregate portfolio of US equity mutual funds is close to the market portfolio, so high active costs show up as lower investor returns. Bootstrap simulations show few funds earn enough to cover costs; before expenses, the tails show some genuine skill, both good and bad.
nodes.source_title: Luck versus Skill in the Cross-Section of Mutual Fund Returns (Journal of Finance 65(5), 1915-1947)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN abstract matches; Crossref: JF 65(5) 2010.

nodes.t: Wilder's RSI is a 0 to 100 momentum oscillator: RSI = 100 - 100/(1 + RS), where RS is average gain over average loss, by default over 14 periods with Wilder smoothing. Wilder treated readings above 70 as overbought and below 30 as oversold.
nodes.source_title: Relative Strength Index (RSI)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: ChartSchool: RS = avg gain / avg loss, 14 periods, Wilder smoothing, 70/30, 1978 book.

nodes.t: True range is the largest of: today's high minus low, high minus prior close, or low minus prior close (absolute values). ATR, from Wilder (1978), averages true range over 14 periods, then smooths it as (prior ATR x 13 + current TR) / 14. It measures volatility, not direction, and is used for stop and position sizing.
nodes.source_title: Average True Range (ATR) and Average True Range Percent (ATRP)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: ChartSchool: three true range methods, Wilder 1978, 14 periods, (prior ATR x 13 + TR)/14, volatility not direction.

nodes.t: Wilder's directional movement system uses +DI and -DI (smoothed directional movement divided by smoothed true range) for direction, and ADX, a smoothed average of their normalized difference, for trend strength. Default is 14 periods. Wilder saw ADX above 25 as a strong trend and below 20 as no trend.
nodes.source_title: Average Directional Index (ADX)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: ChartSchool: +DI/-DI from smoothed DM over smoothed ATR, ADX from smoothed DX, 14 periods, above 25 strong and below 20 no trend.

nodes.t: MACD, invented by Gerald Appel in the late 1970s, is the 12-day EMA minus the 26-day EMA of closing prices. The signal line is a 9-day EMA of MACD, and the histogram is MACD minus signal. It turns two trend-following averages into a momentum oscillator.
nodes.source_title: MACD (Moving Average Convergence/Divergence Oscillator)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: ChartSchool: Appel, late seventies, 12-26 EMA, 9-day signal, histogram = MACD minus signal.

nodes.t: John Bollinger's bands are a moving average (default 20 periods) with upper and lower bands a multiple (default 2) of the population standard deviation away. They show whether price is high or low relative to recent volatility. Companion measures are %b (position within the bands) and BandWidth (band width relative to the middle band).
nodes.source_title: Bollinger Bands
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: bollingerbands.com: 20 periods, 2 standard deviations, population SD, %b and BandWidth described.

nodes.t: Faber's timing model holds an asset class when its month-end price is above its 10-month simple moving average and moves to cash otherwise, checked only on the last day of each month. Faber says the 10-month average corresponds most closely to the 200-day moving average.
nodes.source_title: Timing Model
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page confirms 10-month SMA, buy signals versus moving to cash, month-end-only updates, and 'corresponds closest to the 200 day moving average'. It does not spell out the rule in one sentence; the SSRN paper does. Page says the model was first published in 2006 (journal version 2007).

nodes.n: Cyclically adjusted P/E (CAPE, Shiller PE, PE10)
nodes.t: CAPE divides the index price by the average of the previous 10 years of inflation-adjusted earnings, smoothing the business cycle out of the denominator. It is also called the Shiller PE or PE 10. Multpl credits its data to Robert Shiller.
nodes.source_title: Shiller PE Ratio
nodes.checked: corrected by a second checker: 10-year inflation-adjusted earnings definition confirmed. The page does not mention Campbell and Shiller's findings or shillerdata.com, removed. The 1998 as_of date is not on this page.

nodes.t: The Fed model compares the stock market's earnings yield (inverse of P/E) with the nominal 10-year Treasury yield, calling stocks cheap when the earnings yield is higher. It came from an unnamed Fed report and has no official endorsement. Asness (2003) found it has no power to forecast long-term real stock returns.
nodes.source_title: Fight the Fed Model
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: AQR: earnings yield vs nominal rates, 'allegedly found in the annals of a Fed report', not officially endorsed, no power to forecast long-term real returns, 2003.

nodes.n: New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems
nodes.t: Wilder's 1978 book introduced the RSI, Average True Range and the directional movement system (ADX, +DI, -DI). Its 14-period defaults and smoothing method remain the standard settings in charting software.
nodes.source_title: New concepts in technical trading systems (library record)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Library record: Wilder, New concepts in technical trading systems, Trend Research, Greensboro N.C., 1978, 141 pp.

nodes.n: Technical Analysis: Power Tools for Active Investors
nodes.t: Appel's 2005 book presents trading models built on MACD, which he describes as an indicator he invented in the late 1970s. It is the creator's own account of how to construct and use MACD.
nodes.source_title: Technical Analysis: Power Tools for Active Investors
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: InformIT: Gerald Appel, FT Press, Mar 21, 2005. Intro says MACD is 'an indicator that I invented in the late 1970s'.

nodes.n: Simple Technical Trading Rules and the Stochastic Properties of Stock Returns
nodes.t: Testing moving-average and trading-range-break rules on the Dow Jones index from 1897 to 1986 with bootstrap methods, the authors found returns after buy signals exceeded returns after sell signals, which were negative. The patterns were inconsistent with random walk, AR(1), GARCH-M and EGARCH models.
nodes.source_title: Simple Technical Trading Rules and the Stochastic Properties of Stock Returns (IDEAS/RePEc record)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: RePEc: JF 47(5) 1731-1764, 1992. Abstract matches (DJIA 1897-1986, buy beats sell, sell returns negative, four null models).

nodes.n: Data-Snooping, Technical Trading Rule Performance, and the Bootstrap
nodes.t: Using White's Reality Check over a universe of 7,846 rules and 100 years of Dow data, the authors found the best rule beat the benchmark in 1897-1986 even after adjusting for data snooping. In 1987-1996, out of sample, there was scant evidence of value: the best rule was not statistically significant.
nodes.source_title: Data-Snooping, Technical Trading Rule Performance, and the Bootstrap (LSE FMG Discussion Paper 303)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: FMG DP303 (Oct 1998): 7,846 rules in body, 100 years of DJIA, scant evidence for 1987-1996. Crossref confirms JF 54(5) 1647-1691, 1999.

nodes.n: A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation
nodes.t: Faber proposed a simple month-end trend rule (hold an asset above its 10-month moving average, else cash) across asset classes. The 2013 update on SSRN, adding 2008-2012 data, reports the models performed well in real time, with equity-like returns and bond-like volatility and drawdowns.
nodes.source_title: A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation (SSRN, 2013 update)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN: Faber, Journal of Wealth Management Spring 2007; 2013 update adds 2008-2012 data, 'equity like returns with bond like volatility and drawdowns'.

nodes.n: Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers: Implications for Stock Market Efficiency
nodes.t: Strategies that buy past winners and sell past losers earned significant positive returns over 3 to 12 month holding periods, not explained by systematic risk or delayed reactions to common factors. Part of the first-year excess return reverses over the next two years. This is the founding cross-sectional momentum paper.
nodes.source_title: Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers (IDEAS/RePEc record)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: RePEc: JF 48(1) 65-91, 1993. Abstract matches (3-12 month holding periods, partial reversal over next two years).

nodes.t: Across 58 liquid equity index, currency, commodity and bond futures, an asset's own recent returns predict its future returns. Returns persist for 1 to 12 months then partly reverse. A diversified strategy earns large abnormal returns, has little exposure to standard factors, and does best in extreme markets.
nodes.source_title: Time Series Momentum (SSRN)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN abstract: 58 instruments, persistence 1 to 12 months then partial reversal, 'performs best during extreme markets'. Crossref confirms JFE 104(2) 228-250, 2012.

nodes.n: A Century of Evidence on Trend-Following Investing
nodes.t: Building a time-series momentum strategy across markets with data back to 1880, the authors find trend following was consistently profitable over roughly 110 years, across many economic conditions. They also examine how growth in strategy assets and higher cross-market correlations since the credit crisis affect results.
nodes.source_title: A Century of Evidence on Trend-Following Investing
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: AQR: JPM, Oct 31, 2017. Back to 1880, profitable 'over the next 110 years', covers rising assets and higher correlations since the credit crisis.

nodes.n: Foundations of Technical Analysis: Computational Algorithms, Statistical Inference, and Empirical Implementation
nodes.t: The authors automate chart-pattern recognition (such as head-and-shoulders and double bottoms) with nonparametric kernel regression and apply it to US stocks from 1962 to 1996. Several patterns shift the distribution of subsequent daily returns, suggesting technical patterns carry some incremental information.
nodes.source_title: Foundations of Technical Analysis (NBER Working Paper 7613)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER w7613 (Mar 2000), JF 55(4) 2000. Kernel regression, US stocks 1962-1996, incremental information.

nodes.n: What Do We Know About the Profitability of Technical Analysis?
nodes.t: Surveying the literature, the authors count 95 modern studies: 56 positive for technical trading profits, 20 negative and 19 mixed. Gains were stronger in currency and futures markets than in stocks. They warn that data snooping, ex post rule selection and risk and cost estimation weaken most results.
nodes.source_title: What Do We Know About The Profitability Of Technical Analysis? (IDEAS/RePEc record)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: RePEc: JES 21(4) 786-826, 2007. 95 modern studies: 56 positive, 20 negative, 19 mixed. Caveats match.

nodes.n: Stock Prices, Earnings and Expected Dividends
nodes.t: Using US data from 1871 to 1986, the authors find a long historical average of real earnings is a good predictor of the present value of future real dividends. Prices are too volatile for simple present value models, which implies long-horizon returns are forecastable. This is the root of the CAPE idea.
nodes.source_title: Stock Prices, Earnings and Expected Dividends (NBER Working Paper 2511)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER w2511, JF 43(3) 661-676 (July 1988). Abstract: US data 1871-1986, excess volatility implies forecastable long-horizon returns.

nodes.n: Valuation Ratios and the Long-Run Stock Market Outlook
nodes.t: Using US data from 1871 and 12 countries since 1970, the authors find P/E and dividend-price ratios do poorly at forecasting dividend, earnings or productivity growth and are mainly useful for forecasting future price changes, against simple efficient-markets models. Published in the Journal of Portfolio Management (1998), updated 2001 as NBER w8221.
nodes.source_title: Valuation Ratios and the Long-Run Stock Market Outlook: An Update (NBER Working Paper 8221)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER w8221 (Apr 2001) updates the 1998 JPM 24(2) paper. US data 1871-2000 plus 12 countries since 1970. Abstract matches.

nodes.n: Predicting Excess Stock Returns Out of Sample: Can Anything Beat the Historical Average?
nodes.t: Answering Goyal and Welch, the authors show that predictors with in-sample power, such as valuation ratios, beat the historical average out of sample once sensible restrictions are placed on coefficient signs and return forecasts. The gain is small but economically meaningful, and a true predictor can still underperform for long stretches.
nodes.source_title: Predicting the Equity Premium Out of Sample (NBER Working Paper 11468)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER w11468, RFS 21 (July 2008) 1509-1531. Abstract matches.

nodes.n: A Comprehensive Look at the Empirical Performance of Equity Premium Prediction
nodes.t: Testing dividend and earnings yields, interest rates and other popular predictors, the authors find many look useful in sample, but none would have beaten the historical average equity premium out of sample for a real-time investor, and most would have hurt. They conclude the equity premium has not been predictable in practice.
nodes.source_title: A Comprehensive Look at the Empirical Performance of Equity Premium Prediction (NBER Working Paper 10483)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER w10483 (May 2004), RFS 21(4) 1455-1508, 2008. Abstract matches. NBER page misspells the name as 'Goval'.

nodes.n: Dividend Yields and Expected Stock Returns
nodes.t: The forecasting power of dividend yields rises with the horizon: regressions on D/P explain under 5% of monthly or quarterly return variance but often more than 25% of two- to four-year return variance. The authors attribute this to slowly moving, time-varying expected returns that create temporary price components.
nodes.unit: percent of 2-4 year return variance (often more than)
nodes.source_title: Dividend Yields and Expected Stock Returns (paper PDF hosted by John Cochrane)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Paper PDF (Cochrane link redirects to squarespace): JFE 22, 3-25, 1988. Intro: under 5% for monthly or quarterly returns, often more than 25% for 2- to 4-year returns.

nodes.t: Asness argues the Fed model, which compares the earnings yield with nominal Treasury yields, is intuitive but empirically wrong: it has no power to forecast long-term real stock returns, while the plain P/E has worked well. He suggests its popularity comes from simplicity, flexibility and usually bullish readings.
nodes.source_title: Fight the Fed Model
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: AQR: Asness, JPM 2003. No forecasting power for the Fed model; 'unadjusted P/E alone, have been very effective'; popularity explained by simplicity, flexibility and bullish readings.

nodes.n: Warren Buffett on the Stock Market
nodes.t: In this Fortune essay Buffett called total market value relative to GNP probably the best single measure of where valuations stand. He said buying stocks is likely to work very well if the ratio falls to 70% or 80%, and that approaching 200%, as in 1999-2000, is playing with fire.

nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Wikipedia: Fortune, Dec 10, 2001, with Carol Loomis, GNP based. Quotes on 'best single measure', 70% or 80%, and approaching 200% in 1999 and 2000 confirmed. Secondary source.

nodes.t: EIA describes backwardation as a market condition in which a barrel of crude oil now is more valuable than a barrel delivered later. EIA uses this framing for Brent in 2026, when the Hormuz closure pushed Dated Brent far above front-month futures.

nodes.t: Arbitrage limits how far a futures price can sit above spot: no more than the cost of carry, meaning financing, storage and insurance for holding the physical good. No matching limit applies below spot, which is why steep backwardation can occur when inventories are scarce.

nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: GR w10595 Appendix 2: futures cannot exceed spot by more than cost of carry, with no matching bound below. The appendix defines carry as storage plus interest; insurance appears only in Section 4. Minor.

nodes.n: Carry (as defined by Koijen et al.)
nodes.t: Koijen and co-authors split a security's expected return into its carry and its expected price appreciation. Carry is the return earned if prices stay unchanged, and it can be measured in advance without an asset pricing model.

nodes.n: A Treatise on Money, Volume 2: The Applied Theory of Money
nodes.t: Keynes proposed normal backwardation: hedgers, mainly producers, pay speculators to bear price risk, so futures prices sit below the expected future spot price and long futures holders earn a risk premium over time. Gorton and Rouwenhorst describe their findings as consistent with this theory.
nodes.source_title: A Treatise on Money (Collected Writings of John Maynard Keynes, vols 5 and 6)

nodes.t: Kaldor introduced the idea of convenience yield: holding physical stocks gives the holder a benefit, such as avoiding production stoppages, that rises when inventories are scarce. This explains why spot prices can exceed futures prices (backwardation) even though storage is costly.
nodes.source_title: Speculation and Economic Stability
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: JSTOR metadata: Speculation and Economic Stability, Kaldor, Review of Economic Studies 7(1), Oct 1939.

nodes.n: The Theory of Price of Storage
nodes.t: Working showed that the spread between futures and spot prices acts as a price paid for storage, and that it depends on the level of inventories. With ample stocks, futures trade at a premium near full carrying cost; with scarce stocks, the spread turns negative. Published in the American Economic Review 39, pp. 1254 to 1262.
nodes.source_title: The Theory of Price of Storage (JSTOR)

Published in Financial Analysts Journal 62(2), pp. 47 to 68.

nodes.t: Erb and Harvey find individual commodity futures have had average excess returns near zero and low correlations with each other, but a rebalanced portfolio can earn equity-like excess returns, partly from rebalancing. Term structure and momentum strategies can add return. Commodities diversify stocks and bonds but are a questionable inflation hedge. FAJ 62(2), pp. 69 to 97.

nodes.t: The authors define carry as the expected return if prices stay unchanged and show it predicts returns across and within global equities, bonds, currencies, commodities, Treasuries, credit and index options. nodes.n: Causes and Consequences of the Oil Shock of 2007-08
nodes.t: Hamilton finds the 2007-08 oil price run-up was caused by strong demand meeting stagnant world production, unlike earlier shocks driven by physical supply disruptions. Its effects, especially lower consumer spending and domestic auto purchases, resembled earlier shocks, and he argues oil contributed to the 2007 to 2008 US recession. Brookings Papers, Spring 2009.

nodes.n: Not All Oil Price Shocks Are Alike: Disentangling Demand and Supply Shocks in the Crude Oil Market
nodes.t: Kilian separates oil price shocks into crude supply shocks, global demand shocks for industrial commodities, and oil-specific demand shocks, each with different effects on oil prices and the US economy. Shifts in that mix explain unstable oil-macro regressions; the 2000s surge was mainly global demand. AER 99(3), pp. 1053 to 1069.

nodes.n: A New Interpretation of Information Rate
nodes.t: Shows that a gambler with a noisy private wire who bets to maximize the long-run exponential growth rate of capital can grow wealth at a maximum rate equal to the channel's information transmission rate (for fair odds). The origin of the Kelly criterion: bet to maximize expected log wealth.

nodes.n: The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market
nodes.t: Thorp explains that winning requires both positive-expectation bets and correct sizing, and that Kelly sizing maximizes expected log wealth (the growth-optimal strategy). He recounts applying it to blackjack card counting, a sports betting system and securities investing. Chapter 9 of the Handbook of Asset and Liability Management (Elsevier, 2006), first presented in 1997.

nodes.n: Fractional Kelly, overbetting and risk of ruin
nodes.t: Betting c times the Kelly fraction yields c(2 minus c) of the maximum growth rate: half Kelly keeps about 75% of growth with far smaller drawdowns, twice Kelly yields zero long-run growth, and beyond a critical fraction ruin is almost sure. Thorp advises fractional Kelly when edge estimates are uncertain.

nodes.t: Sets out an axiomatic solution to two-person bargaining: under a small set of reasonableness axioms, the agreed outcome is the one that maximizes the product of the two parties' utility gains over their disagreement point. The foundation of cooperative bargaining theory.

nodes.n: Perfect Equilibrium in a Bargaining Model
nodes.t: Models bargaining as alternating offers over an infinite horizon with costly delay. Shows there is a unique subgame perfect equilibrium in which agreement is immediate and the split depends on the parties' patience: the more patient side gets more.

nodes.t: Roger Fisher and William Ury published Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In in 1981 (Boston: Houghton Mifflin), based on the work of the Harvard Negotiation Project. nodes.n: BATNA: best alternative to a negotiated agreement
nodes.t: A BATNA is a negotiator's best alternative to a negotiated agreement, that is, what you will do if no deal is reached. It sets whether to accept an offer, how much leverage you hold and when to walk away. The concept comes from Fisher, Ury and Patton's Getting to Yes.

nodes.n: The Art and Science of Negotiation (Raiffa, 1982)
nodes.t: Howard Raiffa's book (Harvard University Press, 1982) applies game theory, decision making under uncertainty and fair division to practical negotiation, from selling a house to international agreements, using cases and diagrams. It won the 1985 Leo Melamed Prize.

nodes.checked: corrected by a second checker: PON page lists Harvard University Press, not Belknap Press; examples run to international agreements; 1985 Leo Melamed Prize confirmed.

nodes.n: First offers as anchors: The role of perspective-taking and negotiator focus
nodes.t: Across three experiments, whichever side made the first offer, buyer or seller, got a better outcome, and first offers strongly predicted final prices. The advantage disappeared when the other side focused on information contradicting the anchor: the opponent's alternatives, the opponent's reservation price, or one's own target.
nodes.source_title: First offers as anchors: The role of perspective-taking and negotiator focus
nodes.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 81(4), 657-669
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref and Semantic Scholar confirm authors, JPSP 81(4) 657-669, 2001; abstract withheld by publisher everywhere tried, content matches the paper's known findings.

nodes.n: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
nodes.t: Describes three heuristics people use under uncertainty: representativeness, availability, and adjustment from an anchor. They are efficient but cause systematic, predictable errors; with anchoring, numerical estimates stay biased toward the starting value.
nodes.source_title: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref confirms Science 185(4157) 1124-1131, 1974; abstract names the three heuristics, economical and usually effective but cause systematic errors.

nodes.n: Race and Gender Discrimination in Bargaining for a New Car
nodes.t: More than 300 paired audits at new-car dealerships, with testers using identical scripted bargaining, found dealers quoted white men lower prices than Black or female buyers. Dealers may be guessing buyers' reservation prices, though the data do not strongly support any single theory of discrimination.
nodes.source_title: Race and Gender Discrimination in Bargaining for a New Car
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: RePEc: AER 85(3) 304-321, June 1995; more than 300 paired audits, scripted strategies, lower prices to white males, reservation-price inference, no single theory strongly supported.

nodes.n: Gender differences in bargaining outcomes: A field experiment on discrimination
nodes.t: In Lima's taxi market, where fares are haggled, male passengers using a fixed script faced higher starting prices, higher final prices and more rejections than women. When passengers signaled their valuation first, the gap vanished, consistent with statistical rather than taste-based discrimination.
nodes.source_title: Gender differences in bargaining outcomes: A field experiment on discrimination
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref/RePEc confirm four authors, JPubE 99 35-48, 2013; abstract supports Lima taxis, higher prices and rejections for men, signaling removes gap, statistical discrimination.

nodes.n: The Upstairs Market for Large-Block Transactions: Analysis and Measurement of Price Effects
nodes.t: Studies 5,625 negotiated upstairs block trades (1985 to 1992). Prices move significantly in the trade's direction before the block prints, more so for larger blocks, consistent with information leaking while the block is shopped to counterparties. Temporary price impact rises with size at a decreasing rate.
nodes.source_title: The Upstairs Market for Large-Block Transactions: Analysis and Measurement of Price Effects
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: RePEc: RFS 9(1) 1-36, 1996; 5,625 upstairs trades 1985-1992, pre-trade price moves rise with size (leakage), concave temporary impact.

nodes.n: A Simple, Positive Semi-Definite, Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent Covariance Matrix
nodes.t: Gives a simple covariance estimator that stays valid when regression errors are heteroskedastic and autocorrelated, is positive semi-definite by construction, and is consistent under fairly general conditions. The standard fix for t-statistics on overlapping or serially correlated return data.
nodes.source_title: A Simple, Positive Semi-Definite, Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent Covariance Matrix
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref/RePEc: Econometrica 55(3) 703-708, May 1987; abstract: simple, PSD by construction, consistent under fairly general conditions.

nodes.n: Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife
nodes.t: Introduces the bootstrap: estimate the sampling distribution of a statistic by repeatedly resampling the observed data with replacement and recomputing it, presented as a more general alternative to the jackknife.
nodes.source_title: Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref confirms Efron, Annals of Statistics 7(1), 1979 (pages not in record); no abstract served, content is the paper's standard contribution.

nodes.t: Proposes a bootstrap for dependent time series that resamples blocks of random, geometrically distributed length, so the resampled series is itself stationary. Widely used to bootstrap returns and Sharpe ratios while keeping autocorrelation.
nodes.source_title: The Stationary Bootstrap
nodes.publisher: Journal of the American Statistical Association, 89(428), 1303-1313
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref confirms JASA 89(428) 1303-1313, Dec 1994; no abstract served, content matches the known method.

nodes.n: A New Approach to the Economic Analysis of Nonstationary Time Series and the Business Cycle
nodes.t: Models a series whose growth rate shifts between unobserved regimes (Markov switching), with filtering algorithms to infer the regime and maximum likelihood estimation. On US GNP it identifies recessions objectively and finds a typical recession brings a permanent 3% drop in the level of GNP.
nodes.source_title: A New Approach to the Economic Analysis of Nonstationary Time Series and the Business Cycle
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref/RePEc: Econometrica 57(2) 357-384, March 1989; abstract includes discrete regime shifts, ML estimation, objective recession dating, 3 percent permanent drop in GNP.

nodes.n: Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity with Estimates of the Variance of United Kingdom Inflation
nodes.t: Introduces ARCH, in which the conditional variance of a series depends on past squared shocks, so volatility clusters. Applied to UK inflation.
nodes.source_title: Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity with Estimates of the Variance of United Kingdom Inflation
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref/RePEc: Econometrica 50(4) 987-1007, July 1982; no abstract served, content is the paper's standard contribution.

nodes.t: Generalizes ARCH so the conditional variance also depends on its own past values (GARCH), giving a parsimonious model of persistent volatility. GARCH(1,1) became the workhorse for forecasting return volatility and risk.
nodes.source_title: Generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref: Journal of Econometrics 31(3) 307-327, 1986; no abstract served, content is the standard result.

nodes.n: Co-Integration and Error Correction: Representation, Estimation, and Testing
nodes.t: Defines cointegration: nonstationary series whose linear combination is stationary. Proves a representation theorem linking cointegration to error correction models, proposes a two-step estimator and tests for cointegration. The basis of pairs trading and spread models.
nodes.source_title: Co-Integration and Error Correction: Representation, Estimation, and Testing
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref/RePEc: Econometrica 55(2) 251-276, 1987; abstract: cointegration definition, representation theorem, two-step estimator, tests.

nodes.n: Distribution of the Estimators for Autoregressive Time Series with a Unit Root
nodes.t: Derives the nonstandard distribution of the least squares autoregressive estimator when the series has a unit root, giving the critical values behind the Dickey-Fuller unit root test used to check whether prices or spreads are stationary.
nodes.source_title: Distribution of the Estimators for Autoregressive Time Series with a Unit Root
nodes.publisher: Journal of the American Statistical Association, 74(366a), 427-431
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref: JASA 74(366a) 427-431, June 1979; no abstract served, content is the standard result.

nodes.n: Stock Market Prices Do Not Follow Random Walks: Evidence from a Simple Specification Test
nodes.t: Introduces the variance ratio test, comparing return variances at different sampling frequencies. The random walk is strongly rejected for weekly US stock returns from 1962 to 1985, largely driven by small stocks and not explained by infrequent trading or time-varying volatility.
nodes.source_title: Stock Market Prices Do Not Follow Random Walks: Evidence from a Simple Specification Test
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref/RePEc: RFS 1(1) 41-66, 1988; NBER w2168 abstract: variance ratios, weekly returns 1962-1985 reject random walk, driven by small stocks, not infrequent trading or time-varying volatility.

nodes.n: ... and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
nodes.t: Hundreds of claimed return factors make the usual t-ratio above 2.0 meaningless. Using a multiple testing framework, the authors argue a newly discovered factor should clear a t-ratio above 3.0, and that most claimed findings in financial economics are likely false.
nodes.source_title: ... and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref: RFS 29(1) 5-68, 2016; NBER w20592 (Oct 2014) abstract: t-ratio 2.0 inadequate, hurdle above 3.0, most findings likely false.

nodes.n: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting and Non-Normality
nodes.t: Introduces the Deflated Sharpe Ratio, which corrects a backtest's Sharpe ratio for the number of strategies tried (selection bias) and for non-normal returns, to separate real findings from statistical flukes.
nodes.source_title: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting and Non-Normality
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN: Bailey and Lopez de Prado, JPM 40(5) 94-107, 2014; abstract supports correction for selection bias and non-normality.

nodes.n: Controlling the False Discovery Rate: A Practical and Powerful Approach to Multiple Testing
nodes.t: Proposes controlling the false discovery rate, the expected share of rejected hypotheses that are false, instead of the familywise error rate. A simple step-up procedure controls it for independent tests and gives substantially more power.
nodes.source_title: Controlling the False Discovery Rate: A Practical and Powerful Approach to Multiple Testing
nodes.publisher: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 57(1), 289-300
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref: JRSS B 57(1) 289-300, 1995; no abstract served, content is the standard result.

nodes.t: Combines subsampling with high-dimensional selection methods such as the lasso, keeping variables chosen consistently across subsamples. Gives finite-sample control of false discoveries and a principled way to set regularization.
nodes.source_title: Stability Selection
nodes.publisher: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 72(4), 417-473
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref: JRSS B 72(4) 417-473, 2010; abstract: subsampling plus selection, finite-sample control of false discoveries, choosing regularization.

nodes.n: Sparse inverse covariance estimation with the graphical lasso
nodes.t: Estimates a sparse inverse covariance matrix by applying a lasso penalty, using fast coordinate descent. Solves a 1,000-node problem in about a minute, 30 to 4,000 times faster than competing methods. Used to build sparse networks of asset dependence.
nodes.source_title: Sparse inverse covariance estimation with the graphical lasso
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref: Biostatistics 9(3) 432-441, 2008; abstract: 1000-node problem in at most a minute, 30-4000 times faster.

nodes.n: Better to give than to receive: Predictive directional measurement of volatility spillovers
nodes.t: Measures total and directional volatility spillovers using order-invariant generalized VAR variance decompositions. On US stocks, bonds, FX and commodities (1999 to 2010), cross-market spillovers were limited until the 2007 crisis, then surged, especially from stocks after Lehman's collapse.
nodes.source_title: Better to give than to receive: Predictive directional measurement of volatility spillovers
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref/RePEc: IJF 28(1) 57-66, 2012; abstract: order-invariant generalized VAR, four US markets Jan 1999-Jan 2010, limited spillovers until 2007 crisis, stock spillovers after Lehman.

nodes.n: Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift
nodes.t: Builds online prediction sets around any black-box forecaster that keep the target coverage rate over long periods even when the data distribution shifts, by continually re-estimating a single coverage parameter. Suited to forecast intervals in nonstationary markets.
nodes.source_title: Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift
nodes.publisher: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (NeurIPS 2021)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NeurIPS page: Gibbs and Candes, NeurIPS 34 (2021); abstract: online prediction sets around any black-box predictor, single re-estimated parameter, long-run coverage under shift.

nodes.n: A Linear Non-Gaussian Acyclic Model for Causal Discovery
nodes.t: Shows that the full causal ordering of continuous variables can be recovered from observational data when relations are linear, there are no hidden confounders and disturbances are non-Gaussian, using independent component analysis with no prior variable ordering (LiNGAM).
nodes.source_title: A Linear Non-Gaussian Acyclic Model for Causal Discovery
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: JMLR page: four authors, JMLR 7 2003-2030, 2006; abstract: linear, no hidden confounders, non-Gaussian disturbances, ICA, no prior ordering.

nodes.t: Builds a model with one informed insider, random noise traders and competitive market makers. The insider trades gradually, hiding behind noise trades, and earns profits; prices follow a random walk, market depth is constant over time, and all private information is in prices by the end of trading.
nodes.source_title: Continuous Auctions and Insider Trading, Econometrica 53(6): 1315-1335
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Econometric Society page: Kyle, Econometrica 53(6) 1315-1336, Nov 1985; abstract: one insider, noise traders, market makers, Brownian prices, constant depth, all information in prices by end.

nodes.n: Bid, Ask and Transaction Prices in a Specialist Market with Heterogeneously Informed Traders
nodes.t: Shows that a bid-ask spread can arise purely from adverse selection: a zero-profit dealer widens quotes to recover losses to informed traders from uninformed ones. Trade prices form a martingale, information leaks into prices trade by trade, and if informed trading is too heavy the market can shut down.
nodes.source_title: Journal of Financial Economics 14(1): 71-100
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref/RePEc: JFE 14(1) 71-100, March 1985, Glosten and Milgrom; no abstract available anywhere tried, content matches the paper's known result.

nodes.t: Treats liquidating a large position as a trade-off between market impact cost (trading fast) and price risk (trading slow). Derives an efficient frontier of execution schedules under linear temporary and permanent impact, shows an even-slice schedule is never optimal for a risk-averse trader, and defines liquidity-adjusted VaR.
nodes.source_title: Journal of Risk 3(2): 5-39
nodes.checked: corrected by a second checker: Crossref confirms Almgren and Chriss, Journal of Risk 3(2) 5-39, 2001; 'draft dated December 2000' not verifiable (author PDF unreachable), removed; abstract not served, content matches known paper.

nodes.n: Anomalous Price Impact and the Critical Nature of Liquidity in Financial Markets
nodes.t: Proposes a theory in which the average supply and demand profile is V-shaped and nearly vanishes at the current price. This forces large orders to be split, explaining long memory in order signs, and makes price impact grow roughly with the square root of order size rather than linearly: the square-root impact law.
nodes.source_title: Physical Review X 1, 021006 (arXiv:1105.1694)
nodes.authors: Toth, Lemperiere, Deremble, de Lataillade, Kockelkoren, Bouchaud
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: arXiv: six authors, May 2011, Physical Review X 1, 021006 (2011); abstract: V-shaped profile vanishing at price, metaorder splitting, long memory, square-root impact.

nodes.t: A review of how price impact is measured and modeled. Signed order flow and price changes are strongly linked, but the impact of trades is neither linear in volume nor permanent. Impact is how private information enters prices, and random order-flow fluctuations also add to volatility.
nodes.source_title: Price Impact (arXiv:0903.2428), review chapter
nodes.checked: corrected by a second checker: arXiv page (March 13 2009) shows no Encyclopedia of Quantitative Finance reference; abstract content confirmed.

nodes.n: On the Impossibility of Informationally Efficient Markets
nodes.t: If gathering information is costly, prices cannot fully reflect it, or no one would be paid to gather it. Equilibrium needs an 'equilibrium degree of disequilibrium' where prices are partly informative and informed traders earn a return on research. Noise is needed for trade; perfectly efficient markets would be thin.
nodes.source_title: American Economic Review 70(3): 393-408
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: AEA PDF: AER 70(3) 393-408, June 1980; 'equilibrium degree of disequilibrium' present; noise needed; informative markets very thin.

nodes.t: Argues that noise, in the sense of a large number of small events, makes trading in financial markets possible and lets us observe prices. It also makes markets somewhat inefficient while often stopping anyone from exploiting the inefficiency, and makes theories about markets very hard to test.
nodes.source_title: The Journal of Finance 41(3): 528-543
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref: Black, JF 41(3) 528-543, July 1986; abstract: noise makes trading possible, somewhat inefficient, hard to test theories.

nodes.n: Noise Trader Risk in Financial Markets
nodes.t: Models irrational noise traders whose unpredictable beliefs move prices. Because those beliefs are unpredictable, rational arbitrageurs face risk and cannot bet aggressively against them, so prices can stay far from fundamentals and noise traders can even earn higher expected returns. Helps explain excess volatility and closed-end fund discounts.
nodes.source_title: Journal of Political Economy 98: 703-738
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: RePEc: JPE 98(4) 703-738, 1990, four authors; abstract: unpredictable noise traders move prices, arbitrageurs limited, noise traders can earn higher returns, explains anomalies (Crossref fetch failed).

nodes.t: Real-world arbitrage takes capital and carries risk, and is done by a small number of specialists using other people's money. As a result arbitrage can fail in extreme situations, when prices move far from fundamentals, and the model predicts where anomalies are likely to persist.
nodes.source_title: The Journal of Finance 52(1): 35-55
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref: JF 52(1) 35-55, March 1997; abstract: capital and risk, few specialists using others' money, ineffective in extremes, where anomalies persist.

nodes.n: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk
nodes.t: Shows that people's choices under risk violate expected utility. People value gains and losses relative to a reference point, with a value function concave for gains, convex for losses and steeper for losses (loss aversion). They underweight probable outcomes versus certain ones and overweight small probabilities.
nodes.source_title: Econometrica 47(2): 263-292
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Econometric Society page: Econometrica 47(2) 263-292, 1979; abstract: critique of EU, certainty effect, value function concave gains, convex losses, steeper for losses, low probabilities overweighted.

nodes.n: Taleb (2019), How much data do you need? A pre-asymptotic metric for fat-tailedness
nodes.t: Proposes kappa, a measure scaled from 0 (Gaussian, thinnest) to 1 (maximally fat-tailed), based on how fast the law of large numbers works for sums of n terms. Meant to tell how many observations are needed and to compare distribution classes where kurtosis or tail index fail. International Journal of Forecasting 35(2), 677-686, April 2019.
nodes.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? An Operational, Pre-Asymptotic Metric for Fat-tailedness (arXiv 1802.05495; DOI 10.1016/j.ijforecast.2018.10.003)
nodes.publisher: International Journal of Forecasting (Elsevier); preprint on arXiv
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: arXiv abstract matches; Crossref: IJF 35(2) 677-686, April 2019, sole author Taleb.

nodes.t: With S_n the sum of n i.i.d. draws and M(n) = E|S_n - E(S_n)| (mean absolute deviation of the sum), kappa(n0, n) = 2 - [log(n) - log(n0)] / log[M(n)/M(n0)]. Equivalently M(n)/M(n0) = (n/n0)^(1/(2-kappa)). Shorthand kappa_n0 uses n = n0 + 1; kappa_1 compares one draw with two.
nodes.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? (arXiv 1802.05495v3, Definition 1 and Eq. 1)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Eq. 1 and M(n)/M(n0)=(n/n0)^(1/(2-kappa)) match; kappa_n0 = kappa(n0, n0+1).

nodes.t: The paper states kappa equals 0 for the Gaussian: the mean absolute deviation of a sum grows with the square root of n, the fastest convergence. For stable laws with tail exponent alpha at least 1, kappa = 2 - alpha.
nodes.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? (arXiv 1802.05495v3)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Paper: kappa=0 for Gaussian; kappa=2-alpha for stable with alpha>=1.

nodes.t: From the paper's stable-law relation kappa = 2 - alpha, the Cauchy (stable alpha = 1) has kappa = 1, the maximum: averaging more Cauchy draws does not shrink dispersion at all, so no sample is large enough. The paper also notes a high-sigma lognormal behaves like a one-tailed Cauchy, kappa near 1.
nodes.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? (arXiv 1802.05495v3)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Cauchy value is derived from kappa=2-alpha as the item says (paper gives no explicit Cauchy row); lognormal high-sigma 'one-tailed Cauchy', kappa near 1 confirmed.

nodes.n: Kappa for Student T with alpha 3 (a common fit for equity returns)
nodes.t: Table II gives Student T alpha = 3: kappa_1 = 0.29, kappa_1,30 = 0.191, kappa_1,100 = 0.159. Pareto alpha = 3 is fatter: 0.465, 0.3246, 0.281. The exponential has kappa_1 of about 0.21. Values between 0 and 1 rank how much extra data a distribution needs relative to a Gaussian.
nodes.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? (arXiv 1802.05495v3, Tables I and II)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Table II: Student alpha=3 0.29/0.191/0.159; Pareto 0.465/0.3246/0.281; exponential kappa_1 ~ .21 in Table I.

nodes.n: Taleb and Douady (2013), Mathematical definition, mapping, and detection of (anti)fragility
nodes.t: Defines fragility and antifragility as negative or positive sensitivity to a semi-measure of dispersion and volatility (a 'vega'), model-free and applicable to any payoff with a distribution. Proposes a simple detection heuristic said to reveal hidden risks from size, forecasting and bank tail exposures. Quantitative Finance 13(11), 1677-1689, November 2013.
nodes.source_title: Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility (arXiv 1208.1189; DOI 10.1080/14697688.2013.800219)
nodes.publisher: Quantitative Finance (Taylor and Francis); preprint on arXiv
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: arXiv abstract matches (vega, model-free heuristic, size/forecasting/bank hidden risks); Crossref: Quant Finance 13(11) 1677-1689, Nov 2013.

nodes.t: Fragility is the sensitivity of the left-tail shortfall below a threshold K (the integral of (x - Omega) f(x) from minus infinity to K, not conditioned on probability) to a change in the left semi-deviation of the distribution; an engine can estimate it by bumping volatility and measuring how much expected tail loss grows.
nodes.source_title: Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility (arXiv 1208.1189v1)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PDF defines fragility as sensitivity of unconditional left-tail shortfall xi(K,s-) = integral (x-Omega) f(x) to left semi-deviation.

nodes.t: Their heuristic measures how a valuation or payoff responds to finite shifts of each parameter up and down by a step delta, and compares the two changes as a second-order (convexity) test: losses that accelerate with larger shocks signal fragility. The paper claims this beats stress testing and Value-at-Risk at revealing hidden tail exposure.
nodes.source_title: Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility (arXiv 1208.1189)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PDF heuristic: finite shifts Delta p, second-order ratio H vs 1; abstract says it outperforms stress testing and VaR.

nodes.n: Taleb, Statistical Consequences of Fat Tails (Technical Incerto Vol. 1, 3rd ed.)
nodes.t: Free monograph on why standard statistics (sample means, empirical distributions, PCA, inequality measures) fail under fat tails, built from his journal articles; argues the real world sits in 'medium numbers' between one observation and the asymptote. Third revised edition posted on arXiv September 17, 2025 (v4).

nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Title, Third Revised Edition 2025, v4 dated Sep 17, 2025, abstract points match. Print publisher STEM Academic Press not shown on arXiv page (not material).

nodes.t: Taleb separates ensemble probability (outcomes across many people at once) from time probability (one person repeating a bet). With any chance of ruin these diverge: a repeated bet with ruin risk reaches eventual bust with 100% probability, so average-of-population returns do not apply to the individual and cost-benefit analysis breaks down. Survival comes first.

nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Essay dated Aug 25, 2017 defines ensemble vs time probability, 100% probability of eventually going bust, 'you must first survive'.

nodes.t: Damodaran's method ties every valuation input to a story and every story to an input. nodes.n: McLean and Pontiff (2016): academic research and the decay of return predictors
nodes.t: Studies 97 published cross-sectional return predictors. Journal of Finance 71(1), pages 5 to 32, February 2016. Concludes that investors learn about mispricing from academic publications, so published anomalies shrink after they become known.
nodes.source_title: Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability? (SSRN abstract)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref: JF 71(1) 5-32, Feb 2016 print; abstract gives 97 predictors and investors learn about mispricing. Substance also confirmed on SSRN 2156623. DOI link: https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12365

nodes.t: Across 97 published predictors, long-short portfolio returns are 26% lower in the out-of-sample period (after the original sample ends, before publication). The authors treat this as an upper bound on the data-mining effect.
nodes.source_title: Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability? (SSRN abstract)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN abstract: 97 variables, 26% lower out-of-sample; 'out-of-sample decline is an upper bound estimate of data mining effects.'

nodes.n: Anomaly returns are 58% lower after publication
nodes.t: Predictor portfolio returns are 58% lower after academic publication. The gap over the 26% out-of-sample decline implies about a 32% further drop attributable to publication-informed trading. Declines are larger for predictors with higher in-sample returns.
nodes.source_title: Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability? (SSRN abstract)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN abstract: 58% lower post-publication, 32% attributed to publication-informed trading, larger declines for higher in-sample returns.

nodes.n: Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016): ...and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
nodes.t: Argues that with hundreds of tested factors, the usual t-ratio of 2.0 is far too lenient and that "most claimed research findings in financial economics are likely false." Review of Financial Studies 29(1), pages 5 to 68, 2016 (NBER w20592, 2014).
nodes.source_title: ...and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns (NBER Working Paper 20592)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER page: quote verbatim in abstract, t-ratio 2.0 cited; RFS 29(1) 5-68, 2016; w20592 issued Oct 2014.

nodes.t: Harvey, Liu and Zhu write "We catalogue 316 different factors" proposed to explain the cross-section of returns. Testing that many candidates on the same data makes some false positives nearly certain unless significance thresholds rise.
nodes.source_title: ...and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns (NBER w20592 full text)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PDF contains 'We catalogue 316 different factors.' Dated October 2014.

nodes.n: New factors should clear a t-ratio above 3.0
nodes.t: Accounting for multiple testing, the authors estimate a newly discovered factor needs a t-ratio greater than 3.0, versus the conventional 2.0. An engine can treat a backtest t-statistic between 2 and 3 as weak evidence.
nodes.source_title: ...and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns (NBER Working Paper 20592)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract: new factor needs 'a t-ratio greater than 3.0' versus usual 2.0. Last sentence is editorial.

nodes.n: Harvey and Liu (2015): Backtesting and the haircut Sharpe ratio
nodes.t: Provides a multiple-testing framework to compute the appropriate haircut for any reported backtest Sharpe ratio, given how many strategies were tried, plus a profit hurdle a strategy must clear to count as significant. Journal of Portfolio Management, Fall 2015.
nodes.source_title: Backtesting (SSRN abstract)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN abstract supports haircut framework and profit hurdle. SSRN page lists no journal; JPM Fall 2015 confirmed on the Duke author copy.

nodes.n: The flat 50% Sharpe haircut is a rule of thumb, and a mistake
nodes.t: Practitioners commonly discount backtest Sharpe ratios by 50%. Harvey and Liu write "it is a serious mistake to use the usual 50% haircut" because the right haircut depends on the number of tests and the Sharpe level.
nodes.source_title: Backtesting (Journal of Portfolio Management, Fall 2015)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Duke PDF: 'We argue that it is a serious mistake to use the usual 50% haircut.' JPM Fall 2015.

nodes.n: Haircuts are nonlinear: at most 25% when Sharpe exceeds 1.0
nodes.t: The multiple-testing haircut is nonlinear: the highest Sharpe ratios are only moderately penalized while marginal ones are heavily penalized. In their examples the haircut is at most 25% when the Sharpe ratio exceeds 1.0, but nearly 50% for a weak E/P strategy with 50 trials.
nodes.unit: percent maximum haircut for Sharpe above 1.0
nodes.source_title: Backtesting (Journal of Portfolio Management, Fall 2015)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PDF: haircut nonlinear; 'when the Sharpe ratio is greater than 1.0, the haircut is at most 25%'; 'almost 50%' for least profitable E/P strategy at 50 trials.

nodes.n: Sharpe 0.75 cut to 0.32 after 200 tests (about 60% haircut)
nodes.t: Worked example: an annual Sharpe ratio of 0.75 has a single-test p-value of 0.0008, but with 200 tests the adjusted p-value is 0.15, implying an adjusted Sharpe of 0.32, a reduction of roughly 60%.
nodes.source_title: Backtesting (Journal of Portfolio Management, Fall 2015)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PDF: SR 0.75, p 0.0008, N=200 gives pM=0.15, adjusted SR 0.32, reduction approximately 60%.

nodes.n: Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado and Zhu: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting
nodes.t: Argues hold-out samples are unreliable safeguards for investment backtests and proposes estimating the probability of backtest overfitting (PBO) with combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV), which tests whether the in-sample best configuration ranks poorly out-of-sample. Journal of Computational Finance, 2015.
nodes.source_title: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting (SSRN abstract)
nodes.authors: Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, Zhu
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN abstract: hold-out unreliable for investment backtests, PBO via CSCV; Journal of Computational Finance 2015 (forthcoming). The 'ranks poorly out-of-sample' gloss is not in the abstract but describes the method fairly.

nodes.n: Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism (Notices of the AMS, 2014)
nodes.t: Shows that testing a relatively small number of strategy configurations can produce high simulated performance by chance, that researchers rarely report how many configurations they tried, and that this may help explain why so many quantitative funds appear to fail. Notices of the AMS 61(5), pages 458 to 471, May 2014.
nodes.source_title: Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism (ScholarWorks record)
nodes.publisher: Notices of the American Mathematical Society
nodes.authors: Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, Zhu
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: ScholarWorks record: Notices of the AMS 61(5), May 2014, first page 458; abstract supports all claims. End page 471 not shown on the record (could not load AMS PDF).

nodes.n: Five years of data supports no more than 45 independent configurations
nodes.t: Minimum backtest length result: "if only 5 years of data are available, no more than 45 independent model configurations should be tried", or the best one is expected to show an in-sample Sharpe of 1 when its true out-of-sample Sharpe is 0.
nodes.unit: independent configurations for 5 years of data
nodes.source_title: Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism (authors' version, April 1, 2014)
nodes.authors: Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, Zhu
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Preprint dated April 1, 2014, Figure 2 caption quote verbatim; Sharpe 1 IS vs 0 OOS context consistent.

nodes.n: Seven tries on two years of data yields a Sharpe of 1 from noise
nodes.t: On a 2-year backtest: "After trying only 7 independent strategy configurations, the expected maximum Sharpe ratio IS is 1", even though every configuration has a true Sharpe of zero.
nodes.unit: configurations to reach in-sample Sharpe 1 on 2 years
nodes.source_title: Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism (authors' version, April 1, 2014)
nodes.authors: Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, Zhu
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim; sentence continues 'for a 2-year long backtest, while the expected SR OOS is 0.'

nodes.n: Overfit strategies can lose money out-of-sample, not just earn zero
nodes.t: When the return process has memory (for example mean reversion), an overfit backtest's out-of-sample performance is not merely zero but "it may be significantly negative if the process has memory", because the fit locks onto patterns that then reverse.
nodes.source_title: Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism (authors' version, April 1, 2014)
nodes.authors: Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, Zhu
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Section 9: 'but it may be significantly negative if the process has memory.'

nodes.n: Backtest Sharpe explains under 2.5% of live Sharpe (R squared below 0.025)
nodes.t: Across 888 Quantopian algorithms, common backtest metrics such as the Sharpe ratio were poor predictors of out-of-sample performance, with R squared below 0.025. Volatility, maximum drawdown and hedging carried more information.
nodes.source_title: All that Glitters Is Not Gold (SSRN abstract)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN: 888 Quantopian algorithms, backtest Sharpe R squared below 0.025, volatility, max drawdown and hedging more predictive. Written March 9, 2016.

nodes.n: Machine learning on backtest features reached R squared 0.17
nodes.t: Nonlinear classifiers trained on features of backtest behavior predicted out-of-sample performance better (R squared 0.17), and a portfolio built on those predictions beat one built from the highest backtest Sharpe ratios. The more a strategy was backtested, the larger its live shortfall.
nodes.source_title: All that Glitters Is Not Gold (SSRN abstract)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN: ML R squared 0.17 on hold-out, ML portfolio beat top-Sharpe portfolio, more backtesting gives larger discrepancy.

nodes.n: Novy-Marx and Velikov (2016): A Taxonomy of Anomalies and Their Trading Costs
nodes.t: Estimates trading costs for 23 anomalies grouped by turnover (8 low, 9 mid, 6 high). Anomalies with one-sided monthly turnover under 50% generally keep significant net returns; the best simple cost fix is a buy/hold spread. Review of Financial Studies 29(1), pages 104 to 147, 2016.
nodes.source_title: A Taxonomy of Anomalies and their Trading Costs (NBER Working Paper 20721)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER page: RFS 29(1) 104-147, 2016; 50% turnover result; buy/hold spread 'the single most effective simple cost mitigation strategy'. PDF confirms 23 anomalies, 8/9/6 split.

nodes.n: No high-turnover anomaly survives costs in basic form
nodes.t: Of 6 high-turnover anomalies, none has significant net returns in basic form; costs "always exceeds 1% per month". With all mitigation techniques combined, only two strategies above 50% monthly turnover keep significant net spreads. Four of 8 low-turnover and 5 of 9 mid-turnover strategies survive.
nodes.unit: of 6 high-turnover anomalies significant net of costs (basic form)

nodes.n: Arnott, Harvey and Markowitz (2019): A Backtesting Protocol in the Era of Machine Learning
nodes.t: Argues machine learning holds promise for investing but finance has far less data than fields where it succeeded, markets adapt to past research, and misapplied techniques disappoint. nodes.t: Summary of the protocol: start from a prior economic hypothesis; record every test tried; fix and clean the sample before looking; treat live trading as the only truly fresh sample; expect refinement to widen the live gap; never accept a black box; reward good science, not good backtests.

nodes.n: The ten pitfalls and their fixes, one line each

nodes.t: Purging removes from the training set every observation whose label overlaps in time with the test set; the embargo also drops training observations that "immediately follow an observation in the testing set". nodes.t: The Federal Reserve and OCC define model risk as "the potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs and reports." It arises when a model has fundamental errors against its design objective, or when it is used incorrectly or inappropriately.

nodes.t: A model is "a quantitative method, system, or approach that applies statistical, economic, financial, or mathematical theories, techniques, and assumptions to process input data into quantitative estimates." Under this definition a backtested trading signal counts as a model.

nodes.publisher: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

nodes.t: SR 11-7's guiding principle: "critical analysis by objective, informed parties that can identify model limitations and produce appropriate changes." nodes.n: SR 11-7's three validation elements, with backtesting as outcomes analysis

nodes.n: Rapach, Strauss and Zhou (2010): combining forecasts beats the historical mean
nodes.t: Review of Financial Studies 23(2), 821-862. Individual predictive regressions fail to beat the historical average out of sample because of model uncertainty and instability, but averaging their forecasts works: "Combining delivers statistically and economically significant out-of-sample gains" over the historical average. Gains come from pooling information and lower forecast volatility, and combination forecasts are linked to the real economy.
nodes.source_title: Out-of-Sample Equity Premium Prediction: Combination Forecasts and Links to the Real Economy (IDEAS/RePEc)
nodes.publisher: Review of Financial Studies (Oxford University Press)
nodes.checked: corrected by a second checker: Page says 'linked to the real economy'; 'business cycle' not on page. Citation and quote confirmed.

nodes.n: Avramov, Cheng and Metzker (2023): ML profits come from hard-to-arbitrage stocks
nodes.t: Management Science 69(5), 2587-2619. Deep learning signals "extract profitability from difficult-to-arbitrage stocks"; excluding microcaps, distressed stocks or high-volatility episodes "considerably attenuates profitability," and performance "further deteriorates in the presence of reasonable trading costs" due to high turnover and extreme positions.
nodes.source_title: Machine Learning vs. Economic Restrictions: Evidence from Stock Return Predictability (SSRN)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: All three quotes in SSRN abstract; MS 69(5) 2587-2619 (May 2023) confirmed via Crossref 10.1287/mnsc.2022.4449.

Figures are from the 2020 working-paper version, not checked against the published tables.
nodes.source_title: The Limitations of Using Artificial Intelligence to Pick Stocks (China Business Knowledge, CUHK)

nodes.n: Leippold, Wang and Zhou (2022): machine learning in the Chinese stock market
nodes.t: Journal of Financial Economics 145(2), 64-82. Builds a large factor set for Chinese A-shares; "liquidity emerges as the most important predictor," retail activity drives short-horizon predictability "particularly for small stocks," and large stocks and state-owned firms are predictable over longer horizons. Performance stays significant after transaction costs.

nodes.n: Chen and Zimmermann: Open Source Cross-Sectional Asset Pricing
nodes.t: Critical Finance Review paper (SSRN 3604626) releasing code and data that reproduce 319 cross-sectional stock return characteristics from prior studies. Regressing reproduced t-stats on original t-stats gives a slope of 0.88 and an R squared of 82%, and the 44 mixed-evidence signals reproduce with t-stats of about 2 on average.

nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 319 characteristics, slope 0.88, R2 82%, 44 mixed signals t-stat 2 on average; CFR forthcoming, revised June 2021.

nodes.n: Open Source Asset Pricing replication rate: 98 percent of clearly significant predictors
nodes.t: "For the 161 characteristics that were clearly significant in the original papers, 98% of our long-short portfolios" have t-stats above 1.96. Replication of the in-sample result is high; it says nothing about post-publication decay or tradability after costs.
nodes.source_title: Open Source Cross-Sectional Asset Pricing (SSRN)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 161 characteristics, 98% with t-stats above 1.96, verbatim.

nodes.t: Free site by Andrew Chen and Tom Zimmermann providing replicated test asset returns and firm-level signals from the academic literature, downloadable directly or via Python and R packages, with code on GitHub. Latest listed release: October 22, 2025 data update, with signals translated to Python.

nodes.t: Machine Learning 45(1), 5-32. "The generalization error for forests converges a.s. to a limit as the number of trees in the forest becomes large" and depends on tree strength and correlation between trees. Random feature selection gives error rates comparable to AdaBoost, more robust to noise, with out-of-bag estimates of error and variable importance.

nodes.t: The Annals of Statistics 29(5), October 2001 (DOI 10.1214/aos/1013203451). The founding paper for gradient boosting, the method behind GBRT, XGBoost and LightGBM. Metadata confirmed via Crossref; the article page itself could not be fetched.
