nodes.n: Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer: Algorithmic Learning in a Random World
nodes.t: Springer book (first edition 2005, second 2022) that founded conformal prediction. Its companion site says it shows "the validity of the reliability claimed by conformal predictors" when applied to "independent and identically distributed data." A Vovk working paper listed on the site adds that "conformal prediction relies on data exchangeability."
nodes.source_title: Algorithmic Learning in a Random World (book companion site)
nodes.checked: corrected by a second checker: Exchangeability quote is from Vovk's Working Paper 42 on the site, not the book description; attribution corrected.

nodes.n: Angelopoulos and Bates (2021): a gentle introduction to conformal prediction
nodes.t: arXiv 2107.07511 (v6, December 2022). Practical guide to distribution-free uncertainty sets that are "guaranteed to contain the ground truth with a user-specified probability, such as 90%," wrapped around any fitted model, with sections on covariate shift, distribution drift and a time-series example.
nodes.source_title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: v6 dated 2022-12-07; quote verbatim; sections 4.5 covariate shift, 4.6 distribution drift, 5.3 time series.

nodes.t: With n calibration points exchangeable with the test point, split conformal sets satisfy 1 - alpha <= P(Y_test in C(X_test)) <= 1 - alpha + 1/(n+1). The threshold is the empirical quantile of calibration scores at level ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n. The guarantee is marginal (on average over points), not conditional on today's regime.
nodes.source_title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification (PDF)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Eq. (1) bounds 1-alpha to 1-alpha+1/(n+1), quantile ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n, marginal guarantee all in PDF.

nodes.n: Conformal guarantees assume exchangeability, which return series violate
nodes.t: Angelopoulos and Bates' Theorem 1 assumes calibration and test points are i.i.d.; their time-series example notes "these data points are not exchangeable or i.i.d.; adjacent data points will be correlated." Under drift, coverage can fall below 1 - alpha by an amount tied to distribution shift, so empirical coverage must be monitored in walk-forward tests.
nodes.source_title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification (PDF)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Theorem 1 assumes i.i.d.; quote verbatim; Theorem 4 bounds coverage loss by TV distance.

nodes.n: Fernandez-Rodriguez, Sosvilla-Rivero and Andrada-Felix: nearest-neighbour FX forecasts
nodes.t: FEDEA working paper 2002-05 (related article: International Journal of Forecasting 15, 383-392, 1999). Embeds each EMS exchange rate in 6 lags, picks the closest historical patterns (about 2% of the sample), fits a local least-squares regression on what followed, and adds a simultaneous version that also uses related currencies.
nodes.source_title: Nearest-Neighbour Predictions in Foreign Exchange Markets (FEDEA DT 2002-05)
nodes.checked: corrected by a second checker: Page cites IJF 15, 383-392 without issue number; removed unsupported '(4)'. m=6, k about 2%, SNN confirmed.

nodes.n: Nearest-neighbour FX forecasts: up to 18.9 percent better than a random walk
nodes.t: In the FEDEA study across nine EMS currencies, the "best SNN predictor presenting an improvement of 18.9%" in Theil's U versus a random walk, directional accuracy exceeded 50% in eight of nine cases, and the random walk still won for the escudo and sterling. Analog methods help in some series, not uniformly.
nodes.unit: percent improvement in Theil's U (best case)
nodes.source_title: Nearest-Neighbour Predictions in Foreign Exchange Markets (FEDEA DT 2002-05)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Nine currencies, 18.9% quote verbatim, 8 of 9 above 50%, random walk wins for escudo and sterling.

nodes.n: Lopez de Prado (2018): Advances in Financial Machine Learning
nodes.t: Wiley, February 2018, 400 pages, ISBN 978-1-119-48208-6. Practitioner text covering financial data bars, labeling (triple-barrier, meta-labeling), sample weights for overlapping outcomes, purged k-fold cross-validation, feature importance under substitution effects, bet sizing and combinatorial purged backtesting.
nodes.source_title: Advances in Financial Machine Learning (Wiley)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Wiley: Feb 2018, 400 pp, ISBN 978-1-119-48208-6, chapter topics. Section-level items (bars, triple-barrier, meta-labeling, purged k-fold, CPCV) confirmed on O'Reilly TOC, not the Wiley page.

nodes.t: A label is set by whichever barrier the price path hits first: an upper profit-taking barrier (label 1), a lower stop-loss barrier (label -1), or a vertical time barrier ending the trade. Horizontal barriers scale with recent volatility, typically a multiple of the daily standard deviation of log returns. From Lopez de Prado (2018), section 3.4.
nodes.source_title: Does Meta Labeling Add to Signal Efficacy? (Hudson & Thames)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Hudson & Thames (Singh, Joubert, 30 Apr 2019) supports labels and volatility scaling; book section 3.4 'The Triple-Barrier Method' confirmed via O'Reilly TOC.

nodes.t: A primary model picks the side (long or short); a secondary model learns "whether we should act or pass on the opportunity" and how large to bet. It aims to raise precision by "filtering out the false positives." Introduced in Lopez de Prado (2018), chapter 3.
nodes.source_title: Meta Labeling (A Toy Example) (Hudson & Thames)
nodes.checked: corrected by a second checker: Quotes and chapter 3 attribution confirmed; Joubert JFDS 4(3) 2022 citation not on page, removed.

nodes.t: "A substitution effect takes place when two or more explanatory variables share a substantial amount of information." Then feature importance methods "may not be able to determine robustly which variables are significant." Lopez de Prado presents Clustered Feature Importance, "robust to linear as well as non-linear substitution effects." Engine note: permutation importance can understate each of two correlated features.
nodes.source_title: Clustered Feature Importance (Presentation Slides), SSRN 3517595
nodes.checked: corrected by a second checker: Page does not state the MDA mechanism or that CFI permutes clusters; reworded to abstract and labeled the engine's note.

nodes.n: Advances in Financial Machine Learning treats standard k-fold CV as broken for finance
nodes.t: Chapter 7 of Lopez de Prado (2018) is titled Cross-Validation in Finance, with sections "Why K-Fold CV Fails in Finance" and "A Solution: Purged K-Fold CV"; chapter 12 adds Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation as an alternative to a single walk-forward path. The core issue is leakage from overlapping labels between train and test folds.
nodes.source_title: Advances in Financial Machine Learning, table of contents (O'Reilly)
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: O'Reilly TOC: 7.3 'Why K-Fold CV Fails in Finance', 7.4 'A Solution: Purged K-Fold CV', 12.4 CPCV, 12.2 walk-forward.

nodes.n: Pan et al. (2020): adversarial validation for concept drift at Uber
nodes.t: arXiv 2004.03045. Trains a classifier to tell training rows from new rows; if it can, the new data have drifted, and "the system detects concept drift in new data before making inference." Tested on AutoML3 lifelong-learning data and Uber's MaLTA targeting system. A direct template for flagging that today is out of distribution.
nodes.source_title: Adversarial Validation Approach to Concept Drift Problem in User Targeting Automation Systems at Uber
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Authors, Apr 2020, quote, AutoML3 and MaLTA confirmed.

nodes.n: Rabanser, Gunnemann and Lipton (2019): detecting dataset shift
nodes.t: arXiv 1810.11953. Empirical comparison of shift detectors; finds "a two-sample-testing-based approach, using pre-trained classifiers for dimensionality reduction, performs best," while "domain-discriminating approaches tend to be helpful for characterizing shifts." Useful for choosing between a classifier test and a two-sample test on features.
nodes.source_title: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Both quotes verbatim; v4 2019-10-28.

Ability rises with model size, and "Strategy returns decline as LLM adoption rises."

nodes.n: Glasserman and Lin (2023): look-ahead bias and distraction in GPT sentiment backtests
nodes.t: arXiv 2309.17322. Names two biases: look-ahead, where the model "may have specific knowledge of the stock returns that followed a news article," and distraction, where general knowledge of the firm skews the reading. Anonymizing company names in-sample improved results, implying distraction mattered more than look-ahead in their test.
nodes.source_title: Assessing Look-Ahead Bias in Stock Return Predictions Generated By GPT Sentiment Analysis
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim; anonymized headlines outperform in-sample, distraction larger.

nodes.n: He, Lv, Manela and Wu (2025): chronologically consistent language models
nodes.t: arXiv 2502.21206 (v3, July 2025). Trains ChronoBERT and ChronoGPT only on text available at each date to remove training leakage. Their real-time news-based return forecasts achieve Sharpe ratios comparable to a much larger Llama model, "indicating that lookahead bias is modest," though they stress the bias is model and application-specific.
nodes.source_title: Chronologically Consistent Large Language Models
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: v3 6 Jul 2025; Llama comparison, 'indicating that lookahead bias is modest', model and application-specific confirmed.

nodes.n: a16z: no systemic moats in generative AI
nodes.t: "There don’t appear, today, to be any systemic moats in generative AI." Matt Bornstein, Guido Appenzeller and Martin Casado, a16z, January 19, 2023. They also note AI is easy to integrate where users already work.
nodes.source_title: Who Owns the Generative AI Platform?
nodes.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Verbatim quote present; authors Bornstein, Appenzeller, Casado; January 19, 2023. Integration point supported: "It's easy to integrate AI products where users already work, since the UI is generally just a text box."

nodes.n: a16z: data is not a magic moat

nodes.n: Pearl: proof of work by matrix multiplication
nodes.t: Pearl is a Bitcoin-style Layer 1 that "replaces SHA-256 hashing with matrix multiplication as its proof of work function." "The chain has a fixed 2.1B PRL supply and targets 194-second blocks." Miners commit to their input matrices first, and the result is verifiable by other nodes without re-running the full workload.
nodes.source_title: Pearl: Proof of Useful Work for AI
nodes.checked: confirmed on the publisher's page by the checker, who added it (a single check)

nodes.n: A Pearl-powered inference endpoint at a discount
nodes.t: In May 2026 Together AI launched a Pearl-powered endpoint for Gemma-4-31B-it-Pearl priced at a discount of 25% or more to standard rates; Pearl did not yet have a marketplace where buyers pay PRL for inference.
nodes.source_title: Pearl: Proof of Useful Work for AI
nodes.checked: confirmed on the publisher's page by the checker, who added it (a single check)

nodes.n: Pearl's duplex work: the same matmuls earn twice
nodes.t: "That work is matrix multiplications, the core math behind AI inference (running a trained model to answer requests)." "AI revenue helps pay for the machines; PRL rewards become extra income." Bankless describes Pearl as a fork of Bitcoin that launched in April, with launch inference prices up to roughly 75% below a major provider's standard rates, potentially subsidized by mining rewards.
nodes.source_title: Pearl and the Security Budget Bitcoin Can't Solve
nodes.checked: confirmed on the publisher's page by the checker, who added it (a single check)

nodes.t: Pearl's issuance "follows a smooth, polynomial decay curve rather than Bitcoin's four-year halvings." "About half its supply is mined in the first four years", so inflation falls each year, to roughly 30% by year three and about 11% by year five.
nodes.unit: percent of supply in four years

Panic of 1873, 1873-01 to 1877-06. A railroad-finance bust that began with the failure of Jay Cooke and Company in September 1873 and a long depression after it. Measured from 1873-01 to 1877-06: real S&P 500 prices -31%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -35%, 10-year yield -118bp, consumer prices -22%.

Panic of 1893, 1893-01 to 1896-08. A bank and railroad panic, a run on gold and a deep depression. Measured from 1893-01 to 1896-08: real S&P 500 prices -15%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -19%, 10-year yield -27bp, consumer prices -21%.

Panic of 1907, 1906-01 to 1907-11. A trust-company run in New York, stopped when J. P. Morgan organized the banks; it led to the founding of the Federal Reserve in 1913. Measured from 1906-01 to 1907-11: real S&P 500 prices -40%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -40%, 10-year yield +41bp, consumer prices +6%.

The 1920 to 1921 depression, 1919-07 to 1921-08. A sharp postwar deflation and recession, with prices falling as the Fed raised rates. Measured from 1919-07 to 1921-08: real S&P 500 prices -33%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -36%, 10-year yield -10bp, consumer prices +2%.

The 1920s boom, 1921-08 to 1929-09. Eight years of rising earnings, margin buying and valuations that reached the highest CAPE before 1999. Measured from 1921-08 to 1929-09: real S&P 500 prices +396%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -17%, 10-year yield -124bp, consumer prices -2%.

nodes.n: The 1929 crash and the Great Depression
nodes.t: The 1929 crash and the Great Depression, 1929-09 to 1932-06. The crash of October 1929 and the fall to the 1932 low, with bank failures and deflation. Measured from 1929-09 to 1932-06: real S&P 500 prices -81%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -81%, 10-year yield +14bp, consumer prices -21%.

The 1937 to 1938 recession, 1937-03 to 1938-03. A relapse inside the Depression after fiscal and monetary tightening. Measured from 1937-03 to 1938-03: real S&P 500 prices -43%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -43%, 10-year yield -13bp, consumer prices -1%.

World War II, 1939-09 to 1945-08. The war years, with yields capped by the Treasury and the Fed. Measured from 1939-09 to 1945-08: real S&P 500 prices -10%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -47%, 10-year yield +1bp, consumer prices +28%.

The 1946 to 1949 postwar bear market, 1946-05 to 1949-06. Demobilization, a burst of inflation and a long slide in prices. Measured from 1946-05 to 1949-06: real S&P 500 prices -42%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -42%, 10-year yield +10bp, consumer prices +29%.

The 1949 to 1966 bull market, 1949-06 to 1966-01. The postwar expansion, with low inflation for most of it and valuations rising from deep value. Measured from 1949-06 to 1966-01: real S&P 500 prices +402%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -23%, 10-year yield +230bp, consumer prices +33%.

The 1962 Kennedy slide, 1961-12 to 1962-06. A fast fall in stocks from high valuations in the first half of 1962. Measured from 1961-12 to 1962-06: real S&P 500 prices -23%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -23%, 10-year yield -15bp, consumer prices +1%.

The Great Inflation, 1966-01 to 1982-08. Sixteen years of rising inflation and yields, ending with the Volcker disinflation; stocks lost ground after inflation. Measured from 1966-01 to 1982-08: real S&P 500 prices -62%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -63%, 10-year yield +845bp, consumer prices +207%.

The 1973 to 1974 bear market, 1973-01 to 1974-12. The end of the Nifty Fifty, the oil embargo and stagflation. Measured from 1973-01 to 1974-12: real S&P 500 prices -54%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -54%, 10-year yield +97bp, consumer prices +22%.

The Volcker disinflation, 1979-10 to 1982-08. The Fed under Paul Volcker targeted money growth from October 1979; short rates rose above 19% and inflation broke. Measured from 1979-10 to 1982-08: real S&P 500 prices -19%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -29%, 10-year yield +276bp, consumer prices +30%.

The 1982 to 2000 bull market, 1982-08 to 2000-03. Falling inflation and yields, rising margins and the largest valuation expansion on record. Measured from 1982-08 to 2000-03: real S&P 500 prices +650%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -27%, 10-year yield -680bp, consumer prices +75%.

The 1987 crash, 1987-08 to 1987-12. Black Monday, October 19, 1987: the Dow fell 22.6% in one day, with portfolio insurance selling into the fall. Measured from 1987-08 to 1987-12: real S&P 500 prices -27%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -27%, 10-year yield +23bp, consumer prices +1%.

The 1994 bond rout, 1994-01 to 1994-12. The Fed doubled its policy rate from 3% in a year and long bond yields jumped. Measured from 1994-01 to 1994-12: real S&P 500 prices -6%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -6%, 10-year yield +206bp, consumer prices +2%.

The 1998 Russian default and LTCM, 1998-07 to 1998-10. Russia defaulted in August 1998; the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management was rescued by its lenders in September. Measured from 1998-07 to 1998-10: real S&P 500 prices -11%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -12%, 10-year yield -93bp, consumer prices +0%.

The dot-com bubble and bust, 1995-01 to 2002-10. The internet boom took CAPE above 44 in December 1999; the Nasdaq then fell about 78% to October 2002. Measured from 1995-01 to 2002-10: real S&P 500 prices +52%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -45%, 10-year yield -384bp, consumer prices +21%.

The global financial crisis, 2007-10 to 2009-03. The housing and credit bust, Lehman's failure in September 2008 and the low of March 2009. Measured from 2007-10 to 2009-03: real S&P 500 prices -52%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -52%, 10-year yield -171bp, consumer prices +2%.

nodes.n: The 2011 euro crisis and US downgrade
nodes.t: The 2011 euro crisis and US downgrade, 2011-04 to 2011-10. Sovereign debt stress in Europe and S&P's downgrade of the United States in August 2011. Measured from 2011-04 to 2011-10: real S&P 500 prices -10%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -13%, 10-year yield -131bp, consumer prices +1%.

The 2013 taper tantrum, 2013-05 to 2013-09. Long yields jumped when the Fed signalled it would slow its bond buying. Measured from 2013-05 to 2013-09: real S&P 500 prices +2%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -2%, 10-year yield +88bp, consumer prices +1%.

The 2020 pandemic crash, 2020-02 to 2020-08. The fastest 30% fall on record and the fastest recovery, with emergency rate cuts and asset purchases. Measured from 2020-02 to 2020-08: real S&P 500 prices +3%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -19%, 10-year yield -85bp, consumer prices +0%.

The 2022 inflation and bond rout, 2021-12 to 2022-10. Inflation above 9% and the fastest Fed hikes since the 1980s; stocks and long bonds fell together. Measured from 2021-12 to 2022-10: real S&P 500 prices -25%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -25%, 10-year yield +251bp, consumer prices +7%.

The AI buildout, 2023-01 to 2026-12. The rally led by AI chips and the hyperscalers' capital spending, financed increasingly with debt. Measured from 2023-01 to 2026-09: real S&P 500 prices +74%, worst fall from a peak inside the window -12%, 10-year yield +56bp, consumer prices +11%.

nodes.n: Every step up in complexity fits the past better and the future worse
nodes.t: Each family was trained on the years before 1950, 1980 and 2000 and judged on the decades after, against simply forecasting the training average. Nearest neighbours reach 100% in sample at k = 1 and below -100% out of sample, against -3% at their simplest; boosted trees reach 100% in sample at 400 trees, depth 5 and -94% out of sample, against -1% at their simplest; random forest reach 95% in sample at depth 12 and -58% out of sample, against -3% at their simplest. The in-sample R squared climbs toward 100% because a flexible model can memorize 1,700 months; it cannot memorize the next ones.

nodes.n: Flexible models extrapolate, and the future is outside the sample
nodes.t: Fitted on 1881 to 1948, when the 10-year yield stayed between 1.9% and 5.1%, the eight-predictor regression put a weight of -20.8 on it. From 1950 to 1979 the yield ran from 2.3% to 10.7%, and the model forecast a 12-month return as low as -74% (the worst actual was -41%): out-of-sample R squared below -100%, against +0.8% for CAPE alone. Polynomials do the same thing faster.

nodes.n: The data hold far fewer observations than they seem to
nodes.t: 1,710 months of 12-month returns overlap, so they hold about 142 independent observations (next month's 12-month return is 95% correlated with this month's). Log CAPE's month-to-month autocorrelation is 0.995, a half-life of about 12 years, so valuation itself offers only a handful of independent swings.

nodes.n: The signal is smaller than the cost of estimating it
nodes.t: All eight predictors together explain 10.5% of 12-month returns in sample. Ordinary least squares with 8 predictors on about 142 independent observations loses roughly 5.6% of R squared out of sample, the same order as the signal; a flexible model with hundreds of effective parameters loses far more. CAPE alone costs about 0.7%, which is why the simplest models lose least.

nodes.n: The relationship moves under the model
nodes.t: Re-estimated on rolling 30-year windows, the CAPE slope is negative (high valuation, lower returns) in 22 of 23 windows and ranges from -0.48 to +0.00; a flexible model learns the old regime's details exactly, and the details are what change.

Log CAPE keeps 92% of its level from one year to the next and its shocks move +0.98 with returns, so even a useless predictor shows an average slope of -0.026 over 140 years (Stambaugh's bias). The real slope is -0.076; corrected, -0.050. The naive p-value is 0.033, the bias-aware one 0.120: the effect survives, but it is smaller than the raw backtest says.

nodes.n: Complexity pays only when the signal is strong and genuinely nonlinear
nodes.t: On planted data with a true R squared of 5% and a linear shape, out-of-sample R squared is +2.6% for linear regression, -2.8% for a random forest and -8.1% for boosted trees. With a 40% R squared and a threshold shape, the ranking flips: linear +18.2%, forest +33.2%, boosting +29.1%. Stock returns live in the first case.

nodes.n: Choosing the best backtest is itself a forecast that fails
nodes.t: Picking the configuration that looked best in sample means picking the one that fit the most noise: on this data the in-sample winner landed below the median out of sample in 82% of combinatorial splits (the ML lab's CPCV).

On the site: The shortcut. How the engine runs on matrix multiplication: the mind's question as a vector and its knowledge as a matrix, many questions thought at once, the filter as a scan of matrix products, the graph in 64 numbers per node, and Pearl, where the same matrix math mines a blockchain.

Stocks, Treasuries and gold decided together from regimes, a learner over whole policies, ten years simulated, and one pipeline from 156 years of data to today's sized exposure and hedge: stacked forecasts with a neural-network ensemble, hidden Markov regimes, changepoints, model averaging, a risk budget and an evidence gate, walked forward from 1940.
On the site: Bonds, simply. Set the 10-year and 30-year yields and see every Treasury ETF repriced bond by bond: price, 12-month return, break-even and what it means for stocks.

On the site: The machine-learning lab. Purged walk-forward forecasts, the combination forecast, CPCV and the overfitting probability, and why complex models backtest better than they forecast.
On the site: The mind. Ask anything: recall, spreading activation, weighing and the belief network.
On the site: The labs. The trend lab, valuation lab and the long-history tests on 155 years.
On the site: Technicals and fundamentals. Every chart signal judged on its own asset, every ratio read from the filing.

signals.text: Repriced bond by bond, TLT gains +16.6% if yields fall 1 point and loses -13.4% if they rise 1 point, and its income covers a 37bp rise in a year: at these yields the long bond's payoff is skewed toward the holder.
signals.flip: Yields rising more than the break-even in a year.

signals.text: With inflation between 2.75% and 4.25% (now 2.8% a year over three years), the S&P 500 has moved -2.7% per point of rise in the 10-year since 1871 (t -2.4): stocks and bonds have tended to fall together, so long bonds hedge less.
signals.flip: Inflation crossing into another band.

signals.text: On Oct 22, 2026, TLT was +1.73% while QQQ was -2.65% as AI stocks sold off on earnings and debt worries: the hedge worked on the day.
signals.flip: Stocks and long bonds falling on the same day.

signals.text: On 155 years of data, every model family fits the training years better as it grows more complex and forecasts the years after worse, down to below -100% out of sample; about 142 independent 12-month observations cannot pay for flexible models.
signals.flip: A flexible model beating the historical mean out of sample.

signals.text: Corrected for Stambaugh's small-sample bias, the CAPE slope shrinks from -0.076 to -0.050 a year per log point, and its p-value rises from 0.03 to 0.12: valuation still points down, more weakly.
signals.flip: The bias-corrected slope losing its sign.

signals.text: The hidden Markov model (3 states, filtered) puts next month's odds of the stressed regime at 20%; the chance a new regime began in the last six months is 3%.
signals.flip: The stressed regime's odds rising past 20%.

signals.text: A deep ensemble of small neural networks, walked forward since 1940, forecasts 12-month returns with skill -36.9% against the historical mean (Diebold-Mariano t -2.6); the stack gives it 11% of the weight.
signals.flip: The ensemble beating the mean out of sample.

signals.text: The decision engine's departures from holding improved a risk-averse investor's utility with t 0.4 since 1940, under the 1.1 expected from the best of 7 useless strategies, so it moves the book 0% of the way toward its 1.50x optimum.
signals.flip: The engine's utility gain clearing the bar.

signals.text: The portfolio engine's regime model puts next month in its calm bull state (94%), where stocks and 10-year Treasuries have moved with a correlation of +0.15: bonds have not hedged stocks there.
signals.flip: A shift into a state where the stock-bond correlation is negative.

signals.text: Timing stocks, Treasuries and gold by regime, walked forward since 1940, earned a Sharpe of 0.50 against 0.64 for holding stocks and 0.65 for 60/40; a learner that weights six whole policies by their record reached 0.66 with a worst drawdown of -41% against -52%. Diversifying across policies did better than predicting regimes.
signals.flip: Regime timing beating 60/40 out of sample.
